item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia confronts complexities of schizophrenia after school killing ruling
item.description:
When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began.

“My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia.

“It was so severe to the point that I couldn’t even recognise my own family members. My mother was there, my brother was there, but they didn’t feel like my mother or my brother.”
item.content:encoded:
When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began.

“My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia.

“It was so severe to the point that I couldn’t even recognise my own family members. My mother was there, my brother was there, but they didn’t feel like my mother or my brother.”

Her experience has taken on new resonance in Malaysia after a court acquitted a 15-year-old boy of murdering his schoolmate Yap Shing Xuen, 16, on the grounds that severe schizophrenia had left him legally insane when he killed her at their school in Bandar Utama, outside Kuala Lumpur, last October.

Yap was found dead in a school toilet after suffering at least 180 stab wounds, according to a forensic report, in a killing that shocked Malaysia and intensified concerns over safety in the country’s schools.

On Monday, the Shah Alam High Court accepted testimony from forensic psychiatrist Ian Lloyd Anthony that the teenager had severe schizophrenia and was incapable of understanding the nature of his actions or that they were wrong.

His lawyer Kitson Foong earlier told This Week in Asia that the boy’s condition had gone untreated for several years before the attack.

“The court held that, because of his illness, the child offender did not know the nature of what he was doing and did not know that it was wrong or against the law,” Foong said.

After his acquittal, the boy was sent to Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta, a psychiatric hospital in Perak state, for treatment, counselling and medication.

Foong said the boy would remain there until he was assessed to no longer pose a threat to society, with any eventual release dependent on medical and psychiatric reports presented to the Sultan of Selangor.

But much of the anger since the ruling has centred on the word “acquitted”, with some Malaysians questioning why the boy should escape a murder conviction and others arguing that an insanity verdict had been mistaken for freedom.

In one online forum, the verdict quickly split opinion. Some users called for the death penalty and invoked “a life for a life”, while others stressed that the boy had not simply walked free and remained in psychiatric custody.

Yap’s mother, Wong Lee Ping, has also urged the public to back a petition calling on Malaysia’s Attorney-General’s Chambers to appeal against the acquittal, saying her family had few avenues of its own to challenge the decision.

“We are neither judges nor prosecutors. We are simply a family who has lost our daughter,” Wong said on social media, adding that the family wanted the proper legal process, including any available right of appeal, to be considered.

Cindi said she understood why the case frightened people because her own first psychotic episode in 2016 took her to a place she still struggles to explain.

At one point, frightened and feeling alone, she took out knives. After her mother locked her in an outside kitchen, Cindi repeatedly stabbed the door trying to get out.

“I felt very out of control, basically,” she said. “It’s like I’m witnessing everything from a different point of view, but I don’t know why or how to explain why I do this. I feel like I’m just looking at what I’m doing, but I cannot stop it … by then it was too late because I’ve already done the action.”

Police eventually took her to a psychiatric ward, where she was observed for about two weeks before being diagnosed with schizophrenia.

She then went seven years without another psychotic episode and today works, raises a five-year-old son and attends therapy, although severe stress can still trigger symptoms.

During a recent episode, Cindi called a crisis hotline and told her family she needed their help. As someone on the line talked her through what she was experiencing, she said the negative voices gradually stopped and she began to feel normal again.

“With the right intervention, with the right medication, with the right support, we are just as normal as anyone else,” she said.

Diagnosis in the dock

About 27 million people worldwide, or roughly one in every 300, live with schizophrenia, according to the World Health Organization, which lists persistent delusions and hallucinations among symptoms that can profoundly alter how a person perceives reality.

Mariani Md Nor, a psychologist and vice-chancellor of SEGi University, said severe psychosis could seriously impair judgment and a person’s understanding of their actions, but that was not the experience of everyone diagnosed with schizophrenia.

“We should not assume that schizophrenia means violence. Most people with schizophrenia are not violent,” she told This Week in Asia.

“The risk may increase when someone is experiencing severe untreated psychosis, particularly when other factors such as alcohol or drug misuse are involved. In fact, people with serious mental illness can also be victims of violence, discrimination and stigma.”

We need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia

Chua Sook Ning, clinical psychologist

A review published last year examining 47 longitudinal studies involving more than 203,000 people with psychosis found that a previous criminal history had the strongest association with later violence, followed by substance misuse, with many treatment-related factors linked to a lower risk.

Clinical psychologist Chua Sook Ning, founder of mental health organisation Relate Malaysia, said the danger after a case such as the Bandar Utama killing was that the diagnosis itself could become the explanation for what happened.

“A diagnosis can become a very easy one to reach for. That can make schizophrenia sound as though it explains the violence by itself,” she said.

“Most people with mental illness aren’t violent, and acts of violence can occur in the absence of mental illness, so we need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia.”

Cindi has felt those assumptions in her own life. She kept her diagnosis private for almost a decade and said the father of her son refused to marry her because his family was afraid of her schizophrenia.

“Schizophrenia is a treatable disease. It’s lifelong, but it’s treatable,” she said, adding that she now had an accepting workplace, supportive friends and continued access to therapy.

Much of her attention now is on raising her son, whom she hopes will never have to experience the same illness and upheaval that have marked the past decade of her life.

“I just hope that my son doesn’t get it. That’s all,” Cindi said. “I don’t want my son to go through the same suffering that I have … so let the struggle end with me.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia faces reckoning over maritime safety after deadly ferry disaster
item.description:
Indonesia’s latest ferry disaster has exposed persistent weaknesses in maritime safety oversight, experts have said, with poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continuing to leave passengers vulnerable across the sprawling archipelago.

The capsizing of the Virgo Transport 8 in the Java Sea on Sunday has intensified scrutiny of a system that analysts say too often comes under pressure only after deadly accidents, rather than preventing them.

Six people have been confirmed dead and 129 remain missing after the passenger and cargo ferry capsized amid high winds and rough seas while travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s latest ferry disaster has exposed persistent weaknesses in maritime safety oversight, experts have said, with poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continuing to leave passengers vulnerable across the sprawling archipelago.

The capsizing of the Virgo Transport 8 in the Java Sea on Sunday has intensified scrutiny of a system that analysts say too often comes under pressure only after deadly accidents, rather than preventing them.

Six people have been confirmed dead and 129 remain missing after the passenger and cargo ferry capsized amid high winds and rough seas while travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.

According to Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency, 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – were aboard the vessel when the captain reported bad weather at about 2am local time on September 13.

A total of 108 people were rescued after personnel from agencies including the Indonesian Army and the Search and Rescue Agency were deployed, in the latest of a string of maritime incidents that have renewed questions over how Indonesia regulates and enforces safety at sea.

The latest disaster follows a string of other maritime incidents in recent months.

In August, five people died after a ferry caught fire off the island of Madura, while a blaze aboard another ferry travelling from Bali to Lombok killed one person. In July, a ferry sank in the Bali Strait leaving 19 people dead and 16 missing, and another ferry went down in waters close to South Sulawesi, killing three people with 14 still missing. In May, a tourist boat capsized close to Bengkulu City in Sumatra, resulting in eight deaths.

Following the latest sinking, lawmakers and experts have called for a comprehensive investigation into the incident and a tightening of maritime safety regulations.

In a statement provided to This Week in Asia, Usman Hamid, the head of Amnesty Indonesia, described the Virgo Transport 8 incident as “a humanitarian tragedy” that exposed the state’s failure to protect the safety rights of sea transport users.

Hamid called for an “immediate, independent, impartial and thorough investigation” to determine whether negligence by regulators, the vessel’s owners or other parties had contributed to the disaster, adding that anyone found responsible should be held legally accountable.

He also pointed to survivor testimony that no emergency alarm sounded when the ship capsized in the middle of the night while many passengers slept in cabins below deck.

“The availability of life jackets has also come under scrutiny,” Hamid said, citing survivor accounts that some passengers could not find them and that many people on life rafts were not wearing them.

Data from Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency showed 601 maritime incidents between January and August this year that required search and rescue deployment, including passengers falling overboard, engine failures and fires aboard vessels. In 2025, there were a total of 450 incidents from January to December.

Rise in incidents

Soerjanto Tjahjono, head of the National Transportation Safety Committee, told This Week in Asia he could not comment on the Virgo Transport 8 incident as it was still under investigation but that data compiled by the independent government agency also showed maritime incidents in Indonesia were on the rise.

“However, we do not yet have a definitive conclusion for why that is,” he said.

“What we do know is that extreme weather should never be blamed. We have to learn how to deal with the weather at sea and avoid it. It is not a reason for accidents, but it can be a contributing factor. There are also technical issues such as human factors.”

Tjahjono said the committee was currently conducting a wider investigation into boat safety, and aimed to publish a list of recommendations in the coming months.

One family member still anxiously awaiting news of a loved one aboard the Virgo Transport 8 is Fredy Manuhua, whose younger brother Stefiansa Manuhua, 44, played keyboard in the boat’s band to keep passengers entertained during the voyage.

Manuhua, 48, said he last contacted Stefiansa on Friday and later heard about the ferry incident around 7am on Sunday.

“I went straight to the port in Surabaya and the ferry company confirmed it,” he said. “I have been waiting there ever since and will not leave until there is news.”

Lack of oversight

Aji Suraji, director of postgraduate programmes at the University of Widya Gama in Malang, who specialises in transport safety and engineering, told This Week in Asia that maritime safety was a shared responsibility.

“It is the responsibility of boat operators to ensure that all the standard operating procedures on their vessels are being followed,” Suraji said. “However, it is also the responsibility of external stakeholders such as the Department of Transportation to make sure that vessels are adhering to these procedures.”

While the Department of Transportation had tightened some regulations in recent years, particularly regarding the compilation of accurate boat manifests, Suraji said there was still room for improvement.

“Adhering to standard operating procedures and external oversight of these are weak points in Indonesia when it comes to transport safety,” Suraji said, adding that “there needs to be more control and supervision, with clear and enforced sanctions in place”.

Suraji lamented that too often, transport safety in Indonesia gained attention only when incidents such as the Virgo Transport 8 happened and went viral. “But after that, people forget and are too forgiving. We need to be better at identifying potential issues before they happen and anticipating them.”

The incident has left Manuhua grappling with questions such as why no alarm apparently sounded, and why the captain of the Virgo Transport 8 and 11 crew members left the vessel and were rescued while other passengers were still aboard.

“I hope there will be a full investigation, and I will push for anyone to face the full extent of the law if they were at fault,” he said.

“I am devastated by what has happened. I am so close to my brother and I pray every night to our parents, and tell them that he is still lost and to please send him back to us.

“There are still so many things that we want to do together. I am not ready to lose him.”

item.title: [SCMP] China, US may unveil measures to boost military ties when Xi visits Washington
item.description:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

Sources said both sides were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship.
item.content:encoded:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

Sources said both sides were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship.

They said officials in the two militaries were interacting at various levels, with the frequency and level of engagement increasing substantially in the past few months.

Despite a still-contentious economic relationship marked by tit-for-tat tariffs, export controls and sanctions, military ties between Washington and Beijing have moved in a more positive direction, with regular dialogue and public commitments to maintaining peace and increasing mutual understanding.

Sources said both sides were rebuilding military channels to speak frequently and prevent any misunderstanding and miscalculation about each other’s intentions.

Ending a two-year hiatus, China and the US held command-level talks late last month in Canada, with a meeting between Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the Pacific Command.

The US Pacific Command said Yang and Paparo discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior American and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and to promote safe and professional conduct between forces.

One source said China and the US were seeking military dialogue at three levels. Those talks would be between the two presidents, who are also commanders-in-chief of their countries’ armed forces; also at the ministerial level, including the US defence department and China’s Central Military Commission; and between frontline commanders, in particular the US Pacific Command chief and the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command chief.

“The presidential-level, and frontline commander-level talks are progressing,” the source said, referring to recent meetings between Xi and US President Donald Trump and the talks between Paparo and Yang.

“But actual ministerial-level talks might take a while. One problem has been China’s anti-corruption campaign that [almost] wiped out the CMC, leaving Zhang Shengmin [as the only uniformed official in the body],” he said.

“But we believe they will take place in the near future.”

Another person familiar with the matter said both sides had made clear they wanted new communication channels.

One of the channels could be to revive dedicated arms-control talks between the US State Department and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which gained momentum in 2023 before being suspended in July 2024 over Washington’s continued arms sales to Taiwan.

A source described the talks as a give from the Chinese side that could eventually be broadened to include military personnel – a long-standing US request – “if things go well”.

Washington had planned to send a more senior Pentagon China official to Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum this week, after last year dispatching only the defence attache. But the official withdrew before the forum, with the US delegation instead led by Brigadier General Stacy Kihara of the embassy in Beijing, leaving the official level unchanged from 2025.

A third source said military-to-military contact under Trump’s second term had become more stable but remained “shallow”. The source said deliverables for the Xi-Trump summit were discussed and locked in when Yang and Paparo met face to face in Canada – their first in-person meeting.

The person called that progress “unique” under a Republican president, describing Trump as “a different sort of Republican president”.

A fourth source said the two militaries were working to follow the “strategic stability” guidance agreed by Trump and Xi during their May meeting in Beijing.

After the summit, the two sides referenced the concept of “strategic stability” in their statements, while differing over its phrasing and interpretation.

In July, a senior Pentagon official – for the first time in more than five years – attended and spoke at a reception at the Chinese embassy in Washington marking the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army.

“Under the leadership of Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress,” said Alvaro Smith, deputy assistant defence secretary for China, Taiwan and Mongolia.

He added that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years” and said Washington was not seeking a “conflict with China”.

“This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we made this a reality.”

US undersecretary of defence for policy Elbridge Colby also hosted Chinese Foreign Vice-Minister Ma Zhaoxu at the Pentagon, later saying on social media that the US interacted with its “Chinese counterparts in a spirit of respect, candour, and realism”.

In another sign of closer military engagement, China is cooperating with the US military to recover the remains of American soldiers who went missing in China during World War II.

As part of those efforts, US defence recovery teams travelled to China in early July to resume searches for missing service members.

The renewed engagement marks a significant shift from the Joe Biden administration, when a series of incidents escalated tensions and left military-to-military communication largely stalled.

Beijing suspended several key military dialogue mechanisms with Washington in 2022 after then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi travelled to Taiwan on a high-profile visit.

The Taiwan issue has been the most sensitive between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent nation, but Washington opposes any attempt to seize the self-governing island by force and has pledged to supply it with weapons.

item.title: [SCMP] Teodoro for president? Philippine defence chief draws 2028 election buzz after China clash
item.description:
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has won a burst of online support among Filipinos who see him as one of Manila’s most outspoken senior officials against China, with some already asking whether it could give him enough political momentum to carry him into the 2028 elections.

His latest boost came after a viral moment at the Seoul Defence Dialogue on September 8, where he read out a handwritten note reiterating Beijing’s rejection of the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling while on stage.

Forum organisers said the note came from a military attaché at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who had passed it to a staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has won a burst of online support among Filipinos who see him as one of Manila’s most outspoken senior officials against China, with some already asking whether it could give him enough political momentum to carry him into the 2028 elections.

His latest boost came after a viral moment at the Seoul Defence Dialogue on September 8, where he read out a handwritten note reiterating Beijing’s rejection of the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling while on stage.

Forum organisers said the note came from a military attaché at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who had passed it to a staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.

Teodoro read parts of the note aloud, including Beijing’s position that the 2016 award was “illegal, null and void”, before saying the move was disrespectful to the forum’s South Korean hosts and showed disregard for international law.

“So, perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do … This is actual coercion, bullying and aggression,” he said.

Beijing hit back, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning accusing Philippine officials of “grandstanding and lying” and urging “certain people in the Philippines” to stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea.

China does not accept the 2016 ruling by an arbitral tribunal in The Hague, which found Beijing’s claims to historic rights within the nine-dash line had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Beijing argues the tribunal had no jurisdiction because the case involved territorial sovereignty and maritime delimitation and says the Philippines abused the Unclos dispute settlement mechanism by bringing the case unilaterally.

The Seoul episode followed Beijing’s June sanctions on Teodoro, his wife and child over what China said were erroneous remarks that undermined its interests and damaged bilateral relations.

The move barred them from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau and restricted Chinese organisations and individuals from dealing with them, but Teodoro remained defiant, saying the sanctions would not stop him from doing his job.

Even before his latest viral moment, some social media users in the Philippines had begun urging Teodoro to run for president, vice-president or the Senate in 2028.

On Facebook, a page entitled “Filipinos for Gibo Teodoro 2028” had sprung up by June and had 35,000 followers as of the time of writing. One user commented “if Sec Gibo decides to run for President, we should all support him”, while another said: “He’s my President in 2028.”

His Seoul response also drew support from public figures, including Senator Erwin Tulfo, who said Teodoro had done “the right thing”, and Senator Panfilo Lacson, who said the episode showed what Teodoro’s “brilliant mind” could bring to the world stage.

But political observers said Teodoro’s path to higher office would depend on whether he could translate a burst of online attention into sustained support – a challenge made clearer by his previous unsuccessful runs for national office.

Teodoro was criticised over disaster rescue operations after Typhoon Ketsana in 2009, when he was defence secretary, before running the following year as president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo’s official candidate and finishing in fourth place.

After that defeat, he largely shunned politics until 2022, when he offered to be the vice-presidential running mate of Davao City mayor Sara Duterte-Carpio.

When Duterte-Carpio decided to seek the vice-presidency herself, Teodoro instead ran for one of 12 Senate seats up for election that year under the poorly funded People’s Reform Party, but finished 15th and missed out.

Dr Ranjit Rye, founding president of poll firm Octa Research, told This Week in Asia that Teodoro was “not yet” ripe for the vice-presidential race but said a Senate run could be more realistic.

In Octa’s July poll of the public’s senatorial preferences, Teodoro placed No 29, with 11.2 per cent of respondents saying they would vote for him, while WR Numero Research’s June survey put him at No 35, with 6 per cent support.

Barry Gutierrez, who was spokesman to former vice-president Leni Robredo and is himself an ex-congressman, said survey numbers were “the most immediate measure” of viability, though not the only one.

“Unfortunately, Secretary Teodoro’s numbers are fairly low across the board at this point,” Gutierrez told This Week in Asia, adding that Teodoro “is not even considered in publicly released presidential surveys”.

“To me this indicates that, as of now, he is not top of mind when it comes to choices for the top posts in 2028,” he said.

Ronnie Holmes, Pulse Asia president and a professor of political science and development studies at De La Salle University, said the pollster “will include his name for a long list on presidential preference in our third-quarter survey”.

“I can’t comment on viability until we see the survey results,” Holmes said.

Gutierrez said Teodoro’s numbers could improve if his recent prominence became “the start of a more sustained visibility as a national leader”, but added that this would require “a sustained and consistent effort over time, and not simply one viral moment two years before the elections”.

“Gilberto Teodoro is qualified to run for higher office in 2028. He has the credentials and experience,” said Manuel Mogato, a defence and security analyst.

“But experience, expertise, and his high qualifications are not enough. Winnability is also important,” Mogato said, adding that current opinion polls suggested Teodoro still had significant ground to make up before 2028.

University of the Philippines political-science professor Dr Jean Franco said Teodoro was “definitely viable given his background, experience, and competence”, but that his association with Macapagal Arroyo, elite family background and lack of mass appeal could count against him.

“I believe, however, that if he is paired with a strong presidential candidate and if he has good campaign strategists, he can be a strong contender. He can carry the China issue, which I believe is something that resonates across classes,” she said.

Asked by radio station DZBB on September 11 whether he was eyeing an elective post, Teodoro said he was keeping his options open because “you know it’s hard to plan now. It’s hard to plan because I am focused on my work here”.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 5-year plan, policy continuity offer investors more stability, experts say
item.description:
Longer-term vision and policies with continuity mapped out in Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, along with the latest policy blueprint, offer investment opportunities and greater stability for investors, according to experts and commentators.

Hong Kong marked a historic milestone on Wednesday when Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out the city’s first five-year development plan with his fifth policy address to align with China’s long-term national strategy.

The explicit directions Lee set for Hong Kong in terms of economic and social development are seen as ensuring policy continuity even if there are changes in government leadership. This is Lee’s final policy address of his current five-year term as chief executive.
item.content:encoded:
Longer-term vision and policies with continuity mapped out in Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, along with the latest policy blueprint, offer investment opportunities and greater stability for investors, according to experts and commentators.

Hong Kong marked a historic milestone on Wednesday when Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out the city’s first five-year development plan with his fifth policy address to align with China’s long-term national strategy.

The explicit directions Lee set for Hong Kong in terms of economic and social development are seen as ensuring policy continuity even if there are changes in government leadership. This is Lee’s final policy address of his current five-year term as chief executive.

“It is an important start,” Our Hong Kong Foundation vice-president Kenny Shui Chi-wai said.

“For the first time, the message is clear on the purposes of the two documents. The five-year plan provides mid- to long-term vision with indicators, and the policy address stipulates how to attain the goals.”

The 22 indicators in the five-year plan include five binding and 17 anticipatory goals, which will be covered in Lee’s annual work report to Chinese President Xi Jinping.

In the 60,000-word five-year plan running to 2030, Lee spelled out the city’s core positioning under the “four centres, one hub” concept, which refers to Hong Kong as a financial, maritime, aviation and trade centre, as well as a high-calibre talent hub.

The policy address, at over 40,000 words, offers five major development opportunities spanning talent, industry, business investment, institutional safeguards and international cooperation.

This is in addition to 25 key livelihood initiatives ranging from youth development, housing and healthcare to artificial intelligence and education.

“Many of the developments mean investment opportunities, for example, the Northern Metropolis project,” Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce CEO Patrick Yeung Wai-tim said.

“This time, it gives investors more confidence because previously, the policies on the Northern Metropolis were less organised.”

The centrepiece of development will be the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis, a business, education and housing megaproject near the border with Shenzhen. It will serve the important strategic goals of promoting high-standard tertiary education via a university town, innovation and technology, industrial development and talent aggregation, aligning with the national five-year plan.

The megaproject is subject to a binding target of raising “spade-ready sites” from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030.

Other anticipatory goals include increasing the number of completed homes in the Northern Metropolis to 70,000 from the current 11,000, hitting an average annual increase of 4 to 5 per cent in the number of companies in Hong Kong with parent firms located outside the city, and boosting the value-add of the tourism industry to HK$126 billion (US$16.1 billion) from HK$86.2 billion during the five-year period.

Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services with CBRE Hong Kong, said the five-year plan offered the Northern Metropolis “its clearest and most actionable” timeline yet.

“The next chapter will be defined not by planning ambition but by execution discipline: whether the commercial frameworks attract real capital, whether the transport milestones hold, and whether the talent the university towns are designed to attract actually chooses to live and work in the Northern Metropolis,” she said.

Lee’s call to expedite the building of an international gold trading market and the city’s offshore renminbi businesses, developing an international asset and wealth management centre and risk management centre, enhancing the securities market and expanding fixed-income and commodity trading, also presents greater opportunities to local and foreign investors.

Billy Mak Sui-choi, an associate professor at Baptist University’s accountancy, economics and finance department, pointed to the five-year plan’s emphasis on yuan globalisation, saying it would create synergies with the annual policy and drive the gold trade while consolidating the city’s status as a foreign exchange hub.

“The current problem with offshore renminbi is that its functions are too limited, and the policy address makes it clear that Hong Kong will expand the sales, valuation and clearance of renminbi-denominated assets in the city,” he said.

“When this is promoted, it will help Hong Kong with its foreign exchange business.”

Hong Kong is China’s largest offshore yuan business hub, with 1.1 trillion yuan in offshore deposits as of June and handling more than 70 per cent of all global offshore yuan payments, according to official statistics.

According to Mak, the yuan push went hand in hand with Hong Kong’s vision to build a commodities ecosystem, especially with measures to expand gold trading in the city, as backing renminbi-denominated assets with gold bullion stored in Hong Kong would offer more assurance to investors.

“If Hong Kong, as an offshore renminbi centre, is to further develop the offshore renminbi market, it needs gold to serve as a backup,” he said. “Putting the two together is just the right fit.”

Andrew Gaw, managing director of trader Solid Gold Investments, said the precious metal was a hot asset and gold trading was crucial to the city’s strength as a global financial centre.

“Many investors are sceptical about the US dollar and want to diversify into gold to hedge investment risks,” he said.

“China is a huge market, which means huge opportunities for Hong Kong, so what the government should do is to bring the two markets even closer.”

However, Hong Kong is facing strong competition from markets such as London and Singapore in the gold business.

Gold prices jumped about 17 per cent over the past year to HK$34,099 per ounce on Wednesday.

Yeung of the chamber said gold trading also served to strengthen the financial security of the city and even the country amid intensifying Sino-US rivalry.

“Hong Kong has built a solid foundation in its standing as an international financial centre, which has become an alternative market for gold investors and risk management,” he said.

In February, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to scrutinise more closely Beijing’s use of Hong Kong for sandbox experiments in gold-backed digital assets that could rival the US dollar.

Shui of the think tank said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s plan to introduce a tendering mechanism for seven-day offshore renminbi liquidity and explore issuing short-term debt instruments was among the investor-friendly measures to boost the currency’s liquidity.

He pointed out that government safeguards and initiatives such as building a global capital of mediation and combating the use of artificial intelligence in criminal activities would offer protection to investors.

“In light of the controversies surrounding AI developers like Anthropic and DeepSeek, the AI initiative will at least offer some legal protection, like what the EU and South Korea are offering,” Shui said.

The European Union and South Korea heavily penalise perpetrators of scams using AI.

Yeung of the chamber said the series of investment opportunities, particularly in the Northern Metropolis, would drive the city’s economic growth in coming years, benefitting livelihoods.

“What we will see is a major transformation in Hong Kong,” he said. “The city has to grasp this critical window of opportunity, even though the Northern Metropolis development is very much like crossing the river by feeling the stones.”

Additional reporting by Leopold Chen

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries
item.description:
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.

In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030.

The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.

In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030.

The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

He also focused on improving living standards and social well-being, announcing initiatives ranging from higher baby bonuses to encourage childbirth and increased healthcare spending to more subsidised housing and shorter waiting times for public flats.

“[China’s] 15th five-year plan, which outlines a blueprint for future national development and also places a heightened demand for Hong Kong’s better integration into and service of the overall national development, presents major opportunities and opens up new ground for the growth of our city,” Lee said in his speech to the Legislative Council.

“Hong Kong’s economic structure still leaves room for enhancement, the mission of transitioning to new growth drivers remains formidable, and deep-seated social problems still require speedy resolution.”

The five-year blueprint, a seven-part document described by Lee as “an action agenda” for Hong Kong’s medium- and long-term development, lists 105 indicators, including 22 major targets covering economic and innovation development, livelihoods, and environmental protection.

The major indicators are divided into 17 anticipatory goals and five binding targets, some of which would be affected by geopolitical uncertainties and other external factors.

“If the binding targets are not met at the end of the day, there is a need to be held accountable,” Lee said. “But we need to appreciate that some things may be out of our control, such as economic development. Some countries might suddenly change their policies.”

The anticipatory goals include 10 per cent annual increases in two key technology indicators: nearly doubling spending on innovation activities to 3 per cent from 1.63 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) over five years; and raising the economic share of value-added manufacturing to 5.5 per cent from 3.8 per cent.

Another anticipatory target is to increase by 4 to 5 per cent annually the number of companies whose parent firms are based outside Hong Kong.

Four of the five binding targets concern environmental protection. They include cutting carbon emissions per unit of GDP by 32.5 per cent and raising the share of zero-carbon energy in Hong Kong’s electricity fuel mix to 30 per cent from 25 per cent over the five-year period.

Goals for the Northern Metropolis, the massive undertaking near the Shenzhen border to build a 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) business, education and housing zone, include a binding target to raise the “spade-ready sites” available from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030, and an anticipatory target to increase the number of homes completed in the zone to 70,000 from the current 11,000.

On livelihoods, Lee pledged to raise the doctor-to-population ratio to 2.43 from 2.25 per 1,000 residents, and lower the risk of early deaths caused by chronic conditions to 6.9 per cent from 7.3 per cent.

Lee’s long-term blueprint dedicates a chapter to national security as a priority for the city’s success and prosperity, stressing that “a holistic approach” will be adopted to strengthen economic resilience by improving the city’s legal system and enforcement mechanisms.

The wide-ranging, traditional policy address that followed the announcement of the five-year plan was titled “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era, Driving Reform and Boosting Development, Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihood”.

The address, which was the last of Lee’s current term, set out priorities targeting five major areas of development opportunities, alongside 25 key livelihood initiatives.

Measures offering immediate benefits to residents include one-off cash incentives and subsidies.

While extending the HK$20,000 (US$2,549) newborn bonus for three years, Lee said the government would increase the amount for second and subsequent children to HK$30,000 and offer subsidies to employers providing an extra 10,000 full-time jobs to young people entering the workforce.

Expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis is a key highlight of the policy address, which matches the “dual-core planning” vision set out in the five-year plan that clusters innovation and technology (I&T) sectors near the northern border and places finance sectors south along Victoria Harbour.

Describing the northern development zone as “an important strategic vehicle” for integrating I&T and industry, Lee said selected strategic industries establishing a presence there would receive targeted tax breaks.

While developing three university towns that will span 1,000 hectares in the northern zone, the government will invite universities to build campuses in Hung Shui Kiu from this year. Authorities are also studying the feasibility of a southern extension of the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Western Rail Link to enhance connectivity.

The Northern Metropolis will seek to improve living conditions in space-starved Hong Kong, with its housing projects increasing the proportion of more spacious flats with an area of about 45 square metres (484 square feet) to 25 per cent from the original 20 per cent.

Both policy documents devoted significant space to consolidating Hong Kong’s role as an international financial centre under the broader “Four Centres, One Hub” strategy.

The strategy seeks to strengthen the city’s position as an international financial, maritime and trade centre, develop it into an international innovation and technology centre, and establish the city as a hub for “high-calibre talent”.

The chief executive said the city would introduce an auction system allowing banks to bid for short-term yuan liquidity to meet their short-term financing needs.

Lee said his administration would actively promote the use of the Chinese currency to settle government expenditure, for example purchasing fresh water from Guangdong, and expand the dim sum bond market, while the operator of the city’s stock and futures markets would launch an offshore renminbi bond index and introduce new products.

Following the official launch of Hong Kong’s central clearing and settlement system for gold earlier this year, the government is considering tapping into the Exchange Fund to buy more gold and participate in the spot and futures markets.

The policy address also outlined growth strategies for emerging sectors, including dispute resolution, international property and marine services.

A new task force on frontier technology will spearhead deeper research on aerospace, marine and quantum technologies.

Addressing housing issues that Beijing has often instructed Hong Kong to resolve, Lee said the aim was to reduce the waiting time for subsidised rental flats to 4.5 years from 4.8 years by 2027, and to bring it below four years after 2030.

The long-term plan envisages public rental housing accounting for 40 per cent of total supply, with subsidised sale flats and private homes each making up 30 per cent over the next 10 years.

Lee put a heavy emphasis on leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) in various policy domains, which will include establishing an “AI City Brain” system to strengthen responses to extreme weather events, major incidents and public order management. A new AI commissioner’s post will be created to tackle emerging challenges.

Lee told the media later that while AI boosted efficiency, it also created “operational and societal risks”, prompting his administration to introduce seven risk governance guidelines, with a particular focus on protecting students.

Lee expressed confidence that the targets would improve livelihoods, strengthen economic development and deepen Hong Kong’s integration into the national development agenda.

“I hope and I’m confident that in five years, for everyone, whether it’s their income or development, there will be an improvement,” he said.

“Our industries will be more diversified, education enhanced, [the city] more international, and we will be a highly technologically empowered Hong Kong.”

item.title: [SCMP] Japan’s Natuna port proposal highlights Indonesia’s balancing act on China
item.description:
Japan’s proposed port upgrades in Indonesia’s Natuna Islands reflect Tokyo’s push to bolster South China Sea security without building an overt military footprint. However, analysts stress that the move does not mean Jakarta is siding with Japan in its efforts to contain Beijing.

Japan, which earlier this year eased its restrictions on lethal weapons exports, is ramping up security cooperation with Indonesia – a crucial bellwether for Southeast Asia.

The expanding partnership includes joint defence industry development, intelligence cooperation and expanded military exercises in strategic waterways.
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s proposed port upgrades in Indonesia’s Natuna Islands reflect Tokyo’s push to bolster South China Sea security without building an overt military footprint. However, analysts stress that the move does not mean Jakarta is siding with Japan in its efforts to contain Beijing.

Japan, which earlier this year eased its restrictions on lethal weapons exports, is ramping up security cooperation with Indonesia – a crucial bellwether for Southeast Asia.

The expanding partnership includes joint defence industry development, intelligence cooperation and expanded military exercises in strategic waterways.

Citing Japanese government sources, Kyodo News reported earlier this month that Tokyo was planning to use its official development assistance to help upgrade Indonesia’s fishing ports to allow patrol vessels to operate in more areas.

According to the report, one potential location will be the Natuna Islands, which lie along the southern edge of China’s nine-dash line – a boundary outlining Beijing’s expansive claims in the South China Sea.

In a commentary, state-owned Global Times framed Japan’s offer as a geopolitical tactic to expand Tokyo’s intelligence gathering and strengthen its presence in the South China Sea.

“Japan seeks to push countries like Indonesia to the front lines of South China Sea rivalry, while hiding behind the scenes to orchestrate its ‘proxy gambit’,” it said.

“This allows Japan to avoid risks of direct confrontation yet reap intelligence and strategic dividends. Indonesia and other Asean nations must be particularly vigilant against this ‘wolf in sheep’s clothing’ ploy,” it continued.

The Natuna Islands lie to the northeast of Sumatra and west of Borneo in the South China Sea. The archipelago and its adjacent waters – officially named the North Natuna Sea by Indonesia in 2017 – sit astride a key shipping route. The area is also a hotspot for commercial fishing.

Chinese, Vietnamese and Indonesian fishing vessels, often escorted by coastguard ships, have occasionally clashed over marine resources in recent years.

Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, noted that Jakarta’s push to upgrade the remote resource-rich islands served both economic and sovereign ends.

He said that policymakers in Jakarta had long been wary of foreign military presence in the region, especially the Chinese.

“Indonesia has sought to develop Natuna Islands, particularly its fishing resources, and has looked to expand its military presence in the region so as to consolidate its control in the region,” he said.

Chaula Rininta Anindya, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Indonesia, noted that the project was expected to address the “grey-zone” tactics Jakarta faced in the North Natuna Sea by bolstering frontline maritime deterrence.

However, she said the plan was broader than a simple response to South China Sea issues.

Rather, she said, it reflected Indonesia’s attempt to enhance its “Large Islands Defence” strategy through the dual use of ports – hosting civilian vessels as well as military and coastguard fleets when needed.

Under its “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” strategy, Tokyo has prioritised helping Southeast Asian partners build capacity and increase awareness of maritime threats so they can safeguard critical sea lanes.

Heng Yee Kuang, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said efforts to upgrade fishing ports were a result of the Japan-Indonesia summit in March.

At that meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised cooperation in the fisheries industry, especially as Indonesia faced challenges related to illegal fishing and smuggling in the South China Sea, according to Heng.

He added that the initiative illustrated the continuity of cooperation between the two countries, as Japan had provided patrol boats for the Indonesian coastguard since the early 2000s.

The stakes for Japan are significant. Roughly 80 per cent of its energy imports and much of its maritime trade flow through the South China Sea, making stable sea lanes a core national interest.

“Indonesia’s importance to Japan has grown because of its geostrategic archipelagic location astride maritime chokepoints and key shipping lanes within Japan’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific Vision. Helping Indonesia address its maritime challenges is also in Japan’s enlightened self-interest,” Heng said.

However, Beijing has become increasingly alarmed by Tokyo’s growing security footprint in the region amid a downturn in Sino-Japanese ties.

Chen said that by offering security aid to Southeast Asia, Tokyo might be trying to distract Beijing from territorial disputes in the East China Sea.

“In a sense, Japan is … hoping to use the Southeast Asia region to relieve pressure or draw attention away from the East China Sea,” he said.

“More importantly, I think Japan is now engaged in a full-spectrum competition against China, not just in northeast Asia but in Southeast Asia as well, in terms of the economy, the military and diplomatic influence,” Chen said.

In the past two years, Japan and the Philippines have signed two deals to strengthen the logistics and sustainment capabilities of their armed forces, including the Reciprocal Access Agreement, which came into force last September.

At a defence ministers’ meeting in Jakarta in May, Japan and Indonesia signed a defence cooperation agreement covering military personnel development, defence industry collaboration and a mechanism for integrated defence dialogues. It institutionalises exchanges between senior officials and operational-level engagements between Japan’s Self-Defence Forces and Indonesia’s armed forces.

More crucially, the two sides also agreed to explore cooperation on defence equipment and technology aimed at boosting maritime deterrence, opening the door to future Japanese arms transfers.

Anindya said Indonesia’s role as the largest country in Southeast Asia – by size and by population – and its critical role as a co-founder of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) had made it an agenda setter in the region.

“It seems that Japan is expecting Indonesia to share a common understanding on the issue in the region, then the message could be conveyed as well at the regional level,” she said.

She added that military cooperation between Indonesia and Japan should not be seen as an alliance to counter China but a pragmatic strategy by Jakarta to work with its partners around the world.

“Indonesia is simply being pragmatic, and I believe it does not want to risk escalating tension with China. Indonesia will be careful in establishing cooperation with various countries and will remain committed to its ‘free and active’ foreign policy,” she said.

Heng noted that Japan and Indonesia did not yet have an intelligence-sharing framework for sensitive information.

He said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto had also been careful to balance relations with China, “so Beijing can be reassured on this point”.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s rocket boom has made Hainan a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.

Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan a catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services.

Today, the island province is working to build a more diversified and sustainable growth model and, together with its ambition to host a premier free-trade port, is embracing a hi-tech future increasingly centred on the space economy.

From coconuts to rockets: Hainan’s economic reboot

“Commercial space flight could give Hainan a clearer manufacturing focus while complementing its traditional strengths in tourism and consumer services,” said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

Home to more than 10 million people and comparable in size to Belgium, Hainan now boasts a growing industrial cluster known as Wenchang International Aerospace City. At its centre are two state-owned rocket launch facilities: one serving national programmes and another handling commercial missions.

The Wenchang Space Launch Site staged its first launch in 2016 and focuses mainly on lunar exploration and human space flight. Just a few miles away sits the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, China’s first dedicated commercial launch platform.

Since its inaugural mission in November 2024, the commercial site has completed 21 launches and has sent 221 satellites into orbit, according to Xu Xikai, deputy head of the development department at Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch, the site’s operator.

Two more general-purpose liquid-fuel launch pads were also under construction and could host their maiden missions by the end of this year, Xu noted. Longer-term plans envision as many as eight large coastal launch pads, together with tracking facilities and systems for recovering rockets at sea.

We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains

Xu Xikai, Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch

Wenchang’s coastal geography gives it a major advantage. Massive rockets can be delivered directly by sea, bypassing the road, tunnel and bridge constraints faced by inland facilities. And at about 19 degrees north latitude, rockets gain an extra momentum boost from the Earth’s rotation, reducing fuel requirements or allowing heavier payloads, Xu explained.

“For large-diameter, heavy-lift rockets in the future, coastal launch sites will increasingly have an advantage,” he said.

Geography, however, is also one of Hainan’s economic weaknesses. The island has historically lacked a heavy industrial base, meaning much of the specialised hardware and construction materials required for space manufacturing must be shipped in.

Inside Wenchang’s manufacturing ambitions

The challenge for Hainan is transforming launch sites into the nucleus of a wider industrial ecosystem – and early signs are encouraging.

Wenchang International Aerospace City recorded a surge in revenue amid an “unprecedented” pace of rocket launches, according to a June report by Nanhai Net, a state-run news portal operated by the Hainan Daily Press Group.

The aerospace park’s revenue jumped 85 per cent in 2025 to 23.53 billion yuan (US$3.5 billion), while manufacturing output from its rocket supply chain more than doubled to over 8 billion yuan, the report stated.

Under a provincial action plan from 2025 to 2027, Hainan also aims to raise annual operating revenue at Wenchang’s aerospace cluster to 10 billion yuan by 2027, while building an integrated supply chain spanning rockets, satellites and data services.

The expansion comes as Beijing presses ahead with reforms to open the island further and develop new sources of growth – though competition is intensifying. Two other commercial launch sites have already begun operating in Gansu and Shandong provinces, while at least four more are under development nationwide.

To stay ahead, Hainan’s strategy is to push further up the industrial chain. Its action plan prioritises a “super factory” next to the launch pads, designed to produce up to 1,000 satellites annually. The location would allow freshly assembled satellites to move straight from production line to launch pad with very little transit time, the Star Market Daily, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet focused on technology and capital markets, reported in December.

Described by local authorities as Asia’s largest satellite-manufacturing facility, the industrial complex is also expected to support China’s Qianfan low-Earth-orbit constellation. A planned special bonded zone for satellite data would further leverage Hainan’s free-trade policies to attract data from overseas, according to the report.

“We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains,” said Xu of Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch.

The infrastructure buildout is already reshaping launch activity. After more than two years of development, the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has moved from experimental testing to routine operations. It handled more than 30 per cent of China’s commercial satellite launches in 2025 and successfully carried out the country’s first offshore rocket booster recovery.

Business beyond the launch pad

Putting a rocket into orbit, however, is only one part of the emerging space economy. Ye Shiyang, a Wenchang native who chairs the company behind the Aerospace Supercomputing Centre in Wenchang International Aerospace City, argued Hainan must capture a larger share of the value generated after a rocket launches.

“Over the past few years, we have connected the entire chain – from collecting and receiving satellite data to storing, processing, applying and trading it,” Ye said.

Completed in 2023, the supercomputing centre occupies about 40,000 square metres (about 431,000 square feet), with about 22,400 square metres of floor space. A guide at the centre said it offered peak computing power of 100 petaflops – a measure of processing capacity – and was designed to accommodate about 2,000 server racks.

Meanwhile, three of the centre’s remote-sensing satellites operate as part of Jilin-1, which is described by its developer as the world’s largest commercial sub-metre Earth-observation constellation. The centre has also built 13 ground stations, according to a guide there.

The practical applications could be numerous. Satellite images processed in Wenchang can distinguish food crops from cash crops, identify fallow land and monitor crop growth, assess pest outbreaks and track the effects of typhoons. Such imaging tools can also help to detect water pollution, illegal logging and unauthorised land use.

These services, Ye argued, could generate steady demand from agricultural, environmental and land-management authorities, giving Hainan a revenue stream that is less dependent on the schedule of rocket launches.

The aerospace city is also developing a space tourism business. The Jixing Meteorite Museum, for instance, displays more than 400 specimens gathered from around the world, while exhibitions introduce visitors to satellite data and supercomputing.

“We are developing space tourism in response to market demand,” Ye said. “Visitors should not only watch a launch or see a rocket or satellite. They should also understand the industry and technology behind them.”

In 2025, tourism, modern services, hi-tech industries and tropical agriculture – Hainan’s four pillar sectors – accounted for 65.9 per cent of the province’s gross domestic product, according to the provincial government.

“The Wenchang launch site has already become a tourist attraction, and this could give Hainan an economic model built around tourism, consumer services and aerospace manufacturing – and give its manufacturing sector a much clearer direction,” said Peng of the Guangdong Society of Reform.

For a Wenchang native surnamed Xie, the transformation has been drastic. Growing up in a village in Longlou town, he once walked barefoot along unpaved red-earth tracks. Today, working as a taxi driver, he has watched the sprawling aerospace complex reshape the place he calls home.

As the launch site and surrounding projects expanded, local families were relocated and farmland acquired. While some households received hundreds of thousands of yuan in compensation, Xie noted how traditional livelihoods were quickly fading, leaving coconut processing as one of the few legacy industries remaining.

“Farmers around here barely farm any more,” he said.

In Longlou, the coconut palms still remain – quiet reminders of a past that existed before the rockets arrived, even as a new economy takes shape around them.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese defence chief skirts flashpoints at Xiangshan Forum ahead of Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday.

Speaking at the annual Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Dong took veiled swipes at Washington and its allies but – unlike last year – appeared to pull his punches, skipping mentions of contentious issues such as Taiwan and the South China Sea.

He also said Beijing would share its experience in “military building” and “provide assistance within our capabilities” to foreign armed forces, a rare public offer by the country’s top defence officials.
item.content:encoded:
With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday.

Speaking at the annual Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Dong took veiled swipes at Washington and its allies but – unlike last year – appeared to pull his punches, skipping mentions of contentious issues such as Taiwan and the South China Sea.

He also said Beijing would share its experience in “military building” and “provide assistance within our capabilities” to foreign armed forces, a rare public offer by the country’s top defence officials.

Beijing seems increasingly confident of its military prowess heading into the People’s Liberation Army’s centenary next year, with a belief that it is closing the military gap with Washington.

At the same time, there are signs of improving defence ties between the two powers. A senior Pentagon official said earlier that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years”.

At the forum, Dong described the global landscape as complex and international security as “fragile”, saying there was an “urgent need” to improve global security governance.

“We must promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive, forging a new path to security based on dialogue rather than confrontation, partnership rather than alliance and win-win outcomes rather than zero-sum games,” he said.

While he did not name any country, Dong alluded to the US and its actions in the Middle East on several occasions, including urging “major powers” to shoulder the responsibility of maintaining global stability and upholding multilateralism, and calling on countries to “resist reckless moves that use security as a bargaining chip”.

“We must not tolerate provocations that attempt to hijack the overall interests of countries and regions for private gain or the interests of small cliques. We must work together to rein them in,” he added.

“The persistence of global conflict serves as a sobering reminder that … force cannot resolve the root of the problem. Coercion and pressure only widen rifts and create more difficulties.”

His comments took tacit aim at the United States as the Donald Trump administration resumed strikes against Iran in a bid to end a conflict now in its seventh month.

Dong instead positioned Beijing as a “responsible major country” that has maintained an impartial stance, capable of acting as a “positive and stabilising force” in resolving conflicts.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi hosted his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Beijing on Wednesday.

Even as Dong took veiled jabs at the US, his tone was markedly more measured than at the same forum last year.

A year ago, he still did not name any country but described military alliances as groups driven by “selfish interests”.

Urging countries to stand up against “disguised hegemonic logic and bullying acts”, he also said the time that the world was overshadowed by a “cold war mentality, hegemonism and protectionism” – phrases Beijing routinely uses to describe Washington’s actions.

Unlike last year, when Dong asserted that the return of Taiwan to Beijing was “an integral part of the post-war order” and that Beijing was “ready to thwart any external military interference”, he left out Taiwan from this year’s speech.

Zhou Bo, senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, described Dong’s tone on Wednesday as “relatively mild” but stressed that the omission of Taiwan did not mean the issue was any less important.

“Not mentioning Taiwan does not mean that China is less concerned with the issue,” said Zhou, a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army. “It doesn’t mean that China is not paying attention to it.”

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Beijing has repeatedly said that Taiwan is its core interest and a “red line” that must not be crossed in Sino-US relations. The issue is expected to be raised again by Xi when he sits down with Trump next week.

Nor did Dong make any mention of the South China Sea. Last year, he criticised “extra-regional powers” for using freedom of navigation to stir up tensions in the disputed waterway.

According to Zhou, Dong’s offer to help with military development in other countries reflects Beijing’s growing confidence in its military.

That offer came a day after Dong hosted senior officials attending the forum, including the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar, according to China’s defence ministry.

The PLA has also held a series of joint training exercises with other militaries, including those of Belarus, Egypt, Singapore and Thailand in the past month.

Meanwhile, according to Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, it was good for the world that the US and China had agreed to establish stable relations since Trump’s visit to China in May.

Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s school of international studies, said the forum was aimed at promoting security cooperation between Beijing and the world, so Dong’s speech could not solely focus on “these contentious issues”, referring to the omission of Taiwan and the South China Sea.

Beijing’s offer to help build other militaries stemmed from the turmoil roiling global affairs, Zhu added, saying that while China could deepen cooperation through multilateral platforms, it also needed to work together with smaller states if they faced internal problems.

“This also demonstrates China’s responsibility as a major country in the face of various current tensions,” he said.

With China-Japan relations still strained following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks on Taiwan in November last year, Dong said the world “must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against … hegemonism, militarism and historical revisionism”.

Among other things, the Chinese defence chief also called for countries to deepen cooperation in areas including joint exercises and training as well as engage in dialogue on artificial intelligence, outer space and the deep sea.

The three-day Xiangshan Forum is expected to gather defence delegations from close to 100 countries, regions and international organisations. The forum, seen as Beijing’s answer to Singapore’s annual Shangri-La Dialogue, marks its 20th anniversary this year.

item.title: [SCMP] Is Japan’s Okinawa finally moving past anti-base politics?
item.description:
Okinawa has handed a landslide victory to a conservative who accepts Tokyo’s plans for relocating a controversial US airbase – delivering a blow to 12 years of anti-base politics in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.

Genta Koja’s victory on Sunday over two-term governor Denny Tamaki raised a question cutting to the heart of Okinawa’s post-war politics: is it finally starting to move on from the US military base issue?

Koja, a 42-year-old conservative backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, campaigned on economic revival and accepting Tokyo’s plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station from densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko district in Nago, both on Okinawa Island.
item.content:encoded:
Okinawa has handed a landslide victory to a conservative who accepts Tokyo’s plans for relocating a controversial US airbase – delivering a blow to 12 years of anti-base politics in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.

Genta Koja’s victory on Sunday over two-term governor Denny Tamaki raised a question cutting to the heart of Okinawa’s post-war politics: is it finally starting to move on from the US military base issue?

Koja, a 42-year-old conservative backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, campaigned on economic revival and accepting Tokyo’s plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station from densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko district in Nago, both on Okinawa Island.

Tamaki, by contrast, had opposed the base project for his entire tenure as governor, a stance he inherited from his late predecessor after winning 2018’s election on an anti-base platform.

Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News on Sunday found that nearly half of voters ranked economic revitalisation as their top concern, while barely one-fifth of respondents cited issues related to US bases.

That was reflected in the election results. Koja, a former deputy mayor of Okinawa’s capital Naha, defeated Tamaki with 59 per cent of the vote, officials said on Monday.

He will become the prefecture’s first governor born after its return to Japanese sovereignty by the United States in 1972 and the first in over a decade not to have built his career on opposition to US military bases.

Generational rift

Okinawa has been seen as a bastion of pacifist, left-leaning opposition forces for years.

Despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of Japan’s total land area, it hosts roughly 70 per cent of the land dedicated exclusively to US military facilities in the country – a burden that has made it central to arguments over the US-Japan alliance.

Tamaki and his All Okinawa movement, a broad political and civic alliance that opposes the relocation and construction of US military bases on Okinawa Island, had long framed the dispute as a test of local autonomy against central authority.

Sunday’s result illustrated a generational divide, according to Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science.

While voters over 60 largely backed Tamaki and All Okinawa, “younger voters were more concerned about the economy”, he said.

The outcome reflected “pragmatism as well as frustration” with Tamaki for failing to stop new base construction, Maslow said – though that did not mean voters were unconcerned about national security implications.

Japan’s “Nansei shift” – the build-up of defence capabilities across its southern islands – was expected to continue under the new governor and “this will place an even higher burden on Okinawa”, he said.

Masato Kamikubo, a political scientist and professor at Ritsumeikan University, said successive LDP governments dating back to Shinzo Abe’s administration had cut subsidies to Okinawa in an attempt to “bully” the prefecture for its confrontational approach to central authority.

A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics

Masato Kamikubo, political scientist

“Faced with rising prices and other economic difficulties, Okinawan voters appear to have wanted a way out of the present situation and therefore prioritised the economy over the military base issue,” he said.

The election result reflected a move away from the decades-old contest between conservative and liberal blocs, Kamikubo said, arguing that All Okinawa’s “crushing defeat” revealed a movement built on ideological resistance struggling to hold a new generation’s attention.

“A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics from the grass roots, moving beyond the traditional divide between left and right,” he said. “This election may have symbolised that emerging transformation.”

Meanwhile, Takaichi’s firm stance on national security, particularly the tough line she had taken on China, also resonated with Okinawan voters, Kamikubo said.

“Okinawa is on the front line in confronting the perceived threat from China,” he said, noting that liberal politicians such as Tamaki and the All Okinawa movement had done little more than appealed for peace.

“Some voters are anxious about whether these groups would actually be able to protect them in the event of a crisis.”

Tokyo’s cash carrot

On Monday, following Koja’s victory, Takaichi pledged to raise Okinawa’s budget to more than 300 billion yen (US$1.94 billion) from around 260 billion yen in recent years.

Kamikubo said he expected her “to present Okinawa as a model demonstrating that economic growth can be achieved and rising living costs overcome when the central and prefectural governments work together”.

“For a prime minister struggling with declining approval ratings, the victory in Okinawa will be seen as a significant glimmer of hope,” he added.
