A recent poll by national broadcaster NHK found public approval of Takaichi’s cabinet at 53 per cent, down from 66 per cent in November last year, amid concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living.

Koja’s economic focus and his image as a fresh face – in contrast to Tamaki, who staked his political legacy on opposing the US military presence – had all helped at the polls, said Rintaro Nishimura, a Tokyo-based senior associate at strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.

But Sunday’s result did not mean that Okinawans no longer cared about the base issue, he said, nor that they would accept every central government policy.

“He [Koja] has been clear in how he views his role: a coordinator who will seek out the most practical and best option for the people of Okinawa,” Nishimura said.

Still, the LDP backing a winning candidate for governor in a historically anti-LDP prefecture was “a good narrative for Takaichi to build on”, he said – particularly heading into next year’s local elections, as it helped counter concerns that the party was unpopular at the local level.

Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, said many Okinawans had voted out of dissatisfaction with rising prices and economic hardship rather than security concerns.

“The sense of immediacy regarding a potential conflict stemming from the Taiwan Strait crisis remains relatively limited,” he said, adding that further militarisation of Okinawa was likely to be “tolerated” by a significant segment of voters.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but are opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force.

The two central challenges facing Okinawa today were poverty and the burden of hosting US bases, Gabe said.

“Regardless of who serves as governor, these two challenges continue to exist with unwavering force and successive prefectural administrations have been compelled to confront them,” he said, adding that “the central government holds the upper hand on the base issue and its control over policy is unlikely to be shaken”.

Okinawa consistently ranks as the least economically developed of Japan’s prefectures, with average incomes and employment roughly 20 to 30 per cent behind mainland standards.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore court rejects 90-year-old’s spousal support claim against ex-wife, 89
item.description:
A Singapore family court rejected a 90-year-old man’s claim for spousal maintenance from his 89-year-old wife, noting that both of them are in the twilight of their lives.

The court also noted that the man would receive more than S$2 million (US$1.6 million) from the matrimonial pool, comprising the couple’s assets to be divided in the divorce, and his wife was a retiree living on a pension.

The former couple were married for more than 64 years and have three children, all aged above 60, a judgment published on Wednesday said. They were not named in the judgment, as is usual for a family court ruling.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore family court rejected a 90-year-old man’s claim for spousal maintenance from his 89-year-old wife, noting that both of them are in the twilight of their lives.

The court also noted that the man would receive more than S$2 million (US$1.6 million) from the matrimonial pool, comprising the couple’s assets to be divided in the divorce, and his wife was a retiree living on a pension.

The former couple were married for more than 64 years and have three children, all aged above 60, a judgment published on Wednesday said. They were not named in the judgment, as is usual for a family court ruling.

Most of the value in the matrimonial pool came from their joint asset, a S$5.8 million house.

The couple married in January 1960 and were granted an interim judgment for divorce in September 2024. There were no issues of custody or child maintenance since their children are adults.

Dealing with the division of matrimonial assets, Justice Dedar Singh Gill added about S$14,500 in the man’s name to the pool. Most of this is from his Central Provident Fund (CPF), Singapore’s mandatory social security savings scheme.

He added about S$80,000 from the woman’s assets to the pool, including almost S$20,000 in CPF.

Disputed contributions

The woman argued that she had contributed 100 per cent to the matrimonial home and financed it alone.

She said she had bought their previous property under the Teacher’s Estate housing scheme, which provided homes for educators. The sale proceeds from this property were used fully to buy the matrimonial home, to which her husband contributed “nothing”.

The man sought a 50:50 division of all matrimonial assets, claiming to have contributed to both the Teacher’s Estate property and the matrimonial home.

However, the judge noted that neither side’s account was supported by documentary evidence.

The woman sought a ratio of 80:20 in indirect contributions in her favour, arguing that she bore virtually all the financial and non-financial burdens of the family throughout the marriage.

She said she was the main provider during the first half of the marriage when both of them worked, paying for the children’s tuition and courses, family holidays and a domestic worker to care for the children when she was at work.

She also said that she gave her son S$50,000 to start a business that failed, and footed the bills for her children’s weddings.

After she retired in 1992, she claimed that her husband had no income and contributed “nothing” while she supported the household from her pension of about S$2,400 a month. She gave her husband half of this amount each month, she added.

She also said that she was the primary carer for her children, cooking for the family and supervising the various domestic helpers and overseeing the repairs and maintenance of the household.

The husband sought an equal or near-equal division of indirect contributions, claiming that until retirement, both parties had pooled their incomes in joint accounts. From these, all the household expenses were paid.

After retirement, he said the expenses were paid from their pooled savings in joint accounts, and thereafter from his wife’s joint accounts with their son and oldest daughter.

He said he did his “fair share of being involved in the care and upbringing of the children”.

Justice Gill said the indirect financial contributions for the first half of the marriage were difficult to determine, given the couple’s differing versions of events without objective evidence.

However, the position is clearer for the second half of the marriage after their retirement.

It was undisputed that the man had no income beyond his monthly annuity of S$485.75 from insurer NTUC Income, and that the only income stream was the woman’s monthly pension of about S$2,400, of which she gave her husband half.

The woman also produced payment records showing that she paid the property tax bills up to 2024, as well as receipts for household bills she continued to cover on her own.

Family carer

The judge also found that the wife contributed the greater share in indirect non-financial contributions, with detailed evidence of her caregiving and home-making.

She was the primary carer of her children from birth and even when she worked, helping them with their homework and managing their schooling and activities.

She also ran the household, cooked for the family, organised family gatherings, and trained and supervised the various domestic workers they hired.

“The husband, on the other hand, does no more than assert in general terms that he did his fair share,” Justice Gill said.

“He descends to no particulars of caring for the children, their schooling, their health or their emotional needs. I also consider it significant that the husband neither disputed most of what the wife says she did for the family nor offered any competing account of his own.”

He assessed indirect contributions at 70:30 in favour of the woman.

The woman sought a 2 per cent increase of her share of the matrimonial pool, saying that her ex-husband had illegally excluded her from the home from March 2025 and placed a padlock on the gate. The man, however, claimed that his ex-wife and their oldest daughter moved out of their own accord.

Justice Gill noted that this complaint of illegal exclusion surfaced for the first time only in written submissions, and both parties would obtain substantial sums from the pool in any event. He declined to raise the woman’s share of the assets on this basis.

In total, the ratio across direct and indirect contributions was computed to be 60:40, in favour of the woman. Accordingly, she was to get S$3.5 million, while her ex-husband obtained S$2.4 million.

The man sought maintenance as an incapacitated former husband under the Women’s Charter, pointing to his medical and mobility issues, his inability to earn a livelihood, his minimal income and his wife’s departure from the matrimonial home. This has left him to cover the home’s expenses alone.

If he did not get maintenance, the man asked for a lump sum equivalent to 5 to 10 per cent of his share of the matrimonial assets.

The judge rejected the man’s claim for spousal maintenance and his request for the lump sum payment. He said that both parties are in the twilight of their lives, with neither having any earning capacity nor any expectations of improving their financial positions through work.

Both of them rely on monthly pensions or payouts as their financial source, and they will each have very substantial sums from the matrimonial pool, Justice Gill added.

The sum of more than S$2 million that the man will obtain is “more than sufficient to meet the needs of a 90-year-old retiree for the remainder of his life”.

“Once the division takes effect, he will be amply provided for. In these circumstances, I do not think an order for maintenance against the wife, herself an elderly retiree living on a pension, would be just or necessary.”

The man sought reimbursement from his ex-wife’s share for the property tax he paid on the house for the years of assessment 2025 and 2026, saying that she had paid nothing since moving out in March 2025.

The judge acknowledged that the man should not necessarily bear the entire property tax simply because he lived there, but found his argument for his ex-wife to pay the full bill untenable.

He said that the property tax for the two years must be borne equally by both parties.

The home is to be sold on the open market within six months, with them having joint conduct of the sale.

Each side will bear its own costs.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] How will the Okinawa governor’s race result reshape China’s local messaging?
item.description:
The leadership change in Okinawa could deal a quiet blow to Beijing’s attempts to leverage local opposition to remilitarisation and the US-Japan military alliance, according to analysts.

They added that the shift would compel Chinese academics and state media to recalibrate their messaging and approach towards the strategically vital Japanese prefecture.

Genta Koja, the 42-year-old backed by Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party to become Okinawa’s new governor, defeated incumbent Denny Tamaki on Sunday. This brought an end to eight years of Tamaki’s leadership, characterised by vocal pacifism and active regional diplomacy with Chinese cities that historically maintained ties with Okinawa.
item.content:encoded:
The leadership change in Okinawa could deal a quiet blow to Beijing’s attempts to leverage local opposition to remilitarisation and the US-Japan military alliance, according to analysts.

They added that the shift would compel Chinese academics and state media to recalibrate their messaging and approach towards the strategically vital Japanese prefecture.

Genta Koja, the 42-year-old backed by Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party to become Okinawa’s new governor, defeated incumbent Denny Tamaki on Sunday. This brought an end to eight years of Tamaki’s leadership, characterised by vocal pacifism and active regional diplomacy with Chinese cities that historically maintained ties with Okinawa.

For Beijing, which has long cultivated relationships with Okinawan leaders who challenge Tokyo’s defence policies, Koja’s win represents the loss of a sympathetic subnational partner.

Analysts said the election result served as a reality check for China’s external messaging, requiring it to adjust its approach towards Okinawan voters who were prioritising bread-and-butter issues over opposition to American military bases.

Okinawa prefecture is made up of around 40 inhabited islands and has a population of 1.5 million. It hosts roughly 70 per cent of all US military facilities in Japan despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of the country’s land area.

The United States seized Okinawa from Japan after World War II. Washington returned administrative control of the islands to Tokyo in 1972, but it has maintained a substantial military presence that serves as a crucial node in checking Beijing’s regional ambitions.

Before Japan annexed it in 1879, Okinawa was known as the Ryukyu Kingdom, an independent maritime kingdom that paid tribute to China during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties.

In July 2023, Tamaki visited Beijing as part of a Japanese trade delegation and paid respects at the historic Ryukyu Kingdom cemetery in Beijing’s Tongzhou district.

Concerns have grown in Japan that Beijing may play the “Ryukyu card” – invoking the islands’ history to question Japanese sovereignty over Okinawa and counter Tokyo’s position on Taiwan.

Positioned within the “first island chain”, which stretches along the East Asian coastline from the Kuril Islands down to Borneo, Okinawa acts as a barrier limiting the People’s Liberation Army’s access to the Pacific Ocean. It is expected to play a vital strategic role in the event of a Taiwan conflict.

In addition to the American presence, Japan’s Self-Defence Forces have been expanding their deployments in Okinawa as part of Tokyo’s “southwest shift” – a defence strategy that bolsters the region with new missile systems, radar installations and troop deployments.

Tamaki firmly opposed the construction of new American military facilities on Okinawa Island and also opposed a plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station in southern Okinawa to the Henoko coastal area in the north. Koja supports this controversial plan but has also called on Tokyo to provide a clearer timeline on when the Futenma station will close.

For decades, local Okinawans have protested against the American military presence, with residents long complaining of noise pollution, security risks and recurring cases of sexual assault by US servicemen.

Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said that with Tamaki’s exit, China would lose an important interlocutor who could speak on behalf of the prefectural government to “publicly emphasise dialogue and oppose the expansion of US military bases”.

“Koja’s victory could weaken the leverage Beijing has long relied on to constrain Tokyo through Okinawa’s local politics,” he said.

Xu noted that Koja would be far more mindful of Tokyo’s foreign policy stance and would be likely to scale back reciprocal visits to China that carried obvious political symbolism.

He is also expected to draw stricter boundaries on local matters that concern Beijing, such as the Ryukyu narrative, Taiwan and Japan-US military base arrangements, according to Xu.

In recent years, Chinese state media have played up the historical ties between China and the ancient Ryukyu Kingdom while emphasising tensions between Okinawa residents and the US military.

Chinese academics and state media have even suggested challenging Tokyo’s control of Okinawa. While Beijing has not openly done so, state media have increasingly called for more research into historical and legal claims over the islands.

Xu said that following Tamaki’s defeat, it would be difficult for Chinese media and intellectuals to continue using the narrative that Okinawans generally opposed US-Japan security arrangements. Koja’s victory at least showed that a candidate who did not oppose the air station’s relocation could still win, he added.

“This shift can weaken the credibility and factual foundation of China’s previous narrative, which relied on invoking Okinawan public opinion to criticise Japan-US military activities.”

Xu suggested that Beijing should shift from emphasising the divergence between the prefectural government and Tokyo to focusing on the social consequences of the military build-up.

“China’s focus should be on how these arrangements increase the local burden, exacerbate regional tensions and pose threats to the lives and property of Okinawan residents,” he said.

Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, cautioned against overstating the impact of the election on China’s approach.

“China does not have a formal Okinawa policy in official diplomatic terms, and the change in Okinawa’s leadership may not constitute a shock to existing policy from Chinese cities that have civilian exchanges with Okinawa,” he said.

“During Tamaki’s tenure, he maintained relatively friendly communication channels with China at both the central and local levels. How Okinawa now adjusts and develops its relationship with China will certainly be a test for the incoming governor.”

Yet Koja’s victory signals a recalibration of Okinawan priorities that may still offer Beijing room for regional engagement.

Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News showed that only 21 per cent of voters prioritised issues related to US military bases, while nearly 50 per cent chose economic revitalisation when deciding who to vote for. Over half of the respondents said they supported the Futenma relocation.

During the campaign, Koja pledged to double Okinawa’s average income – which remains among the lowest of all prefectures – expand the local government budget for childcare and increase tourist spending on the island.

According to Xu, Koja’s success stemmed from tapping into Okinawa residents’ economic anxieties.

“This suggests that his administration will still need to preserve commercial ties with China and remain open to advancing tourism, business and cultural cooperation,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Will China’s new local surtax provide relief for its regions’ fiscal headaches?
item.description:
As even China’s wealthiest provinces continue to run deficits and rely on the central government to make ends meet, Beijing is loosening the reins on the country’s highly centralised fiscal system, with legislation for a new tax category – the local surtax – under way.

Late last month, the Ministry of Finance unveiled a draft local surtax law for public consultation. The proposed tax would merge three existing levies – the urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge and local education surcharge – and would be charged on value-added tax (VAT) and consumption tax payments. Provincial governments would be allowed to set rates within an 11 to 13 per cent range.

Analysts described the move as a modest but constructive step in China’s broader fiscal reform agenda. While far from a cure-all for local financial distress, the change would give local authorities much-needed flexibility to manage their spending, they said.
item.content:encoded:
As even China’s wealthiest provinces continue to run deficits and rely on the central government to make ends meet, Beijing is loosening the reins on the country’s highly centralised fiscal system, with legislation for a new tax category – the local surtax – under way.

Late last month, the Ministry of Finance unveiled a draft local surtax law for public consultation. The proposed tax would merge three existing levies – the urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge and local education surcharge – and would be charged on value-added tax (VAT) and consumption tax payments. Provincial governments would be allowed to set rates within an 11 to 13 per cent range.

Analysts described the move as a modest but constructive step in China’s broader fiscal reform agenda. While far from a cure-all for local financial distress, the change would give local authorities much-needed flexibility to manage their spending, they said.

“It appears that the top leadership has heard the calls [for fiscal reform] and is aware that many localities, including coastal regions, are becoming cash-strapped,” said a frontline official with a local finance department in Zhejiang. Although the eastern province is among China’s most financially self-sufficient, it still posted a fiscal deficit of 360.6 billion yuan (US$53.8 billion) in 2025.

During China’s property boom, local authorities were able to rake in huge sums from selling land, enabling them to balance their books even as they handed over most tax revenue to the central government.

But a prolonged slump in the housing market has effectively closed off that source of income, leaving local governments under mounting pressure as they fund an expanding range of public services for a rapidly ageing population – from public transport to healthcare – and work to meet heavy bond repayment obligations.

The proposed local surtax marks the first move towards rebalancing the skewed fiscal relationship between China’s central and local governments – a long-term reform mandate laid out by the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee at a plenum in July 2024.

“There is only one core reason the central government is pushing ahead with this reform this year – it’s time for fiscal rebalancing,” said Li Xin, a partner at Shenzhen-based DeHeng Law Offices. “Local authorities are under such acute fiscal strain that adjustments have become unavoidable.”

Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution

Finance official, Zhejiang

How does the new surtax work?

Representing a “major component of China’s fiscal and taxation reform”, the proposed local surtax is poised to become “the largest single tax category” in China’s local tax system and a pillar source of income for provincial authorities, according to Tian Zhiwei, director of the Institute of Public Policy and Governance at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics.

But it was not designed to boost fiscal revenue, analysts from Moody’s Ratings said in a report this month, adding that the proposed local surtax rate was broadly aligned with the combined effective burden of the three existing charges it would replace, and that overall fiscal revenue was likely to remain broadly unchanged.

Under the current system, the urban maintenance and construction tax is levied at 7 per cent, 5 per cent or 1 per cent of VAT and consumption tax payments, depending on the taxpayer’s location, while the education surcharge and local education surcharge are fixed at 3 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively.

In 2025, the effective combined rate nationwide stood at 11.6 per cent, according to Xinhua, compared with the 11 to 13 per cent range proposed under the new legislation.

The reform would change the institutional status of these revenue streams from three sources distributed across tax, non-tax and government fund accounts to a single tax that would be fully retained by local governments, the Moody’s analysts said, adding that this would improve revenue transparency and simplify fiscal administration.

A key proposed change concerns the two education-related surcharges: by raising their status from fees to taxes, the reform would give provincial governments greater flexibility in spending the proceeds.

Currently, the two surcharges are earmarked for education-related spending, including the purchase of teaching equipment and school building renovations. If enacted, the new law would allow local authorities to use the revenue at their discretion.

In 2025, combined proceeds from the two education-related surcharges reached 396.4 billion yuan, according to Xinhua. If enacted, the reform would allow local governments to redirect the revenue towards repaying maturing debt and meeting civil service payrolls, with civil servants facing pay cuts and delayed salary payments even in some of China’s wealthiest regions.

“Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution,” the Zhejiang official said, on condition of anonymity.

Meanwhile, experts said the reform would also streamline tax collection and cut compliance costs.

“On collection, three separate sets of rules will be consolidated into one … Taxpayers will only need to submit one tax return, lowering manpower-related costs for both businesses and tax authorities,” said Li, the Shenzhen lawyer.

With the two fees’ conversion into taxes, taxpayers who failed to pay or who underpaid their liabilities would face penalties, including overdue payment surcharges and fines, she added.

“This gives local tax authorities much stronger incentives to bolster tax collection,” Li said.

Relief for cash-strapped local governments?

In total, the three revenue sources generated 913.4 billion yuan last year, according to Xinhua. Although the proposed local surtax would be the largest tax source fully retained by local governments, its revenue would remain relatively modest.

Last year, domestic VAT revenue reached 6.9 trillion yuan (US$1.0 trillion), half of which is allocated to local governments under the current revenue-sharing arrangement.

Corporate income tax revenue totalled 4.1 trillion yuan, and personal income tax revenue amounted to 1.6 trillion yuan. The central government kept 60 per cent, leaving 40 per cent for local governments.

Consumption tax for the year brought in 1.7 trillion yuan. Imposed on certain categories of goods – such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel – the income generated goes entirely to the central government.

“The issue is that even with our income dropping, a big portion still needs to be turned over to the central government as state tax, leaving us with limited fiscal resources … The main complaint is that the state is taking too much,” said the Zhejiang finance official.

Daisy Xiao, director of Asia-Pacific international public finance ratings at Fitch Ratings, said the reform should modestly improve local revenue flexibility and spending discretion, but would be unlikely to materially ease structural pressure on local finances because debt growth had far outpaced the expansion of fiscal resources in recent years.

“The extra tax income would be small against persistent structural deficits, which are largely financed through special-purpose bonds linked to capital spending,” Xiao said.

“Even so, the measure is a constructive step in broadening more stable local revenue sources and giving local governments greater fiscal discretion,” she added.

More broadly, the move was consistent with China’s fiscal reform agenda and longer-term objective of reshaping local fiscal incentives away from property-related revenue and towards economic growth, consumption and sustainable tax bases, according to the Moody’s analysts.

“While incremental in nature, it represents a step in expanding provincial fiscal autonomy, supporting a more sustainable local revenue structure,” they added.

Rare autonomy for rate-setting

Under the proposal, provincial governments would be allowed to set the new rate within a range of 11 to 13 per cent, signalling greater flexibility.

“This is notable because most major tax rates in China are set by the central government, leaving local authorities with few levers to adjust revenue,” Xiao said.

Rate-setting discretion within an approved band would give provinces a limited additional countercyclical tool, allowing them to respond to changing revenue needs and local economic conditions, she added.

That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best

Tian Zhiwei, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

Tian, from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, said final tax rates would be the product of provincial governments’ “trade-offs”.

Authorities would need to strike a balance between retaining businesses and easing fiscal pressure: set the rate too high and they risk driving firms away; set it too low and they forgo revenue when public finances are already under strain, he said.

“That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best,” Tian added.

Wealthier provinces may choose lower rates to strengthen their competitiveness, while fiscally weaker regions could opt for higher rates to bolster revenue, according to Moody’s.

“As a result, fiscal management could become incrementally more province-specific, reflecting local economic conditions and policy priorities,” the analysts added.

But the reform could also bring unintended consequences for some localities. Under the current urban maintenance and construction tax rules, a 7 per cent rate applies in urban areas, 5 per cent in counties and designated towns, and 1 per cent elsewhere, including rural areas and oil-producing fields.

As the proposed legislation would replace that system with a single rate across an entire province, businesses in counties and rural areas could face a higher tax burden, according to Li, the lawyer.

“From a provincial perspective, the overall tax burden may see little change, yet for individual companies, it translates into real-world cost increases.”

Additional reporting by Frank Chen

item.title: [SCMP] ‘I just need an answer’: widow haunted by husband’s shooting seeks inquest
item.description:
Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held.

On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home.

Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors.
item.content:encoded:
Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held.

On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home.

Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors.

Little did Mrs Li, who preferred to be identified by her spouse’s surname, expect that the day would end in tragedy.

Police said an officer eventually shot the man at a distance of 1.5 metres (4.9 feet) after he allegedly ignored repeated warnings during a 30-second stand-off and attempted to attack them.

Now, all she wants is for a death inquest to be held as soon as possible to bring closure to herself and her husband, to whom she had been married for 10 years.

“I need no sympathy or pity. I just need an answer and hope to prevent this tragedy from happening again,” she said.

“It’s been two years, yet there is still no news. I’m anxious that this matter will just be left unsettled, and my husband’s death went unexplained.”

The then commissioner of police Raymond Siu Chak-yee defended the officer’s decision to shoot the man because he followed the guidelines on firearms use.

Siu said police would submit a death investigation report to the Coroner’s Court and “recommend the court hold a death inquest as soon as possible”.

But Li barely heard anything about it over the past two years.

In February last year, she received a letter from a coroner confirming that the cause of death was a gunshot wound to the chest.

In early April, she wrote to the court to inquire about a death inquest.

In response, the court said police had been instructed to produce a death investigation report, and a decision on whether to hold an inquest would be made after receiving the complete report.

Since then, she has called the Coroner’s Court general hotline every month to check on the progress, only to be told: “The investigation is still under way.”

On the other hand, she stopped contacting police after the contact person who treated her kindly retired.

Only an officer from the Complaints Against Police Office continued to check on her regularly, but declined to reveal details of their investigation.

“Every step has been very hard for me … I’m always afraid that something bad will happen to me and no one will be left to follow up on my husband’s case,” she said. “I hope everything can go faster.”

In the first few months after her husband’s death, she was unable to eat and sleep well, losing over 20 pounds (9kg) in just one month.

Now, she suffers from a failing memory, slowed reaction times and wakes up repeatedly throughout the night.

Whenever she has a moment to herself, the memory of her husband covered in blood and surrounded by police after being shot floods back into her mind.

“I deeply regret calling police. I made a call, and then he died … I will not forgive myself for the rest of my life,” she said.

“My intention was simply to have my husband taken to hospital, as we did before.”

She questioned why officers discharged a fatal shot to the chest rather than retreating down the stairwell or deploying non-lethal options such as pepper spray and shields.

In response to the South China Morning Post queries, police said they submitted the investigation report to the Coroner’s Court in June 2025.

The court requested further information, which was provided this month, and police were waiting for further instructions from the court.

As for the complaint filed with police, it is being handled in a “fair and impartial manner in accordance with established procedures”.

The judiciary declined to comment on individual cases.

It said the coroner would decide whether to hold an inquest after reviewing the report, and police might be directed to conduct further investigations if needed, with the deceased’s next of kin to be updated on the progress and decision on the inquest.

Under Practice Direction 39 on coronial procedures, which took effect in June last year, if an investigation is not completed within nine months of the date of the interim report, or if no decision whether to hold an inquest has been made, the court will, where appropriate, update the family every three months on the reasons for the delay – which did not happen in Mrs Li’s case.

The guidelines do not set a fixed deadline for supplying supplementary information once a report is submitted.

Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a community organiser at the Society for Community Organisation who helped Mrs Li, said he believed that the case would rely on expert assessment of firearms use and police protocols to evaluate whether the officer’s actions were justified.

“Without disclosing anything, families are left in this situation – with just one letter on hand and they have to reach out repeatedly in anxiety,” he said.

“Even after the report is submitted, it takes time for the pre-inquest [reviews] to be scheduled before the formal hearing; more waiting is anticipated.”

Delays of two to three years before a coroner’s inquest opens are not uncommon in Hong Kong, according to lawyer Jonathan Man Ho-ching.

Man said police handled death investigations alongside routine work without a dedicated unit, according to his understanding.

There are only three designated coroners in Hong Kong handling inquests while performing regular duties such as granting burial and autopsy orders, with their workload further compounded following major disasters such as the Wang Fuk Court fire that claimed 168 lives.

The primary recourse for families is to query the Coroner’s Court directly regarding the progress of their case.

“Just like any case, the longer a death inquest is delayed, the less ideal it is because witnesses might not be able to remember details, or might simply be unreachable any more, as seen during the Lamma ferry disaster inquests,” Man said.

“A wait is often inevitable … which is very hard on families because an inquest allows them to understand what happened to their loved ones, providing closure and helping them move on.”

Man said he believed Hong Kong could do better in strengthening communication with bereaved families during these prolonged periods.

“In some jurisdictions, death inquiries are not treated purely as a legal procedure; caseworkers are assigned to families to help them navigate the process,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Paul French lifts veil on final months of China’s last emperor in the Forbidden City
item.description:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.

In 2018, his City of Devils: A Shanghai Noir was a Kirkus Reviews’ “Best Book of the Year”. In 2024, Her Lotus Year: China, The Roaring Twenties and the Making of Wallis Simpson received much coverage and quotably upbeat reviews (“Her Lotus Year stays in the mind as a bright, shining, lively snapshot,” says The Spectator. “Delightful to read.”).

Now, it’s the turn of Puyi in The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City, which falls into a royalty subgenre that French calls “doomed monarchy”.

Although he’s writing – primarily – for a Western audience, as a category, it has promising global reach. Earlier this year, French was told by his Chinese publisher that only one other foreigner has shifted (and signed) more books in China: British author and historian Simon Sebag Montefiore, whose 2016 work on those quintessential doomed monarchs, The Romanovs: 1613-1918, was a massive hit.

Puyi, of course, didn’t meet his doom with an execution in a cellar. He was six years old in 1912, when the Manchu empire ended and the new Republican government decided to leave him behind the walls of the Forbidden City – an oddity, roaming around the “Great Within”, attended by eunuchs (“teapots without spouts” was the local term). With his peculiar upbringing and background, that child would grow into the adult who, during the second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945), would become his country’s “Great Traitor”.

French, who was a language student in 1980s Beijing and lived in Shanghai for many years before returning to Britain in 2014, had been marinating this story for a while. He sensed that – “a bit like Wallis Simpson”, the American socialite whose relationship with Britain’s King Edward VIII led to his abdication – people sort of knew about Puyi but not really. He’d been struck by the blank stares he met when he mentioned him to Chinese-language students at a couple of British universities.

French realised that it’s been almost four decades since he, along with many others, had been “blown away” by the Bernardo Bertolucci epic, The Last Emperor (1987), which was – an amazing achievement – filmed inside the Forbidden City.

While he was wondering how to tackle the topic, he wrote an article about Puyi’s wife, Wanrong, in 2024, for this magazine. “Wanrong is so beautiful and there are so many pictures of her and I thought it would be fun,” he says. “I did mention, in a couple of lines, that she’d had a tutor and this was one of the things the film had missed.”

In fact, Joan Chen – who played Wanrong in the film – makes a single reference to her tutor as a “Miss Windsor”. Bertolucci, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother-in-law, Mark Peploe, knew Wanrong was educated but not by whom, so they made up a name with British royal resonance. Wanrong’s tutor, however, was not British. Isabel Ingram was an American “mishkid” – a child of missionaries – born in Peking (Beijing) in 1902 and educated at Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, in the US.

After the PostMag piece came out, French was contacted by a man called Kenneth Mayer, who told him he was Ingram’s grandson. “He said, ‘Thank you so much for noticing Isabel; no one else does,’” French recalls. “And then he said, ‘By the way, you really should read her diary and she has some letters from this Johnston guy …’”

French was staggered. He hadn’t known about the diary, and the “Johnston guy” was Reginald Johnston, Puyi’s Scottish tutor, played in the film by Peter O’Toole.

Johnston had written a memoir which, in its 486 pages, makes a single reference to “the Empress’s American friend who had been her teacher of English both before and after the Empress entered the Forbidden City as a bride”; and his letters and journals had been destroyed after his death in Edinburgh, in 1938.

Diary! Letters! Such finds are history’s gold dust. Even better, Ingram, who died in Virginia in 1988, had typed up all of it. (French, who revels in his North London unacademic blokeishness, makes some cheerfully unrepeatable comments about the trials of handwritten research materials.) Once he’d read the Ingram documents, he knew he had his book. Ingram was 20 when she became Wanrong’s tutor, in October 1922. A few months later, on December 1, Wanrong, aged 16, married Puyi, also 16.

French decided to focus The Last Emperor of China on the 23 months between that five-day wedding – “the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see”, he writes – and the couple’s expulsion into the “Great Without” on November 5, 1924, which brought an end to more than 500 years of (occasionally interrupted) dynastic occupation of the Forbidden City.

Apart from sporadic chunks of necessary context, the book is like a wonderfully evocative play with four principal performers – a middle-aged Scottish man, a young American woman and two teenage Manchu royals – on a spectacular stage.

French says he’s only too aware that he joins a long line of Puyi biographers, but what Ingram brings to his version is the voice of modernity. Formal lessons with Wanrong, who had a golden fountain-pen and silver inkwell, rarely took up more than an hour or two. Afterwards, there would be hair-braiding, hat-selecting, wardrobe-rummaging, dancing to gramophone records, chocolates and cigarettes.

Ingram’s language – “I love her for life”; “cute little thing”; “the Empress is still darling”; “he nearly died on the spot” – could be that of a Californian blogger, and the film these scenes evoke isn’t the Bertolucci drama; it’s Clueless, in every sense. Her diary also testifies to Puyi and Wanrong’s genuine friendship as they go cycling and kite-flying and dog-walking around their vast, mouldering compound. Many happy photographs are taken.

For French, Ingram is an important witness to the growing intimacy between the newlyweds. As he says, a great debate among biographers concerns Puyi’s sexuality and whether he was asexual or homosexual. Famously, on his wedding night, the last emperor had sloped off to the Hall of Mental Cultivation for a think.

“He’s 16!” says French, and goes on to note that “the single most surprising thing [in the diary] is when Isabel writes about ‘the curtain being drawn’ and there are no lessons today … Obviously, like all young people, they work out what goes where”.

But Puyi and Wanrong’s isn’t the only unexpected romance in the book. It becomes clear through his letters that Johnston, 28 years older than Ingram, is attracted to her. French believes he was “heartbroken” when she refused him, which is why her name was never mentioned in his memoir. Perhaps. (On the other hand, this reader thinks it was more about Johnston’s considerable, publicity-hogging ego.)

At any rate, Johnston’s letters to Ingram veer in tone from housekeeper (“I am sorry to hear chewing gum has been introduced into the palace”) to stalker (“Who is the young man you kept looking at so earnestly all the time?”). Eventually, he becomes self-deludingly creepy. “Did you explain to the Lockharts how and why you refused to let me kiss you when we were on the Emperor’s swing together?” he writes. “And yet it would only have been a remote, innocuous fatherly salutation!”

By then, the quartet had broken up. On November 5, 1924, several hours after the early-morning palace coup, Ingram was taken by rickshaw to the Forbidden City as usual, but was barred from entering. At the Gate of Divine Prowess, the commandant told her that Wanrong had gone into the “Great Without” “hatless, coatless, baggage-less”. Ingram, who would leave China in 1927, never saw her dressing-up companion again.

In the Bertolucci film, when soldiers arrive to evict Puyi and Wanrong, they are playing tennis. In real life, he was peeling her an apple, that ancient symbol of expulsion, in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Soldiers took a – distinctly unhappy – photo, which is in the book, of his abandoned bedroom: an adolescent muddle of kung fu novels and toys.

“Once they go outside the gilded cage, they’re lost,” says French. “You could write another book about Puyi in Manchuria and try and get into the psychology of what happened to that relationship when he’s manipulated, with no advisers, and she knows that they’ve made a horrendous mistake and slips into opium abuse.”

In this immensely readable book, however, French steps only briefly beyond the palace gates and into that future when Puyi was crowned the emperor of Japan’s puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1934 – another doomed monarchy.

Another sombre note is the contrast between Ingram’s spirited diary and the fate suffered by Wanrong in the final summary, which is heart-wrenching.

Puyi survived and, in the 60s, made several return visits to the Forbidden City. Premier Zhou Enlai liked to keep an eye on him.

Asked what he thinks of Puyi now, French replies, “I do take the Zhou Enlai line. He’s supposed to have invited Puyi to a lunch and told him, ‘You weren’t to blame for becoming emperor and what happened then. But you can be blamed for what happened after.’”

item.title: [SCMP] Brics summit ends with Xi’s AI offer, Modi’s warning on critical minerals as weapons
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded his brief trip to India on Sunday with an offer to help Brics members develop open-source AI and smart manufacturing.

Summit host Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, warned against turning technology and critical minerals into economic weapons.

Experts said the exchange captured the wider picture of the Brics summit. Two days of diplomacy produced a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” pressure with a joint declaration, while heads of institutions Washington once dominated sat at a Global South table. Concerns over minerals and technology, however, exposed clear limits to that unity.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded his brief trip to India on Sunday with an offer to help Brics members develop open-source AI and smart manufacturing.

Summit host Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, warned against turning technology and critical minerals into economic weapons.

Experts said the exchange captured the wider picture of the Brics summit. Two days of diplomacy produced a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” pressure with a joint declaration, while heads of institutions Washington once dominated sat at a Global South table. Concerns over minerals and technology, however, exposed clear limits to that unity.

Speaking on the second day of the summit in New Delhi, Xi identified open-source AI and smart factories as two out of five key initiatives to promote economic growth and technological development in the Global South.

He also said Beijing would offer to train young talent from other member states in advanced technology and innovation, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The bloc has grown rapidly in recent years and is being increasingly seen as one of the strongest voices for the Global South, as the United States becomes increasingly assertive on the world stage.

Against this backdrop, the Chinese leader also issued a rallying call for unity and cooperation within the bloc to counter geopolitical hostilities and disruptive forces that he warned were shattering the stability of supply and industrial chains.

“A world without rules is like an intersection without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder would be inevitable,” he was quoted as saying by Xinhua.

Global rules should be written jointly and applied equally to all countries without double standards, Xi added. “The logic of might makes right should have been discarded long ago.”

Xi’s offer covered some of the key areas of the rivalry between the US and China, where control of resources and technology is vital.

Open-source models and smart factories require magnets, batteries, chips and processing equipment, and the supply chain of the minerals needed to make them run overwhelmingly through China.

But the US is the key gatekeeper when it comes to advanced chips and chipmaking equipment, and has imposed a series of export controls on the most advanced technology.

That leaves many Global South countries caught between two forms of dependence. While Chinese support could be vital to helping Global South countries develop, many are worried about over-reliance on either Beijing or Washington.

Modi, chairing Sunday’s session, marked that fear without naming either side.

“The weaponisation of technology and critical minerals can hinder our shared progress. Therefore, we have emphasised inclusivity in the adoption of technology,” he said.

India already has first-hand experience of how supply chains can be used to exert economic pressure. After the deadly 2020 border clash between Chinese and Indian troops, fertiliser clearances slowed and supplies of some equipment were held up.

In 2025, when China put rare earth magnets under a global export-licence system during its tariff war with the US, Indian automotive production lines felt the impact immediately.

Xi, who arrived in New Delhi early Saturday afternoon local time, skipped a gala dinner hosted by Modi for Brics leaders. Meanwhile, a social media video posted by Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday captured a relaxed exchange on the summit sidelines between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov and Araghchi himself.

At one point, as Lavrov was speaking, Wang reached over to look at the badge pinned to Araghchi’s collar.

Analysts said New Delhi’s aim at the summit was simple: preserve Brics unity without letting its internal tensions take centre stage.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said divisions within Brics were natural – given differences in geopolitics, political systems, levels of development and national interests – and had become more pronounced as the group expanded.

Those differences did not prevent cooperation, he argued, saying consensus and divergence shared a “symbiotic and dialectical relationship”.

But geopolitical trust remained a major weakness, Liu noted, particularly between China and India, something he described as “the biggest problem within Brics”.

While members had found broad common ground on development and economic issues at this year’s summit, disagreements over critical minerals reflected India’s efforts to raise issues with China that were difficult to resolve bilaterally, he said.

“India is trying to maintain ties with both sides,” Liu said, citing its cooperation with China and Russia through Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation while avoiding a break with the US and the West.

Liu said Brics cooperation could also give the Global South including China a greater say in shaping international rules in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) and space.

“Many of the current rules in these fields were shaped primarily by Western countries, with the Global South having limited influence over their formulation,” he said.

If Brics members and other Global South countries worked together to develop new rules, Western countries would have to take their views into account because they represented “huge markets” and “huge numbers of users”, he noted.

Despite US President Donald Trump’s threats of 100 per cent tariffs if Brics nations chose to “play games” with the dollar, the bloc pushed for local currency settlement and linked payment systems to keep trade moving if Washington were to use the dollar as a sanctions or tariff weapon.

However, member states remain divided over how and how much to move away from the US currency.

Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said differences were inevitable given the members’ varying relationships with Washington.

“Such differences are a natural existence under the current circumstances, and they can only reach consensus through long-term interaction and mutual adjustment,” he said.

Lin said the unanimous adoption of the joint declaration also reflected the impact of US policies.

“The measures of the US government are certainly a very important external stimulus,” he said, citing tariffs, sanctions and the “America first” policy, which he said had “damaged the external environment for development across much of the Global South”.

He said Brics had a role to play in emerging areas where the US and other Western countries were “reorganising” their approach, but its ability to shape new global rules remained limited by “the diversity of interests among member states” and their differences.

item.title: [SCMP] Brics members find common ground on AI, trade and alternative payment expansion
item.description:
Brics members agreed in New Delhi on Saturday to continue the push to expand trade and payments in local currencies to counter US pressure.

The member nations also found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits.

In addition, Chinese President Xi Jinping used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
Brics members agreed in New Delhi on Saturday to continue the push to expand trade and payments in local currencies to counter US pressure.

The member nations also found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits.

In addition, Chinese President Xi Jinping used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Xi proposed an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on industry and supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The call came as the bloc was celebrating its 20th anniversary, having grown from a small economic framework into what Xi calls “the most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in today’s world”.

At the same time, the gathering is being held against a backdrop of regional and global turmoil, from the war in Ukraine and the Middle East conflict to protectionism and tariff tensions. And its unity is being tested by divisions such as Iran’s repeated attacks on fellow members, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.

Xi’s attendance at the summit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic activities preceding his trip to the United States, efforts that are expected to give him the upper hand in his meeting with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.

Brics, a bloc of developing nations, has increasingly been viewed as a counterweight to Western-led institutions and a platform for building an alternative international order.

Part of that push includes cross-border payments. The group’s Payment Task Force had studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and would keep working on payments that were “fast, low cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe”.

But the leaders were also clear about just how far they were prepared to go as the declaration said there was “no one-size-fits-all approach” and that national priorities must be respected.

As well as the host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, other high-profile attendees include Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian.

For China, Brics is also seen as a platform to advance Beijing’s vision of a multipolar world and cement its standing as a leader of the Global South.

In that vein, Xi said Beijing was willing to work with Brics countries to play a “due role” in bringing peace to the Middle East, calling on the group of emerging economies to oppose bloc confrontation and the “infringement upon the sovereignty of other countries and interference in their affairs”.

His call for AI cooperation also highlights Beijing’s efforts to advance its own framework, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), widely seen as its answer to Washington’s Pax Silica Initiative.

The two countries are vying for AI dominance and Pax Silica is Washington’s approach to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains among allied nations.

Xi invited all Brics countries to join Waico to shape global AI governance and development.

“China stands ready to work with all parties to jointly produce more research and development and application outcomes, and to deepen cooperation across industrial and supply chains,” he said.

“Facts will prove that ‘decoupling and severing supply chains’ cannot hinder our development process, and ‘small yards with high fences’ will only confine oneself and fragment the world,” Xi said, in a veiled swipe at the US.

“We must firmly … strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, encourage open source and collaborative sharing and push practical cooperation to new heights.”

Xi said the Global South was growing stronger and urged Brics countries to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and lead the international order towards a more just and equitable direction, away from unilateralism and power politics.

Member nations unanimously adopted the 45-page “New Delhi Declaration 2026” on the opening day of the summit, with Modi saying that no member had objected to the text.

In a thinly veiled challenge to Washington’s stance, Xi urged the Brics members to criticise protectionism and unilateralism, calling on emerging economies to defend international institutions such as the United Nations and the World Trade Organization against tariff threats, treaty withdrawals, and efforts to carve out exclusive global trade alliances.

“We must oppose withdrawing from organisations, breaking treaties, and starting anew by setting up separate mechanisms,” Xi said.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Xi’s call for Brics to become “a vanguard for peace and stability” was especially relevant, given India’s efforts, as the group’s chair, to avoid being drawn into geopolitical conflicts.

Xi urged Brics countries to pursue “common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security”, reject cold war thinking and bloc confrontation, and oppose violations of sovereignty and interference in internal affairs.

He also called for constructive efforts to resolve regional hotspots, saying China was ready to work with Brics partners to “contribute to peace and stability in the Middle East and Gulf region”.

Liu said the political and security dimension, part of the three pillars of Brics cooperation, had become increasingly important as global tensions intensified.

“In today’s turbulent global environment, the political and security pillar is especially critical. As Xi emphasised, Brics should play a constructive role in mediating and easing regional tensions to advance global and regional peace.”

Modi, who chaired the opening session, said the voice of developing economies could not remain “a courtesy” and that emerging countries had to write the rules of global governance.

Brics, he said, was “not against anyone” but instead was for everyone.

“The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid,” he added.

“Power and decision-making sit at the top. Those who live with the consequences sit at the bottom, they are affected by every decision, excluded from every one of them.”

China will assume the organisation’s rotating chair next year.

In a sit-down after the summit, Xi told Modi that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.

The grouping first took shape in 2006 when Brazil, Russia, India and China began informal talks before it was officially established in 2009. South Africa joined in 2010, turning the bloc from Bric to Brics.

The grouping has undergone two expansions since, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025. Brics now covers nearly half the global population and about a third of the world’s GDP.

Over the years, the bloc has evolved into a political platform for intergovernmental cooperation in areas ranging from finance and trade to culture and justice.

It has also become increasingly vocal about overhauling global systems, including proposing alternatives to US dollar-based payment systems, a suggestion that prompted warnings from Trump.

But its expansion has also brought fresh challenges to the bloc, with analysts suggesting that there are now more competing voices which have slowed its progress and made it harder to reach a consensus on issues.

Additional reporting by Orange Wang, Nayan Seth, Alyssa Chen, Shi Jiangtao and Victoria Bela

item.title: [SCMP] How one company’s choice – resignation or the factory – left China’s young workers floored
item.description:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.

Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.

The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.
item.content:encoded:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.

Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.

The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.

They could either resign “voluntarily” and receive half a month’s salary, or stay and be reassigned from office-based technical roles to factory-floor work, including tightening screws.

According to the firm, 107 chose the former option. But the uproar that ensued has placed the company firmly in the centre of a media firestorm, with Communist Party news organ People’s Daily calling the move “a blatant trampling of social trust” in a commentary late last month.

The extensive public attention the incident aroused stood as a tangible reflection of corporate workforce contraction, youth employment pressure and growing incidents of labour disputes, phenomena occurring within a broader slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy, analysts said.

While neither the firm nor local authorities specified any violation of labour law by the short-term manoeuvre, which coincided with its application for a listing in Hong Kong, its adverse effects were evident, the analysts warned.

“The company’s planned Hong Kong listing is very likely to be blocked, because the negative impact is simply too damaging,” said Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing.

As for the employment of fresh graduates – an increasingly sensitive issue for Beijing amid a tough job market – “the fact that this incident has escalated to such a degree is also highly unfavourable. Big companies will become very cautious in their future hiring”, he said.

According to its statement, Xingyu had recruited more than 400 college graduates through campus hiring last autumn and this spring, while 372 formally joined the company in July.

About one month into their employment, the company’s human resources department conducted one-on-one meetings with each of them, presenting the binary choice. The decision resulted from a workforce optimisation plan “based on the company’s order pipeline and staffing needs”, it said.

The move sparked backlash from many former employees, who complained to domestic media that after being dismissed, they lost their status as fresh graduates and could only re-enter the job market as social hires with a termination record on their résumés.

Within China’s institutional framework, losing this status stripped them of many competitive job-seeking advantages.

The company and the municipal human resources bureau of Changzhou, where Xingyu is based, have so far arranged for 71 of those dismissed to join new employers, while an additional 22 passed interviews and received offer letters.

The remainder were either undertaking interviews or planning to pursue postgraduate studies, Xingyu said last week.

Previously, both the firm and the bureau responded with apologies and explanations over the incident but failed to quell widespread public scepticism.

On August 25, the bureau confirmed the controversial lay-off – after media reports went viral – noting that the negotiation process was “overly rigid and simplistic, lacking full and effective communication”.

Two days later, the firm issued a public apology, acknowledging “managerial errors in decision-making” and offering a package of remedies including three months’ worth of job-seeking living allowances, free dormitory accommodation and an additional six months’ salary compensation for those who remained unemployed.

At its half-year performance briefing on September 2, the company’s chairwoman and general manager, Zhou Xiaoping, apologised and said the company was “properly implementing remedial measures” under government guidance.

According to its earnings results, Xingyu posted revenue of 6.88 billion yuan (US$1 billion) in the first half of the year, up 1.87 per cent, year on year, with a profit of about 712 million yuan, down 7.78 per cent, year on year.

Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard

Nie Riming, Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law

Its 2025 sales figures showed that it held an 11.6 per cent share of China’s automotive lighting market, ranking first in the country, and accounted for 4.6 per cent of the global market share, ranking seventh.

Nie Riming, a researcher at the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law, said the broader lacklustre job market was primarily why this incident generated such a huge response.

“Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard,” he said.

Another record-breaking army of university graduates – an estimated 12.7 million students – entered China’s job market this summer, up about 4 per cent from last year, according to official data. The youth jobless rate – covering those aged 16 to 24, excluding students – climbed to 17.9 per cent in July from 14.9 per cent in the previous month.

Nie noted that Xingyu’s immediate cash compensation alone could compare favourably with statutory minimums in Germany, where labour protections are generally stronger.

While China has relatively high-standard labour laws on paper, enforcement and compliance are uneven, especially among smaller firms, he said. Against this backdrop, listed companies like Xingyu – along with foreign-invested firms and state-owned enterprises – remain the primary sources of higher-quality jobs in China.

However, these relatively “well-behaved” companies had been steadily reducing their headcount in recent years, and after this incident, such formal, regulated positions were likely to become even more scarce, he added.

“For companies going forward, they will become increasingly cautious when hiring for compliant, formal positions,” he said.

“They will lean more towards non-standard employment arrangements – such as outsourcing and dispatching – to offload their staffing responsibilities. That, in turn, would further reduce formal direct hiring and reinforce labour-market dualisation.”

The most contentious issue remains fresh graduate status, as many recruitment policies, including those for civil service admissions, favour fresh graduates, he said.

“The way graduates are regulated has yet to align with the job market, and this disconnect must be resolved before it causes further frustration,” he urged.

As the economic slowdown persists in China, lay-offs have become a recurring theme in the workplace, and labour disputes are on the rise.

Labour dispute mediation and arbitration bodies at all levels handled 4.54 million cases nationwide in 2025 – a 7 per cent increase from 2024, following a 10 per cent rise over 2023, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security’s annual statistical bulletin.

Meanwhile, Xingyu’s lay-off controversy emerged after it refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July, sparking market speculation that it was a short-term tactic to pad the company’s research workforce and make it look stronger for its listing ambitions.

Among the dismissed employees, about two-thirds held bachelor’s degrees, while the remainder held master’s degrees. The majority were assigned to research and development roles, as well as manufacturing and production positions, while a smaller number were allocated functional support roles, according to last week’s statement.

However, legal experts and academics considered it unlikely that this was the company’s primary intention, given that such a move would offer limited substantive gain while exposing it to significant compliance and reputational risks.

Such risks may soon materialise, such as hindering its listing progress, said Zhao Zhanling, a commercial lawyer from Beijing-based Javy Law Firm.

“The stock exchange and its advisers are likely to demand clarifications on the mass lay-offs, labour law compliance and internal control mechanisms,” he said. “Adverse media coverage may also invite regulatory questions, causing delays – though not necessarily scuttling the IPO altogether.”

The Shanghai Stock Exchange website showed that it issued a regulatory work letter to Xingyu on Wednesday, specifying regulatory requirements regarding the company’s “relevant matters”, without providing further details.

The saga could also lead to a loss of business opportunities, according to Tang, the Beijing researcher.

“It is possible that its international clients would respond positively to public outcry,” he said, “but that does not mean they would punish Xingyu – they may downgrade its supplier tier ... or impose more stringent supply conditions.”

Volkswagen China said earlier this month that it had initiated an investigation into the matter following intense media coverage.

item.title: [SCMP] Politics aside, young Vietnamese are warming to China
item.description:
Vietnam is often held up as proof of China’s underwhelming soft power in Southeast Asia: a millennium of resistance against Chinese domination, a border war within living memory, unresolved maritime disputes and elite surveys that consistently show Vietnamese respondents’ deep distrust of Beijing.

Yet beneath these strategic tensions, a quieter shift is under way. Young Vietnamese are warming to Chinese culture, language, lifestyles and economic opportunity. From crowds queuing for Labubu toys to a scramble for Chinese-language jobs, and from Chinese content going viral on social media to record numbers of Vietnamese students choosing to study at Chinese universities, China is being woven even more tightly into the everyday lives of young Vietnamese.

Four converging forces underpin this shift: cultural attraction, new-media connectivity, facilitation by both governments and economic incentives.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam is often held up as proof of China’s underwhelming soft power in Southeast Asia: a millennium of resistance against Chinese domination, a border war within living memory, unresolved maritime disputes and elite surveys that consistently show Vietnamese respondents’ deep distrust of Beijing.

Yet beneath these strategic tensions, a quieter shift is under way. Young Vietnamese are warming to Chinese culture, language, lifestyles and economic opportunity. From crowds queuing for Labubu toys to a scramble for Chinese-language jobs, and from Chinese content going viral on social media to record numbers of Vietnamese students choosing to study at Chinese universities, China is being woven even more tightly into the everyday lives of young Vietnamese.

Four converging forces underpin this shift: cultural attraction, new-media connectivity, facilitation by both governments and economic incentives.

China’s cultural appeal rests on a mix of cultural familiarity and contemporary trendiness. Chinese dramas have long been a fixture of Vietnamese television and Vietnam is now among Asia’s largest markets for them, their reach amplified by digital distribution. Content from major Chinese streaming platforms such as iQiyi, Tencent Video and Youku is carried on Vietnamese platforms such as VieOn and FPT Play, delivering China’s entertainment industry directly into Vietnamese homes and onto Vietnamese smartphones.

Meanwhile, some Vietnamese celebrities have found wider fame on Chinese reality shows, while hit Chinese formats have been adapted for Vietnamese audiences.

China’s appeal has also spilled into Vietnam’s shopping and lifestyle. Many Chinese brands have won over young Vietnamese with trendy designs and affordable prices. Mixue, the Chinese ice cream and tea chain, had expanded to more than 1,300 Vietnamese outlets by late 2024, making Vietnam its second-largest overseas market. Chagee, Cotti Coffee, KKV and Pop Mart have followed suit, turning shopping centres in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City into showcases of “Made in China” cool.

Algorithmic ambassadors

None of this cultural traction would travel as far, or as fast, without new media. TikTok counts more than 70 million monthly active users in Vietnam, out of 460 million across Southeast Asia, and sits within a broader Chinese digital ecosystem that channels content on Chinese culture and daily life to regional audiences. Vietnamese-language content on TikTok and Facebook – including from Vietnamese influencers living in or travelling through China – offers viewers a window onto Chinese cities, landscapes and the rhythms of life and work in the country.

This bottom-up, peer-driven pull is unfolding alongside a renewed official push for closer people-to-people ties. Since the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations and the designation of 2025 as the “Year of Vietnam-China Humanistic Exchange”, officials on both sides have promoted youth engagement. The joint statement during President Xi Jinping’s state visit in April 2025 invited Vietnamese youth to join “Red Study Tours”. More than 1,000 have done so, visiting sites commemorating the two countries’ shared revolutionary history – among them the former base of the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in Guangzhou – alongside hi-tech hubs that showcase China’s modern development and technological achievements.

Two-way travel has expanded too, supported by growing rail and air links. Since August, Vietnamese citizens have been able to transit China visa-free for up to 10 days, and the Vietnam–China Tourism Cooperation Years 2026–2027 initiative aims to further strengthen people-to-people ties. The numbers are impressive: Chinese visitor arrivals to Vietnam surged 41.3 per cent to 5.3 million in 2025, making China Vietnam’s largest source of tourists, while Vietnam had become China’s fourth-largest source market by mid-2026.
