Education diplomacy tells a similar story: the number of Vietnamese students in China has more than doubled, from 11,300 in 2018 to about 25,000 today – still trailing the numbers in South Korea (43,300), Japan (36,300), Australia (33,000) and the United States (31,300), but expected to climb further as Beijing promises at least 1,000 government scholarships and 1,000 Chinese-language teachers to Vietnam.

Mandarin pays

Underpinning all this is economic pragmatism. Vietnamese attraction to China rests not only on what China represents, but also on what engaging with it offers. As Chinese investment has poured into Vietnam, Mandarin has become a sought-after skill for young Vietnamese. Vietnamese recruitment platform Joboko reported roughly 13,000 openings for Chinese-speaking professionals in 2025, up 50 per cent on the year before, with fluency commanding better pay in industrial estates and Chinese-invested companies. LinkedIn, TopCV and VietnamWorks each list thousands of Chinese-language roles in Vietnam, with monthly salaries ranging from US$500 to US$2,000 – attractive pay by Vietnamese standards.

Demand is such that Vietnam recorded the world’s highest number of registrations for the HSK Chinese-proficiency test in the first quarter of 2025. At some Vietnamese universities, Chinese-language programmes now post higher admission scores than English ones, reflecting surging youth interest. English remains the default foreign language taught from primary school and is moving towards compulsory status by 2030, while Chinese is increasingly picked up later for its practical economic value. But anecdotal evidence points to growing parental demand for early Chinese learning and Vietnam has said it will pilot Chinese, Japanese and Korean lessons for preschoolers to prepare for future workforce competitiveness.

Young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities

All this unfolds as Hanoi emphasises the more productive dimensions of its relationship with Beijing, while keeping long-standing South China Sea tensions in the background. This favourable climate may have helped, but young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities. The 2025 boycott of Chagee after its app and website displayed China’s disputed “nine-dash line” and the removal of some Chinese dramas displaying the same map show how quickly those sensitivities can resurface. Yet such episodes have merely interrupted rather than reversed the broader trend. Chagee is back in Vietnam, just as bilateral ties have recovered from the turbulence of the 2010s, when the maritime dispute overshadowed the relationship.

Whether this societal warming can cushion or withstand the next downturn in relations remains to be seen. Vietnam’s history suggests that affinity with China and resistance to its power have never been mutually exclusive. A younger generation is now living that old paradox on new terms: drawn more directly and intimately into China’s orbit of culture and opportunity, while retaining the instinct to push back when national interests collide.

Hoang Thi Ha is a Senior Fellow and Co-coordinator of the Regional Strategic and Political Studies Programme, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Pham Thi Phuong Thao is a Senior Research Officer at the Asean Studies Centre, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
item.description:
For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent.

That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad.

Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.
item.content:encoded:
For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent.

That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad.

Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.

On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir.

The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement.

It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland.

A role reversal

India has long cast Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker, accusing it of harbouring militants and flouting international norms. But last month’s ruling flips that script, observers say.

“This is particularly attractive to Pakistan, as it turns a long-standing Indian tactic upside-down,” said Daniel Markey, a senior fellow with the Stimson Centre think tank’s South Asia programme, adding that the tribunal’s decision gave Pakistan “a diplomatic opportunity to exploit”.

“Even if Pakistan is only partially successful, it will relish the chance to muddy the waters and claim some high ground,” he said, describing the ruling as another front in a rivalry now “playing out in different forums, including this tribunal”.

Within hours of the ruling being issued, Delhi had rejected it outright, insisting that its decision to hold the treaty “in abeyance” would stand.

Islamabad’s reaction was equally swift and considerably more triumphant, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar declaring on social media that the ruling “vindicates Pakistan’s consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside”.

Delhi disputes the court’s right to rule at all, however, calling it “illegally constituted” because the Indus treaty specifically requires both parties to agree on how an arbitration panel is formed.

“India is challenging the authority of the mechanism,” said Uttam Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in Delhi.

Describing the stand-off as a contest over “sovereignty vs consent”, Sinha said India’s ambition was not to “turn off Pakistan’s water” completely but to finally exploit its own treaty rights on hydropower, storage, irrigation and the like.

“For decades, India had treaty rights and provisions on paper but had not developed the infrastructure necessary to harness them fully,” he said.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and senior fellow at King’s College London’s Department of War Studies, said Delhi was trying to “hide behind a technicality”, having previously turned to the very same court when it suited its own interests – notably in the case of Kulbhushan Jadhav, an Indian national sentenced to death by a Pakistani military court on espionage charges in 2017.

How can India now say that it will not comply? Politically, this will be very embarrassing

Ayesha Siddiqa, political scientist

“How can India now say that it will not comply?” Siddiqa asked. “Politically, this will be very embarrassing, though like the United States, it can refuse to honour the judgment.”

India’s actions are certainly not without precedent on the world stage.

Sriparna Pathak, an associate professor of international relations at O.P. Jindal Global University in India, points to the US’ 2019 exit from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty after Russia deployed a banned cruise missile system as one of several precedents for unilateral treaty suspension.

“States routinely invoke countermeasures … when they judge the other party’s conduct has destroyed the treaty’s object and purpose,” she said, citing a legal principle under which a fundamental shift in circumstances can void an agreement.

But Pathak is clear-eyed about what is really at stake. India has tied the treaty’s suspension to a demand that Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” end its support for cross-border militancy – a condition that is political rather than legal.

“That is a political precondition, not a technical one,” she said. “Compliance with The Hague order would undercut that position.”

It is a dilemma India has long tried to avoid by keeping bilateral disputes, especially over Kashmir, out of international forums altogether – wary that outside mediation legitimises exactly the kind of “internationalisation” Delhi has spent decades resisting.

Weaponised water

Behind the legal arguments lies the reality that water has become a lever for coercion.

In June, India’s minister of water resources, C. R. Patil, vowed that “not a single drop” would flow to Pakistan – prompting Islamabad to accuse Delhi of “weaponising” a shared resource and to warn, as it had in April, that any attempt to block or divert rivers would be treated as an “act of war”.

For now, at least, the threat is mostly rhetorical. India’s existing infrastructure cannot yet shut off Pakistan’s water supply, according to Markey, nor can it “single-handedly cause flooding”.

But as Delhi expands its hydroelectric and water storage capacity, its leverage will grow – and so will the inherent risks.

Bigger Indian dams and barrages would create “a more likely target for Pakistani military attacks in the event of future India-Pakistan hostilities”, Markey said.

“A return to the negotiating table looks unrealistic at the moment, but it will be the wiser course of action over time,” he added. “Neither side will readily benefit from pulling water to the centre of their bilateral dispute.”

Sinha, meanwhile, resisted the idea of a looming “water war”, preferring instead to describe what was happening as the “strategic securitisation of water” – a contest fought not with weapons but with infrastructure, data, timing and design.

That contest is now unfolding across the Indus River system, a vast basin of Himalayan tributaries spanning China, India and Pakistan upon which hundreds of millions of lives depend – and the latest flashpoint in a deep-rooted, acrimonious rivalry.

item.title: [SCMP] Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze
item.description:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.
item.content:encoded:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.

Repeated, prolonged exposure to haze wreaks havoc in the human body, triggering inflammation, asthma attacks and other respiratory problems.

“That is already a signal that their body is not simply being irritated,” Asma said. “It is having a clinically significant response to the exposure.”

Left unchecked, that exposure can scar lungs, cause cardiovascular illness and lead to cancer, as PM2.5 particles small enough to cross into the bloodstream spread the damage far and wide.

In Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index (API) Malaysia uses climbed as high as 519 this week, surpassing a level so hazardous it triggered a state of emergency in the Bornean state’s Serian district that was lifted only once the air was clear enough to breathe.

Singapore, which had gone three years without air quality breaching unhealthy levels, restarted daily haze alerts and in the Philippine capital, more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) from the wildfires, schools were forced to shut their doors.

Climate experts warn of a meteorological double-whammy conspiring to make this the hottest year on record for Southeast Asia. “Super El Nino” – a massive warming of the Pacific Ocean that chokes off regional rainfall – is being stacked on top of a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which cools regional waters, further cutting off moisture.

Together, they act as a force multiplier, fuelling droughts, heatwaves and wildfires from Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra to the Mekong nations of Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

Extreme weather is only part of the story, however. The fuel for the fires is the land cleared, year after year, for palm oil, pulpwood, corn and sugar cane, on plantations that drain water from the region’s peatlands until they become as dry as tinder.

It’s agribusiness vs the atmosphere, observers say – and for now, agribusiness is winning, despite decades of Asean pledges, a real-time satellite-powered fire-detection system and US$1.5 billion in funding to tackle the crisis that has yet to be raised.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, facing an electorate once again struggling to breathe, called on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to take action. “Asean ministers must seriously look at it”, he told reporters, “because it is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies”.

The crisis is also decimating some of the world’s greatest stores of biodiversity. Pitiful photographs from Kalimantan of rescued pangolins curled into defensive balls and orangutans with their fur singed orange-black have refocused the world’s attention on the issue.

But climate advisers warn against a convenient narrative taking hold: that this is simply the fault of this year’s “super El Nino”, rather than the businesses making billions from the burning.

“El Nino and dry conditions are risk multipliers, not the root cause,” said Renard Siew, a climate change specialist at the Centre for Governance and Political Studies in Kuala Lumpur.

“We cannot govern El Nino away,” he added. “But we can manage land better, prevent fires, enforce regulations and reduce the underlying vulnerability. Climate change is effectively making the consequences of weak governance more severe.”

History repeats

By far Southeast Asia’s worst haze offender is its most populous nation and largest economy.

Indonesia’s peatland fires began alarmingly early this year, with hotspots detected way back in January – months before the typical dry season burn.

More than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) have burned so far and police have named 138 arson suspects, including eight companies implicated in forest and land clearance.

But arrests are of little comfort to the families forced to live under a cloud of toxic haze.

Lina Rose, a mother of four in Sarawak, has had to keep her children indoors for most of the recent school holidays.

“I’m worried about my child who has asthma,’’ she said. “The sky looks so gloomy that you think it’s going to rain, but then it doesn’t.”

Residents hark back to 2015, when Indonesia’s worst haze crisis in decades – fuelled by the same slash-and-burn clearance for palm oil and pulpwood – released thousands upon thousands of tonnes of carbon into the atmosphere and blanketed tens of millions of people, from Sumatra to Singapore, in choking smog for months on end.

Jakarta, faced with international fury, labelled that year’s crisis a “crime against humanity of extraordinary proportions” and belatedly signed on to an Asean road map promising haze-fire skies by 2020.

But that deadline came and went – and still the haze continued. A second road map followed in 2023, with a new target year of 2030. Yet few believe this new framework will be any more effective than the first.

The reason comes down to Asean’s modus operandi: consensus and non-interference are not conducive to policing environmental crime across borders, analysts say.

Meanwhile, the palm oil, pulp and paper conglomerates whose business models depend on cheap land clearance have every incentive to keep enforcement weak.

“The fundamental shift has to be from ‘managing haze’ to preventing the conditions that create it,” Siew said. “That means stronger land-use governance, better fire prevention and peatland management, clearer accountability across supply chains and much greater investment in local capacity.”

To its credit, the newer haze-control road map does “contain something its predecessor lacked”, according to Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a legal expert and researcher at Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies – namely, measurable indicators, “including zero days at the highest alert level for two consecutive years”, as well as pledges to reduce burned area by 10 per cent and hotspots by 5 per cent, with a midterm review due in 2028.

But the mechanisms for holding anyone accountable remain weak.

“The consensus principle and the related ‘Asean Way’ approach have led to the creation of mechanisms that are ambitious but have been described as toothless,” said Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of political ecology at the University of Malaya. “This is because the mechanisms often lack strong operationalisation or punitive measures.”

Sanctions would not work, Fahrizal said, as Asean members would never agree to impose them on one another, adding that the latest road map “is not a binding instrument” with reporting done by member states themselves.

Asean’s consensus-based approach has allowed Jakarta to commit to haze-free targets with no penalty attached to missing them. After 2015, it did impose a moratorium on peatland clearance and created an agency to restore affected areas, eventually rehabilitating some 1.6 million hectares (6,177 square miles).

But Indonesia also produces more than half the world’s palm oil and its industry has found ways to adapt, securing permits for “sustainable” farming on the one hand while surreptitiously clearing protected areas on the other. The peatland restoration agency, for all the good it did, was dissolved last year.

Fahriza said the most “realistic” option for enforcing anti-haze measures was to employ independent, third-party verification of data that could be reviewed collectively to impose “consequences for reputation and access to financing”.

Absent that, Asean’s credibility – and relevance – would “ultimately be judged by the citizens breathing the smoke, not by the number of documents signed”, he said.

Patchwork fixes

Advocacy groups are done waiting for another of the bloc’s road maps to fail.

On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights called for the region’s latest haze crisis to be treated as a “human rights emergency”, urging Asean member states to use an October summit in Vietnam to close enforcement gaps and hold corporate offenders to account by forcing companies to publish fire and land-use information for independent scrutiny.

Some smaller-scale bilateral cooperation has also emerged. Thailand and Laos signed a data- and resource-sharing agreement on Wednesday aimed at pre-empting wildfires before they spread, echoing a similar arrangement Bangkok struck with Myanmar last month.

External pressure is building too, with mixed results. The European Union’s threatened ban on palm oil linked to deforestation has been delayed to 2027, after Indonesian objections and Brussel’s own need to lock in a new trade deal amid rising US tariffs.

Then there are the built-in weaknesses in Asean’s own crisis-response tools: under the bloc’s latest haze agreement, accepting emergency firefighting help from abroad remains entirely voluntary.

“At the moment, the arrangement exists, but ultimately it cannot function without the explicit invitation of the host country,” Varkkey said.

“This should be a scientific decision, when the haze is bad enough to warrant external help, not a political one.”

Singapore perhaps best captures the tension between profit and public safety: its companies are heavy investors in Kalimantan’s palm oil sector, yet its people – the region’s wealthiest – no longer tolerate haze imported from beyond their borders.

The city state’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 lets it prosecute companies for haze pollution regardless of where the fire was lit, a legal reach that was tested after the 2015 pollution crisis when six companies, including Indonesia’s Asia Pulp & Paper Group, were investigated – a move Jakarta called an affront to its sovereignty.

As of 2021, four of the cases remained open, Singapore’s environment minister told parliament. There has been no public confirmation of their closure in the years since.

Meanwhile, Singapore still wheezes whenever Borneo burns.

Wildlife photographer Eddie Vanderloot, 47, has learned to recognise a tight chest and itchy eyes as unmistakable signs that the air has turned.

“Constantly planning activities around the air quality gets tiring and it’s hard not to feel worn down by it,” he said.

“Even with all the windows closed, a mask on, an air purifier and air conditioners switched on, the haze still affects me for hours.”

item.title: [SCMP] No pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks
item.description:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.
item.content:encoded:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.

This is the scene in Yimin – one of the five largest open-cast coal mines in China – which launched the world’s first large-scale fleet of cabless, electric autonomous mining trucks in May last year.

More than a year on, the performance of the 100-vehicle fleet offers a chance to assess how the technology has fared beyond the pilot stage – and whether it can be scaled up further to help upgrade China’s traditional energy sector.

“The autonomous electric trucks have helped us cut operating costs, improve safety and increase efficiency,” said Zhao Yaozhong, deputy manager for technology at the mine.

Beyond easing recruitment difficulties caused by harsh working conditions, the deployment has – more importantly – improved safety by reducing the scope for human error, analysts and industry insiders said. This consideration takes on particular importance amid renewed scrutiny of mine safety following a spate of recent accidents.

The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment

Zhao Yaozhong, deputy mine manager for technology at Yimin

Custom-built by heavy machinery maker Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group to withstand extreme cold, the self-driving trucks operate over a 5G network and Huawei Technologies’ cloud-based AI dispatching system, allowing them to navigate the mine and optimise routes in real time, according to the companies.

Automated swapping stations replace depleted batteries in about six minutes, while a dedicated solar microgrid supplies electricity, allowing the fleet to achieve zero-carbon status and run constantly.

“The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment,” Zhao said.

He noted that many mining accidents over the years had been linked to human factors, such as emotions or failures to follow operating procedures. Zhao contrasted this with the autonomous trucks, which he said executed commands precisely once given instructions to haul coal or overburden – the layer of rock and dirt covering a mineral deposit.

Coal mine safety has fallen back under the regulatory microscope in China following a gas explosion in May at the Liushenyu Coal Mine in Shanxi province. The blast killed 82 people, making it the deadliest coal mine disaster in more than a decade.

Aside from safety, the autonomous solution also offered cost savings, Zhao said, remaining cheaper to operate than conventionally driven trucks even after factoring upfront investments in the vehicles, battery-swapping stations and 5G cloud platform, as well as maintenance costs.

The savings have come mainly from lower labour and fuel costs, with the deployment replacing a crew of nearly 270 truck drivers with a smaller maintenance and support team – equivalent to about 220 fewer positions – and saving an estimated 13,300 tonnes of diesel.

Zhao said operating costs for the autonomous trucks were about 6.5 yuan (US$0.97) per cubic metre for hauling coal and overburden, compared with roughly 12 to 14 yuan per cubic metre for conventional haul trucks – almost half the cost.

Since the fleet was deployed in May last year, it has hauled about 28 million cubic metres (988.8 million cubic feet), saving nearly 200 million yuan (US$29.8 million) in operating costs, he added.

Coal has long been the backbone of China’s energy system, powering the country’s rapid industrialisation and still accounting for more than half of its energy consumption. Its dominant role has also helped cushion China from this year’s global energy shock, which saw a rapid increase in oil prices triggered by the US-Israel war with Iran.

Wang Hongzhi, head of the National Energy Administration (NEA), said at a press conference in June that “coal is our biggest source of confidence in maintaining a stable energy supply”, saying China should build up its major coal production bases in line with its national circumstances.

Meanwhile, upgrading and transforming the traditional energy sector has also become part of Beijing’s broader energy strategy.

A blueprint released by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA for China’s “new energy system” during the period covered by the country’s 15th five-year plan called for a “modern coal supply chain”, with wider adoption of green mining practices and the development of smart mines tailored to local conditions.

In another blueprint intended specifically for the coal industry over the period, the two agencies set a target to further advance smart mining across the sector and raise the share of production capacity at smart mines to 75 per cent by 2030.

Analysts from Citic Securities said regulators’ focus on ensuring a safe and stable coal supply amid energy security concerns was driving smart mining, which could also help address labour shortages and cut costs for coal companies.

“The industry’s development is therefore driven not only by central policy coordination and local development plans, but also by coal companies’ own willingness to upgrade,” the analysts said in a report on smart mining last year.

They estimated that smart upgrades could reduce mine staffing by 20 to 30 per cent, with the investment potentially paying for itself in about seven to eight years on labour savings alone.

Since its deployment in May 2025, the Yimin fleet has moved beyond the pilot phase, taking on more demanding operations as the mine prepares to add 200 more trucks by the end of this year.

Initially used to haul topsoil and rock on the surface, the trucks began hauling coal in November, Zhao said. The mine also relocated its battery-swapping stations into the pit to test whether the trucks could navigate more challenging terrain, such as the confined spaces of the coal-preparation plant.

“We need to verify the system’s stability, because we plan to deploy 200 more trucks by the end of this year,” he said.

For Yimin, the experience suggested that technology was no longer the main barrier to wider adoption. But replicating the model across China’s coal mines was another question, with differences in geology, infrastructure and power supply likely to determine how quickly it can scale.

“The technology behind autonomous electric mining trucks is ready for nationwide deployment, but the biggest challenge is whether individual mines have enough power infrastructure to support them,” Zhao said.

Yimin, China’s first coal-and-power integrated project, has an advantage in electricity supply, with the mine able to draw power directly from the affiliated Yimin power plant.

“For other mines, such as those in [the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region], the biggest issue is whether they have enough power supply,” he noted, adding that government efforts to encourage mines to develop microgrids combining solar and wind power with energy storage could offer a potential solution.

Developing smart microgrids in mining areas that coordinate power generation, grids, electricity demand and energy storage is also listed in the coal industry’s five-year plan, which calls for the integrated development and operation of solar and wind power, coal-mine gas generation, energy storage and smart control systems.

According to the Citic Securities analysts, autonomous trucks at open-pit mines and mining robots for underground operations were among the two most mature applications combining artificial intelligence with mining hardware in China, while home-grown large language models for mining provided the technological foundation for such integration.

“We expect … mining-specific large models to incorporate generative AI, further enhancing data analysis and decision-making capabilities while improving safety and energy efficiency in mining operations,” the analysts said.

item.title: [SCMP] Tiananmen vigil leaders jailed for up to 7 years, group fined HK$1.5 million
item.description:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.
item.content:encoded:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.

Lee, 69, and Chow, 41, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months behind bars, respectively.

Former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty ahead of the trial.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the rule of law could only be upheld by imposing severe penalties on the accused.

“The law never allows anyone to blatantly harm their country and compatriots under the guise of promoting human rights, democracy and freedom,” he said.

Central government authorities in Hong Kong hailed the tough sentences as a manifestation of the city’s rule of law, while warning “external forces” against smearing the court’s decisions.

A spokesman for the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said the alliance and the defendants “had long incited public hostility, hatred and disaffection towards the state regime”, adding that their offences had seriously challenged the constitutional order of Hong Kong and gravely violated the city’s national security law.

“They must be severely punished in accordance with the law,” the spokesman said.

The foreign ministry’s arm in Hong Kong said the alliance had undermined the central government’s authority “at both ideological and practical levels”.

Beijing’s liaison office said the defendants deserved severe penalties for attacking the party’s leadership, while the country’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong described the ruling as “widely supported” by society.

Ho is expected to complete his sentence in April 2028, assuming he is not granted a one-third reduction by prison authorities on the basis of good conduct during his incarceration.

Lee Cheuk-yan may be released in September or October 2029, whereas Chow may have to serve her sentence until early 2030. The pair intend to lodge an appeal.

Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said the sentences did not only punish the alliance and its former leaders, but also those who subscribed to the group’s beliefs or previously attended its annual vigil at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay.

“I think free speech is already a thing of the past,” she said. “They were given such heavy sentences even though they had never resorted to any unlawful means.”

Chow’s mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, said her daughter had only intended to “speak the truth”.

The elder Chow added that she was not free to speak her mind because of a police investigation against her.

Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee said the case was serious and warranted five to 10 years’ imprisonment under a two-tier sentencing regime of the national security law.

They noted the offence lasted for 14 months after the law took effect on June 30, 2020, during which the defendants persisted with their offensive conduct on social media and during public events at a time when Hong Kong remained “turbulent and unsettled”.

“Despite the defendants’ belief that their agenda of ‘ending one-party dictatorship’ might be in breach of the [Chinese] constitution and the national security law, they recalcitrantly pursued their course of conduct and strenuously promoted their agenda. This was a premeditated act,” the judges said in a 19-page written ruling.

The European Union said about the sentencing: “This ruling undermines confidence in the rule of law and harms Hong Kong’s reputation.”

The United Nations Human Rights Office said the jailing of the trio highlighted the ever-increasing restrictions on civic space in Hong Kong, including harsh measures taken against civil society actors, since the National Security Law was passed in 2020. The office’s High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for these sentences to be quashed.

Meanwhile, the court adjourned handling the prosecution’s request to confiscate the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture, created by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, pending further arguments.

Galschiot has repeatedly demanded that the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) artwork be returned to him since it was seized by police’s National Security Department in 2023.

Steve Li Kwai-wah, the department’s chief superintendent, argued the sculpture belonged to the alliance and was used to incite others to undermine the party.

“I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” Li said.

Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Galschiot said he intended to request his government to take diplomatic action so that the sculpture could be returned to “its rightful owner”.

Former trade union leader Carol Ng Man-yee, who was released from prison last year after serving 45 months for a subversion offence, and former alliance standing committee member Tang Ngok-kwan were among those who attended the brief hearing on Friday.

Ng said she felt relieved the three defendants finally got to know when they might be released, but said she was still saddened by the outcome.

Tang Ngok-kwan urged the public to continue to honour those who died in the 1989 crackdown in a “reasonable and lawful” manner.

The alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to commemorate the event and called for democratic reforms across the border and the end of one-party rule.

Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

item.title: [SCMP] What’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
item.description:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.

Covering an area more than four times the size of Singapore, the JS-SEZ aims to generate 260 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$63.9 billion) for Johor’s regional economy by 2030 and create more than 20,000 high-skilled jobs, anchored by the coming 4km Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link designed to slash travel times and cement cross-strait integration.

For Malaysia, the early trajectory of Hong Kong and Shenzhen remains the foundational blueprint.

Lee Ting Han, Johor’s state executive councillor for investment and trade, told the South China Morning Post that despite distinct political frameworks, the wealth gap between Singapore and Johor mirrored the historic economic disparity between Hong Kong and Shenzhen.

“Similarly, it is pretty much like the early days of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, where the economic disparity between the two regions was so wide … what we are trying to do now is see whether there’s a way for us from a business standpoint to make it more integrated from trade relationships to investment culture,” Lee said.

He acknowledged that building the JS-SEZ presented unique regulatory challenges because Johor and Singapore operated as sovereign nations without an overarching central authority such as Beijing to coordinate rules.

However, Johor is studying how Shenzhen strategically transitioned over decades from labour-intensive assembly to capital- and technology-intensive hubs by leveraging Hong Kong capital to build home-grown tech giants in the same vein as Huawei Technologies and DJI.

As Asia’s premier financial and technology centres construct massive border-spanning growth corridors, Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis and Malaysia’s JS-SEZ offer a compelling case study in mutual learning.

While Malaysia looks to emulate Hong Kong’s long-standing success in frictionless border flows and joint state-directed planning, the city stands to learn key lessons from Johor’s aggressive strategy in nurturing talent pipelines and deploying state-backed infrastructure to secure a low-cost, high-reliability energy grid for power-hungry tech industries.

Key to Johor’s rapid rise is its approach to energy, an area where Hong Kong could draw valuable operational insights. Highlighting the power requirements of data centres, Lee noted that Malaysia’s utilities were largely state-backed.

This allows the government to take a long-term, strategic view by investing heavily in power infrastructure upfront, insulating critical digital hubs from the short-term profit pressures faced by purely private, commercial utility entities.

Malaysia adopted a forward-looking approach by making heavy infrastructure investments ahead of the cycle.

Chew Chong-sin, a former Mengkibol state assemblyman who has analysed the region’s economic integration, noted that by combining Singapore’s global financial and connectivity hub status with Johor’s land, energy, and industrial capacity, the zone aimed to mirror Shenzhen’s early evolution into a technology powerhouse.

However, he cautioned that significant operational hurdles persisted – most notably easing severe bottlenecking at the world’s second-busiest land checkpoint and resolving head-on competition in ports and logistics – even as the coming RTS Link aimed to streamline cross-border mobility by 2027.

Crucially, the zone was positioning itself to absorb global supply chain diversification, offering a neutral, disaster-free base for multinationals and mainland Chinese enterprises looking to de-risk, Chew said.

He added that this momentum had already drawn increased interest from Hong Kong firms, including sustainable aviation fuel producers and hospitality enterprises.

As Malaysia and Singapore finalise a comprehensive 10-year master plan, he said that the zone’s ultimate success would depend on maintaining the strict execution discipline needed to translate high-level blueprints into lasting economic integration.

To spur investment ahead of its full master plan launch in late 2026, authorities introduced sweeping tax incentives starting January 2025.

Firms deploying at least 500 million ringgit in high-growth fields such as AI, quantum computing and aerospace enjoy a 5 per cent preferential corporate tax rate for years, paired with stamp duty waivers.

These incentives have caught international attention.

A representative from a Mexico-based construction and information technology enterprise, who did not wish to be named, confirmed to the SCMP that the company would visit Malaysia to explore data centre sites, citing the country’s strong connectivity within Asean, widespread English proficiency and attractive tax environment.

Following stops in Kuala Lumpur and coming visits to Johor, he commended Malaysia’s proactive tech push.

Turning to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, however, the representative observed that while the city retained distinct institutional advantages, its position within China imposed inherent geopolitical limitations when manufacturing high-end, sensitive semiconductor chips.

The Northern Metropolis has been touted repeatedly as a top priority for Hong Kong’s administration, capped most recently by a visit from Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, who underscored Beijing’s call to accelerate construction.

The megaproject aims to transform 30,000 hectares into a major housing hub and an economic growth engine.

Both the Northern Metropolis and the JS-SEZ are strategically positioning themselves as multifaceted growth engines that integrate international education hubs, hi-tech innovation corridors and vibrant ecotourism circles.

Joining the call for deeper integration, Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers Hong Kong, said the city could take reference from Johor as a benchmark for cross-border development by aligning its land-grant policies with Shenzhen and leveraging universities to spearhead innovation.

She noted that Johor’s experience showed how robust research and technology ecosystems relied heavily on close synergies with academic institutions.

To build a sustainable tech ecosystem, Lee urged authorities to synchronise housing and talent policies with project completion timelines, anticipating a resurgence in demand as new infrastructure came online.

Given the intensive energy requirements of advanced technology and data centres, she recommended that the government initiate joint feasibility studies with mainland Chinese authorities on cross-border electricity supply to secure a reliable, green power source for the city’s tech sector.

Echoing the push for seamless integration, former lawmaker Edward Lau Kwok-fan argued that Hong Kong should draw inspiration from the JS-SEZ by speeding up the implementation of bespoke legislation for the Northern Metropolis to unlock the fluid movement of people, goods, capital and data.

He also called on higher education institutions to take greater initiative.

“I feel universities have not done enough yet. In the future, universities could evolve towards an industry-oriented development path,” said Lau, a member of the Advisory Committee on the Northern Metropolis.

“Universities need to reflect. There is a need to rethink course offerings and review academic programmes going forward.”

In response, Hong Kong’s Development Bureau said that the Northern Metropolis operated as a strategic cross-boundary hub under the “one country, two systems” governing principle, utilising coming Hetao-specific legislation to facilitate fluid cross-border resource sharing within the Greater Bay Area.

The bureau highlighted that by pairing the city’s five global top-100 universities and a planned 1,000-hectare university district with Shenzhen’s industrial scale, Hong Kong provided a platform, backed by common law, capable of rapidly converting lab discoveries into mass production.

The Education Bureau also said in a reply that it was encouraging University Grants Committee-funded universities to revamp their academic offerings, backed by a fund launched in 2023 to drive digital teaching reforms.

The Chinese University of Hong Kong said in a reply that it offered AI degree programmes across its engineering and science faculties, which delivered structured training to foster AI talent equipped for real-world innovation and academic research.

The SCMP also reached out to the University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

Under the 2025-28 triennial planning cycle, local universities were introducing 27 new undergraduate degree programmes tailored to STEAM fields, the bureau said.

STEAM refers to an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths.

Addressing Hong Kong’s internal bottlenecks, lawmaker Aaron Bok Kwok-ming, a former president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers (HKIE), stressed that the city had to aggressively tackle its ongoing engineering talent shortage similarly to Malaysia.

To supply future high-value talent for the JS-SEZ, the Johor Talent Development Council acts as a centralised talent engine by partnering with universities, institutions and agencies to deliver industry-aligned upskilling, matching programmes and specialised training.

Bok called for targeted manpower forecasts, particularly in electronic engineering, to pinpoint exact deficit areas as Hong Kong advanced its innovation ambitions.

He urged government leaders to conduct official, comprehensive surveys rather than relying on industry estimates, while establishing structured pathways to entice overseas Hong Kong engineers back home and expanding domestic university training.

According to a manpower forecast report by Hong Kong’s Construction Industry Council released in 2023, the sector is expected to face a shortage of about 6,000 to 6,500 professionals by 2027, with civil, mechanical, structural and environmental engineering listed among the most severely affected specialisms.

Drawing on the forecast report, the HKIE noted in 2023 that the city would face a shortfall of about 3,000 professional engineers over the five years through 2027, stressing that engineers played an indispensable role in supporting the government’s push for new industrialisation and biotechnology.

This deficit is already affecting local businesses. Some tech companies previously said that while they struggled to find veteran talent, such as experienced electronics engineers, locally in Hong Kong, they could easily recruit skilled professionals on the mainland.

Addressing these industry concerns over projected workforce shortages, including the estimated shortfall of 3,000 engineers, engineer and former technology minister Alfred Sit Wing-hang said that emerging technologies such as AI, robotics and building information modelling required more sophisticated technical expertise rather than diluted entry criteria.

Sit added that as Hong Kong’s economic landscape underwent a structural shift towards advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries, local universities and professional bodies were actively overhauling their training frameworks.

AI had increasingly become a core component of undergraduate engineering curricula, while new certification programmes were being developed to upskill mid-career professionals in fields such as smart industrial engineering and automation, he said.

On the energy front, lawmaker and energy sector expert Chan Siu-hung noted that Hong Kong already possessed top-tier infrastructure for data centres and computing hubs, but suggested the government could accelerate the roll-out of power infrastructure blueprints to match coming industrial investments.

On the city’s digital expansion, he noted that major development zones such as the Lok Ma Chau Loop and the San Tin Technopole were well positioned, with strong power supply nodes.

Responding to queries on energy security, the Environment and Ecology Bureau said that the government had signed Scheme of Control Agreements (SCAs) with the city’s two power companies.

Under these agreements, the suppliers are obliged to support the development of Hong Kong including the Northern Metropolis, by providing, operating and maintaining sufficient electricity-related facilities to meet the needs of various industries.

Chan stressed that actual energy demand would ultimately depend on incoming corporate investments.

“To ensure long-term energy security, Hong Kong’s two power suppliers need to finalise power agreements with mainland supply, securing cross-boundary supply options while advancing low-carbon energy goals,” he said.

“Officials should provide clearer and earlier timelines for these infrastructure plans to give operators certainty.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why I am grateful for Asean’s endless meetings
item.description:
I remember 2011 well. Indonesia was chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and I was serving as deputy foreign minister for Asean cooperation. I learned a great deal, although if I had to summarise the experience in one word, I would say: meetings.

Asean members meet. They talk. They disagree. They issue statements. Then, quite remarkably, they meet again. We meet in conference rooms, coffee shops and restaurants. We speak by telephone and online. And when matters become particularly serious, there is always durian.

To outsiders, Asean consensus can appear tedious. Where is the breakthrough? Why does everything take so long?
item.content:encoded:
I remember 2011 well. Indonesia was chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and I was serving as deputy foreign minister for Asean cooperation. I learned a great deal, although if I had to summarise the experience in one word, I would say: meetings.

Asean members meet. They talk. They disagree. They issue statements. Then, quite remarkably, they meet again. We meet in conference rooms, coffee shops and restaurants. We speak by telephone and online. And when matters become particularly serious, there is always durian.

To outsiders, Asean consensus can appear tedious. Where is the breakthrough? Why does everything take so long?

Yet the longer I work in diplomacy, the more I appreciate the willingness to meet again, especially after a disagreement. Agreement is important, but it is not the only measure of successful diplomacy. Sometimes, the achievement is simply that disagreement does not end the conversation. This is what I understand as the habit of dialogue.

Working in Beijing, I see something familiar around Chinese dinner tables. A round table has no visible head, creating a sense of equality. Yet it does not remove order. Everyone has a place and everyone is expected to contribute.

Those who have conducted business in China will understand that many important decisions are shaped around such tables. Trust is built gradually, through conversation, shared food and the willingness to spend time understanding one another.

I wonder whether this habit offers a modest lesson for a world accelerating towards multipolarity. I use the word “accelerating” because the changing distribution of global power appears to demand immediate adjustment. Yet multipolarity does not tell us how power will be exercised or what kind of order will emerge.

China’s vision of an equal and orderly multipolar world recognises this challenge. Its Global Governance Initiative similarly places sovereign equality at the centre. But how can sovereign equality become a working practice? How can countries create order without simply recreating hierarchy?

Perhaps Asean can offer part of the answer.

International order needs power to sustain it, but it also needs limits on how power is used. Institutions make those limits more durable. Countries accept restraint because predictability benefits everyone: they know broadly what others may do, what they are unlikely to do and how disagreements will be managed.

The difficulty arises when power shifts. Established powers may fear that restraint gives rivals room to advance. Rising powers may question rules they had little opportunity to shape. When countries no longer believe restraint will be reciprocated, rules begin to give way to transactions. Every concession has a price. Every act of self-restraint starts to look like a favour that must be repaid.

Cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon

This is especially complicated because power today takes many forms. One country may possess greater military strength, another greater manufacturing capacity, another financial influence, advanced technology or essential mineral resources. Strength in one area often exists alongside dependence in another.

Countries will not always share the same interests. But perhaps they can develop a shared understanding of how their different forms of power should be exercised.

Indonesia has Asean’s largest population and economy. By accepting consensus, Indonesia accepts a restraint on its weight. This restraint is useful because, as Bilahari Kausikan, a good friend of mine, has explained, consensus reassures smaller members that Indonesia cannot impose decisions upon them. It also reassures Indonesia that smaller members cannot simply combine to outvote it.

Each accepts limits in exchange for reassurance. No one gets everything but no one is expected to surrender everything either. This matters in a region of different political systems, cultures, levels of development and national interests. Such diversity complicates collective decisions. It also makes Southeast Asia difficult for any outside power to capture entirely behind a single agenda.

Its members may not converge on every interest, but they can converge on certain procedures, protocols, principles or concepts, for example, the non-use of force, a zone of peace, freedom and neutrality, a nuclear-weapon-free zone, Asean centrality and Asean-plus.

We have learned, imperfectly, how to disagree without immediately reaching for the divorce papers.

There are, of course, limits to Asean’s experience. Consensus can take time. Dialogue can become repetitive. Meetings can produce more meetings, sometimes followed by preparatory meetings for the next meeting. I would therefore hesitate to present Asean as a complete model for the global order. Its lesson is more modest: cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon.

The habit of dialogue helps sustain this process. Equality gives every country a voice. Humility helps each country listen and recognise that it may not possess the whole answer. Repeated interaction gradually creates predictability.

Admittedly, habitual dialogue cannot erase power differences. It cannot resolve every dispute. But it can do something essential. It can create time when decisions are moving too quickly. It can lower the temperature when tensions are rising. And it can help countries adjust to power shifts without allowing every disagreement to become a crisis.

This is why I view the first Indonesia-China comprehensive strategic dialogue, held in Jakarta last month, with hope. Its importance lies not only in what was discussed but in the habit that made the discussion possible.

And there is quite a momentum to protect. Since 2015, the bilateral trade volume has tripled and Chinese investment has risen over 12-fold. At this pace, US$300 billion of trade in the next four to five years is within reach.

Through my years in China, I have walked its streets, met its people and spoken to many who will inherit whatever we build today. I do not know whether I have done enough. But I take some comfort in believing I have helped nurture the habit of dialogue. As long as we remain willing to meet again, we will always have something on which to build.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong guqin devotees embrace the ancient zither’s history, philosophy and craft
item.description:
When civil servant Jackel Wan Chak-kui, 28, first heard a guqin being played, he was a young boy wandering through Chi Lin Nunnery, in Diamond Hill. He remembers being entranced by the instrument’s music, at once subtle and comforting. It seemed to envelop him like a warm embrace, complementing the natural beauty of the gardens, melding with stone, water, wood and stillness.

Years later, as a student at Baptist University, Wan chanced upon the sound again, while scrolling through YouTube. He delved deeper this time, yearning to learn more. He ordered his first guqin from Taobao (“Not a good one, but at least I could have a touch [of the instrument],” he says) and taught himself from scores found in the university library, learning where to place his fingers on the seven silk strings.

A seven-stringed zither, the guqin (“ancient stringed instrument”) was once the preserve of noblemen and royal courts, poets and scholars, and has been part of a musical tradition that has existed for more than 3,000 years in China, played in small, elite gatherings.
item.content:encoded:
When civil servant Jackel Wan Chak-kui, 28, first heard a guqin being played, he was a young boy wandering through Chi Lin Nunnery, in Diamond Hill. He remembers being entranced by the instrument’s music, at once subtle and comforting. It seemed to envelop him like a warm embrace, complementing the natural beauty of the gardens, melding with stone, water, wood and stillness.

Years later, as a student at Baptist University, Wan chanced upon the sound again, while scrolling through YouTube. He delved deeper this time, yearning to learn more. He ordered his first guqin from Taobao (“Not a good one, but at least I could have a touch [of the instrument],” he says) and taught himself from scores found in the university library, learning where to place his fingers on the seven silk strings.

A seven-stringed zither, the guqin (“ancient stringed instrument”) was once the preserve of noblemen and royal courts, poets and scholars, and has been part of a musical tradition that has existed for more than 3,000 years in China, played in small, elite gatherings.

Since Unesco first recognised guqin music as part of humanity’s intangible cultural heritage in 2003, the seven-stringed zither has become more widely appreciated, with the instrument itself having been inscribed on China’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2006. Virtuoso Chen Leiji played a specially composed piece on the guqin during the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, reaching millions of viewers worldwide, and today, it’s commonly seen being played in concerts and online videos, with younger musicians being drawn to the instrument.

In Hong Kong, the guqin’s renaissance goes beyond simply renewed popularity, say scholars and players, many of whom construct their own. What they want to preserve are not just the rich sounds of an ancient instrument, but also a traditional way of life.

When it comes to the instrument and its music, “the guqin may be more accessible than before, but true revival is not just about more people playing it. It is about whether people understand its inner life: its craft, philosophy, subtle sound, cultural memory and intensely personal mode of expression”, Wan explains. “Because the more you understand Chinese culture, the more you realise that the guqin goes beyond music to explore other cultural aspects, such as Taoism, philosophy and history.”

A player’s understanding of those references can shape their interpretation of the music.

Wan gives as an example the piece Li Sao (“Encountering Sorrow”) – a lament to Qu Yuan (circa 339BC-278BC), the poet-politician whose exile, grief and moral idealism are central to one of the great works of Chinese literature, also titled Li Sao. To perform such a piece properly, Wan says, it is necessary to enter the emotional and philosophical world behind the notes, rather than just play them.

“It is like the first-, second-, third-person thing – the player might perform as if they are Qu Yuan, or they could be a storyteller, telling the story of Qu Yuan. Or [they could] consider themselves as humming the Li Sao prose,” says Wan, explaining that “to acquire these perspectives, one must cultivate not just the musicality, but also the culture, in a broad sense, of the qin”. He continues, “It is a good mix of understanding traditional culture and the current situation of ourselves.”

Players should learn to develop an appreciation for the guqin’s silences, too, says John Yiu Shek-on, an art historian and the deputy director of the Jao Tsung-I Petite Ecole academic research and cultural centre, at the University of Hong Kong.

“It has so much void – the space between the musical notes,” he says.

As a child in Hong Kong, Yiu played Western instruments, including the piano, but was later drawn to the guqin through its cultural and literary presence.

“I didn’t start with the music,” Yiu admits. “I actually started from writing about it, because it is a very revered instrument in Chinese poetry.”

He notes that the music’s silences remind him of “negative space”, referring to the intentionally untouched areas of silk or paper in Chinese paintings, which are not so much empty but alive with suggestion.

In 2005, he began learning to play the guqin and was soon appreciating the lingering pauses before notes, as part of the music’s emotional landscape. He found himself drawn not only to the instrument’s sound, but also to its refusal to overwhelm the listener – a quiet invitation to slow down and listen inwardly.

Unlike many old-school qin players, Yiu says, both private enjoyment and public performance matter to him. “I enjoy playing just for myself […] and actually, just last year, I had a concert with my teacher in Shanghai.”

Yiu is a member of the Deyin Qin Society, founded in 1998 by disciples of Tsar Teh-yun (1905-2007), a guqin master, poet and calligrapher who relocated to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1950s. “She is widely regarded as one of China’s last great literati,” says Yiu, whose own teacher learned from her directly.

Tsar was born in Huzhou, Zhejiang province, into what Yiu describes as a scholar-gentry family. She received an education in traditional arts, poetry and Kunqu – a polished, flowing style of singing that originated in Suzhou more than six centuries ago – and spent around 30 years teaching in Hong Kong. “Importantly, she did not teach for a living, and treated her students like friends. Many of her students later became established scholars or successful professionals. What united them was not only musical ability, but a temperament suited to the guqin; they’re all quite low-key people,” says Yiu.

Nowadays, the Deyin Qin Society has fewer than 80 members but “we hold regular, semi-private yaji [‘elegant gathering’] salons every two months. We also do public concerts sometimes”, at venues such as the Xiqu Centre and Hong Kong City Hall.

Appreciation of the seven-stringed zither is passed on through other intimate circles as well. Wee Lian-hee is a professor at the Academy of Language and Culture at Baptist University, and his initial encounter with the guqin came in the 80s.

Living in Singapore, he read about the seven-stringed zither while researching Chinese instruments, but struggled to find much information. It wasn’t until the early 2000s, while pursuing a PhD in linguistics in the United States, that he learned of Choi Chang-sau (1933-2025), the third-generation owner of Hong Kong’s Choi Fook Kee Musical Instrument Factory, a producer of Chiuchow and Hakka instruments, as well as violins and guitars. Choi was a foremost expert in crafting, restoring and preserving the guqin.

Established players choose their disciples with care. When Wee visited the master’s workshop, expressing an interest in learning how to make the instrument, he was advised to return after he had settled in Hong Kong. In 2001, Wee moved to the city for work but, preoccupied with his career, postponed his guqin studies.

In 2012, he sought out Lau Chor-wah, an esteemed guqin musician and philosopher, and a founding member of the Deyin Qin Society. Lau refused to teach him for two years, a test to see if he was worthy and genuinely interested. Eventually, he proved his dedication, and she agreed. Her teaching was strict and rigorous, says Wee, requiring weekly attendance at a fixed time, and the first three months were dedicated solely to learning how to string the instrument, a process that requires enormous focus and patience, and can take a novice hours. Precision and gentle finesse are required to maintain the correct tension on each silk string if the right pitch is to be attained.

With a recommendation from Lau, Wee was accepted by Choi as a student, although the master insisted that, to become a maker, one must first be an accomplished player. “Both playing the guqin and crafting it are equally fulfilling,” says Wee. He views both as integral to developing a connection to the instrument.

Of the 50 or so students who studied under Choi, as many as 10 are still making guqin in Hong Kong, among them Sou Si-tai, chairman of the Deyin Qin Society.

A guqin’s body is traditionally fashioned from thoroughly seasoned wood, typically that which has been dried in the shade for about a century. Wee explains that a range of wood is used for different parts of the qin: “The top board is typically paulownia or cedar, the bottom board is more varied and the inlaid parts may be various kinds of hardwood.” After careful selection, the wood is hollowed and shaped before layers of ash and lacquer are applied, polished and adjusted.

Constructing a guqin usually takes more than 200 person-hours, spread over nine painstaking steps that must be planned according to the season. Every detail affects the sound: the thickness of the boards, the curve of the body, the placement of the bridges, the tension of the strings and the way the surface responds to a player’s touch.

“Historically, the guqin is a niche instrument,” says Wee. “Sudden popularity has led to commercialisation and changes that should raise discussion.”

One area of contention is the use of metallic strings, which are louder, more stable and less expensive, but alter the instrument’s sound dynamics and are harsh on the fingers. Unsurprisingly, they are not favoured by purists.

Wee is unsure how many guqin he owns, with several still under construction. Although he appraises and repairs antique guqin for friends and collectors, he says he would never consider selling one of his own creations, as they are “my personal explorations into creating the sounds for my music”.

Says Wee, “It takes me an average of three years to make a guqin, so even if I were to imagine selling it, I wouldn’t know how to price it. I usually lend my instruments to like-minded friends and musicians for their playing pleasure.”

For his wife, he carved a guqin from the beam of a 200-year-old school in Yuen Long that was demolished, and decorated the instrument with a symbol representing his name, inlaid in sheep bone. Using material found in the vicinity of his village, in the Lau Fau Shan area, Wee fashions many of his guqin in memory of deceased pets. In one instance, the ashes of their dog Lily were incorporated into the guqin he made for his wife, an instrument that bears a carving of one of Lily’s paws.

Wan recently made his first qin, an undertaking he estimates took more than 200 hours. He shares that the process demanded a different kind of attention than that needed for playing. It meant learning to understand the instrument not only through sound, but through wood, lacquer, strings and touch, and to consider how small changes in shape, tension and surface alter the way it resonates.

“Both crafting and playing [the guqin] are a means of connecting with nature, to the world around you,” says Wan. “I’d say it’s a way of life.”

item.title: [SCMP] J-50 designers reveal leapfrog tech for China’s next-gen stealth fighters
item.description:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.
item.content:encoded:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.

China’s future fighters, including the J-50 and J-36, are considered rivals to the US Air Force’s sixth-generation main fighter programme, the F-47, being developed by Boeing.

The lead researcher is chief flight-control designer Zhang Dong at the institute, and his team’s paper – rare for its public details – was published in a peer-reviewed journal Aircraft Design in August.

China’s next-generation stealth fighter programmes were undergoing a “leapfrog transformation from being able to fly steadily to being able to win in combat”, wrote Zhang and his colleagues.

Zhang’s study presents a future of pilots handing over control during periods of extreme workload or incapacitation, quantum navigation technologies supporting operations in satellite-denied environments and crewed fighters coordinating attack, reconnaissance and protection missions with reconfigurable wingman drones.

The team’s institute is part of the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China, which oversees much of the country’s aircraft research and development.

Its subsidiary, Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group, is also developing the J-36 fighter, widely regarded as another candidate for China’s next-generation sixth-generation combat aircraft.

In 2025, an investigation by defence news website, The War Zone, using satellite imagery found that the Chengdu J-36 and the Shenyang J-50 aircraft were both based at an experimental military airfield near Lop Nur, a highly secretive site for aerospace test flights that has often been compared to the United States’ Area 51.

Their simultaneous presence at the same base suggested that China’s military was actively supporting the parallel development of the two programmes.

Zhang’s paper presents a rare technological road map for future combat aircraft, describing a fundamental restructuring of the flight-control system from a device concerned mainly with flight quality into a core enabler of collaborative engagement, intelligent manoeuvre and mission effectiveness.

The change reflected what the authors described as three successive eras of air combat.

In the earlier “energy manoeuvrability” era, victory depended heavily on physical manoeuvring performance in close-range combat, while flight-control systems were largely closed and centralised, with specialised hardware and software designed mainly to keep the aircraft stable, controllable and responsive to pilot inputs.

The rise of long-range radar, stealth shaping and precision-guided weapons shifted combat towards “information manoeuvrability”, where detecting, tracking and attacking an opponent before being detected became increasingly important.

Fifth-generation aircraft such as the F-22 and J-20 use full-authority digital fly-by-wire systems and increasingly integrate flight control with fire-control and propulsion systems through high-speed data links.

The authors argued that the next phase was “cognitive manoeuvrability”, in which artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and distributed networking allowed air combat to move from platform-versus-platform competition towards system-level contests involving manned-unmanned formations.

This changes what flight control is expected to do.

“The functional positioning of the flight control system is undergoing a fundamental restructuring – from a platform controller merely pursuing flight quality to a core enabler of collaborative engagement management, intelligent manoeuvre decision-making and closed-loop mission effectiveness,” Zhang and his co-authors wrote.

The first major capability is autonomous flight control.

Instead of making pilots constantly turn high-level battle plans into precise stick movements, the new system would let on-board intelligent algorithms do that job automatically, translating tactical orders into smooth, continuous flight actions while keeping the aircraft safely within its physical limits, even during extreme manoeuvres.

The aircraft would constantly monitor its own health by fusing data from sensors such as inertial navigation, airspeed indicators, control-surface positions and engine performance.

This would allow it to assess its flight state, estimate remaining manoeuvrability and detect potential problems before they develop into emergencies.

The system could then automatically adjust control settings and redistribute on-board resources while strictly enforcing safety boundaries to avoid stalls, loss of control or stuck control surfaces.

In particularly stressful situations, the aircraft could take over from the pilot.

The paper proposes allocating control authority between humans and autonomous systems so that pilots can spend less effort on low-level aircraft handling and more on battlefield assessment and tactical decisions.

During periods of excessive workload or if a pilot loses the ability to control the aircraft, the system could take control and continue executing the intended tactical task while prioritising flight safety.

The second major change concerns navigation.
