Koukyo Yoneta, a fifth-generation Buddhist priest in a small town in Japan’s Hokkaido, was struggling to keep up with the maintenance needs of his century-old temple, so he chose a path that would have been unthinkable for his predecessors – rather than wait for his congregation to give money they do not have, he invested what they had already donated.

The move paid off. Within two years, his portfolio of US treasuries, Japanese real estate investment trusts and stocks including BYD and Hyundai Motor returned more than 10 per cent annually, helping to cover part of the roughly 25 million yen (US$160,000) in needed repairs. The extra money even allowed him to expand the renovations beyond the original plan.

Having previously worked in retail sales at Daiwa Securities Group, Yoneta is an unusually finance-savvy priest but is also part of a growing wave of temple owners turning to financial markets to make ends meet.
item.content:encoded:
Koukyo Yoneta, a fifth-generation Buddhist priest in a small town in Japan’s Hokkaido, was struggling to keep up with the maintenance needs of his century-old temple, so he chose a path that would have been unthinkable for his predecessors – rather than wait for his congregation to give money they do not have, he invested what they had already donated.

The move paid off. Within two years, his portfolio of US treasuries, Japanese real estate investment trusts and stocks including BYD and Hyundai Motor returned more than 10 per cent annually, helping to cover part of the roughly 25 million yen (US$160,000) in needed repairs. The extra money even allowed him to expand the renovations beyond the original plan.

Having previously worked in retail sales at Daiwa Securities Group, Yoneta is an unusually finance-savvy priest but is also part of a growing wave of temple owners turning to financial markets to make ends meet.

Costs for the upkeep of the ornate wooden buildings are soaring while the country’s Buddhist population has dropped about 14 per cent in the last two decades as elderly adherents die and younger generations in larger cities lose their ties to religious practices.

“I’m just so thankful that the investments performed well,” said the 46-year-old, who inherited the Kongo-ji temple from his father in 2018 after leaving his job in finance and training as a monk.

“With the funeral business shrinking, more and more temples will find they can’t just rely on donations to meet their funding needs; they will have to build up reserves and invest those funds.”

The shrinking number of followers is hitting temples’ finances. About half bring in less than 4 million yen per year, according to a 2021 survey of 7,000 temples by one of the largest Buddhist groups, Jodo Shinshu Hongwanji-ha.

The situation is particularly severe in rural areas, where it is common for monks to oversee multiple temples while also working day jobs like schoolteachers or civil servants.

Moral dilemma

Traditionally, funerals and maintaining graves have helped sustain temples as bereaved families would pay for more elaborate ceremonies and prayers.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, people began spending less on funeral rituals and the trend has continued, particularly as inflation has increased households’ daily costs. Some temples that are popular with tourists charge entrance fees, but most lack other means.

The need to cover higher costs through price hikes or investments poses a moral dilemma for some monks, whose religious principles call for detachment from greed.

Daian-ji temple in Nara prefecture still holds most of its assets in cash, with around 10 per cent now allocated to foreign-currency denominated insurance products, which earn higher interest returns.

Their investment style is “purely defensive” to avoid any conflict with the religion’s teachings, according to the deputy priest Yusho Kono.

“There is an inherent contradiction in our position,” Kono said. “In principle, monks should not engage in profit-making activities. But if we do not take any action now, the temple could cease to exist.”

Production costs for some of Daian-ji’s traditional silken amulets, which visitors buy to guard against misfortune or to bring good luck, have surged in the last two years.

Monks should not engage in profit-making activities. But if we do not take any action now, the temple could cease to exist

Yusho Kono, Daian-ji temple deputy priest

Shifting attitudes among priests underscore the strain that persistent inflation is placing on traditional institutions long accustomed to stable prices.

Although Japan’s consumer price inflation has fallen below the central bank’s 2 per cent target, thanks to a series of subsidies, rising prices are continuing to disrupt social and financial practices shaped by decades of deflation.

Rising costs

Issues surrounding surging living costs are a major political issue for the Sanae Takaichi administration.

Opinion polls show her approval rating hovering near its lowest level after 11 months in office, after she was seen by voters to be concentrating too much on less pressing issues than the cost-of-living crunch.

Temples’ limited ability to charge adherents more for services strengthens a case for asset management, according to Tsuyoshi Kawata, a senior researcher at SMBC Nikko Securities’ corporate investment strategies department, who published a study on asset management by religious organisations in 2023.

“When the overall market is shrinking, raising prices is not really an easy option,” Kawata said. “Leaving cash sitting idle is probably no longer an option either. They would want to use whatever means they can to increase income, even if only slightly.”

For some temples, returning to financial markets also means overcoming painful lessons from the past. In 2013, the Koyasan Shingon-shu sect was embroiled in a financial ordeal after reporting unrealised losses from its exposure to structured bonds. The sect declined an interview request, saying they were considering revising their asset management strategy.

Even so, rising bond yields following the end of negative interest rates offer comfortable investment opportunities for risk-averse monks.

Soto-shu, a Buddhist sect overseeing around 15,000 temples nationwide, has been taking advantage of higher yields.

Of the 13 billion yen it manages across eight accounts, around 10 per cent is now invested in Japanese government bonds that it plans to hold to maturity, while another 2 per cent is invested in debt issued by the Japan International Cooperation Agency to finance development in emerging economies.

Religious groups, schools and other non-profit organisations are collectively becoming a buying force of fixed-income products.

Non-profit organisations, including schools and religious institutions, held roughly 5 trillion yen of corporate bonds as of March, about double the amount in 2023, according to Bank of Japan figures. Holdings of Japanese government bonds also increased to 2.9 trillion yen from 2.5 trillion yen over the same period.

At Kongo-ji temple in Hokkaido, Yoneta hopes his investments will help fund future repairs as revenue continues to decline. At the same time, he is trying to safeguard the future by regularly hosting investment seminars for adherents at the temple, building a support network that the temple might one day be able to rely on.

“The days when temples and their priests enjoyed a privileged status are completely over,” Yoneta said. “How temples plan their finances and manage their assets is becoming an issue we simply cannot afford to ignore.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will ‘transactional’ America assist India in a future border crisis with China?
item.description:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi last week on the sidelines of the Brics summit, another country loomed large in the background, even in its absence: the United States.

After the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintain peace at the disputed border and strengthen economic ties.

Beijing’s readout, however, offered a pointed reminder of the US factor in India-China ties.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi last week on the sidelines of the Brics summit, another country loomed large in the background, even in its absence: the United States.

After the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintain peace at the disputed border and strengthen economic ties.

Beijing’s readout, however, offered a pointed reminder of the US factor in India-China ties.

The official Chinese statement claimed that Modi assured Xi that India adhered to an “independent foreign policy” and that its ties with China are “not influenced by any third party”, an apparent reference to Washington.

While India did not endorse Beijing’s assessment, analysts said Washington’s shifting priorities in the Asia-Pacific region and strained US-India ties are reinforcing New Delhi’s instinct for strategic autonomy and influencing its approach to China.

However, they added that despite uncertainty about Washington’s strategy, it would likely stand by India in a potential border crisis with China as it did during the 2020 Galwan clashes, but New Delhi should be ready to defend the territory on its own.

“American assistance cannot be treated as automatic,” said Nirupama Rao, a former Indian foreign secretary.

“If China attempted a significant unilateral alteration of the status quo. American support would likely be substantially stronger.”

“India is going to its default position, which is strategic autonomy and multi-alignment,” said Aparna Pande, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, adding that the policy has been “reinforced over the last year and a half because of concerns over the global order under the second Trump administration”.

During his second term, US President Donald Trump has frequently criticised allies and partners for taking advantage of the US, launched trade wars against them and questioned the security architectures in Europe and Asia as well as the costs of maintaining them.

In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to significantly reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, citing their cost and saying the drills sent an inappropriate message to North Korea.

His approach has unsettled America’s friends, prompting a scramble among them to manage rivalries and forge new partnerships.

India’s attempts to stabilise ties with China come as its relations with Washington have frayed over trade and tariffs, oil sanctions, visa restrictions and rising anti-India rhetoric and racism from Trump’s Maga base.

While not a treaty ally of the US, India still maintains strong defence ties with Washington, focused on maintaining peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, a euphemism for checking China’s growing influence.

Xi, Modi emphasise need for border stability

During his bilateral talks with Xi, Modi emphasised that “peace and tranquillity in the border areas remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”, while Xi said both sides should commit to “parallel development and mutual promotion of bilateral relations and border issues”.

Xi’s first visit to India in seven years followed the prolonged freeze in ties after the deadly Galwan clashes in June 2020, which killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops. Both sides deployed thousands of troops and heavy weaponry along the ill-defined border for more than four years.

Border arrangements that began in 2024 eased tensions and revived high-level dialogue, regular flights and people-to-people exchanges.

However, disagreements appeared to resurface last month over patrolling points in Arunachal Pradesh, a province in India’s northeast that Beijing claims as Zangnan or south of Tibet.

The two sides contained the latest crisis and agreed to an eight-point consensus, including an “early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management”.

Despite multiple border arrangements, thousands of troops remain deployed on either side, while the two countries continue to expand physical infrastructure across the difficult terrain.

India’s Ministry of Defence said in its annual report last week that it witnessed a “significant reduction in the deployment of People’s Liberation Army [PLA] forces” along the LAC in the northern front, with around 40,000-50,000 PLA troops at the border and an equal number in designated training areas.

The report did not disclose India’s troop numbers, describing its deployment as “robust, well poised and prepared to deal with any emerging contingency”.

“All India is trying to do is manage, to the extent possible, the border issue so that it doesn’t flare up,” said Pande of the Hudson Institute.

She added that New Delhi is attempting to balance a “very strong” China, a weaker Russia and a less dependable, transactional and “semi-isolationist America”.

“India has to manage that,” Panda said.

Rao, who has served as India’s ambassador to both China and the United States, said that “difficulties with Washington undoubtedly reinforce India’s instinct for strategic autonomy and increase the value of stabilising relations with China”.

But she cautioned that there isn’t a “direct causal connection” between the two, noting that the India-China stabilisation process began well before the recent deterioration in India-US ties.

Will US support India in a Galwan-like clash with China?

During the 2020 India-China border crisis, the US largely stayed in the background but played an important supporting role, providing India with surveillance drones and logistical assistance.

It reportedly provided India with MQ-9 drones for surveillance in record time, along with cold-weather clothing, tents, rifles and spare parts.

In 2022, Washington shared real-time intelligence on Chinese positions along the LAC with New Delhi, according to reports, in what was the first known instance of the US providing such active assistance.

Hundreds of Indian and Chinese troops wielding spiked clubs and tasers engaged in fistfights in December that year in the Tawang sector of Arunachal Pradesh.

Neither side officially confirmed the extent of the US assistance, as details of the cooperation remain classified.

On whether the US would extend its support to New Delhi again despite tensions in bilateral relations, Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he was optimistic and confident that it would.

“I think our relationship is even better now than it was in 2020,” he said, adding that “there’s a lot more structural support” for defence cooperation.

The India-US defence relationship has expanded in recent years from arms sales to technology cooperation and plans for greater defence co-production in India.

Under the current administration, the two countries signed a new 10-year framework last October, focusing on operational coordination, information sharing and bolstering defence industrial capacity.

The previous Joe Biden administration launched INDUS-X, the India-US Defence Acceleration Ecosystem, in 2023 to connect US and Indian defence companies, start-ups and investors.

New initiatives help strengthen US-India relations

The Trump administration has since strengthened the partnership through TRUST, a broader technology initiative, and INDUS Innovation, a network connecting defence start-ups, investors and research institutions in the two countries.

The two militaries have also expanded joint exercises, including the tri-service Tiger Triumph and the Malabar naval exercise, alongside cooperation across air, land, sea, space and cyberspace.

They also cooperate through the Quad, an informal grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia that focuses on maritime security, including maritime domain awareness, coastguard cooperation and disaster response.

Rao argued that the “precedent of 2020 is important” and any valuable assistance “would probably be discreet”.

She added that Washington would probably “encourage de-escalation” and avoid “unnecessarily internationalising the incident” in the event of a small patrol confrontation, but American support would likely be “substantially stronger” if China attempted a significant unilateral alteration of the status quo at the border.

“The essential qualification is that India is not a US treaty ally,” she cautioned.

“US partnership should multiply Indian capability, not substitute for it.”

According to Lalwani, India is seeking to build guardrails with China through the latest border arrangement to prevent “inadvertent crisis escalation”, but a meaningful thaw remains unlikely.

“These two countries are clearly rivals, if not adversaries,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Scott Bessent confirms weekend meeting with He Lifeng days before Xi’s US visit
item.description:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed that he will meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend for the final preparatory talks between the two sides, less than a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping travels to Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.

“With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart Vice [Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing.

Bessent was responding to a question about the alleged role of Chinese banks in facilitating commercial transactions with Iran and whether Washington planned to take action against them.
item.content:encoded:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed that he will meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend for the final preparatory talks between the two sides, less than a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping travels to Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.

“With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart Vice [Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing.

Bessent was responding to a question about the alleged role of Chinese banks in facilitating commercial transactions with Iran and whether Washington planned to take action against them.

Bessent is expected to discuss the likely economic outcomes of the Trump-Xi summit and begin preparatory dialogue on artificial intelligence safety and governance.

Last week, the South China Morning Post reported that Washington and Beijing are set to fold the long-awaited AI dialogue into a broader economic meeting.

The two leaders agreed in Beijing in May to establish an intergovernmental dialogue on AI, which ran separately from the economic talks led by Bessent and He for months. The AI channel has struggled to make progress, with basic details of the planned talks still unresolved as Xi’s visit approaches.

Bessent set to address AI and economic issues in meeting with He

Sources said Bessent is now expected to address both AI and economic issues in a single meeting with He, rather than hold separate high-level talks. Bessent leads the US side in both channels, while the tight schedule ahead of the summit has made arranging a second meeting increasingly difficult.

The latest arrangements mirror those in May, when Bessent and He held talks in Seoul just days before Trump met Xi in Beijing.

Another source familiar with the discussions said the upcoming AI talks are expected to be “fairly preliminary” and more about “agenda setting” than grappling with complex issues.

On Tuesday, Bessent also weighed in on the AI safety debate, highlighting the tension between addressing concerns about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and maintaining US competitiveness with China in the race for AI leadership.

“It does matter whether the good guys or the bad guys have this,” Bessent said in response to Massachusetts Democrat Stephen Lynch, who argued it probably wouldn’t matter whether the good or bad guys developed superintelligence if it couldn’t be controlled.

“As a person who manages the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal,” Bessent added.

Trump on Monday dismissed growing concerns about AI, claiming America already has guardrails to regulate the industry and warning that casting doubt on development only benefits China.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ ‌that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on social media.

“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these ⁠companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data ‌Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

Bessent echoed Trump’s stance on Tuesday, arguing that “AI is the most important technology of this century, and that we must maintain US leadership”.

Bessent’s testimony came on the same day that Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump White House aide Steve Bannon joined forces at a Washington conference, dubbed the Pro-Human Assembly, to call for new policies to curb the rapidly accelerating development of AI.

The AI safety issue gained prominence last week when a former Anthropic employee warned that the technology may lead to human extinction in the next decade.

On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-step framework to slow the pace of AI development and give policymakers and companies more time to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology.

The proposal quickly won support from other prominent industry leaders, including xAI chief Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

However, the Trump administration is prioritising AI competition with China as a key driver of AI development and is unwilling to slow down.

Concerns rise over Chinese AI models using ‘distillation’ from US rivals

The Treasury Secretary once again raised concerns about Chinese AI models using “distillation” from US models, which he described as one area where the US could challenge Beijing.

“One of the ways we can push back against China, because the Chinese models distil from the US models, which is a polite scientific word for steal,” he said.

Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones.

Last week, three US agencies – the National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI – accused leading Chinese AI companies of engaging in “aggressive, malicious and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale”. They alleged that the practice was carried out “likely with Chinese government awareness”.

During an afternoon press conference at the White House on Tuesday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked whether the US Justice Department would “go after” China over the alleged distillation or whether Trump would bring it up when he meets with Xi next week.

“When you say China, you’re talking about an entire country, and so those two presidents have a great relationship, and they get along, they make deals together,” said Blanche.

“Are there separate issues with actors in China and companies in China and bad actors? That has existed long before this administration and will exist for the next several years.”

Blanche said the US Justice Department and other executive branch agencies would continue to combat theft “in the right way”.

“I don’t think it’s fair to just label China as a country,” he added. “There’s bad actors in China that are doing it, which we’re definitely going to go after.”

The Chinese embassy in Washington rejected US allegations, terming distillation “a common technical practice used by AI developers worldwide, including US companies”.

“The US allegations are unfounded and politicise a normal technological and commercial practice,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang told the SCMP.

As Chinese companies have narrowed the capability gap in frontier AI models, US firms and Trump administration officials have increasingly accused Beijing of stealing and copying American technology to speed up the development of its own systems.

Additional reporting by Mark Magnier

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore ministers earn millions. What do other Asian leaders make?
item.description:
Singapore’s ministers are among the world’s highest paid, a system its leaders have defended as necessary to attract capable people into public service and reduce the temptation of corruption.

Its latest salary review has once again put the spotlight on that approach, while highlighting a wider regional divide over how Asian governments value political leadership and public service.

Under the city state’s formula, the prime minister’s salary is pegged at twice the benchmark for an entry-level minister, which is based on the median annual income of the country’s top 1,000 Singaporean earners after applying a 40 per cent public-service discount.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s ministers are among the world’s highest paid, a system its leaders have defended as necessary to attract capable people into public service and reduce the temptation of corruption.

Its latest salary review has once again put the spotlight on that approach, while highlighting a wider regional divide over how Asian governments value political leadership and public service.

Under the city state’s formula, the prime minister’s salary is pegged at twice the benchmark for an entry-level minister, which is based on the median annual income of the country’s top 1,000 Singaporean earners after applying a 40 per cent public-service discount.

When Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s annual pay benchmark rises to S$3.6 million (US$2.83 million) on October 15, it will be almost four times the basic annual salary of Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu.

Wong has pledged to donate his S$1.4 million increase over five years, while serving ministers will only gradually move towards the S$1.8 million entry-level benchmark.

For analysts, the issue extends far beyond the size of any one leader’s salary. Political pay structures reveal what governments value, what they expect citizens to accept and how much of a leader’s total compensation is visible to the public.

While Singapore defends high salaries as a way to attract talent and guard against corruption, the balance looks very different across the rest of Asia – shaped instead by bureaucratic hierarchy, austerity, symbolic restraint or off-the-books perks that do not always appear in headline figures.

Premium on talent

Singapore’s high ministerial salaries stem from a broader choice about who should govern, according to Donald Low, a former civil servant in the city state and professor of practice in public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

Rather than relying only on politicians who rise through party ranks, the long-ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) routinely recruits mid-career professionals and senior public servants.

However, these new political entrants must still stand for election, engage voters and face public scrutiny, Low said. “It’s a very unusual model of how politics is done, and high ministerial salaries are almost inevitably a consequence of this model.”

Low said Wong’s donation pledge and the gradual phase-in for serving ministers showed that public expectations remained a factor, even within a market-linked system.

Hong Kong’s administrative benchmark

Hong Kong’s chief executive also sits near the top of regional salary rankings, but that figure is set through a different system.

Following a 1.3 per cent adjustment in July, Lee’s cash pay stands at about HK$475,600 (US$61,000) a month, or HK$5.71 million annually. Since 2007, the chief executive’s salary has been pegged at 112.5 per cent of the wages received by the chief secretary for administration.

“Rather than asking what a political leader might earn in the private sector, Hong Kong has positioned the chief executive’s salary within an established public-service hierarchy,” Low said.

The contrast also reflects different career arcs. Hong Kong’s principal officials often serve one or two terms before returning to another profession, making any private-sector pay cut temporary.

“In Singapore, a ministerial appointment is more likely to become the final major phase of a person’s career,” Low said.

Hong Kong’s former chief executives remain subject to a three-year post-office employment control period, which includes a total ban on outside jobs during their first year out of office.

Institutionalised austerity in Japan

Until December 2025, Japan’s prime minister and cabinet members who were also Diet members were entitled to additional executive pay and bonuses, in addition to their standard legislators’ salaries.

However, Japanese leaders have long maintained a tradition of returning their executive pay and bonuses – a practice started by former prime minister Naoto Kan in the wake of the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

What began as an emergency response survived as a long-standing norm of financial restraint under subsequent administrations.

The practice was formalised when legislation was enacted last year stating that Diet members appointed as prime minister or ministers would receive no additional pay.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the change as “mi wo kiru kaikaku” – or self-sacrificing reforms.

The revised law means Takaichi now receives standard Diet pay and year-end allowances, totalling about 21.9 million yen (US$141,000) annually, down from the 40 million yen figure often cited in older comparisons of Japanese prime ministers.

Hidden figures and off-the-books perks

In Malaysia, Anwar Ibrahim has refused a salary for both his roles as prime minister and finance chief since taking office in 2022. His cabinet also implemented a 20 per cent monthly pay cut that remains in place – gestures meant to show solidarity with citizens facing economic pressures.

Bryan Cheah, a senior researcher with the anti-corruption non-government organisation Centre to Combat Corruption and Cronyism, said modest salaries and voluntary pay cuts could not answer wider questions about politicians’ wealth, investments and business interests.

Malaysia has no statutory requirement for ministers and elected representatives to make comprehensive public asset declarations.

“Such disclosures are entirely voluntary and lack a common protocol,” Cheah said.

He pointed to instances where candidates published their bank statements during the last general election, calling them “wholly inadequate” as such documents “[do] not exclude the possibility that their wealth may be deposited with a family member”.

Cheah cited enforcement cases involving the seizure of assets worth millions of ringgit as a reason official salary figures alone did not necessarily reassure the public.

“Without the requisite institutional reforms that demonstrate the real earnings of ministers and elected officials, this gesture remains a gesture alone,” Cheah said.

Indonesia presents a sharper divide between headline salary and the overall value of political office.

A cabinet minister’s basic monthly salary is 5.04 million rupiah, with a 13.61 million rupiah position allowance bringing the published total to about 18.6 million rupiah (US$1,056).

But ministers can also receive an official residence, vehicle and driver, health coverage, travel expenses and ministry-specific performance allowances.

“No single public document tells a citizen what a minister actually takes home in total,” said Yanuar Nugroho, a visiting senior fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and senior lecturer at the Driyarkara School of Philosophy in Jakarta.

“The 18.6 million rupiah figure is real, but it is a small and slightly misleading fraction of the real value of holding office.”

President Prabowo Subianto has also floated salary cuts for ministers to improve budget efficiency.

Nugroho said the gesture could matter politically, but not financially.

He cited independent estimates that the move would save about 6.5 billion rupiah a year in basic pay, or 47.9 billion rupiah including allowances – roughly 0.0005 per cent of Indonesia’s 2026 state budget.

Public anger over political privilege has already proved combustible. Protests erupted last August over a 50 million rupiah monthly housing allowance for legislators, before spreading nationwide after ride-hailing driver Affan Kurniawan was killed by a police vehicle.

Indonesia could borrow Singapore’s clearer consolidation and disclosure of political pay, Nugroho said, without adopting its link to elite private-sector incomes.

“Transparency travels,” he said. “The market-rate aspiration does not.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Doing a North Korea’? Why the Middle East could be entering a new nuclear age
item.description:
The Middle East stands on the precipice of a new nuclear age, with Saudi Arabia set to acquire American uranium enrichment technology and Turkey eager to follow suit, as Iran weighs withdrawal from the treaty that bars it from making atomic bombs.

Momentum is building: last week, the United States and Israel both threatened further air strikes against Iran’s nuclear facilities, accusing Tehran of attempting to resurrect its nuclear programme. The country’s three main complexes were buried deep underground after the US and Israel bombed them during their first, brief air war against the Islamic Republic in June 2025.

The warnings from US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu followed the publication on September 9 of a study by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) claiming that a surge in construction activity at the so-called Pickaxe Mountain site “likely” meant it was being developed into an underground fortress for Iran’s nuclear programme.
item.content:encoded:
The Middle East stands on the precipice of a new nuclear age, with Saudi Arabia set to acquire American uranium enrichment technology and Turkey eager to follow suit, as Iran weighs withdrawal from the treaty that bars it from making atomic bombs.

Momentum is building: last week, the United States and Israel both threatened further air strikes against Iran’s nuclear facilities, accusing Tehran of attempting to resurrect its nuclear programme. The country’s three main complexes were buried deep underground after the US and Israel bombed them during their first, brief air war against the Islamic Republic in June 2025.

The warnings from US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu followed the publication on September 9 of a study by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) claiming that a surge in construction activity at the so-called Pickaxe Mountain site “likely” meant it was being developed into an underground fortress for Iran’s nuclear programme.

The CSIS report said the facility could either be a centrifuge assembly plant, an enrichment site or a safe haven for other “nuclear weapons-relevant” work such as uranium metal conversion.

That same day, Trump said Western intelligence agencies had flagged the Pickaxe facility as a likely storage site for nuclear material.

“We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard,” he threatened.

In a video message on September 10, Netanyahu alleged that Iran, “after we destroyed its immediate capability to produce nuclear bombs … is trying again”.

However, the CSIS findings were hotly disputed by eminent American nuclear weapons expert David Albright, founder of the Institute for Science and International Security.

In a social media post on Monday, Albright argued that the construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain spotted by satellites in August had in fact been under way since last year’s air strikes and more likely showed Iran preparing the site for a potential US attack.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed the CSIS report on Tuesday as “much ado about nothing”.

Still, its publication coincided with an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) decision to refer Iran’s file to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years.

The resolution, brought by Britain, France and Germany, accused Iran of non-compliance with the nuclear non-proliferation treaty (NPT) on the grounds it had withheld information on its stockpiles of highly enriched uranium stored in the three facilities rendered inaccessible by American bunker-buster bombs and by denying IAEA inspectors access to the sites.

The referral is not expected to yield further UN Security Council action against Iran, because of opposition from veto-wielding permanent members China and Russia.

But the political fallout is already being felt in Tehran, where hardliners have seized on the move to renew calls for withdrawal from the NPT.

Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned that the IAEA’s “politicised and disruptive actions will push countries towards withdrawing from the NPT”.

Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said further US-Israeli strikes could prompt Tehran to take that very action.

Barbara Slavin, distinguished Middle East fellow at the Stimson Centre, said such attacks would “increase political support within the regime for such a step”.

Sina Azodi, author of Iran and the Bomb, called withdrawal “quite likely” given the war and Iran’s “strong dissatisfaction with the IAEA and the NPT itself”.

Ali Alfoneh, author of Political Succession in the Islamic Republic of Iran, was more cautious, suggesting Tehran would only leave the NPT “if and when it has completed production of two nuclear weapons: one for testing and another to retain as a deterrent”.

Slavin agreed that the likelihood of Iran “doing a North Korea” was increasing.

Azodi also noted growing support within Iran for “weaponisation” since the previous strategy of enriching uranium to near weapons-grade without actually building a bomb had failed to deter the US and Israeli attacks.

“Whether Tehran can actually sneak out and test a device is a separate issue,” Azodi said.

Alfoneh similarly said he suspected that “technical obstacles, rather than an absence of political resolve, are the principal constraint on Iranian weaponisation”.

A July 22 agreement between the US and Saudi Arabia to develop the kingdom’s nuclear power industry was expected to further strengthen Iran’s resolve to keep its uranium enrichment capabilities, analysts said.

The deal, which Alfoneh calls “a sad joke”, has alarmed nuclear non-proliferation experts because it includes scope for future uranium enrichment activities using American reactors and Saudi uranium reserves.

At the IAEA’s annual general conference in Vienna on Tuesday, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman announced the discovery of 110 million tonnes of uranium-bearing ore near the holy city of Medina.

The agreement with the US makes proliferation safeguards a bilateral matter, sparing Saudi Arabia the intrusive nationwide inspection regime required by the IAEA.

The Arms Control Association said in a statement published on September 1 that the Trump administration had “rejected key non-proliferation conditions for US nuclear cooperation that have long-standing bipartisan support and are internationally recognised best practices” in negotiating the agreement with Riyadh.

While Saudi Arabia had insisted its interest in enrichment is purely for civilian purposes, the association observed that the same technology could create fissile material for a bomb – a risk it called “particularly troubling given that Saudi officials have openly threatened to pursue nuclear weapons to match any Iranian capability”.

Analysts said Nato member Turkey was closely following all these developments.

According to Gonul Tol, senior Turkey fellow at the Middle East Institute, Ankara sees the US-Saudi deal as “evidence that regional states are becoming more serious about preserving a nuclear option”.

“Just as importantly, Turkish officials see Washington itself as becoming more flexible about non-proliferation,” Tol noted in a September 10 research paper.

The Iran war, Turkey’s expulsion from the F-35 programme, Trump’s threats towards Nato and broader questions about US security guarantees had also “strengthened doubts in Ankara about whether Turkey can rely indefinitely on the American nuclear umbrella”, she said.

Turkey would likely hedge by seeking “greater control over its nuclear supply chain and more indigenous nuclear capabilities”, Tol added.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s Prabowo appoints third finance minister in under 2 years
item.description:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto abruptly removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa on Monday after just over a year in the job, turning to veteran ministry technocrat Suahasil Nazara as his government grapples with mounting fiscal pressure and questions over economic policy coordination.

Suahasil, who had served as deputy finance minister since 2019, becomes Prabowo’s third finance minister in less than two years, following Purbaya and his internationally respected predecessor Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

No official reason was given for Purbaya’s removal, which came after a tenure marked by an aggressive push for faster economic growth and, more recently public friction over government finances and the management of state funds.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto abruptly removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa on Monday after just over a year in the job, turning to veteran ministry technocrat Suahasil Nazara as his government grapples with mounting fiscal pressure and questions over economic policy coordination.

Suahasil, who had served as deputy finance minister since 2019, becomes Prabowo’s third finance minister in less than two years, following Purbaya and his internationally respected predecessor Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

No official reason was given for Purbaya’s removal, which came after a tenure marked by an aggressive push for faster economic growth and, more recently public friction over government finances and the management of state funds.

The surprise nature of the reshuffle was underscored by Purbaya’s movements on Monday: he had been attending a parliamentary hearing when he left after receiving a phone call, shortly before Suahasil was sworn in at the presidential palace.

“The priority is to run a credible state budget,” Suahasil said after taking office. He said Prabowo had instructed him to safeguard the health and credibility of state finances while pledging to keep the fiscal deficit below Indonesia’s statutory ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP.

He also sought to portray his appointment as continuity rather than a sharp policy shift, pointing to his long tenure inside the finance ministry.

Analysts said Suahasil’s extensive experience inside the finance ministry could help steady policy after a turbulent period.

“To help restore market confidence and stabilise macro-fiscal management, President Prabowo finally made the decision to appoint Suahasil Nazara, an experienced internal fiscal expert, amid growing frictions over revenue targets, state budget implementation, and policy coordination – including debates over state fund transfers and contributions from Danantara,” said Harry Su, managing director at brokerage Samuel Sekuritas Indonesia.

One of the most visible disagreements in Purbaya’s final weeks concerned state investment fund Danantara Indonesia.

Purbaya said late last month that Danantara would contribute about 120 trillion rupiah (US$6.8 billion) to the state budget this year, describing the payment as a decision by Prabowo and saying the funds could provide an additional fiscal buffer as the government sought to contain its deficit.

But Danantara chief executive Rosan Roeslani subsequently said the institution had not internally discussed such a 120 trillion rupiah payment, contradicting Purbaya’s account of the proposed payment.

Bhima Yudhistira, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, said Danantara had mounted “strong protests” over the finance ministry’s proposal.

“Purbaya’s internal coordination methods, including his communication style, have been deteriorating over time. He was also overconfident. That’s what led to his reshuffle,” Bhima said, although the presidential palace has not officially disclosed the reason behind the dismissal.

Questions over Purbaya’s management style had also surfaced over tax refunds after businesses complained that delays were squeezing company cash flows.

Purbaya said last week that he had instructed officials to increase scrutiny of tax refunds in the coal sector but acknowledged that implementation had apparently extended more broadly than he had intended and promised to investigate the problem.

Bhima said the dispute reflected internal coordination problems involving tax and customs officials and had angered businesses whose refunds were held back.

“This upset many business owners, as tax refunds were initially withheld for audits in the natural resources sector but they ultimately affected all sectors,” he said.

The episode added to a reputation Purbaya had cultivated as an unusually outspoken economic policymaker.

After replacing Sri Mulyani last year, Purbaya pursued a more expansionary approach aimed at accelerating an economy that has grown at roughly 5 per cent for much of the past decade, including moving large amounts of government cash into state banks to spur lending.

He repeatedly said Indonesia could achieve growth of around 6 per cent, a target broadly in line with Prabowo’s ambitions but above the country’s recent trend.

Bhima said Suahasil was likely to bring a markedly different tone to the job, with communications that would be “more careful, more credible” than what he called Purbaya’s “cowboy style” rhetoric.

“He’s a veteran in the Ministry of Finance bureaucracy since the Sri Mulyani era and understands internal matters. He’s considered capable of moderating internal conflicts and relationships,” Bhima said.

Suahasil is a former academic who headed the finance ministry’s Fiscal Policy Agency before becoming deputy finance minister in 2019, making him one of the most experienced officials inside the institution.

But analysts said a calmer style would not remove the difficult fiscal arithmetic awaiting him.

Indonesia’s 2026 budget deficit is forecast to widen to 2.85 per cent of GDP from an original projection of 2.68 per cent, bringing it closer to the legal 3 per cent ceiling as higher expenditure puts pressure on state finances.

Dipo Ramli, a researcher at the Center of Reform on Economics Indonesia, said Suahasil’s biggest challenge would be navigating “limited fiscal space”, particularly for regional governments, while Prabowo continued to pursue ambitious spending programmes.

“At the national level, [our financial situation] might still be considered safe, but we know that many regions have problematic [fiscal] situations,” Dipo said.

Prabowo has made costly programmes – including free nutritious meals for schoolchildren and pregnant women and the development of tens of thousands of Red and White village cooperatives – central to his economic agenda.

At the same time, his government is targeting growth of 6 per cent under its proposed 2027 budget while seeking to narrow the deficit, leaving the finance ministry with the task of reconciling faster expansion and heavy expenditure with Indonesia’s long-standing fiscal guardrails.

The immediate market reaction to Purbaya’s removal was mixed. Jakarta stocks recovered most of an earlier sell-off to finish 0.1 per cent lower on Monday, while the rupiah weakened 0.33 per cent against the US dollar.

This latest reshuffle follows Prabowo’s replacement of Sri Mulyani last year and the unexpected resignation in July of Bank Indonesia governor Perry Warjiyo, who has since been succeeded by Destry Damayanti.

Dipo said frequent changes in such positions could signal to foreign investors that the administration was still “trying to find its groove”.

“For foreign investors, the minister of finance and Bank Indonesia [governor] are usually considered stable positions. Replacing them is not a good idea, but considering our fiscal situation, I think adjustments are necessary,” he said.

“It’s true that the market might not like it, and foreign investors might not like it, but given the numerous problems, I don’t think there’s a problem with replacing the minister of finance.”

Additional reporting by Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.

“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.

Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.

Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.

These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.

Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.

“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.

Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.

“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore jails armed Malaysian gang for US$3.9 million ‘lightning heist’ at bungalow
item.description:
After learning that a woman regularly hosted high-stakes poker games at her home in Singapore’s affluent Bukit Timah area, two men plotted to rob the house, recruiting a group of people from Malaysia and conducting surveillance before carrying out the plan.

Prosecutors said seven men entered the King Albert Park good class bungalow in the early hours of April 18, 2024, in a “lightning heist”, some of them armed with machetes and baseball bats. They tied up the people inside and stole about S$4.9 million (US$3.9 million) in cash, valuables and cryptocurrency.

The men then fled Singapore with the loot in two cars, crossing the border into Malaysia through the Tuas and Woodlands checkpoints in what the judge called an “audacious and well-planned” operation disrupting peace and security.
item.content:encoded:
After learning that a woman regularly hosted high-stakes poker games at her home in Singapore’s affluent Bukit Timah area, two men plotted to rob the house, recruiting a group of people from Malaysia and conducting surveillance before carrying out the plan.

Prosecutors said seven men entered the King Albert Park good class bungalow in the early hours of April 18, 2024, in a “lightning heist”, some of them armed with machetes and baseball bats. They tied up the people inside and stole about S$4.9 million (US$3.9 million) in cash, valuables and cryptocurrency.

The men then fled Singapore with the loot in two cars, crossing the border into Malaysia through the Tuas and Woodlands checkpoints in what the judge called an “audacious and well-planned” operation disrupting peace and security.

Most of the men in the group were subsequently arrested and taken back to Singapore to face prosecution. One man, 33-year-old Malaysian Muhammad Yusuf Kassim, remains at large and is believed to have left Malaysia for Thailand, court documents stated.

On Monday, the six Malaysian men pleaded guilty to various charges, including armed gang robbery and removing criminal benefits from jurisdiction. They were sentenced to jail terms of between seven years and eight months and 12 years and 11 months, along with 24 strokes of the cane for those aged below 50.

They are: Wong Chi Shan, 35; Goh Boon Tong, 30; Mohd Hamidon Ahmed, 49; Kartik Palaniappan, 34; Mohd Hashim Ismail, 51 and Muhammad Tauffiq Ahmad Fauzi, 34.

The prosecution said this was one of the highest-value robberies in Singapore, if not the highest, in nominal terms. A gold bar case in the 1970s would be higher if inflation were accounted for.

In November 2023, Wong and Goh learned that high-stakes poker games were being held at a house in the King Albert Park area, where many landed properties and good class bungalows are located.

They knew someone who had taken part in the games, court documents stated.

The games involved stakes of up to a few hundred thousand dollars, with payments settled using cryptocurrency, the court heard.

Wong and Goh visited the house and observed that the gate was left open and the wooden door unlocked during the poker game.

Several months later, in March or April 2024, Wong suggested robbing the house. But he and Goh knew they would need more people to carry out the plan.

Goh approached Hamidon, whom he had met at an event where Hamidon had provided private security. Hamidon ran his own private security firm as well as debt-collection services.

Wong and Goh met Hamidon to discuss the operation. Hamidon was to recruit men to intimidate and subdue the victims in exchange for 1.5 million ringgit (US$368,515), which would be split among his team.

Hamidon obtained a deposit of 10,000 ringgit before recruiting the others. He did not initially tell them the details of the operation but they knew it involved illegal activity.

Wong and Goh decided the robbers would wear black clothing, gloves and ski masks.

On April 15, 2024, Wong drove into Singapore via Woodlands Checkpoint and checked into a hotel. However, despite a poker game ongoing at the house, Hamidon’s team was not ready and the robbery did not take place.

Meanwhile, Hamidon’s team prepared themselves with black clothing, ski masks, gloves, duct tape and cable ties.

The following day, Wong and Goh drove past the house but found that no poker game was taking place. They instructed Hamidon’s team to remain in Johor Bahru, Malaysia.

The next night, however, a poker game was in progress.

Goh and Wong instructed Hamidon to meet them at a car park in Geylang. Hamidon and his team entered Singapore through Woodlands Checkpoint in a vehicle at about 10.45pm on April 17.

They met Wong and Goh at the car park, where they were shown photographs of the house and briefed on how to enter it. Machetes and baseball bats were placed in Hamidon’s vehicle.

Before 2.05am on April 18, 2024, the seven men drove to the house and parked outside.

Three of them were armed with machetes, while two carried baseball bats.

The men entered through the unlocked gate and main door while the poker game was still taking place.

Those in the house were:

Li Xiaoyu, a Chinese national and the hostess of the game.

Li Yang, her husband who was a tenant at the house.

Hu Zhi Peng, a Chinese national who stayed at the house and helped Li with organising the poker game.

Mo Ran, a South Korean woman hired as a card dealer.

Yap Kian Yeap, a Malaysian hired to provide massages during the poker game.

Seven poker players: Indonesian Andrew Halim, Chinese national Liu Yi and Singaporeans Macus Yap Jin Xin, Ceesvin Abraham Abdulla, Lim Yah Loon, Hoo Teng Yang and Ho Bao Qiang.

The robbers first encountered Hu, who had just exited the toilet near the main door. They pointed a machete at him and taped his mouth, wrists and ankles before telling him to sit in the toilet.

The robbers then moved into the living room and ordered the victims to put their hands in the air, lower their heads and place their phones on a table.

The victims complied. They were tied up and had their mouths taped while the robbers searched the house for valuables.

Goh and Wong checked the victims’ phones for cryptocurrency applications and discovered sizeable amounts of cryptocurrency in the hostess’ phone apps.

The group carried out cryptocurrency transfers to a wallet they controlled, emptied cash from a safe in the living room and ransacked a bedroom.

In total, this is what they took:

From Li: S$210,000 in cash, about US$40,000 in cash, S$55,500 worth of Emirati dirhams, about S$3.6 million in cryptocurrency and a Patek Philippe watch worth more than S$500,000.

From Abdulla: S$1,300 in cash and one Rolex watch worth S$55,000.

From Hoo: S$3,000 in cash and one Rolex watch worth S$55,300.

From Macus Yap: A Samsung Galaxy smartwatch worth S$452.

From Yap Kian Yeap: A Huawei watch worth S$400 and S$1,000 in cash.

From Ho: A Richard Mille watch worth S$320,000 and a Ferrari car key worth S$1,000.

‘Audacious’ armed gang robbery

The seven men then left in their vehicle for another location where they split up from Goh and Wong.

As part of their escape plan, Wong and Goh left in their car via Tuas Checkpoint at about 2.15am while the rest left via Woodlands Checkpoint in a second vehicle at about 2.40am. They arranged to regroup in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

They discarded the weapons and clothing used in the robbery along the way.

Meanwhile, the victims managed to free themselves and called the police. They sustained minor injuries from being bound.

Goh and Wong drove to Kuala Lumpur that same day, where Wong transferred about 1.1 million USDT to Goh as his share of the loot. USD Tether is a cryptocurrency pegged to the US dollar.

Goh and Wong managed to find buyers for their coins while in Kuala Lumpur, receiving 1.49 million ringgit in cash for an unspecified amount of USDT.

They handed the cash over to Hamidon and Yusuf in Kuala Lumpur as the remaining payment to Hamidon’s team in exchange for the stolen cash and valuables.

Hamidon and Yusuf gave 100,000 ringgit to two friends in Malaysia who had helped to coordinate their activities. Hamidon kept 445,000 ringgit, while Tauffiq, Hashim and Kartik each received 100,000 ringgit. Yusuf kept 645,000 ringgit, of which his share was to be 245,000 ringgit. He claimed that he would safely keep the remainder for the team.

The six Malaysian robbers were arrested in Malaysia by the Royal Malaysian Police between April 2024 and November 2024. Tauffiq was caught before he boarded a flight to Kota Kinabalu, while Goh was arrested at the airport before getting on to a plane for Japan.

Of the S$4.9 million stolen, the Singapore Police Force managed to recover only about S$1.69 million. About S$3.21 million has been lost, lead prosecutor Dillon Kok said.

Wong and Goh also pleaded guilty to other charges involving sex work by Japanese women.

Kok sought various jail terms for the six men according to their relative culpability, with Wong and Goh pegged at the highest culpability.

The jail terms sought by the prosecution range from the lower end of seven years and eight months to 13 years and one month, with 24 strokes of the cane.

Wong was represented by Don Tan, while Goh was represented by Thangavelu, Tan Jun Yin and Sugenya Manogaran. James Gomez Jovan Messiah defended Kartik, while Ariffin Sha represented Hashim. Estelle Tai represented Tauffiq, while SS Dhillon acted for Hamidon.

Gomez and Ariffin said their clients received only 100,000 ringgit each, while Tai said her client was largely kept in the dark about details of the robbery. Tan said no injuries were caused in the robbery.

Dhillon said his client Hamidon was turning 50 in the coming months but did not cause any undue delay in the matter going to court to avoid caning.

He said Hamidon had refused to prepare weapons for the robbery, instead preparing duct tape and cable ties. He was not armed at all during the robbery, the lawyer said.

Sugenya said Goh helped authorities recover about 800,000 USDT out of the 1.1 million USDT he received, which she called a substantial recovery.

In sentencing, Justice Aidan Xu said this was an “audacious and well-planned” armed gang robbery “which has disrupted the peace and security”. He said the sentence must deter any future such attempts and punish those involved.

Justice Xu said Singapore is by and large a safe country, thanks to the efforts of law enforcement agencies and members of the public.

“We expect our homes to be secure … those who disturb that peace and security … can only expect to be treated severely,” he said.

Wong and Goh were each sentenced to 12 years and 11 months’ jail, 24 strokes of the cane and a fine of S$4,000.

Hamidon was jailed for 10½ years and given 24 strokes of the cane, while Kartik and Tauffiq received seven years and eight months’ jail and 24 strokes of the cane.

Hashim, who cannot be caned due to his age, was sentenced to eight years and eight months’ jail.

For armed gang robbery, an offender can be jailed for between five and 20 years and is liable to 24 strokes of the cane.

The Attorney General’s Chambers has been contacted about whether any action has been taken against the victims for illegal gambling.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Japanese delegations flock to China, but thaw hinges on Takaichi mending ties
item.description:
With bilateral ties in a deep freeze since late last year, a flurry of planned China visits by Japanese lawmakers and business leaders has been interpreted as an attempt to break the ice ahead of November’s Apec summit in China.

However, analysts warned that these efforts to carve out a diplomatic opening with Beijing might not achieve much unless Tokyo sends a clearer signal to mend ties from the very top.

Relations reached their lowest point in a decade following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks last November that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence.
item.content:encoded:
With bilateral ties in a deep freeze since late last year, a flurry of planned China visits by Japanese lawmakers and business leaders has been interpreted as an attempt to break the ice ahead of November’s Apec summit in China.

However, analysts warned that these efforts to carve out a diplomatic opening with Beijing might not achieve much unless Tokyo sends a clearer signal to mend ties from the very top.

Relations reached their lowest point in a decade following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks last November that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence.

An eight-member cross-party delegation of junior lawmakers led by the Liberal Democratic Party’s Masahiro Takamura is visiting Beijing this week.

Meanwhile, Keidanren – Japan’s largest business lobby – and the Osaka-based Kansai Economic Federation are also planning China trips in the coming months.

Later this month, former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya will lead a high-profile delegation from the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade, which is seeking to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

These efforts are not going to lead to much unless there is a clear message from the very top – that is, the prime minister or her cabinet – to make proactive efforts to mend ties

Rintaro Nishimura, senior associate at The Asia Group

Rintaro Nishimura, a senior associate at The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, noted that Beijing probably viewed progress as requiring clearer signals from Japan’s top leadership.

“These efforts are not going to lead to much unless there is a clear message from the very top – that is, the prime minister or her cabinet – to make proactive efforts to mend ties,” he said.

“Diet members and business delegations seem to be trying to create that opening, but Beijing is also drawing a clear line between the Japanese government and other actors.”

“These successive visits are largely intended to lay the groundwork and break the ice for a potential meeting between Takaichi and Xi in November,” said Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University.

Takaichi is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen in mid-November, but whether she will secure a meeting with Xi remains uncertain.

Wang said he was sceptical about the effectiveness of the business and lawmaker visits given the depth of deterioration in China-Japan relations and the gravity of what he called Takaichi’s “erroneous remarks” on Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Wang added that it was unclear whether these delegations had received a mandate from Takaichi or her cabinet, or whether the prime minister even wanted them to visit China now.

The fragile limits of parliamentary diplomacy were exposed in late August when a group of Japanese lawmakers met Lu Kang, vice-minister of the Communist Party’s International Department.

According to a statement from the department, Lu told the delegation that history and Taiwan were at the centre of tensions between the two nations, and Tokyo needed to take “concrete actions” to improve ties.
