Lu added that he hoped Japanese politicians could urge their leadership to learn from history and handle the issue “honestly and faithfully in accordance with the one-China principle”.

Toru Horiuchi, a China-Japan relations expert at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, noted that while these visits helped keep communication channels open, Japanese lawmakers “have not been able to meet with anybody in the Chinese leadership, and business delegations so far have been rather small”.

He suggested watching who from the Chinese side would meet the delegation led by Iwaya – who is viewed as more China-friendly – as a potential sign of Beijing’s willingness to accept greater political contact with Japan.

“China still demands that Takaichi retract her remark on Taiwan and continues to put pressure on Japan,” Horiuchi said. “So as long as Japan does not compromise in some way, a major breakthrough is unlikely.”

During the 2014 Apec summit in Beijing, Shinzo Abe, Japanese prime minister at the time, had an ice-breaking meeting with Xi following a two-year freeze triggered by territorial disputes and Abe’s visit to the Yasukuni Shrine.

Before that meeting, former prime minister Yasuo Fukuda went to China on a “secret mission” to ease a rapprochement and deliver Abe’s request for dialogue.

But Wang said a similar breakthrough was out of reach today because the current rift was centred on Taiwan – a “red line” on which Beijing allows no compromise.

“Both sides lack intermediaries with sufficient political capital and a foundation of mutual trust,” he added.

According to observers, a deeper structural problem compounds the difficulties facing Beijing-Tokyo ties: a generation gap in Japan’s vital conduits to China.

Older politicians such as Yohei Kono – who died in June – and Toshihiro Nikai previously wielded considerable influence within the Liberal Democratic Party and maintained long-standing trust with Chinese counterparts.

The LDP’s former junior coalition partner Komeito, which positions itself as a party of peace and acted as a bridge between China and Japan, is no longer in government.

“The major problem we’re facing now is that as this cohort of older-generation ‘China-knowledgeable’ politicians collectively exits the political stage, the younger generation has not done a good job in maintaining continuity in communication channels,” said Wang of Fudan University, describing it as an “alarming gap”.

Nishimura noted that Japanese politicians today faced mounting domestic pressure that made China engagement politically perilous.

“With sentiment towards China souring in Japan, it is becoming increasingly challenging for lawmakers to visit China or engage with Chinese stakeholders without being seen as ‘too cosy’ with Beijing or under Beijing’s influence.”

He said this perception carried huge political costs, potentially damaging their standing within the LDP and alienating voters.

“The recent acceptance of business and Diet member delegations suggests that Beijing is keen to gauge how Tokyo is thinking about China engagement and to encourage these delegations to communicate back to Tokyo that it needs to make efforts to re-engage Beijing, not the other way around,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Brics leaders act to hedge – not revolt – against US dollar dominance
item.description:
The family photograph did the political work the summit’s final declaration could not.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi stood shoulder to shoulder as the Brics summit closed in New Delhi on Sunday – a single frame capturing an 11-nation bloc that now spans four continents and nearly half the world’s population.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres attended the gathering of emerging economies alongside World Trade Organization Director General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, New Development Bank president Dilma Rousseff and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank president Zou Jiayi.
item.content:encoded:
The family photograph did the political work the summit’s final declaration could not.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi stood shoulder to shoulder as the Brics summit closed in New Delhi on Sunday – a single frame capturing an 11-nation bloc that now spans four continents and nearly half the world’s population.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres attended the gathering of emerging economies alongside World Trade Organization Director General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, New Development Bank president Dilma Rousseff and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank president Zou Jiayi.

As Washington leans on tariffs and steps back from the institutions it once dominated, the United Nations, the WTO and the WHO sat at a table built by the Global South.

What the leaders signed – the New Delhi Declaration – was neither a revolt against the dollar nor a blueprint for a new world order. It was a hedge.

Experts say the document treats de-dollarisation as insurance. By promoting local-currency settlement, linked payment rails and a louder voice within the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, Brics members aim to ensure trade keeps moving even if the United States turns its dollar, or the institutions around it, into a political weapon.

“As we move irreversibly to a multipolar world, all countries must work to strengthen and safeguard a multilateral system that delivers for all with the United Nations at its centre,” Guterres told the summit.

Multipolarity, he said, required “reforming multilateral institutions, including the UN Security Council and the Bretton Woods system, to reflect the world of today”.

“From Gaza, to the broader crisis in the Middle East, to Ukraine, Sudan and beyond, our world needs peace.”

Brics finance ministers and central bank governors had already set the economic demand. Before the summit they called for quota changes at the IMF, a bigger voice for emerging economies at the World Bank, and leadership contests not locked to the West.

“We reiterate the urgent need to reform the Bretton Woods Institutions to enhance their legitimacy,” their joint statement said.

India closed the door on the idea of a common Brics currency – a door US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to slam.

“There is no proposal in the Brics for a Brics currency, as of now,” Sudhakar Dalela, India’s Brics sherpa, told reporters on Saturday.

He added that local-currency settlement was “a practical mechanism to reduce transaction cost in bilateral trade” and had been “encouraged as complementary to the global payment and settlement system”.

The declaration sent the Brics Payment Task Force back to work on interoperable payment and messaging channels and on settling trade in members’ own currencies, “acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach”.

Chinese scholars who follow the grouping describe a double movement: press the old institutions to make space, and build parallel machinery in case they do not.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, pointed out that “dissatisfaction with the US-led international order” was one of the key reasons Brics was established.

Members were seeking both to reform the existing system and to build new mechanisms. Liu said moves towards a Brics payment system and greater use of national currencies were “especially driven by the constraints imposed by the US dollar-dominated financial system, particularly on countries such as Russia and Iran”.

“These measures will gradually change the international financial system and enhance the strategic autonomy of Brics countries,” Liu said.

Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies said these efforts were easy to misread. “I’d say it’s less about de-dollarisation, since much of their trade will continue to be denominated in dollars, and more to do with lessening the capacity for dollar weaponisation,” he said.

Invoices can stay in dollars. Gupta said payment itself could move to infrastructure over which the US Treasury did not have jurisdiction, such as a network of correspondent banks, and be “routed amongst themselves but outside the plumbing of the dollar-based system.”

The secondary aim is slower. Members want to “build out their own local currencies-based trading and settling directly with counterparts”, he said. “But this process will take a much longer time. That’s where central bank digital currencies come in too, at a later date.”

According to Gupta, the nearer-term prize is more precise: “Transact in dollars, and instantaneously, while sitting outside the back office market infrastructure that is an essential basis of the dollar’s centrality, and via which Treasury can flex its jurisdictional powers.”

That infrastructure is why the dollar is more than a unit of account. Cross-border dollar payments still run, in large part, through correspondent banks, the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (Swift) messaging network and US-centred clearing.

After 2022, Russia learned what happens when those channels close. Iran has lived with that constraint for far longer. Other Brics members have watched tariffs and secondary sanctions and drawn the lesson without wanting to announce it.

A more public experiment is Brics Pay, developed through the Brics Business Council rather than as a finished intergovernmental system, which aims to let people pay in national currencies across member countries. It is not yet operational.

Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, was sceptical about the scale of any shift. Members had a shared interest in reducing reliance on the US dollar after facing sanctions from Washington, he said, adding that local-currency payments were moving “slowly but steadily”, though a Brics currency remained unrealistic.

“Even if local currencies are used for settlement, it would not have a major impact on the dollar system,” Lin said, because Brics’ economic power remained fragmented and its members were not sufficiently united. The work still mattered, he added, because it was strengthening members’ “strategic autonomy” and their ability to respond to US pressure.

Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South Programme at the Quincy Institute, put the retail project in that same modest frame.

“The idea is that of a decentralised system based on blockchain technology in which Brics-wide settlement will be done of transactions by, say, a Brazilian tourist paying a restaurant bill in Mumbai or a Chinese student buying a T-shirt in a store in Cape Town,” he said.

“They’ll be able to do these transactions on their phone via QR codes. It will cut out intermediary credit card companies that charge fat commissions and are typically American, and also avoid intermediate steps of dollar conversion.”

Even success would leave the core of dollar power untouched. “The system has ways to go before being adopted, with barriers present, including the question of political will,” Shidore said.

“Several Global South states don’t want to create the impression that they are trying to ‘de-dollarise’.”

“Brics Pay, even if it were fully functional, would not touch the big wholesale trade transactions between countries that matter much more to dollar usage,” Shidore said.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore is open to chemical castration, but what are ethical, health concerns?
item.description:
Singapore’s openness to chemical castration for sex offenders has cast light on the ethical questions surrounding the treatment, with the discussion centred on whether it would fill any gap left by existing legislation.

Experts point to how safeguards would be set regarding who receives the treatment, the duration of the process and if resulting medical consequences would be proportional to the offence.

The debate comes after Senior Minister and Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam’s written parliamentary reply last week, where he said Singapore was open to considering chemical castration if there was clear evidence that the measure was effective in lowering crime rates.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s openness to chemical castration for sex offenders has cast light on the ethical questions surrounding the treatment, with the discussion centred on whether it would fill any gap left by existing legislation.

Experts point to how safeguards would be set regarding who receives the treatment, the duration of the process and if resulting medical consequences would be proportional to the offence.

The debate comes after Senior Minister and Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam’s written parliamentary reply last week, where he said Singapore was open to considering chemical castration if there was clear evidence that the measure was effective in lowering crime rates.

But Shanmugam stressed that evidence around the method remained inconclusive, pointing out that the country already had “heavy penalties” in place for such crimes.

Chemical castration, also referred to as pharmacological anti-androgen treatments, involves the administration of drugs to reduce libido, compulsive sexual fantasies and capacity of sexual arousal, and is usually reversible.

Singapore recently strengthened its framework for dealing with high-risk sexual and violent offenders.

Rapists can be jailed up to 20 years, fined and caned. If the victim is aged under 14, the offender will be imprisoned for at least eight years and face a minimum of 12 strokes of the cane. Molestation is punishable with a prison term of up to three years, a fine and caning.

The Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection, which took effect on July 31, allows courts to impose minimum detention periods of between five and 20 years on serious violent or sexual offenders assessed as posing a substantial risk of reoffending. Before release, offenders undergo an updated psychiatric assessment and can remain detained if they are still considered a public threat.

Sexual drive and reoffending

The existing framework already fulfilled the objectives of punishment and keeping convicted sex offenders away from society, said Chen Siyuan, a law professor at the Singapore Management University.

Any push for chemical castration would then have to show additional benefits delivered, particularly for those deemed most likely to reoffend.

“If the objective is to target the likeliest reoffenders, then one still has to balance it against proportionality, such as whether the punishment has undue permanent effects,” Chen said.

He called for stronger medical evidence and research into whether the treatment actually served that purpose.

Reported sexual offences are on the rise in Singapore – police figures showed 261 rape cases in the first half of this year, compared with 230 during the same period last year. Molestation cases rose to 762 from 739.

But experts cautioned against assuming that suppressing sexual drive would necessarily stem reoffending.

Mervyn Cheong, an associate law professor from the National University of Singapore, said the penalty had to be balanced carefully with the existing framework. “It raises real operational and policy questions of when it should be deployed instead of, or in addition to, present custodial measures,” he said.

“Chemical castration does not map cleanly onto the four traditional pillars of deterrence, retribution, prevention and rehabilitation.”

Cheong described the treatment as “controversial” due to its punitive nature as it continued to burden offenders physiologically even after release from prison.

Medical professionals have similarly warned that although the effects of anti-androgen treatment are generally reversible, they can be substantial. Studies have linked such treatments to conditions including osteoporosis, depression and cardiovascular issues.

Tan Kok Kuan, medical director at Dr Tan Medical Centre and a specialist in men’s health, said recovery after treatment could also depend on an offender’s age and how long the drugs had been administered.

“If the patient is of advanced age when the treatment is stopped, fertility or bone strength may not return to 100 per cent,” he said.

Cheong added that policymakers would also have to consider less easily measurable consequences, including whether compulsory treatment could generate resentment or grievance among offenders and undermine rehabilitation.

For criminal lawyer Zachary Lim of IRB Law, these concerns mean any move to implement the treatment should have a far narrower threshold than simply applying chemical castration to broad categories of sexual offenders.

If introduced, he said, its use should be discretionary, preceded by medical assessment and confined to the most serious cases.

“A statutory threshold drawn any wider would be difficult to defend,” Lim said.

Other Asian countries have moved to implement the penalty, although experts note that studies on its effectiveness have been limited.

South Korea in 2011 approved its use on convicted paedophiles for a maximum period of 15 years, and later included sex offenders such as attempted rapists and offenders whose sexual crimes led to injury or the death of minors.

In 2020, Indonesia’s then president Joko Widodo signed a regulation that required offenders who inflict or threaten sexual violence against those under the age of 18 to undergo chemical castration for a maximum of two years.

In 2023, Thailand provided the treatment as an option to sex offenders in return for an early release from prison. Offenders are first evaluated by a psychiatrist and an internal medical specialist.

Human rights activists have criticised such laws for being improperly coercive, voicing concerns that inmates may be forced to choose between staying in prison and undergoing treatment. Medical professionals have also expressed concerns about side effects, such as osteoporosis, and the ability of offenders to make informed decisions.

US-based advocacy group Human Rights Watch has denounced chemical castration as a “cruel and degrading form” of corporal punishment.

Public attitudes in Singapore, meanwhile, are considerably less hesitant.

Singaporean content creator Athalie Yi, 33, said she believed medically supervised treatment should be considered if it lowered the danger posed by repeat offenders.

“I think it’s fair to also consider whether a medically supervised treatment could help reduce the risk of reoffending, especially once someone returns to society,” she said.

“The comfort and consideration afforded to convicted sexual offenders should never carry more weight than the safety and assurance we owe victims and potential victims.”

But Lim acknowledges the risk of the treatment’s wider appeal to society overtaking evidence of what it can actually achieve.

“A measure of this kind carries a symbolic weight well beyond its practical reach, and public expectations of what it can deliver should be managed carefully from the outset.”

item.title: [SCMP] US-led Luzon corridor in Philippines faces growing scrutiny over real local benefits
item.description:
While Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr was pitching the Luzon Economic Corridor to a 600-strong delegation of foreign investors and officials last week, protesters outside were clashing with police, accusing the US-backed initiative of exploiting the country’s resources.

The backlash mirrored opposition against the Pax Silica AI supply chain drive – a separate proposal but again, American-led. It underscored mounting tension over the ambitious corridor, since expanded from a transport and logistics project into development plans for energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing.

Analysts say the pushback does not necessarily signal a wider rejection of Washington in a country where public trust in the US remains relatively strong. But the latest stirrings point to scepticism over local benefit from such foreign investments.
item.content:encoded:
While Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr was pitching the Luzon Economic Corridor to a 600-strong delegation of foreign investors and officials last week, protesters outside were clashing with police, accusing the US-backed initiative of exploiting the country’s resources.

The backlash mirrored opposition against the Pax Silica AI supply chain drive – a separate proposal but again, American-led. It underscored mounting tension over the ambitious corridor, since expanded from a transport and logistics project into development plans for energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing.

Analysts say the pushback does not necessarily signal a wider rejection of Washington in a country where public trust in the US remains relatively strong. But the latest stirrings point to scepticism over local benefit from such foreign investments.

The inaugural Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum on Thursday and Friday at the Grand Hyatt Hotel in Bonifacio Global City was sponsored by the US Trade and Development Authority and co-hosted by the Philippines, the United States and Japan – countries that had announced the initiative during a summit in 2024.

Tensions erupted outside the venue, with human rights group Karapatan claiming that over two dozen supporters were injured and five paralegals arrested while protesting against what the group called a “US-backed open house for the plunder of Philippine resources”.

Initially envisioned as a project linking three main ports and two international airports across four cities on the main island of Luzon, the corridor is now also drawing investments in energy, digital systems, cybersecurity, shipbuilding and advanced manufacturing.

Marcos said in his speech that it had drawn “wider support” from other like-minded nations. Canada, Australia, Denmark, France, Italy, South Korea, Sweden and the United Kingdom pledged support in May while Spain and the EU announced their participation at the forum.

“This growing interest reflects confidence in the Philippines as a reliable partner and an attractive destination for long-term investment,” the president said. “Across all these sectors, our goal is not simply to attract investment. We want investment that strengthens our economy and expands Filipino capability.”

The protesters also rallied against the proposed Pax Silica hub, a 1,620-hectare (4,000-acre) industrial zone that will sit in New Clark City, part of the Luzon Economic Corridor.

Pax Silica is a US-led coalition aimed at countering Chinese dominance in critical supply chains such as AI and semiconductors. The Philippines and Singapore are the only Southeast Asian countries to join the 13-member bloc. It has seen online backlash due to concerns over resource extraction and the widespread displacement of farmers and indigenous communities.

Younger dissent

Net trust among Filipinos for the US, though, remains “good”, according to Pollster Social Weather Stations. The June survey of 1,200 Filipinos found that 60 per cent were still positive about the US compared with 18 per cent who voiced distrust.

Dissent towards the two US-led projects likely came from Gen Z, experts said.

Sonny Africa, executive director of Manila-based non-profit think tank IBON Foundation, called the backlash “extremely significant politically”.

“They show that reported positive views of the US don’t translate into public acceptance of every US economic or military initiative, and that the public is receptive to seeing these for what they really are beyond predictably glowing US and Philippine government hype,” Africa said.

“If this leads to greater understanding of US historical dominance of the Philippines and of worsening global US economic and military aggression today, the Pax Silica protests could eventually snowball into a generalised anti-American turn.”

Online access allowed people to decide for themselves. “Reports on the displacement of indigenous peoples strengthen the sense that these projects are more exploitative than beneficial,” said Gino Trinidad, a political science instructor at Ateneo de Manila University.

“It does not help that a considerable number of Filipinos – especially the youth – have had access to reports of how the building of data centres in the US and elsewhere have contributed to the depleting of natural resources and polluting of water.”

A Momentum Research survey of 1,487 Filipinos from August 18 to 23 found that while 33.9 per cent decried the Pax Silica project, opposition was highest among Gen Z compared with others at 43.2 per cent, with adequate power and water supply for data centre operations topping their concerns.

Gen Z Filipinos were also the most concerned about environmental effects and the displacement of farming and indigenous folk, the polling firm said.

“For a country that has locations still facing problems of accessing potable water, the potential ill-effects of the initiatives become harder to ignore,” Trinidad said.

While initiatives such as the Luzon Economic Corridor promise “1 million jobs” for Filipinos, their critics are sceptical that these would provide higher value for the country and offset resource exploitation.

“My sense is that the main promise of these initiatives is job creation … Jobs will indeed be created, but what kinds and if these jobs are high-value are questions that must be addressed clearly,” Trinidad said, pointing out that Central Luzon was already in the top three regions for total gross domestic product.

“The level and potential effects of the exploitation of the Philippines’ natural resources by these projects should be clearly addressed. Furthermore, the redistributive potential of such projects must be scrutinised. Will these projects really lead to a more equitable distribution of economic growth?”

‘Minor’ benefits

Africa called the expected benefits for the Philippines “shallow, minor and incidental at best if the overriding logic of the initiatives is another country’s strategic purposes”.

“There will be construction activity, some foreign-oriented infrastructure with limited domestic use, and perhaps some foreign-owned mineral processing aside from how the government can report additional exports, jobs and foreign investment,” he said. “However, there is not likely to be much in terms of the Filipino firms, technology, profits and strategic productive capacity that constitute real Philippine industrial development.”

US desire for technological dominance in semiconductors and AI would result in the Philippines staying in its “subordinate role in US-led value semiconductor chains”, Africa said, adding that it had been the case for decades despite billions of dollars in investments by American firms.

“There’s also the opportunity cost. Philippine infrastructure, minerals and public resources will be directed towards the requirements of US semiconductor, AI and military supply chains instead of the country’s own national industrialisation and development priorities.”

He warned that increased economic dependence on the US “becomes another mechanism to reinforce strategic alignment with the US, while excluding potentially productive relations with countries the US seeks to isolate such as China”.

“National industrialisation and development is difficult enough as it is without these major external constraints,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Are Chinese students learning English just to ‘tell China’s story’?
item.description:
For generations of Chinese schoolchildren, English textbooks offered a glimpse of an unfamiliar world, from London’s Tower Bridge and Big Ben to American school life and Halloween traditions.

Today, students opening an English textbook are more likely to encounter passages on late Qing dynasty (1644-1912) thinker Liang Qichao, the Dragon Boat Festival and China’s overseas aid projects.

These changes are part of a nationwide overhaul of China’s primary and middle-school textbooks, which have shifted their focus towards Chinese culture and “telling China’s story” of national achievements, sparking debate over the purpose of English education in China.
item.content:encoded:
For generations of Chinese schoolchildren, English textbooks offered a glimpse of an unfamiliar world, from London’s Tower Bridge and Big Ben to American school life and Halloween traditions.

Today, students opening an English textbook are more likely to encounter passages on late Qing dynasty (1644-1912) thinker Liang Qichao, the Dragon Boat Festival and China’s overseas aid projects.

These changes are part of a nationwide overhaul of China’s primary and middle-school textbooks, which have shifted their focus towards Chinese culture and “telling China’s story” of national achievements, sparking debate over the purpose of English education in China.

The revised textbooks – which have been introduced in stages since 2024 and were fully rolled out at the start of this year’s autumn semester – have dropped much of the content on foreign cultures found in older editions as Beijing seeks to align education more closely with national priorities, including strengthening patriotism and boosting China’s image overseas.

The changes have been praised by some parents and teachers who argue they will boost students’ cultural confidence, while others worry that they will limit children’s exposure to the wider world and undermine their English proficiency.

Integrating Chinese cultural content into English courses was a growing education trend, state news agency Xinhua wrote in April 2025.

The changes are reflected throughout primary and middle-school textbooks. Lessons place a strong emphasis on traditional festivals, Chinese historical figures, archaeological discoveries and the country’s modern economic, social and technological developments, according to teachers and Chinese media reports.

The textbooks also introduce contemporary government policies, such as the idea of a “new socialist countryside” and the goal of building a “community of a shared future for mankind”.

“I’ve been waiting for this change for many years,” a veteran English teacher wrote on social media.

“Learning a language has never been just about the language itself. It is about learning how to use it to engage with the world. In the past, we learned to ‘listen to others’. Now we are finally learning to ‘speak for ourselves’.”

Many others questioned whether the shift had gone too far.

“There’s simply too much Chinese culture, ideological content and local elements in today’s English textbooks,” said another English teacher with a decade of experience.

“We all agree that building confidence in Chinese culture is absolutely a good thing,” the teacher wrote.

“But at its core, language learning is about entering other cultures, understanding different ways of thinking and seeing a diverse world.”

The teacher argued that the generations who grew up using the older textbooks were not “eroded” by foreign cultures.

They added that without exposure to foreign cultures and customs, students could struggle to develop a sense of curiosity about the language. Without any novelty, they said, studying English could easily become dull and formulaic.

Some teachers criticised the new textbooks for turning English lessons into nothing more than “exercises in translating Chinese culture into English”.

They said China needed people who could use English to present its culture to the world, but using a foreign language to express ideas and content already familiar to students could undermine the point of learning it in the first place.

Some also noted that parts of the new textbooks were in “Chinglish”, saying students were learning how to fit Chinese ways of thinking into English sentences rather than developing more natural ways of expressing themselves in English.

But while teachers debate the impact on language learning, Beijing’s top leadership has made clear that political direction takes priority.

The latest high-level signal on textbooks and ideology came last week when senior officials at a national conference called for building a “high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics”.

Speaking at the conference last Tuesday, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang highlighted the “political, people-centred and strategic” nature of education and said textbooks should have the “correct political direction and value orientation”.

The textbook overhaul is part of a broader national push to promote “cultural confidence”, a term used by President Xi Jinping to describe a belief in the value and vitality of Chinese culture.

In 2016, Xi described the essential “Four Confidences” – confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The formulation was later added to the Communist Party’s constitution.

The push to strengthen patriotic education and cultural identity building in schools has been solidified through successive policies.

In 2020, the Ministry of Education announced a ban on foreign-published textbooks in primary and junior high schools.

The approach was given legal backing in 2023, when the Patriotic Education Law required patriotic education to be incorporated into different subjects and textbooks, stressing the importance of preserving and developing China’s traditional culture.

What kind of identity is being shaped by textbooks is especially sensitive in China’s ethnic minority areas. In 2021, the former head of the Xinjiang education department was handed a suspended death sentence for his role in writing and publishing a number of school textbooks that were deemed “problematic” by the local authorities for encouraging “separatist thoughts”.

The education ministry began to revise textbooks in March 2022, following the release of a new national plan for the compulsory education curriculum.

The new textbooks were rolled out in stages from autumn 2024, beginning with primary grade one and middle-school grade seven. The roll-out expanded in 2025 to primary grades two and three and middle-school grade eight, before covering all primary and middle-school grades this autumn.

Supporters of the revisions argue that the shift is intended to correct a long-standing imbalance.

“Over an extremely long period in the past, our foreign-language textbooks, including English textbooks, were seriously lacking in content on China’s fine traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture,” said Dong Hongdan, an education ministry official, according to the 2025 Xinhua report.

English was particularly well suited to carrying out patriotic and cultural education, he said.

“If we want Chinese culture to reach the world, we first need to use language and forms of expression that others can understand to tell China’s stories well,” he said.

On social media, one teacher warned that a child who studied English without learning about the cultures of English-speaking countries might end up with “not cultural confidence, but a closed sense of self”.

“English textbooks should first and foremost be a bridge,” the teacher said. “Students need to learn to understand the world before they can truly speak to it.”

“Good English education,” they added, “is not about telling students what we already have, but showing them what else the world has to offer.”

item.title: [SCMP] Man up, break down: unpacking the Philippines’ male suicide crisis
item.description:
Richardson Mojica is no stranger to thoughts of ending it all. The 40-year-old university professor and mental health advocate was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and depression in his early 20s.

He finds fulfilment in his job, yet suicidal ideation has always lingered.

“We call it passively suicidal – you don’t want to live, but you don’t want to stop everything,” he said, revealing that he had survived a self-inflicted attempt on his life months ago.
item.content:encoded:
Richardson Mojica is no stranger to thoughts of ending it all. The 40-year-old university professor and mental health advocate was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and depression in his early 20s.

He finds fulfilment in his job, yet suicidal ideation has always lingered.

“We call it passively suicidal – you don’t want to live, but you don’t want to stop everything,” he said, revealing that he had survived a self-inflicted attempt on his life months ago.

Survival is a daily discipline: continuous medication, regular therapy, psychiatrist check-ins and a support network he has learned to lean on.

But seeking help meant confronting stigma – first at age 23 following a panic attack at work, then for years afterwards as he kept his condition to himself.

Eventually, he told his family, but he found it difficult. “I’m the eldest son, so it wasn’t easy for me to be vulnerable in front of them, to cry in front of them,” he said.

Mojica’s experience is emblematic of a wider struggle among men in the Philippines.

Around 80 per cent of the country’s suicide deaths are men, according to the World Health Organization, and two in five are among those aged 15 to 29. The Philippine Statistics Authority recorded 3,379 deaths from intentional self-harm in 2024, up from 3,133 in 2023.

Studies consistently showed men were less likely than women to seek help for mental health concerns, said Kristine Faith Moral, a clinical psychologist at Ateneo de Manila University.

“This is also reflected in the ratio of men vs women who inquire about my professional services,” she said. “Even more so among those who eventually push through with seeking help.”

Rigid expectations around masculinity, such as being self-reliant, could act as barriers, Moral warned.

If the expectation is that a man should be the one who solves problems, then asking for help can itself feel like a failure

Kristine Faith Moral, clinical psychologist

Mental health professionals say women actually attempt suicide more often, but more men die by suicide because they use more lethal methods.

“This is one possible way of understanding what is sometimes referred to as the gender paradox in suicidology: women tend to report suicidal ideation and suicide attempts more frequently, while men are more likely to die by suicide,” Moral said.

“This does not mean men necessarily experience less psychological distress. Rather, there may be differences in how distress is understood and expressed.”

Yves Miel Zuniga, co-founder of civil society organisation #MentalHealthPH, agreed.

“Suicide is a preventable public health issue,” he said. “But we should be careful about reducing it to the idea that it’s simply because men don’t talk about their feelings … there’s no single explanation for why someone dies by suicide.”

‘Boys don’t cry’

Cultural expectations rooted in gender norms shape how men perceive mental health, advocates say.

Moral said this largely came down to how boys were socialised, reinforced by media depictions of masculinity.

“From a very young age, boys may receive messages that discourage vulnerability, such as ‘boys don’t cry’ … they may be told to ‘suck it up’ or ‘man up’,” she said.

Zuniga warned against treating Filipino men as “one homogeneous group”, noting that gender only added to the complexity of suicide.

Supposedly “masculine” traits such as resilience and self-reliance only became problematic when they were interpreted to mean men should suffer alone, he said, adding that the affordability and accessibility of mental health services was another major issue.

Moral argued that underlying stressors – financial difficulties, work pressures or relationship troubles – could be similar for both men and women.

“Gender expectations can influence the meaning they attach to those experiences and the ways they believe they are allowed to cope,” she said.

Much of that conditioning begins at home, according to Moral.

“Filipino family expectations can be particularly potent drivers of behaviour,” she said, adding that many men were expected to take on the role of provider, protector and problem solver.

“If the expectation is that a man should be the one who solves problems, then asking for help can itself feel like a failure to fulfil that role.”

Losing a job could therefore become more than a financial setback, Moral said. It could challenge a man’s sense of self-worth “particularly when his identity is strongly tied to being a provider or someone who is supposed to have things under control”.

Mojica knows that feeling of vulnerability, sharpened by the social stigma associated with mental health struggles.

“As a man, I think what bothered me was saying it out loud, telling people that I have this condition and letting everybody know,” he said. “Being vulnerable in public, being vulnerable to a lot of people and showing that I am weak, for a certain period of time, when these things happen … when I need to breathe, I need to cry, it’s hard.”

Where change begins

Advocates advise against trying to lecture men out of their instincts, saying what they need instead are peer groups where they can speak plainly to others facing similar struggles.

For Zuniga, a lot has changed in the Philippines over the past decade or so, but much work still needs to be done.

Depression used to be “perceived as being dramatic” rather than a public health issue, he said – reflecting progress, even as stigma and problems with cost and access to care remained.

Filipino culture was capable of silencing men, but also protecting them, Zuniga said.

“Research on help-seeking behaviour among Filipinos shows social support is very important, and Filipinos frequently turn to friends or family before formally entering the mental healthcare system,” he said.

“So the question is: how do we make sure we have a society where Filipino men feel safe enough to speak, and know they’ll be taken seriously?”

Moral’s answer is not to strip away the values that men hold dear, but to build upon them.

“For many Filipino men, being a provider, protector or someone their family can depend on can be deeply tied to their identity,” she said.

The goal was “to show that being strong and dependable can also include knowing when to ask for help”, Moral added.

“Allowing yourself to be cared for and being emotionally present … it needs to start somewhere.”

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] Why AI experts are ‘freaked out’ over safety fears ahead of Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China.

The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg.
item.content:encoded:
A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China.

The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg.

OpenAI may coordinate the slowdown with other leading AI laboratories, though some firms may decline to participate, the report said, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Altman’s remarks underscored a growing reckoning in Silicon Valley over the risks of rapid AI advancement.

[Industry leaders are] racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives

Jacob Coxon, former OpenAI researcher

Paul Christiano, a prominent AI safety researcher who recently joined OpenAI’s non-profit board to serve on its safety and security committee, warned on Thursday of a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term” based on the current trajectory of the technology.

In a Thursday post on X that drew more than 1.5 million views and 10,000 likes, OpenAI safety team member Julie Steele wrote in a personal capacity: “I also think we need to slow down.”

Steele cited a viral post from former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon, who said earlier this week that he had resigned from Anthropic because both industry leaders were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.

Political momentum is also building. US Senator Bernie Sanders pledged on Thursday to introduce legislation to “pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether”.

Safety alarms intensify at US labs

The urgency behind these warnings has been heightened by growing security breaches and monitoring difficulties across the industry.

Anthropic said on Wednesday that an early version of its flagship Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorised access to a third-party computer system during testing in January. The incident, which went undetected during a previous company-wide audit, marks the fourth time an Anthropic model has breached security boundaries.

Meanwhile, OpenAI said last week that GPT-6 Astra – its first model to reach what it called a “critical” level of cybersecurity capabilities – was harder to monitor than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol.

If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents

Ben Hayum, Centre for a New American Security

Security analysts warned that as models became more capable, developers could be sacrificing internal visibility for performance.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said AI labs in both the US and China faced intense market incentives to push boundaries, “even if this means diminishing control or legibility”.

Theo Bearman, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, cautioned that cutting back on chain-of-thought monitoring could trigger a “race-to-the-bottom dynamic” across the industry.

Ben Hayum, a research assistant for the Technology and National Security Programme at the Centre for a New American Security, said: “The fact that the Hugging Face incident happened, and then right afterwards, [OpenAI is] releasing a model that’s harder to monitor – that’s why so many people are freaked out.”

He added that if “substantial gains in internal processing continue without external visibility, AI model alignment becomes a lot harder from the get-go in terms of creating a safe model”.

Analysts also warned of heightened risks as labs pursue recursive self-improvement, a milestone where AI models autonomously build and refine their own successors in an accelerating feedback loop.

“If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents,” Hayum said.

“These are national security threats to America, China and the globe.”

However, pushback against calls to slow down remains fierce, driven by fears of ceding ground to Beijing.

Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham argued on X on Thursday that if China held the lead in AI, researchers would not have the freedom to sound public alarms about potential threats.

Others contended that America’s current lead provided a buffer for a pause.

“Given how far behind China is on compute and how dependent Chinese progress is on US capabilities, pacing AI progress in America would not immediately concede the lead,” said Konstantin Pilz, co-founder of Centre for Technology and Statecraft, on social media.

Pre-summit tensions heighten

The safety concerns come at a delicate time for diplomatic relations between Washington and Beijing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lead bilateral talks on AI governance ahead of Xi’s visit to Washington later this month, with agenda items expected to include joint frameworks for monitoring AI-driven cyber threats.

Speaking in Dallas, Texas, on Tuesday, Bessent accused Chinese developers of freeloading on US breakthroughs through model distillation, a common industry technique where smaller AI systems are trained using outputs from larger ones.

“The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation,” Bessent said. “So, the Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us.”

On the same day, three US federal agencies accused major Chinese developers – including DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding, Moonshot AI and Z.ai – of conducting aggressive, large-scale distillation “likely with Chinese government awareness”.

China’s Ministry of Commerce on Wednesday called the accusations factually and legally groundless, accusing Washington of using safety and intellectual property concerns to consolidate computing power and maintain a technological monopoly.

Anthropic on Thursday said in a report that Chinese AI companies DeepSeek and MoonShot re-routed users’ queries to Claude, passing off the generated answers as output from their own models.

Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

item.title: [SCMP] Openness must not be sacrificed in US science and tech policy on China
item.description:
When President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his planned September 24 visit – his first state-level visit to Washington in more than a decade – artificial intelligence is expected to be near the top of the agenda. Both administrations are preparing for their first formal dialogue on AI.

Washington has framed much of that conversation around the need for tighter controls on sensitive technologies. That framing is the problem.

For much of the debate over US science and technology policy towards China, Washington has been stuck on a false choice between engagement (scientific exchange, international students and collaborative research) and security (export controls, research restrictions and visa limits). The real choice is between indiscriminate restriction and disciplined risk management.
item.content:encoded:
When President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his planned September 24 visit – his first state-level visit to Washington in more than a decade – artificial intelligence is expected to be near the top of the agenda. Both administrations are preparing for their first formal dialogue on AI.

Washington has framed much of that conversation around the need for tighter controls on sensitive technologies. That framing is the problem.

For much of the debate over US science and technology policy towards China, Washington has been stuck on a false choice between engagement (scientific exchange, international students and collaborative research) and security (export controls, research restrictions and visa limits). The real choice is between indiscriminate restriction and disciplined risk management.

The security concerns are genuine. Some advanced technologies have clear military or intelligence applications. Universities must take seriously undisclosed affiliations, conflicts of commitment and improper technology transfer. Federal research security policy already requires extensive disclosure of appointments, foreign support, affiliations and potential conflicts of interest and commitment. Advanced computing, semiconductors, quantum science, biotechnology and AI all raise legitimate national security questions, largely because so much of the work is dual-use[end optional trim.

But acknowledging those risks does not require treating every interaction with China as equally dangerous. The challenge is to protect what truly matters without damaging the openness that has long been one of America’s greatest scientific strengths.

Smart openness starts from a simple premise: technologies are not equally sensitive and not every Chinese institution carries the same risk. Military-relevant quantum sensing is not cooperation in basic mathematics or astrophysics. A researcher who conceals ties to a defence laboratory has little in common with a Chinese graduate student studying theoretical chemistry.

Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing.

Policy too often blurs those distinctions. Once national security becomes the primary lens for nearly every scientific interaction with China, agencies and universities turn deeply risk-averse. Restrictions spread, compliance burdens grow and institutions abandon perfectly legal activities because they look politically risky.

The result can be self-defeating: measures meant to protect American technological leadership can erode elements of the research system that produce it. Research Caroline Wagner and I conducted for the Quincy Institute has argued that a more sustainable approach would distinguish genuine security risks from ordinary international scientific collaboration, rather than treat broad categories of China-related activity as inherently suspect.

American pre-eminence in science was built in substantial part on imported knowledge and talent. The National Science Board reports that foreign-born workers accounted for 43 per cent of the US science and engineering workforce at the doctorate level in 2021; among foreign-born science and engineering workers, China is one of the two leading countries of origin.

Chinese students and researchers have made tangible contributions to American science and technology. China has also gained substantially from its access to the US research ecosystem, and concerns about technology transfer are well founded. Policy has to hold both facts at once.

Washington should begin by defining critical technologies more narrowly and updating those definitions regularly. Controls should focus on identifiable capabilities with plausible national security consequences, not on sprawling categories like “AI” or “biotechnology.” A “small yard, high fence” approach works only if the yard stays small.

The government should also build a genuinely tiered framework for international research collaboration. The most sensitive technologies, and institutions closely tied to China’s military and security apparatus, warrant heightened scrutiny or outright prohibition. Dual-use research should proceed under disclosure rules, access controls and institutional review. Fundamental research outside those categories should remain open.

Washington should move away from nationality-based screening as well. Visa and research-access decisions should turn on affiliations, research fields, access to controlled information and disclosure records – not on citizenship or country of birth. A Chinese passport is not evidence of a security threat.

Universities receiving substantial federal funding should maintain serious research-security capabilities, conduct due diligence on sensitive collaborations and enforce disclosure requirements. In return, universities need clearer and more consistent federal rules. Institutions should not be punished after the fact because a government assessment shifted.

Washington also needs a firmer distinction between disclosure violations and espionage. Researchers who hide material foreign affiliations or funding should face consequences. But a disclosure failure is not by itself proof of illicit technology transfer.

The United States should treat talent attraction as a national security asset. Foreign students who earn advanced American degrees in important scientific and engineering fields deserve clearer pathways to stay, subject to appropriate screening. It makes little strategic sense to educate exceptional people, then push them to build their careers elsewhere.

The importance of this talent pool is particularly evident in advanced science and engineering: more than half of doctorate-level computer and mathematical scientists and engineers working in the US were born abroad. In the competition for scientific talent, the ability to attract and retain such researchers is one of America’s most important structural advantages.

Finally, major restrictions should face a competitiveness test. Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing.

The competition runs deeper than technology. It is a contest over where the world’s best scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs choose to build their careers, and openness remains a decisive American advantage. Access to China’s talent pool has real strategic value.

The US does not have to choose between security and openness, though it does have to get better at both. A good place to start is by re-energising the US-China Science and Technology Cooperation Agreement, revised and extended for five years in December 2024. The amended agreement already comes close to the model we need: it limits government-to-government cooperation to basic research while adding stronger safeguards concerning national security, intellectual property, transparency, data reciprocity, and researcher safety and security.

Rather than retreat from scientific engagement, Washington should build on it, drawing sharper lines around genuinely sensitive technologies while preserving room for collaboration where the risks are manageable.

The measure of a successful China policy is not how many doors America can close. It is whether the country can protect what needs protecting without sacrificing the openness, international talent and collaboration that have long been among its greatest sources of strength.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s shrinking population may be a blessing, not a curse
item.description:
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.

But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.

While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.
item.content:encoded:
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.

But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.

While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.

The reaction was swift and familiar: China will grow old before it grows rich, its workforce will hollow out, its pension system will buckle, its ascent will end.

Some concerns are warranted. If 2.1 children per woman is the population replacement rate, then those countries with the lowest birth rates – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.6, and South Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to experience population declines of 20-30 per cent relative to 2023; their share of the population aged 65 and over to reach 30-40 per cent; and older workers (aged 45 and over) to comprise 60 per cent of the labour force.

But that’s not the whole story. In fact, much of it is missing, and the alarm has outrun the analysis. “What if the historical evidence tells us that collapsing birth rates, paradoxically, are good for the economy,” economist Joeri Schasfoort asks in his YouTube channel, “because they force companies to innovate?”

He was referring to a groundbreaking paper, “Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy”, which was published in July by the National Bureau of Economic Research in the United States and has attracted widespread interest in academic and policymaking circles.

The four economists – Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne and Andrew Scott – studied seven decades of demographic change across more than 100 countries and 722 American local labour markets. They find that countries where birth rates fell earlier and further did not grow more slowly. Rather, they grew faster per head, and total output did not decline.

Something is compensating for the missing hands. The authors argue that it’s technology

“Contrary to the widespread expectation that these trends hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings,” they wrote.

They found that these patterns could not be explained by educational upgrading and other likely factors. Rather, they reflected “the endogenous, labour-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers”.

The size of the effect is striking. A country with a birth rate one percentage point lower in 1950 saw income per working-age adult roughly a quarter higher 50 years later, or about half a percentage point (0.46 per cent) of additional growth every year, compounding across two generations. The same pattern appears in American regions, measured through wages.

There is an obvious mathematical objection: the same output divided among fewer workers naturally produces a higher figure per worker. But the study finds no meaningful decline in total output either. Something is compensating for the missing hands.

The authors argue that it’s technology. When young workers become scarce and expensive, employers buy machines. Economies with falling birth rates register faster productivity growth, heavier investment in equipment, a shift of employment from labour-intensive industries towards research-intensive ones, and more patenting in automation. The productivity gains are large enough to offset the lost labour entirely.

The most persuasive test uses the second world war. Military casualties fell overwhelmingly on young men; civilian casualties fell across all ages. Fifty years later, countries that lost population to civilian deaths were poorer per head. Those that lost young men were measurably richer. It is not population loss that damages an economy, but the wrong kind of it.

As the economists wrote: “Exploiting cross-country variation in WWII military and civilian deaths, we find that declines in younger population, rather than population size per se, drive our results [of productivity and growth].”

China’s record is consistent with this. It does not have a labour shortage; rather the opposite. Youth unemployment reached 17.9 per cent in July as a record 12.7 million graduates entered the market. That is an argument for patience rather than panic: the cohorts that will genuinely be scarce are yet to come.

Its factories installed 295,000 industrial robots in 2024 – 54 per cent of the global total – bringing the operational stock past two million units, the largest anywhere. Robot density rose 17 per cent in a single year, and Chinese manufacturers outsold foreign suppliers at home for the first time. That’s 166 robots per 10,000 employees, according to China’s statistics bureau. Robotics, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing sit at the centre of the 15th five-year plan. The economy grew by 5 per cent last year on a record trade surplus.

None of these neglect genuine problems. The state pension fund for urban workers may be exhausted by the middle of the next decade. In 2023, 11 of 31 provinces were running deficits. But that is a question of who pays, not whether the wealth exists. If output holds steady while the workforce shrinks, the resources are there. Moving them from prosperous coastal provinces to depleted industrial ones is a political task, not a demographic one.

The researchers themselves are cautious. The decline in China, they note, will be faster and larger than anything in their data, and their evidence for the technological mechanism is indirect. Or, as Schasfoort has observed, their findings describe the past and may not predict the future.

However, that caution cuts both ways. The pessimistic case rests entirely on projections. The optimistic case rests on what has actually occurred across 70 years and most of the world.

China now contemplates spending an estimated 180 billion yuan (US$26.76 billion) this year alone to lift the birth rate – subsidies, free preschool, funded fertility treatment. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore have all tried variations of this, with more generous provisions and greater personal freedom. All have failed.

The focus should be on preparing for a smaller, older, more automated workforce than trying to get women to have more babies when most other socio-economic factors cause them to have fewer or no children.

Demography is not destiny. Beijing should focus on fighting the right war – advancing technology on all fronts.

item.title: [SCMP] For China, H-6N bomber enhances nuclear deterrence and second-strike capability
item.description:
Last month, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) released footage showing its H-6N bomber flying with a nuclear-capable Jing Lei-1 (JL-1) air-launched ballistic missile (ALBM), offering a rare look at China’s airborne nuclear strike capability.

The H-6N is one of the latest modernised variants of the H-6, the country’s only strategic bomber. Its flight carrying the ALBM during a joint anti-ship exercise was featured in a documentary by state broadcaster CCTV for the PLA’s 99th anniversary.

The unveiling comes as China expands the scope of its H-6 bombers’ activities beyond its nearby airspace.
item.content:encoded:
Last month, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) released footage showing its H-6N bomber flying with a nuclear-capable Jing Lei-1 (JL-1) air-launched ballistic missile (ALBM), offering a rare look at China’s airborne nuclear strike capability.

The H-6N is one of the latest modernised variants of the H-6, the country’s only strategic bomber. Its flight carrying the ALBM during a joint anti-ship exercise was featured in a documentary by state broadcaster CCTV for the PLA’s 99th anniversary.

The unveiling comes as China expands the scope of its H-6 bombers’ activities beyond its nearby airspace.

In July 2024, two H-6s were spotted conducting joint patrol near Alaska for the first time with their Russian counterpart, the Tu-95, prompting the US-Canadian North American Aerospace Defence Command to scramble their fighter jets.

For the past six decades, the H-6 has served as Beijing’s primary strategic strike aircraft. With the JL-1 ALBM able to be mounted on the H-6N bomber, China is now considered to have completed its nuclear triad, boosting its nuclear deterrence and second-strike capability.

History and development

Manufactured by the Xian Aircraft Industrial Corporation, the H-6’s design is based on the Soviet-made Tu-16 strategic heavy bomber, one of the earliest Soviet jet bombers, developed in 1952.

Beijing began licensing production of the Soviet-made warplane after it signed an agreement with Moscow in 1957 to acquire components and manufacturing data to make the Tu-16, later designated as H-6, in China.

In 1959, the first Chinese-assembled Soviet Tu-16 bomber conducted its maiden flight and was transferred to the PLA.

However, following the Sino-Soviet split in the 1960s, Beijing had to independently build the H-6 without the Soviet Union’s help.

After encountering significant delays in the first years of the Cultural Revolution, China’s first fully domestically produced H-6 bomber made its maiden flight in December 1968.

Since the aircraft’s inception, China has produced more than 230 H-6 bombers, with modernised variants remaining in production. It also exported the bomber to Egypt and Iraq. Iraq deployed its fleet during the first Iran-Iraq war.

During the 1991 Gulf war, Iraq’s entire H-6 fleet was destroyed on the ground by US-led coalition forces. Egypt retired its H-6 fleet in 2000.

China’s variants of the H-6 have served in various roles. Among those currently in service in the PLA with recent upgrades are the H-6K and H-6N with the air force and the H-6J with the navy.

The H-6K, known as the “god of war”, and the naval variant H-6J are conventional bombers, responsible for launching precision-guided land-attack cruise missiles and striking maritime targets using anti-ship missiles, respectively.

In contrast, the H-6N, nicknamed the “god of thunder”, is designed to carry large, nuclear-capable ALBMs.

By introducing this capability, China restored the airborne leg of its nuclear triad, supplementing its intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBM) and submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBM).

H-6N variant specifications and armaments

Reportedly entering service in 2018 and making its first public appearance at China’s 2019 military parade, the H-6N variant is a redesigned, modernised strategic bomber capable of carrying the nuclear-capable JL-1 ALBM.

According to an estimate by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, a Swedish think tank, as of 2026, there are about 20 H-6Ns in service, with up to 20 nuclear warheads assigned to them.

The H-6N bears a modified fuselage, replacing the traditional internal bomb bay used in other H-6 variants with a recessed underbelly designed to carry oversized external payloads such as an ALBM.

It is also notable for its nose-mounted aerial-refuelling probe, allowing the aircraft to refuel in flight with a YY-20A tanker aircraft. This significantly extends its combat radius to more than 3,500km (2,175 miles).

The H-6N would play an important role in China’s nuclear deterrence, with the recent introduction of the JL-1 ALBM, which appeared at the country’s large-scale military parade in Beijing in September last year.

The JL-1 is China’s first long-range air-launched strategic ballistic missile mounted with a nuclear warhead, and its design is thought to be derived from the land-based DF-21 medium-range ballistic missile.

In contrast to the DF-21, whose range is 1,700km, the JL-1 reportedly achieves an operational reach of up to 8,000km. This intercontinental reach is made possible by combining the bomber’s extended combat radius with the initial altitude and speed provided at launch.

Strategic implications and future development

The delivery of the H-6N and JL-1 to the PLA Air Force made China one of only three countries worldwide to operate nuclear-capable strategic bombers. The other two are the United States and Russia.

Although China’s second-strike retaliatory capability relies primarily on its land-mobile ICBMs and ballistic missile submarines, the airborne platform adds operational flexibility.

By being able to scramble on early warning of an incoming attack, the H-6N can survive an initial enemy strike and deliver a retaliatory counter-attack.

The aerial refuelling capability of the H-6N extends the PLA’s operational reach into the western Pacific Ocean. When paired with the ALBM, the system provides a total strike radius exceeding 11,000km, giving the air force an intercontinental nuclear and conventional strike capability that could reach US territory.

The role played by bombers in the PLA, currently using the H-6N and other H-6 variants, is poised to evolve once the H-20 bomber, announced in 2016, completes development to become the country’s first domestically produced strategic bomber.

While there has been no official confirmation of the H-20’s development progress, multiple reports and computer-generated pictures have surfaced online suggesting it will have a flying wing design with at least 10 tonnes of payload for either conventional or nuclear weapons.

Despite multiple reports that the H-20 is nearing its maiden flight and public unveiling, there are no official updates as yet. The Pentagon’s annual China Military Power Report assesses that the H-20 is unlikely to make its operational debut until the 2030s.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s anti-corruption law is going global. What does it mean for overseas firms?
item.description:
China’s new draft law on combating cross-border corruption is as much a weapon against foreign interference as it is a tool against illicit financial flows, analysts say.

The draft sets out ways to block extraterritorial investigations and to retaliate against foreign anti-corruption enforcement, drawing a firm legal boundary against foreign jurisdictions while establishing its own mechanism to police overseas assets.

In doing so, legal specialists warn, Beijing is also creating a double-edged regulatory framework that will force multinationals and Chinese businesses operating in regional hubs such as Singapore to navigate data compliance dilemmas.
item.content:encoded:
China’s new draft law on combating cross-border corruption is as much a weapon against foreign interference as it is a tool against illicit financial flows, analysts say.

The draft sets out ways to block extraterritorial investigations and to retaliate against foreign anti-corruption enforcement, drawing a firm legal boundary against foreign jurisdictions while establishing its own mechanism to police overseas assets.

In doing so, legal specialists warn, Beijing is also creating a double-edged regulatory framework that will force multinationals and Chinese businesses operating in regional hubs such as Singapore to navigate data compliance dilemmas.

The draft Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was submitted to the country’s top legislature in late August for its first reading, and the public has until September 26 to give feedback.

During panel discussions about the legislation, lawmakers said the measures filled a crucial statutory void.

Wang Ke, a member of the National People’s Congress’ Standing Committee, said that in the past, provisions covering the area had been scattered across the Supervision Law and Criminal Procedure Law, complicating asset recovery and procedures for trials in absentia.

However, the new draft was a “fundamental law” that integrated prevention, punishment and international cooperation “into a single chain”, Legal Daily quoted Wang as saying on September 1.

The legislation will add another layer to the legal firewall that China has steadily erected over the past five years against perceived Western legal overreach.

Ryan Mitchell, an associate professor of law at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said “foreign-related factors in the fight against corruption are on the rise” and “the intertwining of domestic and overseas corruption is intensifying”, making the draft bill part of Beijing’s “overall push for intensifying ‘foreign-related rule of law’”.

“The rising globalisation of major Chinese firms makes cross-border corruption an ever more significant issue for Beijing. International perceptions regarding the fairness of Chinese competition, or the benefits of [Belt and Road Initiative] projects, are also tied to such genuine concerns,” Mitchell said.

The rising globalisation of major Chinese firms makes cross-border corruption an ever more significant issue for Beijing

Ryan Mitchell, law professor

To some extent, the draft law resembles some anti-corruption laws in the West, such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Britain’s Bribery Act.

All three extend anti-corruption jurisdiction beyond domestic borders to target overseas bribery and cross-border commercial misconduct, and put corporate compliance programmes, internal accounting integrity, and third-party due diligence at the centre of enterprise liability and risk management.

However, the US act focuses on bribery of foreign public officials and accounting controls, while the British model establishes broadly framed bribery offences and a corporate failure-to-prevent offence, according to Wang Jiangyu, a law professor at City University of Hong Kong.

“The Chinese draft is much more institutionally and politically integrated,” he said.

The Chinese bill covers not only outbound bribery but also corruption involving Chinese public officials, state organs and state-owned enterprises (SOEs), overseas misconduct by Chinese public-sector actors, flight by suspected persons, cross-border transfers of corrupt assets, and certain foreign conduct producing effects in China.

“Beijing is borrowing some internationally recognisable elements of modern anti-bribery law, but embedding them in a distinctly Chinese model combining punishment, prevention, asset protection, supervisory governance, international cooperation and resistance to what China considers abusive foreign extraterritorial enforcement,” he said.

That Chinese model includes establishing a centralised mechanism led by the National Supervisory Commission, which comes under the Communist Party’s top anti-corruption body. The commission will coordinate with a dozen or so state bodies, ranging from public security and finance to cyberspace administration.
