“This is important because cross-border corruption cases rarely involve bribery alone. They commonly require the tracing of payments, corporate records, beneficial interests, electronic data and overseas assets,” Wang said.

China’s decision to adopt a framework like the US act carries a touch of historical “irony”, according to Matthew Erie, an associate professor of law at the American University Washington College of Law.

Erie said that in 2011, then US Department of Commerce general counsel Cameron Kerry advocated for China to adopt a law equivalent to the American legislation.

Beijing responded by amending its Criminal Law that year to criminalise bribes paid to foreign officials, fulfilling its obligations under the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, he said.

But those statutory provisions remained dormant for over a decade until October 2023, when a court in the southern city of Guangzhou enforced them in a landmark case, convicting two former executives of state-owned China Railway Tunnel Group of bribing a government official in Singapore, Erie said.

It was a signal that China’s foreign bribery laws were being enforced.

What started out as a US effort to encourage trade has become a state-led push to resist Western legal dominance and American long-arm jurisdiction.

Behind Beijing’s legislative shift lies a decade of deep frustration with international legal cooperation. Before turning to a statutory extraterritorial framework, Beijing tried for years to combat cross-border corruption and repatriate fugitives through traditional bilateral diplomacy.

At its height, China negotiated 59 bilateral extradition treaties, believing that formal international agreements could serve as the legal backbone for anti-graft campaigns such as Operation Fox Hunt and Operation Sky Net, which were launched between 2014 and 2015 and continue today.

However, Western scepticism – which Chinese authorities view as an unreasonable double standard – blocked this bilateral framework from expanding where Beijing needed it most. Key Western destinations for fugitives, including the United States, Canada, Britain and Australia, either refused to negotiate bilateral extradition treaties with mainland China or left signed treaties unratified due to human rights and judicial concerns.

That left China with only around 45 active extradition treaties in force globally, mostly with non-Western nations.

This lack of an enforceable international framework turned Western capitals into safe havens for scores of high-profile fugitives well known for their corrupt activities.

Denied a functional multilateral repatriation pipeline, Beijing was left with little choice but to pivot to a statutory mechanism – creating what is, in effect, China’s own version of long-arm jurisdiction to police corrupt assets and actors overseas.

Now, Beijing appears to be summoning its full legislative powers to take a far tougher line than the US and Britain.

Mitchell said that both the US and British acts were widely regarded as being underused, with foreign officials seldom pursued and convicted of bribery.

That enforcement is only set to decline further. In February last year, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order pausing enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act before the Justice Department unveiled new guidelines in June restricting prosecutions to cases directly threatening American economic competitiveness and national security.

“The Trump administration has reduced usage [of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act] to promote the ‘competitiveness’ of American companies,” Mitchell said.

“In contrast, Beijing is continually making its own anti-corruption framework more strict and far-reaching. The draft law indicates that this process of increasingly tight regulation continues to be a major focus for the party.”

Provisions such as Article 17, which establishes rewards and legal protections for whistle-blowers, were key legislative tools aimed at bolstering enforcement capabilities, Mitchell said.

One of the major features of China’s draft law is its power to fight foreign scrutiny and retaliate against overseas enforcement.

Erie said the draft was “a confluence of two reform trajectories: domestic anti-corruption concerns and foreign adversarialism”.

In particular, Article 6 was a reaction to perceived “unlawful US extraterritoriality”. The article authorises retaliatory and blocking measures if foreign states use anti-corruption enforcement “as a pretext” or improperly apply extraterritorial laws to suppress Chinese interests.

Article 26 also targets sovereignty, banning foreign entities and individuals from conducting anti-corruption investigations or gathering evidence within China without explicit state approval. And Chinese domestic entities cannot help foreign authorities without prior clearance.

Wang said Article 26 was “particularly important” because it was “a strong assertion that cross-border investigations must proceed through authorised government channels”.

If enacted, the law’s broad reach will be tested in key financial and trading hubs across Asia, such as Singapore, which hosts regional management, treasury functions, intermediaries, and holding structures for many Chinese enterprises.

Because cross-border investigations often involve offshore bank accounts, corporate structures, trusts and professional intermediaries, Chinese enforcement efforts will frequently require data and assets located within Singapore.

Wang said there was a “solid foundation” for bilateral cooperation, as both nations were signatories to the UN Convention Against Corruption and maintained formal channels for legal assistance and information sharing.

But it may not be automatic or unilateral.

Wang said that any requests from Beijing would have to navigate Singapore’s independent judicial process, where local authorities – such as the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau and the Attorney-General’s Chambers – process inquiries strictly according to Singaporean domestic law, evidential thresholds and procedural due process.

This raises three potential points of friction.

“The first is data disclosure, particularly where a company faces a Chinese demand to cooperate but is also subject to Singaporean confidentiality, privacy or regulatory obligations,” he said.

“The second is asset restraint, because Singaporean authorities or courts would need an adequate domestic legal basis before freezing or confiscating property.

“The third is competing investigations, especially where China and Singapore characterise the same transaction differently or both wish to prosecute.”

The broad scope of the law has also raised concerns over definitions of certain behaviour.

Bing Ling, a professor of Chinese law at the University of Sydney law school, warned that the text lacked statutory definitions of core terms in Article 3 such as “power rent-seeking” and “waste of state assets”.

“In practice, these concepts will likely derive their meaning from Chinese criminal law and internal disciplinary practice rather than internationally recognised standards, creating significant uncertainty for foreign firms dealing with Chinese SOEs,” he said.

Another area of ambiguity is Article 18, which authorises Chinese authorities to demand evidence and require foreign corporate cooperation in major cases based on “reciprocity”.

Ling said the draft did not define “cooperation” or how reciprocity operated in practice.

While international law prohibits unilateral enforcement on foreign soil without state consent, the provision’s open-ended language fuels concerns that Chinese enforcers might seek evidence outside formal channels.

For foreign multinationals, parallel-enforcement risk could increase significantly where a China connection exists

Will Wu, Chance Bridge Law Firm

For businesses, the draft law transforms internal compliance from a voluntary corporate safeguard into an independently enforceable statutory obligation.

According to Will Wu, a Shanghai-based partner at Chance Bridge Law Firm, the draft law reshapes cross-border risk for both foreign and Chinese entities in distinct ways.

“For foreign multinationals, parallel-enforcement risk could increase significantly where a China connection exists,” he said.

Under Articles 29 to 34, all enterprises engaged in cross-border operations – including domestic firms operating abroad and foreign multinational corporations operating within China – are legally required to establish “integrity compliance” management systems.

Wu said multinationals must evaluate China-related risks from the start and align their evidence handling, legal privilege, disclosures and remediation strategies across all involved jurisdictions.

For overseas Chinese enterprises, compliance duties would become far more direct and stringent, he added.

Article 33 spells out third-party due diligence, while Article 45 makes compliance failures an independently punishable administrative offence.

Companies failing to rectify control flaws would face business suspensions or licence revocations, even without proof of an actual bribe.

And while a parent company would not be automatically liable for an offshore agent’s misconduct, weak third-party oversight could trigger direct penalties and, together with other evidence, help legally link the company to suspected bribery involving that third party.

Additionally, offshore proxies or nominees used to transfer or hold illicit funds linked to suspected corruption across borders would fall directly under the law’s asset-tracing, restraint and recovery provisions, Wu added.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines bets big on rail, but can it fix a broken transport network?
item.description:
A two-hour commute for a 14km (8.7-mile) journey. For Julius Dalay and millions of other Filipinos, this is just how public transport works in Manila: a mishmash of jeepneys, trains and buses that commuters are left to figure out for themselves.

Dalay, an environmental planner, is resigned to the chaos. Reaching his destination usually involves hailing a jeepney, then cramming into a packed train and enduring a slow bus crawl along the capital’s main thoroughfares.

“You either wait the jeepney out, or you pray to God that the vehicles aren’t packed,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
A two-hour commute for a 14km (8.7-mile) journey. For Julius Dalay and millions of other Filipinos, this is just how public transport works in Manila: a mishmash of jeepneys, trains and buses that commuters are left to figure out for themselves.

Dalay, an environmental planner, is resigned to the chaos. Reaching his destination usually involves hailing a jeepney, then cramming into a packed train and enduring a slow bus crawl along the capital’s main thoroughfares.

“You either wait the jeepney out, or you pray to God that the vehicles aren’t packed,” he said.

The Philippine government now says it wants to change that, with the roll-out of its biggest transport spending plan in years.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration is proposing to more than double the transport department’s budget to 300.96 billion pesos (US$4.8 billion) next year, as it races to push forward major railway projects meant to transform mobility across the congested capital and its surrounding provinces.

The Philippines was ranked Asia’s most congested country in the 2025 TomTom traffic index, with Manila placed 14th among the world’s 492 metropolitan areas and Davao City faring even worse, at 11th.

But transport planners and commuter advocates warn that money alone will not fix Metro Manila’s problems. The bigger challenge, they say, is making sure existing buses, jeepneys and other modes of public transport are not neglected while costly new projects – still years in the making – get built.

For Dalay, the daily commute has turned into even more of a headache since state-owned operator Philippine National Railways suspended services to make way for the North-South Commuter Railway, a 147km (91-mile) link that is slated to connect New Clark City to Calamba in Laguna province by 2029.

Services between Malabon in the northwest and Alabang in the south were paused two years ago, pushing commuters onto other rail lines and forms of transport – despite their partial resumption this June.

Dalay, who founded the advocacy group Commuters of the Philippines, called the budget increase “necessary”, but warned against putting all the government’s financial eggs in one basket at the expense of other transport systems.

He points to the EDSA Carousel, a dedicated bus rapid transit system running along the capital’s main expressway, as a case in point.

“Some projects, like the carousel, are getting zero budget – this is detrimental. We can’t neglect the existing systems for the sake of future ones, simply because people need transport now,” Dalay said.

Creating a transport ecosystem in which different forms of transport compete for funding rather than complement one another was a “major shortcoming” of the government, said Patricia Mariano, director of AltMobility PH, an advocacy group for pedestrian and commuter rights.

“Every mode serves a specific purpose and meets different mobility needs,” she said.

Rail baggage

The Marcos administration’s decision to sharply increase transport spending comes as the government faces mounting costs for major railway projects, many of which rely on a mix of internal funding and substantial foreign loans.

Rail projects in the Philippines could take years to move from planning to operation, said Manuel Jose Camagay, a mechanical engineer and transport, urban and logistics specialist.

The Metro Manila subway was one such example, he said, with the project delayed partly because the capital’s development had for decades been planned around roads and private vehicles rather than rail infrastructure.

“All developed economies, especially in Europe and Japan, prioritised rail or mass transit as the effective solution to development instead of single-car driving,” he said.

Camagay suggested that the proposed budget increase might reflect pressure to accelerate railway construction before Marcos leaves office in 2028.

Transport researcher Sandy Mae Gaspay, an associate professor at UP Diliman Institute of Civil Engineering, said financing would still be a challenge given the nature of the loans involved.

“It is the Philippines’ obligation to provide the counterpart funds for these loans,” she said, adding that railways were “disproportionately more expensive to build compared to other transport projects”.

Gaspay warned that projects such as the North-South Commuter Railway and the Metro Manila Subway could not meet the transport needs of the wider capital region on their own.

“They don’t replace the need for a genuinely networked system across Metro Manila and its surrounding regions,” she said. “That network shouldn’t be understood as rail alone. Buses and jeepneys still carry the bulk of daily trips and will continue to for the foreseeable future, so a real network has to integrate rail with these other modes.”

Camagay said commuters would eventually benefit from the railway projects, but argued that bus rapid transit systems could deliver faster gains in urban mobility in the meantime, without the need for extensive construction.

Corruption was also a concern, he added, warning that simply building infrastructure would achieve little if public works were compromised by dishonest practices.

Mariano said the government should also look beyond the capital’s transport demands to other parts of the country.

“Considering the rapid growth we’ve been seeing, investments and road space would be best allocated to rail or other mass transit … rather than roads and highways,” she said, adding there was “a strong case for mass transit in other metropolitan cities like Cebu and Davao.”

A new hope

Even with the Philippines’ chronic public transport issues, analysts welcomed the sheer scale of the projects now under way as a positive shift away from piecemeal infrastructure planning.

“What gives me optimism is that there are many ongoing initiatives that are leading to a more integrated outlook,” Gaspay said – though she added that weak coordination between government agencies and local authorities remained a major obstacle.

“I’m always hopeful that better days are coming,” said Gene Lambert Giron, an assistant professor on land-use planning at the University of the Philippines Open University. “But the big question is when?”

Even Laos, a country which is not as economically prosperous as the Philippines, has long-distance railway infrastructure

Gene Lambert Giron, urban planning specialist

Giron contrasted the Philippines’ progress with that of other countries in the region.

“Imagine, years ago, the economy and infrastructure of Vietnam were behind us. Look at Vietnam now,” he said. “Even Laos, a country which is not as economically prosperous as the Philippines, has long-distance railway infrastructure. Indonesia, also an archipelago, has a functioning long-distance railway infrastructure.”

A study published last year by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that the country’s public transport system seriously lagged behind that of its Southeast Asian neighbours.

Manila’s ambitious transport agenda would only succeed if it stayed focused on the seamless movement of both vehicles and people, Mariano.

“Our hope is for the administration to dream bigger: to pursue a mobility renaissance, with a greater focus on the needs of the nearly 90 per cent of Filipinos who rely on public and active transport in their daily lives,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] As Asia rapidly ages, who cares for the carers when they grow old?
item.description:
Bessie* left the Philippines for Malaysia more than a decade ago to care for other people’s children. She stayed to look after their parents instead.

Certified as a carer, she now freelances around Kuala Lumpur’s Klang Valley, earning up to 25 ringgit (US$6) an hour for round-the-clock shifts, with clients providing her meals, transport and housing.

“My former employer was very understanding and offered to release me earlier so I could earn a higher salary as a caregiver,” the 50-year-old said.
item.content:encoded:
Bessie* left the Philippines for Malaysia more than a decade ago to care for other people’s children. She stayed to look after their parents instead.

Certified as a carer, she now freelances around Kuala Lumpur’s Klang Valley, earning up to 25 ringgit (US$6) an hour for round-the-clock shifts, with clients providing her meals, transport and housing.

“My former employer was very understanding and offered to release me earlier so I could earn a higher salary as a caregiver,” the 50-year-old said.

Her career path is, in miniature, the story of many of Southeast Asia’s carers. Malaysia is often a way station: a place to earn a certificate and some experience before moving on to better paid work, sometimes with a path to residency, in Japan, Canada or Europe.

“A lot of caregivers from the Philippines come to Malaysia or Singapore to work for a while, before they relocate,” Bessie said, adding that, unlike so many others, she planned to stay put.

The region’s wealthier economies are now competing for a workforce that is thinning out as it moves around.

Taiwan employed about 225,000 migrant social welfare workers as of March, 186,000 of them Indonesian, while Japan reached the end of last year with 67,871 foreign nationals employed in its skilled nursing-care category.

Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia are all scaling up recruitment just as two major source countries for carers – the Philippines and Indonesia – are themselves greying. . Over-sixties already accounted for more than 10 per cent of Filipinos in 2024 and almost 12 per cent of Indonesians the following year.

The dilemma now facing Asean governments is how to combat a regional shortage of carers without simply offloading the problem onto poorer states.

Ready buyers

Malaysia illustrates the strain from the buyer’s side. The country has no dedicated immigration pathway for foreign carers, so most arrive as domestic helpers or on temporary work passes – the route Bessie took.

That mismatch has consequences, according to Delren Douglas, president of the Association for Residential Aged Care Operators of Malaysia (Agecope).

“Many of our members have had the Immigration Department coming in and deporting foreign caregivers for doing work that is different from their permit,” he said.

In May, Agecope put the national shortfall at roughly 1,400 carers across some 12,000 nursing-home beds. Douglas said it had worsened since, although he gave no updated figure. “We are being left with carers not adventurous enough to travel abroad or who lack the education required to work elsewhere,” he said.

Local nursing home operator Christine Yee sees the same churn from the training side: carers gain confidence and skills on the job, then leave for Singapore or beyond.

“It’s already very difficult to recruit people who have the temperament, the patience and passion for this type of work, because taking care of the elderly is not easy,” she said.

Money explains much of the drift. Carers in Malaysia start on around 2,000 to 2,500 ringgit (US$490 to US$615) a month, while Singaporean employers pay about triple that, between S$2,200 (US$1,740) and S$2,500.

Singapore’s response, outlined in parliament in March, is to “diversify the sources of foreign recruitment” and secure bilateral labour deals, with talks on care-worker cooperation taking place between acting manpower minister Jasmin Lau and her Philippine counterpart Francis Tolentino last month.

The city state estimates its healthcare workforce will grow by a fifth by the end of the decade, to about 156,000, on top of the 300,000 or so migrant domestic workers who increasingly provide care for the elderly.

Thailand, meanwhile, is entering the bidding rather late. The International Labour Organization (ILO) projects that the country may need over 250,000 additional paid care workers by 2037, roughly 55,000 of them migrants, and has flagged “increased competition for Asean migrant care workers”.

In January, Thailand’s then labour minister Trinuch Thienthong warned that demand for foreign workers could climb by more than half, adding that future labour-import policies “must be clearly defined”. They still have not been.

‘Brain waste’

Indonesia illustrates how the shortage travels. Of the 153,049 Indonesians placed overseas in the first half of this year, 30,514 were carers – the largest single occupational group.

Ferry Efendi, a community health nursing professor at Airlangga University, attributed the outflow to a shortage of jobs at home. “Indonesia has more than 700 nursing schools graduating about 50,000 nurses a year, far beyond what the domestic health sector can employ,” he said.

Some graduates inevitably ended up caring for the elderly overseas, despite their qualifications – creating “brain waste rather than brain circulation”, as Efendi put it.

Indonesia has no national long-term care system or regulated care-worker profession for them to return to.

Malaysia’s proximity and linguistic familiarity could continue to attract Indonesian carers despite lower wages, Efendi added. “A nurse with young children in Sumatra may rationally prefer Malaysia to Taiwan even at a lower wage. But Malaysia would have to recognise her nursing background rather than repeat Taiwan’s practice of hiring nurses as care attendants.”

The Philippines faces a somewhat similar contradiction. Its skills authority certifies about 41,000 carers annually, according to paper from the Philippine Institute for Development Studies published in May. Yet Japan, under a bilateral economic partnership agreement, takes in only about 200 of them a year.

Filipino carers had become an expensive “gold standard” that Japanese employers were increasingly abandoning in favour of cheaper alternatives from India, Nepal and Myanmar, the paper said.

Jean Clarisse Carlos, the paper’s co-author, warned that a training pipeline built for export became a liability once it collided with realities at home, including “persistent vacancies and high turnover in local care services, rising unmet care needs among older persons and continued dependence on unpaid family caregivers”.

Her paper calls for a national care and migration strategy to mitigate what it termed the “care drain”.

An invisible workforce

Behind all of this sits a regulatory blind spot.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ 2006 mutual recognition arrangement on nursing left licensing power with national regulators while entirely excluding carers – “where most of the movement is actually happening”, according to Efendi.

Because so much care for the elderly happened behind closed doors, classified as domestic work rather than a profession, it was invisible to regional skills initiatives, Carlos said.

When Asean labour ministers met in Bangkok on August 26, their published communique focused on skills certification, without once mentioning care.

Today’s employment surplus should not be read as tomorrow’s care surplus

Ferry Efendi, community health nursing professor

The International Labour Organization said in a statement that there was “no comprehensive mechanism within Asean or at the global level” to stop wealthier countries outbidding poorer ones. If workers obtained the right to migrate, restricting where they could work raised “significant labour rights concerns”, it said.

The agency advocates for fair recruitment, portable social security and skills recognition, but that still leaves unresolved the question hanging over the region: whether today’s labour-exporting countries will have any carers left to spare once their own citizens grow old.

“Today’s employment surplus should not be read as tomorrow’s care surplus,” Efendi said.

*Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] When Indonesia burns, these women run towards the fire
item.description:
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick, yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.

She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives straight into the impenetrable smog emanating from wildfires devouring the peatland and ancient forests of Borneo.

“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother told This Week in Asia, moments before disappearing into the murk that has settled over the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan.
item.content:encoded:
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick, yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.

She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives straight into the impenetrable smog emanating from wildfires devouring the peatland and ancient forests of Borneo.

“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother told This Week in Asia, moments before disappearing into the murk that has settled over the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan.

Irma, who like many Indonesians only goes by one name, is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit that heads out every day during the dry season to battle blazes smouldering deep beneath the island’s peatlands.

They fight fires lit, deliberately or otherwise, by the agricultural burning of poor farming communities clearing land the cheapest way they know how. This year, those fires arrived earlier and burned harder than most can remember, fuelled climate anomalies and drought conditions.

“We are the ones who feel its effects most,” said Irma, who is the group’s coordinator, explaining that it was women who were left to care for housebound children through increasingly long stretches of the year.

“The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it.”

Indonesia has an estimated 206,000 square km (79,500 square miles) of tropical peatland, making up about 10.8 per cent of its total land area and the most carbon-dense store of its kind anywhere on Earth.

When the peatlands burn, they release thousands of tonnes of greenhouse gases into the air, fuelling a vicious cycle that drives global warming and worsens each year’s drought.

Smog from the wildfires then drifts over Singapore, Malaysia and further afield – poisoning the air and damaging lungs as it does so.

Peatlands are normally waterlogged, but most of Borneo has not seen heavy rain since late June.

Decades of deforestation and drainage for palm oil plantations and other intensive agriculture have helped create a wildlife crisis that each year consumes vast tracts of the country, destroying the last natural habitat of some of the world’s rarest species, from orangutans and hornbills to pangolins.

From her village in Ketapang regency, Irma has witnessed the damage first-hand.

“We used to see wild boars, deer, muntjacs and even sun bears; we had hornbills, but now it seems as if they have disappeared,” she said.

Authorities say more than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) of Indonesia burned between January and July – an area nearly twice the size of Hong Kong.

The Sipongi monitoring website of Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry had recorded 8,638 hotspots across Kalimantan by the end of August. Ketapang, where Irma lives, accounted for about one in five of those fires, placing her volunteer group right on the front line.

Hard hats and hosepipes

Wearing hard hats or motorcycle helmets over their jilbabs, the Power of Mama volunteers haul long hosepipes into singed forest and fields, their bright red uniforms the only splash of colour against the scorched earth.

Most wear thin surgical masks or cloth coverings for protection while they carry out their gruelling, unpaid work.

The small creeks and rivers that once served as natural firebreaks had been drying up since June, Irma said – forcing the volunteer firefighters to linger at the edge of forests or plantations as they try to douse the flames wherever they can.

The group was formed in 2022 by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), the local affiliate of global non-profit International Animal Rescue. Translating to the Indonesian Nature Rehabilitation Initiatives Foundation, YIARI operates with a mandate that extends well beyond firefighting.

“This isn’t just about putting out fires,” YIARI founder and CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said. “It’s about seeing these women become more confident and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.”

Members are trained to fly surveillance drones and lead community outreach as well as fight the fires, which can be very difficult to put out.

“You can’t see the flames,” Sanchez explained. “But the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.”

Back on patrol, Suriati, 32, and Ratinah, 56, both of whom also go by a single name, pick their way along a narrow track towards the edge of the forest.

“We often fall off our motorbikes,” Ratinah said. “Particularly during the rainy season when it’s slippery and muddy.”

Fire is not the only obstacle. In a conservative, male-dominated society, the women’s authority is regularly tested by the neighbours they are trying to protect.

“Sometimes they won’t accept it,” said Suriati, a housewife who runs a small grocery stall alongside her firefighting duties. “They feel that we are being patronising. They say ‘what do housewives know’? With the older people in particular, we cannot simply forbid them … we have to treat them gently.”

When the rains finally do arrive, the volunteers will turn to advising farmers on controlled burning and nitrogen-restoring alternatives to slash-and-burn agriculture, rehabilitating degraded mangroves and teaching schoolchildren about how to steward the land their parents have been setting alight.

The night shift

For Ely Marlina, 46, the fires are personal. She joined the volunteers after the 2019 fire season, when Ketapang regency alone logged more than 1,000 hotspots and doctors reported an alarming spike in chronic breathing conditions among children.

By day, Ely teaches at a junior high school. By night, she fights fires.

It was already dark when word reached her of a recent blaze less than 3km (1.86 miles) from her home in Sungai Awan Kiri village, West Kalimantan.

“Some of the residents’ houses were about 100 metres away and the distance to the densely populated residential area was only about 200 or 300 metres,” she recalled.

At the scene, she climbed onto a fire truck to rig water pumps, hosepipes and portable tanks, then joined the other members of her team hauling the equipment towards the flames.

“The area was peatland,” the 46-year-old said. “The ground was very dangerous. My leg even slipped and sank half a metre into the peat.”

Hours later, the fire was finally extinguished – a small victory for Ely and her exhausted team, in a battle that begins again with every sunrise.

“Like it or not we have to stay on guard during the dry season,” she said. “The people depend on us.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Chelsea football shirts are making Hong Kong fans nervous about crypto laws
item.description:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.

Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.

Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.

Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.

Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.

Only two stablecoin issuers are currently licensed in Hong Kong – Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC.

Ahead of the enactment of the Stablecoins Ordinance on August 1, 2025, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned on its website that “it will be illegal for any person to … actively market the issue of unlicensed [fiat-referenced stablecoins] to the public”.

Winnie Choi, a Chelsea fan of 12 years, was among those worried about breaking the law.

“After looking up the law, I still do not understand whether it is a problem to wear the jersey,” she said.

Choi suggested that the HKMA issue a clear, “down-to-earth” guideline on whether wearing the shirt with the USDC logo constituted promotion.

Danny*, a club supporter for more than 20 years, said ordinary football fans would not have the awareness to identify if the shirt promoted an unregulated stablecoin.

“If I wear it, who will enforce the law? Will I be arrested by police?” he said.

Danny said he would not buy the new jersey until authorities clarified whether it was legal to wear it.

Hammer Chung, owner of football apparel shop DirectSoccer in Mong Kok, said he was unsure whether it was legal to sell replica jerseys with the USDC logo.

He added that he hoped regulators would clarify the matter.

But Chung noted that many of the kits for other football clubs that he sold also bore the logos of illegal gambling websites.

“Are we also promoting for them by selling the shirts?” he said.

The HKMA said it would not comment on individual cases, but noted the ordinance prohibited the “active marketing” or advertising of unauthorised stablecoin activity in Hong Kong.

Whether an act constituted actively marketing to the public was determined on a case-by-case basis, a spokesman said.

Factors considered by the HKMA included the languages used in the marketing messages, whether they targeted people living in the city, whether a Hong Kong domain name was used and whether a detailed marketing plan was in place to promote the activity.

A specific exemption was provided to publishers and live broadcasters who merely published content created by others, as long as they satisfied the relevant conditions set out in the provision and considered the relevant facts and circumstances, he said.

Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung expressed concerns that fans donning the new Chelsea shirt in public could be “problematic”, as it all depended on how the HKMA defined active marketing.

“There are so many grey areas,” he said, adding that he dared not wear T-shirts sporting the logos of unlicensed crypto trading platforms after the licensing regime was put in place by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).

Li said USDC was the second-largest stablecoin in the world, and it was ridiculous that it was labelled as “unlicensed” under local legislation.

He also said it was difficult to regulate the promotion of cryptocurrencies within a certain jurisdiction in the age of the internet because they were issued globally. “How can you say something legal in other countries is illegal here?”

The ordinance provides an exemption for promoting unlicensed stablecoins across various media and digital platforms, including live broadcasts, provided the person did not devise and exercised no control over the content of the advertisement.

“A group of players on TV is wearing [shirts with] this logo … it’s impossible that it isn’t an advertisement. We’re looking at them the entire game, right?” Li said.

Tanna Chong, head of public policy at VerifyVASP, a digital assets compliance company, called for enhanced consumer protection through disclaimers before every match, similar to warning messages in moneylending advertisements.

“They would be clear reminders that the programme contains these materials [about cryptocurrency], and that those companies actually do not have a licence in Hong Kong,” she said.

Chong, who helped draft the ordinance during her time in government, said there was no hard and fast rule to define active marketing, noting that it was a concept determined on a case-by-case basis considering various contextual factors.

She said neither Circle nor Chelsea had control over the broadcasting of matches in Hong Kong, which involved a deal between NowTV and the Premier League, and had not actively implemented a marketing campaign in the city.

Circle was not “by way of business providing services” in the city either, she added.

She also reassured fans that there was no problem with wearing the Blues’ shirt with the USDC logo, as wearers were not the service provider.

“Unless [the wearer] is a Circle employee walking down the street in a Chelsea jersey. In that case, you need to establish that Circle instructed him to wear it with the intent of targeting a Hong Kong audience,” she said.

An HKT spokesman said Now TV strictly complied with all relevant Hong Kong laws and regulations.

The South China Morning Post has reached out to Circle and Chelsea FC for comment.

The West London club’s latest deal followed a collective agreement by all 20 Premier League clubs to phase out front-of-shirt gambling sponsors. But the Blues are not the first team to partner with the crypto sector.

OKX and Kraken, both virtual asset trading platforms unlicensed in Hong Kong, are the sleeve sponsors of Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur.

Chelsea itself also partnered with crypto platform BingX, which is also unlicensed in Hong Kong, for an official training kit front sponsorship.

During their visit to the city last month, Chelsea players wore the training kit with the BingX logo during an open training session at Kai Tak Stadium.

Players from City and Spurs also wore kits sporting the OKX and Kraken logos during their friendlies in Hong Kong in August this year and July last year, respectively.

Similar clauses regulating the promotion of unlicensed virtual asset trading platforms are present in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance.

The SFC said it would not comment on specific cases. It added that it would take into account all marketing and advertising activities in their totality in considering the appropriate course of action.

Kraken said that it maintained jurisdiction-specific controls designed to ensure its activities complied with applicable local laws.

The trading platform also stressed that its partnership with Tottenham Hotspur was a global brand sponsorship.

It did not reflect an offer, solicitation or promotion of Kraken’s virtual asset trading services in jurisdictions where those activities were restricted, it added.

The SCMP has reached out to Manchester City, OKX, Tottenham Hotspur and BingX for comment.

*Name changed at interviewee’s request.

item.title: [SCMP] Social media must join the fight against teen suicides
item.description:
As we observe World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, the global community reflects on a sobering reality: suicide remains a leading cause of death among young people. Every year, more than 720,000 people die by suicide – each life a story cut short, a family shattered, a community left to grapple with unbearable loss.

In Hong Kong, the Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention (CSRP) at the University of Hong Kong estimates last year’s suicide rate at 13.0 per 100,000 in the population – a slight improvement from 13.8 in 2024. But let me be clear: this is no cause for complacency. The rate among our young people, particularly boys, remains stubbornly high, and that is where my deepest concern lies.

We can no longer afford to ignore the role of social media in the mental health crisis facing our teenagers. Social media has become the landscape of modern adolescence. In the United States, reports indicate that up to 95 per cent of adolescents use social media, with over one-third reporting near-constant use. For young people, these digital spaces are not merely entertainment – they are where identities are formed, relationships are navigated and self-worth is measured.
item.content:encoded:
As we observe World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, the global community reflects on a sobering reality: suicide remains a leading cause of death among young people. Every year, more than 720,000 people die by suicide – each life a story cut short, a family shattered, a community left to grapple with unbearable loss.

In Hong Kong, the Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention (CSRP) at the University of Hong Kong estimates last year’s suicide rate at 13.0 per 100,000 in the population – a slight improvement from 13.8 in 2024. But let me be clear: this is no cause for complacency. The rate among our young people, particularly boys, remains stubbornly high, and that is where my deepest concern lies.

We can no longer afford to ignore the role of social media in the mental health crisis facing our teenagers. Social media has become the landscape of modern adolescence. In the United States, reports indicate that up to 95 per cent of adolescents use social media, with over one-third reporting near-constant use. For young people, these digital spaces are not merely entertainment – they are where identities are formed, relationships are navigated and self-worth is measured.

Their impact on mental health deserves attention. For decades, my team at the CSRP has tracked the data, studied the patterns and advocated for evidence-based solutions. The evidence is overwhelming. Excessive use of social media is correlated with poor mental health and deteriorating family relationships. The causes of youth suicide are complex – home and school problems are major, intertwined contributors – but the digital environment has become a significant amplifier of distress.

We have long known that irresponsible media reporting can trigger the Werther effect – where sensational coverage of suicide leads to imitative behaviour. Social media has made this problem exponentially more complicated. A single post, whether a careless comment or misguided “awareness” message, can reach thousands of vulnerable young people instantly. Specificity in describing methods or locations – even when framed as a warning – drives contagion risk.

Yet the responsibility does not rest solely with individuals. The platforms design their algorithms to maximise engagement, often at the expense of well-being. The recent US$18 billion settlement by Meta Platforms – agreeing to examine its algorithm design to improve mental health among young users – should be a wake-up call for the industry.

The tragic case of American Sophie Rottenberg, who ended her life after months of confiding in a ChatGPT therapist, illustrates the dangers of unregulated digital environments. In our work on chatbot development, we have observed that overly empathetic responses can inadvertently reinforce a user’s negative thoughts, create a dangerous feedback loop and validate harmful ideation.

For years, we have partnered with local media to promote safe reporting practices. But the landscape has shifted dramatically. Passive audiences have become content creators. The old guidelines were not designed for this reality. That is why, with the support of The Better Hong Kong Foundation, we worked with the Hong Kong Press Council to produce an updated 2026 edition. For the first time, we have incorporated targeted guidance for social media alongside traditional recommendations.

So, what does responsible social media use look like? First, pause before posting. If your post describes methods, means or locations in specific detail, do not share it. Do not speculate on causes or spread rumours. Always obtain consent before sharing someone else’s experience with suicide.

Second, promote hope, not despair. Whenever suicide is mentioned, attach help-seeking resources. These can make a tangible difference. Share recovery stories that highlight coping strategies and resilience.

Third, use mindful language. Avoid phrases that frame suicide as noble, peaceful or an act of empowerment. Such framing normalises it for at-risk individuals. Describe the pain, not the act.

But individual action is not enough. We must hold platform operators accountable. With their sophisticated algorithms, these companies have the ability to identify at-risk users – the same algorithms that deliver personalised advertisements can be repurposed for early detection and intervention. Platforms worry that intervening might affect traffic volume. But we cannot accept profit motives as a justification for inaction.

Platforms should detect and remove harmful content using automated tools, but they must route flagged items to human moderators before removal to avoid overreach. They should deprioritise borderline high-risk content in recommendation feeds while reserving outright restriction for clear violations like content that promotes suicide methods, pacts or graphic acts. They must act swiftly against cyberbullying, which remains a major class of harmful content. And they should pin help resources prominently alongside sensitive posts.

I am pleased Meta has suggested a two-hour daily limit for young users and content filtering for children under 15. These are potentially effective measures. But we need systemic change.

Our government has committed to continuing the three-tier system to support mental health in secondary and upper-primary schools. That is welcome. However, I must highlight a critical point often overlooked: by our estimates, about 75 per cent of suicides occur among those who do not have depressive symptoms. By focusing solely on depression, we are missing most of those at risk. This is a central reason our suicide rate remains stubbornly high despite increased mental health awareness.

To truly move the needle, we must think beyond clinical interventions. We must promote a healthy lifestyle: a balanced diet, regular exercise and adequate sleep are all essential. We must make schools and homes safe places where young people feel valued and supported. And we must give them something to look forward to – a meaningful future, hope and a strong support network.

There is no silver bullet to solving the suicide problem among teenagers. The path forward is difficult and requires coordinated effort across families, schools, governments and technology companies. But it is not impossible. We have seen progress: the rate has come down from 13.8 to 13.0. That shows our efforts are working. We just cannot afford to ease up.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline.

You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s ‘Tesla imitators’ have a new mission: build affordable humanoid robots for consumers
item.description:
When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots.

“I think robotics will represent a natural extension of our carmaking capabilities and business acumen,” Li told reporters at a media briefing after Nio posted its first-ever quarterly profits for the three months ending December.

“Don’t you think that every car we produce in the future will actually be a robot? Its perception, decision-making, and execution will all be based on artificial intelligence.”
item.content:encoded:
When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots.

“I think robotics will represent a natural extension of our carmaking capabilities and business acumen,” Li told reporters at a media briefing after Nio posted its first-ever quarterly profits for the three months ending December.

“Don’t you think that every car we produce in the future will actually be a robot? Its perception, decision-making, and execution will all be based on artificial intelligence.”

While Li has adopted a “latecomer” strategy in robotics to avoid potential big losses in early-stage investment, he is convinced that robotics and carmaking have synergistic benefits.

The premium cars Nio is building already embody perception, decision-making and control systems – similar to those of robots.

That perspective on the future of mobility, buoyed by rapid growth of physical AI, is typical of the more than 10 Chinese manufacturers of intelligent vehicles that have ventured into robotics.

These players, from BYD – the world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) maker – to Stellantis-backed Leapmotor, are once again being labelled as Tesla imitators because the US carmaker is accelerating commercialisation of its humanoid robot Optimus.

Some of the Chinese firms – with clear-cut time frames to begin production and deliveries of self-developed robots – could compete against Elon Musk’s Tesla on an equal footing in robotics, buoyed by government support, an integrated supply chain and consumer willingness to embrace new technologies, according to analysts.

“AI’s enhanced role in cars provides a catalyst to automotive companies’ diversification into robotics,” said Qian Kang, owner of a vehicle circuit board factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “More importantly, Tesla’s business scope and model is inspiring Chinese companies to explore embodied AI.”

The robotics sector has supply chain synergy with smart EV production because key components like cameras and radar, as well as software, are needed for both.

Other key parts, from motors to heat control systems, are strongholds for automotive firms but also actively sought after by robot builders.

Chinese EV maker Xpeng and autonomous driving technology developer Baidu got off to an early start in building robots. Five years ago, they offered a sneak peek into their vision of the future of mobility, underscoring the role of robotics technology.

In August 2021, when Baidu founder and CEO Robin Li Yanhong unveiled a prototype “robocar”, he said that in the future “a car will be equivalent to a robot”.

The two-seat vehicle looked like something out of a science fiction movie. It had no steering wheel or pedals, featured two retractable doors, and the cockpit was dominated by a large curved intelligent display and a control pad.

A month later, Guangzhou-based Xpeng announced its plan to release a four-legged robot pony for children, banking on its design and manufacturing capabilities to churn out robotic products equipped with power modules, motion controls, intelligent navigation, and emotional interaction capabilities.

Today, Chinese carmakers are viewed as strong rivals to Tesla as they meld the latest AI technologies with mobility, industry officials and analysts said.

In December, Musk endorsed Xpeng’s Iron humanoid robot on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla.

Tesla has yet to sell any of its Optimus humanoid robots, and Musk is now transforming the EV maker from a hardware-centric business into a ­physical AI firm.

Tesla has halted production of its Model S and Model X cars at its plant in Fremont, California, and instead will build humanoid robots in the facility.

In April, Tesla’s China president, Allan Wang Hao, said the company’s Shanghai Gigafactory had the potential to produce humanoid robots, taking advantage of the mainland’s complete supply chain and advanced manufacturing techniques.

The contest between Chinese carmakers and Tesla in humanoid robots takes on broader importance in the context of the heated China-US tech rivalry.

The two countries are battling for supremacy in a number of fields, with humanoid robotics one of the key areas where Beijing and Washington hope their companies can establish global dominance.

Thanks to the country’s diverse supply chain and large production scale, upstream Chinese suppliers could make high-quality, cost-efficient and innovative components for various types of robots, including humanoids, according to Lu Hancheng, former director of the Shenzhen-based Gaogong Robot Industry Research Institute.

Mainland China was now home to more than 150 humanoid robot makers, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. They delivered 97 per cent of the total humanlike robots on the global market in the first half of the year, according to Morgan Stanley.

Early this year, the US bank predicted that the global humanoid market would achieve US$7.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2050.

Morgan Stanley also forecast in July that China’s humanoid robot shipments could hit 446,000 units by 2030, jumping nearly ninefold from about 50,000 units this year, spurred by competition to reach deployment scale and to close the real-world data feedback loop.

Among the Chinese carmakers diversifying into robotics, BYD and Xpeng are now under the spotlight due to their development and manufacturing heft as their mass production plans draw near.

At the end of July, BYD said in a statement to the South China Morning Post that its first humanoid robots would debut in August at the firm’s Di Space experience centres, but that timetable has now been delayed.

In June, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice-president, predicted that China would become the first market to “see full commercialisation of humanoid robots”.

However, automotive giants do not just see themselves as just making robots to sell on the open market. They also aim to achieve a high level of automation in production by gaining experience in embodied AI technology.

In late July, BYD formed a strategic partnership with Chinese robotics start-up PaXini Tech to deploy robots in manufacturing. The carmaker will create real-world industrial environments for the robots, generating operating data to help train embodied AI models.

Xpeng’s robotics subsidiary Dogotix received US$900 million in its latest round of financing last month, which valued it at US$6.3 billion. The fundraising, which attracted Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the SCMP, and IDG Capital, marked the biggest single private-equity deal involving a Chinese robotics maker.

The company said it planned to begin producing its Iron humanoid robots at the end of 2026, targeting an initial volume of 1,000 units, to be deployed as sales assistants at its domestic showrooms.

Iron runs on the firm’s Vision-Language-Action 2.0 AI model. Unlike older systems that translate images into text-based code before executing a movement, the newer model allows the robot’s neural network to convert visual data directly into motion, improving task efficiency and reducing information loss.

Xpeng CEO He Xiaopeng said in November that the company aimed to sell 1 million robots annually by 2030, when costs would be brought down to a level to make the products affordable for household use.

Rivals Li Auto, Xiaomi and Leapmotor have all ramped up the development of humanoid robots, which are expected to perform tasks such as factory work and elderly care.

Since early 2024, Chery Automobile has been working with AI company Aimoga to develop Mornine, a humanoid robot capable of understanding natural language and interpreting human intentions.

At the World Robot Conference in Beijing last month, the industry’s mindset had firmly pivoted towards real-world application ramp-up, Goldman Sachs said.

“While demonstrations of locomotion and entertainment still attract interest, discussions are now centred on quantifiable metrics such as task performance, success rates, throughput, and payback periods, reflecting a healthy maturation of the sector,” the bank said in a research report. “Logistics sorting has emerged as one of the most visible early commercialisation directions.”

Shao Yu, chief economist with the Sci-tech Innovation Centre at Fudan University’s School of Management, said tech industries, propelled by government support and an influx of private capital, were acting as the major growth driver for the Chinese economy.

Shao added that tech sectors, from advanced semiconductors to embodied AI, would sustain their strength over a period of time despite worries of an AI-generated bubble.

“With the trend of innovation, more investment will be made to those hi-tech areas to reflect the K-shaped structure of the Chinese economy,” Shao said. “The crux point is how to leverage hi-tech companies and products to benefit society as a whole.”

A K-shaped divergence refers to China’s economic structure, where hi-tech manufacturing and exports are thriving while consumption, property and traditional industries are experiencing slower growth.

But Xu Mingqi, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, threw a wet blanket over investors’ expectations for quick returns from investing in physical AI.

Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly

Xu Mingqi, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences

“No AI technology with material impact on people’s lifestyle has been in sight yet,” he told reporters in a media briefing this month. “Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly and it will still turn out to be a long drawn-out process.”

item.title: [SCMP] From Ohio to Hong Kong: former NBA player Bryant Austin’s basketball journey
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Lima, Ohio, a small city in the United States, to high-school sweethearts, in 1987. My childhood was split between the inner city and my great-grandparents’ farm: livestock, a wood-burning furnace, the whole thing. Although both my parents had been athletes, I never saw them in their prime. Instead, I watched my older sister. My parents split up when I was six or seven, and we moved to Columbus. My mum worked four jobs to support us. Money was tight, but there were constants: Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan films, and a meal at a Chinese restaurant as a reward when I did well at school.

AT MY GRANDFATHER’S house, I’d sit for hours watching old VHS basketball tapes. There was Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan. One clip stayed with me – a young Kobe Bryant growing up in Italy, speaking Italian, playing basketball on the other side of the world (his father played for an Italian team). Something shifted in me. I started to dream of playing overseas. I was also quietly obsessed with Asia. I watched anime, drew constantly – it felt like a world I couldn’t explain to anyone in Ohio. Every year, our teacher asked us what our top three ambitions were. Mine never changed: professional basketball player, marine biologist, or lawyer. In that order. I was already manifesting it.

MY SISTER IS two years older than me, and she was my hero before I knew what that meant. At school, she protected me from bullies, from older boys who wanted to jump me. When I was 13, a group of men broke into our home and held our family hostage at gunpoint for hours. While two of them left to move what they had stolen, one stayed behind. My sister – 15, maybe 16 then – wrestled the gun away from him. She shot him in the face. She saved all of us.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Lima, Ohio, a small city in the United States, to high-school sweethearts, in 1987. My childhood was split between the inner city and my great-grandparents’ farm: livestock, a wood-burning furnace, the whole thing. Although both my parents had been athletes, I never saw them in their prime. Instead, I watched my older sister. My parents split up when I was six or seven, and we moved to Columbus. My mum worked four jobs to support us. Money was tight, but there were constants: Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan films, and a meal at a Chinese restaurant as a reward when I did well at school.

AT MY GRANDFATHER’S house, I’d sit for hours watching old VHS basketball tapes. There was Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan. One clip stayed with me – a young Kobe Bryant growing up in Italy, speaking Italian, playing basketball on the other side of the world (his father played for an Italian team). Something shifted in me. I started to dream of playing overseas. I was also quietly obsessed with Asia. I watched anime, drew constantly – it felt like a world I couldn’t explain to anyone in Ohio. Every year, our teacher asked us what our top three ambitions were. Mine never changed: professional basketball player, marine biologist, or lawyer. In that order. I was already manifesting it.

MY SISTER IS two years older than me, and she was my hero before I knew what that meant. At school, she protected me from bullies, from older boys who wanted to jump me. When I was 13, a group of men broke into our home and held our family hostage at gunpoint for hours. While two of them left to move what they had stolen, one stayed behind. My sister – 15, maybe 16 then – wrestled the gun away from him. She shot him in the face. She saved all of us.

I WASN’T AN immediate star. I have always been super-introverted, and had anxiety interacting with crowds and fans. I didn’t make varsity until my senior year. No one was knocking down my door offering scholarships. So, I started clicking through university websites, cold-emailing coaches. That’s how mundane it was. I ended up playing at Notre Dame College, then Columbus State and Indiana Tech. After graduating, I played in the professional minor leagues, but it wasn’t enough.

MY TURNING POINT was a high-profile tournament in Portsmouth, Virginia, where I was up against players from Duke, Kentucky, North Carolina – the big blue-blood universities. I didn’t just hold my own; I dominated. There was a rage in me, the accumulated weight of being overlooked for years. My trainer and mentor, Greg “Radar” Williamson, spent two years helping me prepare for that moment.

BY THE END, three NBA (National Basketball Association) agents were competing to represent me: Andre Buck, who worked with LeBron James; Sean Rooks, who had played alongside Kobe and Shaq (Shaquille O’Neal); and John Spencer, who had a past playing in Hong Kong’s A1 Division against Yao Ming and China’s national team. I signed with John. At the time, I didn’t realise how significant he would become to me.

AT 25, I WAS drafted into the NBA Development League by the Fort Wayne Mad Ants. It was overwhelming. You’re meeting Magic Johnson and all these star players. So, on one side, you’re starstruck and on the other side, you’re thinking, “I’m supposed to be here.”

I BROKE MY thumb the day before training camp. I decided to play through it without a cast because the NBA is so cutthroat, I couldn’t risk losing my shot. I also had a newborn son at home and no room for excuses. That season, I was also working as an overnight carer for disabled adults and as a substitute teacher. Three jobs, one broken thumb, a new baby. On the court, I was playing beside Khris Middleton, who would go on to become an NBA All-Star. I was proud, exhausted and watching every penny.

AT THE END of that season, the team president, Jeff Potter, sat me down and was honest with me. He advised me to go overseas, build my profile and then come back, as I wasn’t getting much court time alongside so many more experienced players. John Spencer helped me get a contract in Israel. And when I landed in Tel Aviv (in October 2013), I was in heaven. I had an apartment right by the sea. The city was beautiful: new culture, new language, new food. Then came the blood clot.

I PLAYED THROUGH what I thought was a severe calf strain for a month – it felt like my leg was being sawn off – but ego and pride refused to let me sit it out. I had developed a blood clot in my leg and then one in my lung and didn’t know it. The pain started in my chest, and nearly ended everything – not just my career, but my life.

I WAS BACK home in the US (by December 2013), had almost died and was injecting blood thinners daily. The doctors told me I couldn’t play. I was depressed for six months. I didn’t talk to many people, I just retreated into myself and stopped training. I’d fought all those years to have my name on that jersey. Having it taken away so suddenly left me in a dark place. Then, a new drug, Xarelto, appeared and gave my cardiologist enough confidence to clear me. That same week (in April 2014), without knowing any of this, John Spencer called out of nowhere and asked if I’d go to Hong Kong. The league had been closed to American imports since the 2008 financial crisis, but had just reopened and the money was good. I call that timing a call from God.

I STEPPED OFF the plane into the heat and humidity, and looked up at the skyline. Instantly, I fell completely in love. I saw bamboo scaffolding around glass towers and felt like I’d walked onto a Rush Hour set. Apparently, I was all over the local media. My American teammate, Reggie Johnson, had full culture shock; the density, the noise, strangers staring at two tall black guys on trains and in lifts. But I didn’t mind any of it. It felt like arriving somewhere I’d been dreaming of since I was a kid.

THE BASKETBALL SYSTEM in Hong Kong is unlike anywhere else; it’s fast-paced and kind of chaotic. We won the championship with the Eastern Long Lions (now Hong Kong Eastern) team. I flew my mum over for the final and we celebrated with champagne.

IN AUGUST 2014, I went to Bangkok to party for a week, to celebrate my Hong Kong championship with my close friend and NBA G League teammate, Tommy Smith, who works with me today. I asked to train with his team to stay sharp between nights out. They begged me to stay and I said yes. I played in the Thai Super League season, and then for an Indonesian team in Surabaya.

INSTEAD OF GOING back to the US, I realised that life had a plan for me in Asia, and specifically in Hong Kong – it always drew me in. Now, I play forward and point guard for Chongde Flying Eagle here in the A1 Division. When I first got here, the Hong Kong fans were crazy, following me around, asking for autographs, photos. I just love that they love basketball as much as I do. I started a basketball academy with just five kids. I’d turn up in my jersey on the street courts of Southorn Playground, Nathan Road and Victoria Park, and ask to join games. Kids would clock who I was and ask if I coached. That’s how my academy, League MVP, started – organically.

TODAY, OUR TEAM works with up to 150 local boys as well as international students here on holiday camps. We’ve worked with refugee children from Africa, India and Pakistan. One of the players I coached, Hong Kong-born David Muoka, became the first from the city to be drafted into the NBA.

WHAT I WANT for Hong Kong basketball is more visibility, more opportunity. There’s talent here. It just needs investment, time and belief. Hong Kong is an underdog, but there are a lot of passionate players, and I want them to win.

MY SON IS 13 now. Every summer, he comes over from Ohio. I wake him early – he hates it – and we’re in the gym by 5am. I never forced basketball on him, but once he chose it, I made it clear: no short cuts. We train hard, then we enjoy the city – Disneyland, Ocean Park, beaches, hotpot, the MTR. I push him to explore independently; this city is safe enough to do that.

TWELVE YEARS AFTER I arrived, Hong Kong is home – not a posting, or a chapter. I’m 38, still playing, still growing my business, still up early doing weights – my life is kind of consumed by basketball. I’m manifesting my end game – the best is yet to come. And I know I want to be here when the next kid from a Hong Kong court makes it somewhere nobody expected, and gives the city another reason to believe.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Xi tells Modi China and India bear ‘significant responsibilities’ as Global South powers
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.

Xi said that although the countries had different national circumstances, “there is ample scope for us to learn from each other’s strengths, offer mutual support, achieve shared success and pursue common development”.

“Over the past two years, Prime Minister Modi and I have met twice, guiding the relationship from a ‘fresh start’ to a ‘new level of advancement’,” Xi said, according to a readout from Xinhua.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.

Xi said that although the countries had different national circumstances, “there is ample scope for us to learn from each other’s strengths, offer mutual support, achieve shared success and pursue common development”.

“Over the past two years, Prime Minister Modi and I have met twice, guiding the relationship from a ‘fresh start’ to a ‘new level of advancement’,” Xi said, according to a readout from Xinhua.

“Institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the list of cooperative initiatives has steadily expanded, and the volume of bilateral trade has hit a new high. This situation was hard-won and deserves to be cherished.”

On the border issue, Xi said that both sides should maintain peace and tranquillity in boundary areas and commit to “parallel development and mutual promotion of bilateral relations and border issues”.

The two sides have sparred repeatedly along their ill-defined border, including the 2020 Galwan Valley clash in which at least 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.

Even the length of the border is not agreed upon, with India recording it at around 2,160-miles (3,476 km) while China puts it at less than half that.

Xi looks to ‘future of humanity’, ‘well-being of our people’

The two leaders met on the sidelines of the Brics summit in New Delhi, where trade, investment, the long-running border dispute and the normalisation of ties took centre stage.

“We must keep the future of humanity and the well-being of our people at heart, join hands to drive high-quality cooperation within the expanded Brics framework, advocate for an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive,” the Chinese leader said.

Xi also called for both sides to inject greater positive energy into promoting global peace, stability and prosperity.

The Chinese president acknowledged that the two countries, with their combined 2.8 billion people, are in “different” economic and geopolitical positions. But he said they could “learn from each other’s strengths”, offer mutual support, prosper and pursue common development.

China’s economy is currently four times larger than India’s in nominal GDP terms, compared with rough parity in 1987.

Xi outlined a vague four-point plan for future China-India relations that was short on specifics, in keeping with many of Beijing’s foreign policy initiatives.

He called on the neighbours to align on “objective and rational” strategy; engage in “win-win” cooperation; overcome differences through “political wisdom” and mutual understanding; and collaborate to bolster the global good in part by working together in multilateral groupings.

“China and India are partners rather than rivals, and present opportunities for each other’s development rather than threats,” he said, according to Xinhua.

Xi, Modi address lingering China-India border questions

The meeting began at 5.45pm, with Cai Qi, a close aide to Xi and China’s fifth-ranking official, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi taking part.

India was represented by National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and Vikram Doraiswami, India’s ambassador to China.

The two countries have been trying to turn their fragile diplomatic thaw into a broader reset following years of military tensions, frozen political engagement and sharply curtailed economic and people-to-people links.

New Delhi’s statement on the meeting said the two leaders “reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties”, and that “differences should not become disputes”.

Modi “emphasised that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”, underlining “the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues”.

“The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples,” the statement read.

According to China’s version, India also said it “adheres to an independent foreign policy” and its relationship with China is “not influenced by third parties”, an apparent reference to any role by Washington.

Beijing further noted that India’s policy and stance regarding Taiwan and Tibet-related issues “remain unchanged”, adding that New Delhi “does not permit any forces to engage in anti-China activities on Indian soil”. More than 70,000 Tibetans live in India, including the 91-year-old Dalai Lama.

Xi arrived in New Delhi around midday on Saturday leading about a 70-strong delegation. He is scheduled to attend Sunday morning’s Brics summit session before leaving the country.

A separate Chinese business delegation is also visiting, underscoring the economic dimension of the trip.

The meeting is taking place amid tight security, and Chinese personnel were spotted in New Delhi ahead of Xi’s visit.

Deadly Galwan clash colours China-India relations

The optics of the visit are significant. Xi’s last trip to India was in October 2019, when he held informal talks with Modi. His first trip as leader took place in 2014, and he also took part in the 2016 Brics summit in Goa.

But high-level engagement between the two countries came to a near-standstill after the deadly Galwan confrontation.

The incident led to a multi-year military stand-off along their disputed frontier, with direct flights and several official dialogue channels being suspended.

Pilgrims were also barred from travelling from India to sacred sites such as Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar in Tibet.

The first major political opening came in October 2024, when Modi and Xi met on the sidelines of the Brics summit in Russia after the two sides reached an understanding on disengagement along the border.

The two leaders also met on the sidelines of last year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organisation meeting in the Chinese city of Tianjin.

Meanwhile, direct flights have resumed and pilgrims have been permitted to travel to the sacred sites. The Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination and the Special Representatives’ Dialogue on the Boundary Question have also resumed.

Last month, after the latest border talks between Wang and Doval in Beijing, the two sides issued a rare joint statement, signalling an effort to build momentum ahead of Xi’s India visit.

They also produced an eight-point consensus that included commitments to keep the frontier quiet, create new working groups, add military communication channels and continue talks on pilgrimages, border trade and rivers.

The next round of boundary talks will be held in India in 2027.

The bigger test now may be whether the diplomatic thaw can translate into an economic reset.

Saturday’s Indian statement said the two leaders also agreed to intensify people-to-people exchanges and pledged to address concerns regarding market access, trade imbalances and supply chains, points echoed in China’s version.

Two-way goods trade has continued to grow, exceeding US$150 billion in the latest full-year figures, according to publicly reported customs data. But the economic relationship remains heavily skewed and politically sensitive.

For Beijing, a stable relationship with India could help restore one of its most consequential Asian economic partnerships.

For New Delhi, the question is whether greater economic engagement can take place while it has concerns over market access, trade imbalances, investment and national security.
