“India appreciates China’s support for its hosting of the Brics summit and pledges full support for China’s Brics chairmanship next year,” according to China’s readout.

“India is ready to coordinate and cooperate closely with China to strengthen Global South cooperation, promote a multipolar world and economic growth and serve as a force for stability and progress in a turbulent world.”

item.title: [SCMP] Foie gras, puppies, water parks: North Korea gets a glow-up
item.description:
Coffee bars. Water parks. Retail therapy. ⁠North Korea – a country few would associate with leisure or pleasure – is experiencing an ⁠unlikely outbreak of fun.

Leader Kim Jong-un, himself no stranger to indulgence, is orchestrating new ways for his citizens to spend ⁠their wealth. North Korea’s imports of massage equipment have surged 40-fold over the past decade, according to Chinese customs data. Treadmill shipments jumped over 600 per cent. Pianos and even bumper cars are pouring in, too.

The consumption drive extends to luxury malls, beach resorts and ski destinations that are popping up around North Korea, according to a review of trade statistics and state media reports, and interviews with five recent visitors and two defectors.
item.content:encoded:
Coffee bars. Water parks. Retail therapy. ⁠North Korea – a country few would associate with leisure or pleasure – is experiencing an ⁠unlikely outbreak of fun.

Leader Kim Jong-un, himself no stranger to indulgence, is orchestrating new ways for his citizens to spend ⁠their wealth. North Korea’s imports of massage equipment have surged 40-fold over the past decade, according to Chinese customs data. Treadmill shipments jumped over 600 per cent. Pianos and even bumper cars are pouring in, too.

The consumption drive extends to luxury malls, beach resorts and ski destinations that are popping up around North Korea, according to a review of trade statistics and state media reports, and interviews with five recent visitors and two defectors.

It’s not just about expanding access to life’s little luxuries, analysts say. By channelling personal spending through state-controlled leisure and retail networks, Kim strengthens government control of commerce, squeezes informal markets and unlocks new sources of revenue and growth for the nuclear-armed country.

The strategy drew “the production, distribution and capital flows concentrated in the markets into an official economic space managed by the state,” said ‌Kang Seong-hyeon, a research fellow at the Seoul-based Hyundai Research Institute think tank.

Avenues for consumption have proliferated even as North Korea faces heavy UN sanctions – including on luxury goods, energy and mineral trade – designed to impede Kim’s weapons programme. North Korea’s economy grew 3.5 per cent in 2025, a third consecutive year above 3 per cent, the South Korean central bank said in July.

The glow-up has attracted the attention of outsiders. After visiting Pyongyang in May, Singapore’s foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan called the capital’s progress “remarkable”, saying it resembled “any modern city” in East Asia.

Residents drink cappuccinos and browse home appliances at the Rangnang Aeguk Kumgang Service Complex, a luxury shopping centre in Pyongyang that opened last year, according to social media videos verified by reporters.

A hard-earned thirst can be quenched at the Hwasong Taedonggang Beer Restaurant, a two-year-old drinking den celebrated in state media.

In April, Kim toured a new pet shop with his daughter, Kim Ju-ae, who was drawn to the kittens and puppies.

Pyongyang’s leisure blitz is bankrolled by revenue streams including cryptocurrency heists, the deployment of North Korean troops to fight for Russia in Ukraine and exports of coal and other minerals, according to South Korean researchers.

The United States and other foreign officials and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly tied crypto theft to North Korean state-sponsored ⁠hackers. The Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy, a South Korean government-funded think tank, estimates North Korea earned up to US$14.4 billion from its involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war between August 2023 and December 2025.

The influx of cash trickles through North Korea’s economy, where many have also made money from informal trade.

But accumulated wealth created a problem: “a ‌middle class of roughly 8 million people with savings and nowhere to spend them”, said Ruediger Frank, a professor of East Asian economy and society at the University of Vienna.

Consumption was Kim’s answer, Frank said: it reduced frustration, channelled money away from bidding up prices of essentials such as rice and generated growth through domestic demand.

With its fortunes uplifted, North Korea has less need for sanctions relief and fewer incentives to restart nuclear negotiations with Washington, analysts have said, despite US President Donald Trump’s stated desire for another ‌meeting with Kim.

North Korea’s embassy in Beijing did not respond to questions about the domestic-consumption drive. Russia’s foreign ministry and the White House also did not comment.

China’s foreign ministry said it maintained trade and cooperation with North Korea while implementing UN Security Council resolutions, adding that sanctions should not ⁠affect the country’s livelihood.

Mentions of tourism, leisure and cultural life in ⁠North Korean state media have increased since 2022 as attractions have been opened or refurbished, a review of more than 1,200 articles found.

These developments include the Wonsan Kalma beach resort, which launched in the summer of 2025; five luxury hotels that opened in December in Samjiyon, on the Chinese border; a ski resort under construction nearby; and a water park and yet-to-be-finished equestrian club in the northeast.

State media coverage of a heatwave ‌in August showed the Wonsan beach resort packed with domestic visitors.

“One local contact even told me that when taking his family there, several members had to share a twin room because everything else had already been booked,” said Rowan Beard, co-founder of travel operator Young Pioneer Tours.

Wonsan Kalma received more than 300,000 domestic visitors in the latter half of 2025, according to China’s embassy in Pyongyang, which mentioned the figure in a February ‌post about its ‌ambassador’s visit.

Saunas, pools, video-game arcades and sports centres had also sprung up in northeastern Rason city, said a Chinese businessman who gave his surname as Cui.

As part of a regional development plan, Kim is also building leisure complexes containing libraries, restaurants and cinemas across the country, with at least two dozen completed or under construction, ‌according to state media.

But the most lavish additions are in Pyongyang. State media has described a new housing district containing a gaming arcade, car showroom and a barbecue restaurant that serves salmon belly and foie gras burgers.

The range of goods available in North Korea also has expanded, according to three recent visitors.

At Ryugyong Golden Plaza, ⁠which opened in 2023, shops display the logos of watchmakers including Rolex, Omega and Herbelin, and an electronics store features Huawei branding, according to social media footage verified by reporters.

Rolex and Huawei declined to comment. Omega and Herbelin said they had no official retailers or distributors in North Korea.

North Koreans shop online using mobile ⁠apps, according to images published by Beard and NKTechLab, an analysis project of the US-based Stimson Centre think tank. Beard, who visited Pyongyang in May, said mobile app payments were used “everywhere” and for “anything available for sale”.

Trade statistics show how the leisure drive encompasses both personal goods and state-led infrastructure.

Chinese customs data reveal surging shipments of pianos, watches and amusement equipment – including merry-go-rounds, rollercoasters and waterslides. North Korea imported more than 3 tonnes of bumper cars from China, worth more than US$20,000, between January 2025 and July this year.

Trade with China has rebounded broadly since the Covid-19 pandemic. A ‌flourishing car culture has even emerged in Pyongyang, fuelled by Chinese imports.

After North Korea’s famine in the 1990s, semi-legal markets flourished as the state could not supply residents. Attempts to close them early this century failed because the state lacked the distribution infrastructure to replace them, according to Jung Chang-Hyun, director of the Peace Economy Research Institute in Seoul.

Now, Kim’s consumption gambit served that purpose: building state commercial infrastructure that could compete with and eventually undermine private markets, he said.

Payment and delivery apps also enable official scrutiny of private spending, analysts say. In 2023, Pyongyang passed a law requiring every bank and store to accept electronic payments.

Not everyone benefits from the consumption boom. Yang Il-cheol, who worked as a driver in Pyongyang before defecting to South Korea last year, said people like him had little access to the new restaurants and leisure facilities.

While cellphones had become ubiquitous in the capital, many North Koreans distrusted the government and preferred cash payments, Yang said.

Frank, the professor, said Kim’s campaign to boost domestic spending appeared to be paying off – for now.

“Consumption buys time,” he said. “It does not buy loyalty forever.”

item.title: [SCMP] As Singapore weighs joining China-led AI body, does it risk US retaliation?
item.description:
As Singapore considers joining a China-led body on artificial intelligence, analysts say membership would give the city state a bigger say in global governance matters related to the technology but may invite an unfriendly response from Washington.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo revealed in parliament earlier this week that Singapore had received an invitation to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Singapore would consider the proposal alongside its broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives, she added.

Launched in July, the Shanghai-based bloc aims to build cooperation in areas such as AI governance, technical standards and development strategies.
item.content:encoded:
As Singapore considers joining a China-led body on artificial intelligence, analysts say membership would give the city state a bigger say in global governance matters related to the technology but may invite an unfriendly response from Washington.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo revealed in parliament earlier this week that Singapore had received an invitation to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Singapore would consider the proposal alongside its broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives, she added.

Launched in July, the Shanghai-based bloc aims to build cooperation in areas such as AI governance, technical standards and development strategies.

Responding to a parliamentary question on Singapore’s strategic positioning between Waico and the US-led Pax Silica initiative, Teo said on Wednesday: “Whether we participate in any particular initiative depends on its objectives, the substantive areas of common interest, how it complements our existing engagements, and Singapore’s overall interests.

“It is therefore less meaningful to make one-to-one comparisons between individual initiatives.”

The Pax Silica initiative aims to help partners strengthen supply chains for minerals essential to AI. Singapore was among seven signatories that agreed to collaborate during its launch last December.

The government said the initiative aligned with its approach of pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation with international partners and reflected a “shared commitment to advance prosperity, technological progress and economic security”.

Teo added: “What matters most is the overall relationships we have with each of our partners, and how we can continue to work with them in ways that advance Singapore’s interests and contribute constructively to international cooperation on AI.”

‘Less about China’

Joining the China-led bloc would, in principle, be in Singapore’s interests by providing a platform to shape AI governance. But an intensifying superpower rivalry over the fast-evolving technology might complicate decision-making, analysts said.

Beijing has positioned Waico as a way to advance “AI for good and for all”.

William Heidlage, senior director of technology at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, said Singapore was likely to evaluate Waico membership based on whether it would have a say in AI issues.

“For Singapore, joining Waico is less about China and more about whether it can shape emerging AI governance from inside the room,” he said.

Teo said on Wednesday that it was in Singapore’s interest to ensure AI interoperability, noting that diverging international standards would pose difficulties for companies based in the city state.

Heidlage said the objectives of Waico and Pax Silica were complementary rather than contradictory for Singapore. “One seeks to prevent fragmentation in governance and the other seeks to prevent concentration in capability,” he said.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said accepting Beijing’s invitation could give Singapore a larger say in shaping governance standards. “This could be useful for Singapore if the organisation ends up being substantive and independent.”

Miguel Alberto Gomez, a senior research fellow at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, noted that joining Waico would give Singapore greater access to AI technology that could not be developed domestically, while reducing the risk of over-dependence on the United States and its partners.

But analysts cautioned that the decision could not be viewed independently of broader geopolitical friction.

Growing competition between Washington and Beijing made the invitation “less straightforward than before”, said Chong, suggesting that dual membership could prompt the US to impose restrictions that Waico’s benefits might not offset.

The invitation comes as countries face escalating pressure to choose between both superpowers in the AI race. While Pax Silica does not explicitly target China, its objective to reduce “coercive dependencies” is widely interpreted to reference China’s dominance and rare earths.

Reuters reported last month that Washington was preparing to tell a dozen countries to pick sides, warning they would be excluded from Pax Silica if they were to sign up for the Chinese framework. Kazakhstan is the only nation so far with membership in both initiatives.

Beijing, however, has said it firmly opposes forcing countries to take sides or creating bloc confrontation in AI.

Joining Waico might also limit Singapore’s ability to engage with parties leaning strongly towards either AI bloc, Gomez said. “This is not a novel situation for Singapore, and ultimately it must prioritise its own strategic interests.”

The city state, which has long maintained a stance of non-alignment, had to prioritise its own strategic interests while maintaining cordial relations with both powers, Gomez said.

“I do not think this reality is lost on both the US and China. Moreover, I would think both are aware of the value of having Singapore on side in the long run, especially in this region.”

Unified Asean position?

While a collective Asean position on Waico and Pax Silica would give the 11-nation bloc greater bargaining power, analysts said a consensus among its members would be unlikely due to diverging national interests.

Teo confirmed on Wednesday that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations had no position on either organisation.

Chong said Asean members could wield greater influence in shaping regulations and norms for AI initiatives if they used their collective weight. “It could also have the option of setting its own standards, given the accumulated economic, population and geographic size of Asean,” he said.

However, reaching an agreement would be challenging for a bloc operating on the principle of consensus. Tensions arising from competing AI frameworks could further strain internal cohesiveness, Chong added.

Singapore and the Philippines are the only two Asean members in Pax Silica, which is widely perceived as an effort to isolate China from key technology supply chains. Five other Asean members – Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia and Myanmar – were among the 29 original signatories at Waico’s launch.

A consolidated Asean position would require members to navigate competing interests and priorities, said Elina Noor, a non-resident scholar in the Asia programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

“In theory, it’s possible for Asean to form a common or consolidated position, but in reality, its members compete with each other on both the supply chain and governance fronts,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Marcos’ Brics trip is ‘low-risk opportunity’ for Philippines to make new friends
item.description:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr is set to be the first Philippine leader to join the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend – presenting him with the perfect “low-risk opportunity” to engage the grouping as Manila continues to diversify its ties, analysts say.

“The president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel said in a press briefing on Wednesday.

“This participation is a strategic opportunity to monitor emerging economic frameworks and to represent the priorities and perspectives of the region, while directly engaging leaders of major emerging economies.”
item.content:encoded:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr is set to be the first Philippine leader to join the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend – presenting him with the perfect “low-risk opportunity” to engage the grouping as Manila continues to diversify its ties, analysts say.

“The president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel said in a press briefing on Wednesday.

“This participation is a strategic opportunity to monitor emerging economic frameworks and to represent the priorities and perspectives of the region, while directly engaging leaders of major emerging economies.”

Brics, an international organisation formed in 2009 of emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members.

While Marcos is attending the event in his capacity as Asean chair, he is also scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and business executives on the sidelines. Issues to be discussed include the progress of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership, a review of the implementation of an action plan for 2025 to 2029, and a follow-up with business leaders on the US$5.8 billion investment pledges Marcos secured during a state visit to India in August last year.

Analysts say the summit is Marcos’ chance to engage Brics members and diversify beyond its traditional ties with the US amid geopolitical tensions with China. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to be attending, marking his first trip to India in seven years.

“The Asean chairship provides President Marcos with a relatively low-risk opportunity to engage Brics more closely without necessarily signalling that the Philippines is already moving towards membership or changing its broader strategic orientation,” said Enrico Gloria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

The engagement was “not particularly unusual” given that Association of Southeast Asian Nations members already have varying degrees of ties with Brics, he said. Indonesia is a full member and Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam are partner countries. “For the Philippines, this is less as choosing another geopolitical camp and more as a way for it to continue diversifying its partnerships.”

‘Friends to all’

Marcos’ attendance reflected his “friends to all and enemy to none” stance on foreign policy, said Chester Cabalza, founder and president of the Manila-based think tank International Development and Security Cooperation. Under Marcos, the Philippines has signed defence pacts with countries such as Japan, Canada, New Zealand and France.

“Marcos should not ignore this opportunity, not only because he represents Asean, but also due to India’s benevolent acts to the Philippines. The Philippines has India to thank for the Brahmos missiles,” he said. “The growing economic potential of Brics is unprecedented in terms of its energy and AI global outputs.”

For a smaller power such as the Philippines, “expanding the number of countries and institutions it can work with increases its room to manoeuvre”, Gloria said.

Last year, Marcos said he was open to considering Brics membership for the Philippines. But this visit appeared to be “exploratory rather than preparatory”, Gloria said, adding it was not “evidence that Manila is already moving towards a formal plan of accession”.

There is an important difference between being open to something and having made it a foreign-policy objective. Marcos himself framed it last year largely in terms of giving the Philippines more options, rather than announcing an intention to join,” he said.

This is a good chance to re-engage China and India amid uncertainties from the global oil crisis, according to Cabalza. “Manila should learn from India’s non-alignment policy even as Delhi experienced a territorial rift with Beijing in 2000,” he said. “Navigating this tedious diplomatic stunt is important for a country that needs to bring home barrels of oil, employment through investments, and latest AI protocols.”

Despite the finalisation of the code of conduct in the South China Sea remaining an Asean priority, it was unlikely that Marcos would tackle China on maritime issues, he added. “He is going to India as Asean chair, so Marcos’ policy recommendations and contributions to the conversation must attribute to the needs of Asean. He is a statesman from Southeast Asia and not only of the Philippines in that summit.”

Beyond India

One of the most consequential goals of Marcos’ visit would be a deepening engagement with India, both analysts said.

“⁠Following up on the Indian investment commitments should certainly be one of the most tangible objectives of the visit,” Gloria said. “A meeting with Prime Minister Modi offers an important opportunity to assess how much of that potential can actually move towards implementation.”

Manila can also explore further partnerships with India – especially as it looks to strengthen its position as a hub for diversified supply chains. One possibility is the multi-country Pax Silica initiative to secure global supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals.

“This could help move the conversation beyond individual investment pledges towards a more strategic discussion of how Philippine-Indian economic cooperation can contribute to more resilient and diversified regional supply chains,” Gloria said.

Predicting that India would be the “future second-largest economy of the world”, Cabalza said it would be good to “enhance our ties to secure investments in agriculture, business process outsourcing, medical and spaceport ventures”.

However, Gloria cautioned that the Philippines should not focus solely on India as the forum presented a chance for Manila to develop a diverse range of partners beyond traditionally aligned states.

“One weakness of Philippine foreign relations historically has been the concentration of our diplomatic emphasis and economic attention on a relatively small number of major partners. A more multipolar world requires the Philippines to develop a multipolar diplomatic portfolio as well,” he said.

“As the current Asean chair, the Philippines is poised to leverage that institutional power not just for the region but for its own interests as well to diversify existing partnerships.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s export machine strengthens in August as US critiques trade imbalance
item.description:
China’s exports continued to beat expectations in August, buoyed by strong demand for tech products and pre-Christmas orders that offset severe weather disruptions, though analysts warned the country’s widening trade imbalances remained a concern among Western policymakers.

The country’s exports rose by 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion last month, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday. The reading was above a forecast of 21.93 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. That compared with 23.9 per cent growth in July.

China also saw imports grow by 28.2 per cent last month to US$282.36 billion, slightly above the Wind poll’s projections of 28.07 per cent growth.
item.content:encoded:
China’s exports continued to beat expectations in August, buoyed by strong demand for tech products and pre-Christmas orders that offset severe weather disruptions, though analysts warned the country’s widening trade imbalances remained a concern among Western policymakers.

The country’s exports rose by 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion last month, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday. The reading was above a forecast of 21.93 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. That compared with 23.9 per cent growth in July.

China also saw imports grow by 28.2 per cent last month to US$282.36 billion, slightly above the Wind poll’s projections of 28.07 per cent growth.

That brought China’s trade surplus to US$119.09 billion last month, up from US$112.5 billion in July. This marked the fourth consecutive month the surplus had stayed above US$100 billion.

China’s export sector has remained resilient this year, as the global artificial intelligence boom and energy security worries linked to regional conflicts – including the US-Israel war on Iran – have driven up shipments of goods as well as prices.

Exports have also benefited from seasonal pre-Christmas orders, though a series of typhoons last month caused widespread delays at Shanghai’s two major container ports.

Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said that demand related to AI offset the effects of adverse weather, with high-priced tech shipments boosting export figures, while tariff uncertainty continued to front-load US import demand.

However, looking ahead, Xing said he expected overall export growth to slow later in the year due to a higher base, noting exports may be close to their peak and fourth-quarter growth “may not be so strong”.

Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, also noted that tech-related export categories outperformed in August. “The trade data came in broadly in line with expectations, and illustrates that external demand remains strong.”

He added he expected China’s balance of trade to keep growing, with another record trade surplus likely by the end of this year. The cumulative surplus had already reached US$805.51 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up about 3 per cent from the same period last year, customs data showed.

That figure, which hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year, has drawn intensified scrutiny from the West and prompted trade restrictions over Beijing’s industrial policy.

Speaking publicly after a meeting of Group of 20 finance ministers last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called China’s current account surplus “unsustainable” and cited opposition from Beijing as the reason the group failed to issue a unanimous statement.

As China continues to rely on exports to support the economy, trade imbalance has become an area of discussion among policymakers, said Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.

He added that while the recent appreciation of the Japanese yen and South Korean won had built up pressure on the yuan to appreciate, exchange rate adjustment would likely be modest this year, with limited impact on trade imbalances.

President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington later this month, with trade, AI and the Iran war expected to be high on the agenda.

In August, China’s exports to the United States rose 34.4 per cent year on year, against a low base for the same period last year.

Exports to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, China’s largest trading partner by bloc, rose by 30.21 per cent year on year, while shipments to members of the European Union increased by 6.61 per cent.

The world’s second-largest economy is taking steps to further boost trade with Southeast Asia. The 134km (83-mile) Pinglu Canal is set to open to navigation next week, linking south China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region to Vietnam and other countries in the region via the Gulf of Tonkin, also known as the Beibu Gulf.

Meanwhile, the EU’s trade deficit with China has become a point of contention for Brussels. Amid marathon trade talks with their Chinese counterparts at the end of June, the bloc’s trade officials set a three-month deadline for the two sides to make “tangible progress” in disputes spanning several areas.

EU policymakers and business leaders have expressed fears that cheap Chinese imports – aided by hefty state subsidies – are helping to deindustrialise swathes of the continent’s manufacturing economy.

Separated by product category, the data showed tech-related exports continued to rise as automobile exports slowed.

Shipments of integrated circuits fell by 7.92 per cent year on year in volume terms last month but surged by 129.83 per cent in value – driven by higher prices amid a memory chip shortage fuelled by a global AI infrastructure buildout. The pace improved upon July’s 116.57 per cent growth, as well as June’s 121.9 per cent growth rate.

Outbound shipments of automatic data-processing equipment and related components also jumped last month, growing by 76.52 per cent year on year. Export growth for automobiles, however, was 43 per cent in value terms, down from the 60 per cent rate recorded in July.

China’s rare earth exports fell by 18.25 per cent year on year by volume, as Beijing continues to exert tight control over shipments of the minerals, which are essential to the production of a range of hi-tech products.

Meanwhile, imports came in a little softer than expected, Song said.

Both the import volume and value of automobiles dropped in August, falling by 50 and 32 per cent, respectively.

“China’s import profile is undergoing a clear structural shift in autos, where heavy domestic competition has also driven a sharp drop in demand for foreign imports,” Song said.

The country’s crude oil imports reached US$22.72 billion last month, down 8.85 per cent year on year in value terms, while shipments fell by 23.36 per cent.

Among emerging economies, China’s imports from Africa slowed to just 3.7 per cent year on year compared with a 25 per cent surge in July. Last week, Xi paid a state visit to Egypt, his first in 10 years, aimed at boosting economic and trade ties.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore investigates racism related to China-Nepal disaster, Air India investment
item.description:
Police are investigating “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the China-Nepal disaster and Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday.

Mr Shanmugam told reporters that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will also ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines.

“The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Mr Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security.
item.content:encoded:
Police are investigating “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the China-Nepal disaster and Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday.

Mr Shanmugam told reporters that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will also ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines.

“The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Mr Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security.

“I have asked police to look into these comments.”

Under CNA’s social media moderation policy, users who post hate speech, racist or offensive comments are blocked from commenting on CNA’s social media pages.

In cases where such comments are widespread and persistent, CNA may totally turn off comments on its posts, as it did for several news posts related to the China-Nepal disaster.

MP Alex Yam (People’s Action Party) also called out such comments earlier this week, describing them as “not just racist” but “downright heartless”.

Nine Singaporeans remain missing after devastating floods caused massive destruction in Nepal on August 26.

Mr Shanmugam gave several examples of racist remarks made online about the missing Singaporeans, including “no, they are not our own” and “all ABNNs look the same”. He noted that “ABNN” is a derogatory term for Indians.

More than a thousand people died in the disaster and Singaporeans remain unaccounted for, he said, yet such remarks continued to circulate online.

Mr Shanmugam added that most Singaporeans do not share these views, pointing to more than S$3 million (US$2.4 million) raised by the Singapore Red Cross for relief efforts in Nepal.

“Singaporeans are generous, across all races. And it is important that we don’t allow a minority to poison the entire well.”

Racist backlash over Air India investment

Meanwhile, news that Air India is seeking fresh equity from shareholders, including SIA, has sparked a new wave of “anti-Indian, racist ranting” online, such as “references to snakes, curry, prata, black magic”, Mr Shanmugam said.

An “online mob” has also attacked various parties, including the CEO and senior management of Temasek, over their ethnicity. Temasek is the majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines.

“It has been said that because the CEO is of Indian ethnicity, he would favour Air India. In the eyes of these people, the CEO’s sin is that he is of Indian ethnicity, even though he is as Singaporean as any of us, he was born here, studied here. That is nasty and libellous,” Mr Shanmugam said.

“But for this online mob, however, all of that, the facts don’t matter. What matters is their racism and their own prejudices. If we allow this, in future, everyone can be attacked for their decisions based on their ethnicities.

I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things, slowly it becomes normalised, then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it

Singapore’s Senior Minister K Shanmugam

“These people should be unmasked and dealt with rather than be allowed to hide behind online anonymity.”

Singapore is not exempt from “latent racism”, Mr Shanmugam said, adding that authorities have taken a “tough line” to protect the country’s multiracial, multi-religious fabric and preserve social harmony.

“I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things; slowly it becomes normalised; then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it,” he added.

“Public discourse is then debased. Social harmony is affected. Violence against people of a different skin colour and different religion becomes acceptable.”

Racist comments, particularly against Indians in Singapore, have grown more frequent of late, with some originating and “fanned from overseas”, Mr Shanmugam said.

“We are a very small multiracial, multi-ethnic country. If we are divided along racial or religious lines, we will lose the unity that has made Singapore strong. There will be feelings of ill will, suspicion, and we will all suffer,” he added.

“We should not tolerate this. This is not who we are as Singaporeans.”

Temasek’s role in SIA’s decisions

A Reuters report last month cited sources as saying that Air India is seeking a further US$1.5 billion in support from owners Tata Sons and SIA, just months after it posted a record annual loss.

An SIA spokesperson said last week that the board would “carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the group’s other capital requirements and Air India’s business strategy”.

Workers’ Party MP Kenneth Tiong said in a Facebook post on August 26 that he would not support nor expect any future use of Temasek’s funds to “prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines”.

Whether it is SIA or Temasek that “writes the cheque”, there will be a “significant impact” on Temasek, he wrote.

“No one, least of all Singaporeans, owes Air India a living … if Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek’s.”

Mr Shanmugam said it is SIA’s responsibility to assess its investments in Air India against the resources it has for its “long-term growth and profitability”.

“Any decision to invest in Air India lies with SIA, and Temasek as a shareholder in SIA, along with other shareholders, will expect SIA to make its investment decisions responsibly.”

Temasek is accountable to the government for its overall portfolio and long-term performance, Mr Shanmugam said, but not for individual investment decisions of its portfolio companies.

“Temasek and its subsidiaries decide how to invest across a wide portfolio with investments of varied risks and varied time horizons. Once governments or politicians start directing individual investment decisions, commercial discipline will be compromised,” he added.

“Decisions will become politicised – shaped by political considerations, rather than commercial judgment. In the end, Singaporeans will bear the cost.”

The government’s general principle is not to intervene in individual investment decisions or pressure companies on how to invest, Mr Shanmugam added.

Its role is to ensure professional management in Temasek, and then provide Temasek and its portfolio companies with the “political cover and the confidence which will allow them to make properly considered commercial decisions, free from untoward pressures”.

Temasek and many of its portfolio companies, including SIA, Sembcorp, Singtel and CapitaLand, have made substantial investments in India over the years, Mr Shanmugam said.

“Temasek’s website says that 43 per cent, nearly half, of its country exposure is to the Americas and China, and seven per cent is in India. But its website also says that India has in fact been its best-performing market over the last decade,” he said.

“Mr Tiong is entitled to his views. He is entitled, like any other Singaporean, to ask questions about SIA and Temasek.

“But neither his views, nor that of any minister, or any other MP, should substitute for the commercial judgment of SIA’s management and board of directors – boards which have knowledgeable and independent members, and management which has professionals whose primary responsibility is to consider and make these decisions.”

Asked by a reporter to respond to Mr Tiong’s statement that no one “owes Air India a living”, Mr Shanmugam said: “I think he ought to do his homework and look at SIA’s letter and the facts that I put out today, and ask if he is being responsible.”

This article was first published by CNA: Police investigating ‘shameful’ racist online comments about Nepal-Tibet disaster, Air India: SM Shanmugam - CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Singaporean who filmed couple on rooftop and demanded sex, cash gets jail
item.description:
A man who hid behind some plants to film a couple having extramarital sex at a rooftop garden in Singapore later used the video to threaten the woman while asking for sex and cash.

When the police began investigating, the offender asked the woman to drop the case, even approaching her sister at a supermarket.

Despite this ongoing investigation, the man targeted another couple having sex in a parked car and took a photograph of them before confronting them.
item.content:encoded:
A man who hid behind some plants to film a couple having extramarital sex at a rooftop garden in Singapore later used the video to threaten the woman while asking for sex and cash.

When the police began investigating, the offender asked the woman to drop the case, even approaching her sister at a supermarket.

Despite this ongoing investigation, the man targeted another couple having sex in a parked car and took a photograph of them before confronting them.

On Tuesday, Mohammad Sharulnaim Miswan, a 33-year-old Singaporean, was sentenced to two years and 10 months’ jail, along with three strokes of the cane.

He pleaded guilty to three charges which include putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, obstructing justice and wrongful confinement.

Another two charges were taken into consideration.

In sentencing, the judge told Sharulnaim that his actions had been most hurtful to his wife, who wept in court with a newborn baby in her arms.

Addresses and names of the victims were redacted from court documents due to gag orders protecting their identities.

At about 1am on January 15, 2024, Sharulnaim walked past a 35-year-old woman and a 39-year-old man at the rooftop garden of a multi-storey car park.

Suspecting they might engage in sexual acts as the man was touching the woman, Sharulnaim hid behind some plants to catch them in the act.

He took five videos of the pair having sex, capturing their faces in some of the clips and moving to another spot at one point for a better view.

Months later on May 6, 2024, the woman took her son to a clinic and was waiting to see the doctor when she was approached by Sharulnaim.

He introduced himself and asked if she was married and whether the boy with her was her son.

The woman’s turn at the clinic was next and she took her son to see the doctor. While the woman was waiting to collect medication, Sharulnaim approached her again.

He said he had a video of her having sex on the rooftop and showed her a screenshot, getting her to agree to meet him in his car to discuss it.

In his vehicle, Sharulnaim told the woman that he wanted to post the video online.

She pleaded with him not to do it, saying her son had special needs.

Sharulnaim dropped the woman and her son off, exchanged numbers and continued to communicate with her on how to settle the issue.

He said he intended to report the video to the police or make it go viral. The woman offered him S$300 (US$236) but he said it was “too low”.

Sharulnaim told her that if she was charged with an offence relating to the video, she faced months in jail and a fine of up to S$5,000.

He then sought S$2,000 and later S$1,500, but the woman could not afford either sum.

Sharulnaim then asked for S$1,000 and for the woman to have sex with him. He said he could pick her up and they could have sex at a car park, after which he would delete the video.

The woman refused the sex request and agreed to pay him S$1,300 by the following day. However, on the advice of the man in the sex video, she lodged a police report.

Unaware of this development, Sharulnaim sent the woman a photograph of a police station, saying he was going to lodge a report.

When the woman did not reply, Sharulnaim called the man in the sex video and repeated the threat.

The man felt threatened and said he would pay S$1,000 as the woman had only S$300. He pleaded with Sharulnaim to leave her alone because she had a young son and mother to take care of.

No payment was ultimately made and the police arrested Sharulnaim. While his statement was being recorded, he learnt that he was being investigated for putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion.

Months after this, in September 2024, Sharulnaim approached the woman’s sister in a supermarket and said he had an explicit video of her sister.

The woman was also present but did not speak to him until Sharulnaim approached her. He asked her to tell the investigation officer that she no longer wished to pursue the case.

To placate him, the woman said she would consider it. She refused to take down Sharulnaim’s new number and instead told the investigation officer about what happened.

Sharulnaim saw the woman with her sister and son at the supermarket again the following month and begged the woman to drop the case.

He asked for forgiveness, saying he was the sole breadwinner and that his parents and wife had learned about what happened. He claimed that he wanted to kill himself.

He also asked the woman to tell the police they were family, even though they were not. His friend had told him that this might help get the case dropped.

He also offered gifts and financial help to the woman if she let the matter go.

The woman’s sister lodged a police report that same day.

While the case was ongoing, on February 25, 2025, Sharulnaim came across another couple having sex in a parked car at a multi-storey car park.

He took a photograph of them before knocking on the window and gesturing to them to step out.

Lying that he was a former police officer, Sharulnaim asked the pair in their 20s for their ages and schools.

He said he had taken a video of them having sex and said he would lodge a police report, scaring the man.

Sharulnaim said he wanted to lodge a police report against them and that they would be fined for engaging in such acts in public.

The couple tried to leave and walked away, but Sharulnaim drove his vehicle and cornered the pair.

He rolled down his window and insisted that the man leave while he took the woman home.

The woman said her home was nearby and she would walk, but Sharulnaim insisted. He locked the doors and drove off, complimenting the woman on her looks and asking why she was in a relationship with her boyfriend.

When Sharulnaim came to the woman’s home, he saw her boyfriend waiting there for her and said he would not let her alight until her boyfriend left.

He told the woman she should not be with her boyfriend because she was too pretty for him.

Eventually, he unlocked the doors and let her go. She later lodged a police report and Sharulnaim was arrested again.

Deputy public prosecutor Niranjan Ranjakunalan sought two years and 11 to 13 months’ jail for Sharulnaim, along with three strokes of the cane.

Sharulnaim has prior convictions for theft and desertion from civil defence, among other charges.

Defence lawyer S Balarumugan said his client had a daughter and a month-old baby. He said he was also financially supporting his aged parents, who had medical conditions.

He said his client apologised to the victims for the ordeal he caused and assured the court he would be “more responsible” in future.

District Judge Samuel Wee allowed Sharulnaim’s wife to stay in the courtroom to hear sentencing remarks instead of leaving to tend to her crying baby.

He told Sharulnaim that his actions were premeditated and planned.

“You know the hurt it has caused your family,” said Judge Wee. “I would say … [it] has been most hurtful to your wife. Despite that, she’s still here today.”

Sharulnaim’s wife began to break down in the courtroom, surrounded by family.

The judge asked Sharulnaim to look at him as he was talking and told him about the consequences of his actions.

“Because of what you did … your children are going to grow up for a short period of time without their father,” Judge Wee said.

“And your wife, who has already had to bear the brunt of your very hurtful conduct, is going to be the one continuing to care for them while you are away.”

He asked if Sharulnaim had anything to say to his family, to which the man said he had already spoken to his wife and was grateful that she had stayed by his side.

The judge then reminded him to think about what he did while in jail and be clear on what he wanted for his future and his family on his release.

He allowed Sharulnaim time to speak to his various family members before being taken to jail. He said goodbye to his baby through a hole in the glass.

For putting a person in fear of harm to commit extortion, he could have been jailed for between two and five years and caned.

For obstruction of justice, he could have been jailed for up to seven years and fined.

For wrongful confinement, he could have been jailed for up to three years and fined.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Brics summit: Xi urges states to stand on ‘right side of history’, floats AI plan
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Speaking at the bloc’s summit in New Delhi on Saturday, Xi proposed an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on industry and supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The call came as the bloc was celebrating its 20th anniversary, having grown from a small economic framework into what Xi calls “the most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in today’s world”.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence.

Speaking at the bloc’s summit in New Delhi on Saturday, Xi proposed an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on industry and supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The call came as the bloc was celebrating its 20th anniversary, having grown from a small economic framework into what Xi calls “the most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in today’s world”.

At the same time, the gathering is being held against a backdrop of regional and global turmoil, from the war in Ukraine and the Middle East conflict to protectionism and tariff tensions. And its unity is being tested by divisions such as Iran’s repeated attacks on fellow members, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.

Xi’s attendance at the summit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic activities preceding his trip to the United States, efforts that are expected to give him the upper hand in his meeting with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.

Brics, a bloc of developing nations, has increasingly been viewed as a counterweight to Western-led institutions and a platform for building an alternative international order.

As well as the host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, other high-profile attendees include Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian.

For China, Brics is also seen as a platform to advance Beijing’s vision of a multipolar world and cement its standing as a leader of the Global South.

In that vein, Xi said Beijing was willing to work with Brics countries to play a “due role” in bringing peace to the Middle East, calling on the group of emerging economies to oppose bloc confrontation and the “infringement upon the sovereignty of other countries and interference in their affairs”.

His call for AI cooperation also highlights Beijing’s efforts to advance its own framework, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), widely seen as its answer to Washington’s Pax Silica Initiative.

The two countries are vying for AI dominance and Pax Silica is Washington’s approach to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains among allied nations.

Xi invited all Brics countries to join Waico to shape global AI governance and development.

“China stands ready to work with all parties to jointly produce more research and development and application outcomes, and to deepen cooperation across industrial and supply chains,” he said.

“Facts will prove that ‘decoupling and severing supply chains’ cannot hinder our development process, and ‘small yards with high fences’ will only confine oneself and fragment the world,” Xi said, in a veiled swipe at the US.

“We must firmly … strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, encourage open source and collaborative sharing and push practical cooperation to new heights.”

Xi said the Global South was growing stronger and urged Brics countries to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and lead the international order towards a more just and equitable direction, away from unilateralism and power politics.

Brics countries also agreed on Saturday to expand trade and payments in local currencies, edging further towards de-dollarisation as the bloc seeks to counter an assertive US.

Member nations unanimously adopted the 45-page “New Delhi Declaration 2026” on the opening day of the summit, with Modi saying that no member had objected to the text.

In a thinly veiled challenge to Washington’s stance, Xi urged the Brics members to criticise protectionism and unilateralism, calling on emerging economies to defend international institutions such as the United Nations and the World Trade Organization against tariff threats, treaty withdrawals, and efforts to carve out exclusive global trade alliances.

“We must oppose withdrawing from organisations, breaking treaties, and starting anew by setting up separate mechanisms,” Xi said.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Xi’s call for Brics to become “a vanguard for peace and stability” was especially relevant, given India’s efforts, as the group’s chair, to avoid being drawn into geopolitical conflicts.

Xi urged Brics countries to pursue “common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security”, reject cold war thinking and bloc confrontation, and oppose violations of sovereignty and interference in internal affairs.

He also called for constructive efforts to resolve regional hotspots, saying China was ready to work with Brics partners to “contribute to peace and stability in the Middle East and Gulf region”.

Liu said the political and security dimension, part of the three pillars of Brics cooperation, had become increasingly important as global tensions intensified.

“In today’s turbulent global environment, the political and security pillar is especially critical. As Xi emphasised, Brics should play a constructive role in mediating and easing regional tensions to advance global and regional peace.”

Modi, who chaired the opening session, said the voice of developing economies could not remain “a courtesy” and that emerging countries had to write the rules of global governance.

Brics, he said, was “not against anyone” but instead was for everyone.

“The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid,” he added.

“Power and decision-making sit at the top. Those who live with the consequences sit at the bottom, they are affected by every decision, excluded from every one of them.”

China will assume the organisation’s rotating chair next year.

In a sit-down after the summit, Xi told Modi that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”.

The grouping first took shape in 2006 when Brazil, Russia, India and China began informal talks before it was officially established in 2009. South Africa joined in 2010, turning the bloc from Bric to Brics.

The grouping has undergone two expansions since, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025. Brics now covers nearly half the global population and about a third of the world’s GDP.

Over the years, the bloc has evolved into a political platform for intergovernmental cooperation in areas ranging from finance and trade to culture and justice.

It has also become increasingly vocal about overhauling global systems, including proposing alternatives to US dollar-based payment systems, a suggestion that prompted warnings from Trump.

But its expansion has also brought fresh challenges to the bloc, with analysts suggesting that there are now more competing voices which have slowed its progress and made it harder to reach a consensus on issues.

Additional reporting by Orange Wang, Nayan Seth, Alyssa Chen, Shi Jiangtao and Victoria Bela

item.title: [SCMP] AI fight shadows final preparations for Xi Jinping’s White House visit to meet Donald Trump
item.description:
Rising tensions over artificial intelligence are shaping the final preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States.

Washington and Beijing are discussing the possibility of folding a long-awaited AI dialogue into a broader economic meeting in the days before Xi meets US President Donald Trump, according to several people familiar with the arrangements.

The two leaders agreed in Beijing in May to launch an intergovernmental dialogue on AI. For months, that channel was treated separately from the trade talks led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, with both sides struggling to make progress in the dialogue.
item.content:encoded:
Rising tensions over artificial intelligence are shaping the final preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States.

Washington and Beijing are discussing the possibility of folding a long-awaited AI dialogue into a broader economic meeting in the days before Xi meets US President Donald Trump, according to several people familiar with the arrangements.

The two leaders agreed in Beijing in May to launch an intergovernmental dialogue on AI. For months, that channel was treated separately from the trade talks led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, with both sides struggling to make progress in the dialogue.

Sources now say Bessent is expected to handle the two issues in one meeting. Bessent is the American lead on both the AI talks with Beijing and the economic talks. The sources said that holding a second high-level meeting so close to the summit was becoming difficult to arrange.

Development of AI in China has always been part of He’s portfolio, as the Chinese vice-premier is in charge of the National Development and Reform Commission, China’s powerful economic planning agency overseeing industrial development in the country, including AI.

The arrangements are similar to the ones in May, when Bessent and He met in Seoul days before Trump sat down with Xi in Beijing.

Officials have not confirmed the exact date or venue for the coming session, but it could happen just days ahead of the Xi-Trump handshake.

A person familiar with the discussions said He and Bessent were likely to cover all three economic initiatives: the Board of Trade, the Board of Investment and an AI working group, though only the Board of Trade was expected to yield a deliverable in time for the summit.

Beijing and Washington have invested heavily in making the reciprocal visit happen.

According to another person familiar with the discussions, officials on each side say “strategic stability benefits both sides and will be better defined by this visit” and both sides see it as an important opportunity before major political events in both countries: US midterm elections for Trump, and for Xi, a Communist Party plenum next month and a party congress next year.

Both sides were trying to “manage expectations and clarify red lines periodically”, the person said, as competition between the two countries, especially in AI, was “very intense”.

Trump and Xi were described as “having to manage opposition inside their own systems to ensure the visit does not go off course”, the person added.

The decision to hold the AI conversation in the Bessent-He session is being presented in private as a scheduling fix. It would take place in a harsher political climate than when the AI dialogue was first proposed.

Several people following the talks said the concern was that a stand-alone dialogue could shift away from risk reduction and towards semiconductor chips, model access and export controls.

One person said the Chinese side was unhappy with how the US was approaching the AI dialogue, viewing American requests as aimed at limiting harmful outcomes from AI as well as constraining China’s ability to develop its own capabilities.

One person familiar with the Chinese assessment of the process said a combined session was understandable on logistics alone.

Beijing was not given a clear picture of which US agencies would sit on the American side of an AI table until late July, the person said, and with Bessent leading that track as well as trade, asking him to appear twice so close to the leaders’ meeting created an obvious clash.

Another source said the AI file now spanned semiconductor controls, distillation and intellectual property, safety rules, cybersecurity and military constraints.

With such a broad spectrum and amid divergent expectations, they did not expect much from this round. AI security, they said, was the one area where some overlap looked possible.

Such is the context in which American AI companies have been “aggressively lobbying” the White House for a harder line, according to a person following the talks, while the Chinese side was expected to resist any US attempt to “impose a global ban on Chinese AI models”.

Earlier this week, Bessent warned that “nothing else would matter” if China pulled ahead in AI. That same day, American agencies accused six Chinese firms, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of industrial-scale distillation of frontier US models since late 2024, likely with “Chinese government awareness”.

On Thursday, US-based Anthropic alleged Alibaba alone ran more than 151 million Claude exchanges between May and July, while Moonshot and DeepSeek routed tens of millions more queries, in some cases exposing sensitive military and government data.

Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

Beijing rejected the claims, calling them groundless and accusing Washington of trying to suppress competition. Beijing said it was still willing to hold “constructive and professional discussions” under the dialogue as the two leaders agreed in May.

According to Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies, the wide range of issues in the AI file suggested the track should ideally run in parallel to, but separately from, the broader trade, technology and economy channel.

“[If He] is indeed Bessent’s counterpart on the AI track, it makes more sense to conduct the AI conversation at the same time and venue as the broader trade, tech and economy discussion without necessarily merging the two tracks together,” Gupta said.

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank, said that if the AI discussion was folded into the Bessent-He economic track, “it would constitute a modest downgrade in institutional status but not necessarily a substantive abandonment of AI risk reduction”.

Simon said that a stand-alone AI session would give officials a protected block of time for issues that rarely survived a ministerial agenda: military applications, autonomous cyber operations, accident notification, frontier model evaluation, and the relationship between AI and nuclear command and control.

Folded into a Bessent-He economic meeting, AI would compete with tariffs, overcapacity, rare earths, farm purchases, investment rules and summit deliverables, he added.

“Those issues are politically immediate and economically quantifiable,” Simon said, adding that “nuclear AI risk reduction is neither. In bureaucratic terms, it is therefore especially vulnerable to being pushed towards the end of the agenda”.

Bessent himself had simultaneously cast AI as something Trump and Xi should discuss, he said, “but that does not make Treasury the natural institution for sustained military AI or nuclear command discussions”.

item.title: [SCMP] Fresh photos offer clearest view yet of China’s ‘WZ-X’ spy drone
item.description:
Fresh clues are emerging about a new type of Chinese drone being developed as a long-range intelligence and surveillance platform intended to operate deep inside contested airspace.

New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified.

Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh clues are emerging about a new type of Chinese drone being developed as a long-range intelligence and surveillance platform intended to operate deep inside contested airspace.

New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified.

Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality.

Rupprecht said he was “100 per cent certain” the photographs showed what military aviation watchers have dubbed the “WZ-X”, citing its dimensions, proportions and other visible details. Beijing has not publicly confirmed the aircraft’s designation, purpose or specifications.

The aircraft was first publicly identified by US defence website TWZ in satellite imagery from May last year showing the Chinese air force’s Malan test facility in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Its estimated wingspan of around 52 metres (170 feet) is comparable to that of a US B-2 stealth bomber.

Rupprecht said the aircraft was designed as an intercontinental high-altitude, long-endurance (Hale) intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drone – a platform intended to operate deep inside defended airspace and function as an advanced communications relay node.

He likened its probable role to that of the RQ-180 – a secretive US high-altitude stealth flying-wing drone believed to be designed for reconnaissance inside defended airspace – describing the Chinese aircraft as an “RQ-180 XXL”.

He stressed that the comparison was about the expected mission and likely sensor role rather than proven performance, saying it remained unclear whether the WZ-X’s larger airframe translated into greater altitude, range or endurance.

Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said the WZ-X was likely intended as a strategic high-altitude reconnaissance platform.

Compared with smaller medium-altitude, long-endurance drones, large Hale aircraft could offer advantages in speed, survivability and capacity for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads, according to Bosack, a former US Air Force drone maintenance unit commander who worked on MQ-9 Reaper strike-capable drones.

“The speed comes from the larger engine and allows the aircraft to get to its target faster,” he said. “The survivability comes from its ability to fly higher than traditional air-defence systems can detect and reach.”

He added that the WZ-X’s airframe appeared to be shaped to minimise its radar signature. Its high operating altitude could protect it from many conventional air-defence threats, he said.

Bosack said a practical challenge would be shelter and maintenance, since keeping it out of satellite view would require sufficient hangar space.

But he cautioned that size and design alone would not determine whether the aircraft became operationally useful.

“Airframes like this are meaningless without the systems they carry,” Bosack said. “However, if they can achieve the right flight profile and carry the most useful ISR equipment, then they can stay operationally relevant for decades.”

“Simply put, until we know what sensors or other payloads the Chinese will put into the aircraft, we cannot really determine how useful it will be.”

Other key details remain uncertain, including the aircraft’s inlet configuration, engine count, sensor fit and whether more than one airframe has been built.

Bosack said the drone’s ability to contribute to real-time operations would depend on whether China could move large amounts of sensor data quickly and securely across the battlespace.

Without that, he said, the aircraft could be more useful for collecting intelligence for later analysis than directly supporting fast-moving combat operations.

He also considered a strike role unlikely, arguing that weapons would detract from its more useful reconnaissance mission.

Tate Nurkin, founder of OTH Intelligence Group, also sees the WZ-X mainly as an intelligence and communications platform rather than a strike aircraft, pointing to its potential for wide-area maritime surveillance, target identification and tracking, as well as data relay.

The WZ-X could fit into a broader People’s Liberation Army effort to expand and integrate specialised uncrewed reconnaissance systems. Last month, Chinese state media showed the new GJ-3A armed reconnaissance drone operating alongside WZ-10 and WZ-7 systems, with the three drone types described as providing intelligence support across the PLA.

“Everything points towards networking, joint and inter-service interoperability,” Rupprecht said, adding that the WZ-X could initially complement and eventually replace the WZ-7 and WZ-10 while performing similar missions in more demanding environments.

Open-source research has linked the Malan facility in far western China to the PLA Air Force’s 178th UAV Brigade and identified it as a major testing and training facility for unmanned aerial vehicles.

Rupprecht described Malan as the Chinese air force’s principal drone test centre, saying the WZ-X’s presence there clearly showed the programme’s importance.

Western China, which falls within the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and includes the frontier with India, could serve both as a testing area and as an early environment for evaluating the drone in scenarios involving India, according to Rupprecht.

He said operations around Taiwan were unlikely to be a priority for the WZ-X, given the island’s proximity to mainland China.

“For Taiwan you don’t need such a range and endurance – it’s almost on the doorstep,” he said.

Given the WZ-X’s likely reach, Rupprecht said the South China Sea, waters around Japan and the Korean peninsula, and potentially the eastern Pacific were other possible operational theatres for the drone.

Nurkin placed greater emphasis on the western Pacific, arguing that the aircraft appeared to be tailored for the “longer ranges, better air defences, [and] more complex maritime environment” of a broader regional conflict. He noted that while Taiwan itself was nearby, a crisis over the island could expand “north to Japan, east to Guam, and south to the Philippine Sea and South China Sea”.

In such a contested environment, a stealthy uncrewed aircraft capable of long-range operations could bolster China’s existing surveillance network.

For now, the WZ-X is known mainly through imagery and analyst assessments rather than official information. Its significance may depend less on size than on the sensors and communications systems it ultimately carries.

item.title: [SCMP] Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
item.description:
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.

It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.

“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.

It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.

“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.

“If I have to do a massive round of work just to sail for one or two days, I might as well sail in Hong Kong.”

He added that he would rather take a commercial ferry to Dongao for a holiday.

Still, the 66-year-old veteran mariner gave the voyage a score of 60 out of 100 and viewed it as a worthwhile test run.

Yu was among 139 participants aboard 16 yachts from Hong Kong and Macau that sailed to Dongao under the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme. Launched in June, the scheme allows eligible Hong Kong and Macau vessels to enter designated Guangdong waters for tourism.

The voyage, which took place over the weekend, was the scheme’s largest cross-border flotilla to date. It gave visitors a taste of the island’s seafood, hotel suites and natural scenery.

An eventful voyage

Early on August 29, the flotilla left the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in Causeway Bay for Dongao, about 36 nautical miles (53.7km) southwest of the city.

The journey took between 6½ and 8½ hours, depending on the yacht’s speed.

For participants such as 60-year-old financial executive Noel Chan and his 16-year-old son Nigel, it was family time. Chan sailed his 45-foot cruiser, Rampage, in 15-knot winds, while the pair chatted and shared drinks on deck.

“The wind speed was very good, conditions were great,” Nigel Chan said.

Mabel Tsim, an IT professional and sailor, described the eight-hour journey as a stress-relieving bonding experience.

She compared Dongao Island’s idyllic setting and sea views with those of a Southeast Asian resort in Thailand or Bali, Indonesia.

“For us as crew members, we focus on the journey itself,” she said. “The destination is a place for leisure, but more importantly, the process is sailing … For city dwellers, it is very stress-relieving.”

But hardware limitations soon became apparent. Immigration procedures at the designated port on Guishan Island took about 20 minutes – visitors entered a building, went upstairs for home return permit and baggage checks, then waited downstairs while officers checked vessel documents.

However, there was only one yacht berth, meaning vessels had to circle at sea for about 15 minutes while waiting for the previous yacht to clear.

One yacht suffered an incident at the port when its propeller broke off and sank to the seabed.

After navigating intermittent rain, the fleet arrived at Dongao, an island heavily reliant on mainland families visiting at weekends. But its temporary pontoons proved inadequate, with one yacht running aground twice in shallow water.

In the end, 13 of the 16 yachts stayed on the island for one night, while the rest remained for two.

Before setting sail, a yacht typically had to spend thousands of Hong Kong dollars to meet government requirements, including a US$1,500 vessel inspection and 3,000 yuan (US$447) in clearance fees, excluding hotel, food and other expenses.

For some participants, the time and expense were still worthwhile.

“I think out of 100 marks, I would say 85 to 90, so no such complaint … [the mainland is] really, really helpful for this [scheme] … [they] didn’t give you any hassle,” Noel Chan said.

His son Nigel compared the cost of sailing to Zhuhai with a friend’s experience in the United Kingdom.

“It’s 100 per cent more affordable, and it’s a much more pleasant experience,” he said.

While committed sailors and industry advocates regard the scheme’s early problems as necessary growing pains on the path to a world-class Greater Bay Area maritime economy, more pragmatic yacht owners remain divided over whether sailing north is worth the effort.

The yacht economy

For those with a team to navigate the administrative hurdles, the value proposition can be striking. Noel Chan said he spent just several thousand yuan on Marriott sea-view suites and other expenses for his group of 12.

He said the trip cost a fraction of a comparable stay in Hong Kong, and voiced concern that it could lead to a further outflow of Hong Kong consumer spending to the mainland.

“You go to Hong Kong, have a bad dinner, you spend that money already. So I think it’s a big challenge [for the] Hong Kong economy,” he said. “The money moved here again by sea instead of Hong Kong cars going [through the northbound vehicle scheme].”

The flotilla was a boon for some hotels.

A representative from the island’s five-star Gree Dongao Hotel said that the flotilla booked nearly 70 rooms, filling the 268-room property on August 29.

The hotel is part of the state-owned Zhuhai Gree Group, which has invested about 4 billion yuan since 2009 to develop a high-end hotel cluster on Dongao. The cluster also includes a 257-room Marriott and the cliffside Alila resort, which has 103 suites and is already attracting Hong Kong yachting people.

Dongfa Seafood Restaurant co-owner Zhou Shunfang, 60, marvelled at the flotilla but said she had not seen an influx of high-spending yacht guests. She suspected touts had intercepted them at the pier before they discovered her long-established restaurant.

Charting a smoother course

Liao Kai, president of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said about 50 yachts had obtained temporary nationality certificates, allowing them to use the scheme to travel to the Greater Bay Area.
