Participants broadly agreed that the cross-border experience would require major upgrades to both its policy framework and physical infrastructure before it could unlock the full economic potential of Greater Bay Area waters.

At the policy level, reducing the barriers to entry is crucial. The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club had called for cross-border costs to be harmonised, vice-commodore Joseph Chu said. He suggested that northbound fees should be cut from thousands of Hong Kong dollars to match the nominal HK$58 charged for southbound vessels.

He argued that equalising the fees would turn special expeditions into more frequent trips, similar to Hong Kong residents travelling to Shenzhen for afternoon tea before returning home.

Yu echoed the call for less bureaucracy. He urged authorities across the border to drop the allegedly redundant “temporary nationality certificate” and accept surveys carried out by Hong Kong-approved professionals, rather than requiring separate and costly mainland inspections.

Workarounds to reduce costs are also emerging. Liao said traditional commercial shipping agencies had charged tens of thousands of dollars for customs clearance, prompting the Zhuhai Yacht Association to set up a dedicated agency to deal with paperwork. The move helped reduce outbound clearance fees to around 3,000 yuan for the flotilla.

On the water, relatively simple logistical changes could reduce delays. Noel Chan recommended staggered arrival times for yachts at clearance ports such as Guishan, to prevent bottlenecks that leave vessels circling offshore.

Tsim said authorities should find a way to process several boats at once. She also called for less rigid point-to-point travel rules, allowing yachts to visit more than one destination on the same itinerary.

Infrastructure remains a major constraint. Both Yu and Noel Chan said robust floating moorings, and more of them, were urgently needed at destinations such as Dongao Island to stop yachts having to “double park” in unsafe conditions.

Gao Jun, an associate professor at Sun Yat-sen University’s school of tourism management, said Zhuhai needed to improve tourist spending opportunities and amenities to extend the value chain beyond its 20-year manufacturing base in Pingsha.

By taking advantage of new self-navigating repair policies in Jinwan, cross-border access points and related services, Zhuhai aims to capture longer-term value from yacht maintenance and berthing, rather than relying solely on weekend tourism.

Liao said four yachts had successfully sailed to Jinwan, undergone major repairs and returned to Hong Kong since the self-navigating vessel repair policy was launched in March.

He added that more than 20 other vessels were applying to use the service.

Industry leaders urged patience. Chu compared the scheme’s early administrative and infrastructure problems with the chaotic early days of Hong Kong International Airport before it developed into a global aviation hub.

Stakeholders are now preparing for the anticipated launch of southbound travel.

Liao said he had heard from local authorities that the southbound scheme might open in September.

item.title: [SCMP] How Asian shipyards in Japan, Korea and Philippines keep US warships battle ready
item.description:
After being stranded in the South China Sea following a power failure in July, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold was towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for emergency repairs.

The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home.

The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations.
item.content:encoded:
After being stranded in the South China Sea following a power failure in July, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold was towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for emergency repairs.

The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home.

The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations.

While US law mandates that major warships be built domestically, outsourcing MRO to foreign yards offers more flexibility, especially for forward-deployed vessels.

Naval vessels homeported outside the United States are not strictly prohibited from receiving foreign MRO services and deployed US-homeported ships may also be serviced by foreign workers under specific conditions.

The capacity of regional allies in the western Pacific, including Japan and South Korea, is particularly vital, given their distance from the continental US as well as Washington’s intensifying strategic competition with Beijing.

“By establishing the ability to repair and sustain larger numbers of ships closer to potential conflict areas in the Indo-Pacific, the United States could potentially support extended deployments – including during wartime – by reducing the need to recall ships to the US mainland for repairs,” the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies said in a recent report.

South Korea and Japan’s advanced shipbuilding industries rank second and third in the world, respectively, in terms of capacity. The Philippines and Singapore, meanwhile, occupy strategically important positions in the region and have long served as key partners for the US military.

Meanwhile, China at No 1 accounts for more than half the world’s shipbuilding capacity, providing a solid industrial base for its rapidly expanding navy.

Shipyards in the region

The US Navy runs the US Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Centre (SRF-JRMC) at its bases in the region. It is headquartered at the Yokosuka Naval Base in Kanagawa prefecture, with detachment sites in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, and Singapore’s Changi Naval Base.

The organisation employs local workers and occasionally outsources certain tasks to local contractors.

In addition to the directly operated SRF-JRMC, the US Navy has been expanding a network of private companies in the region through its Master Ship Repair Agreement (MSRA). The certification qualifies a shipyard to bid on and perform MRO work on military and support vessels.

For instance, the US Navy issued solicitation notices last month, inviting bids from MSRA and Agreements for Boat Repair (ABR) holders to carry out minor repair and maintenance of the America-class amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS New Orleans, both homeported in Sasebo.

Japan

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI)’s Yokohama Dockyard & Machinery Works is the largest ship repair yard in Japan, with abundant experience in repairing civilian and naval vessels. It has two dry docks, seven piers and seven jib cranes. The dock can accommodate huge ships of up to 270,000 tonnes, according to the company.

The yard serviced the Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Milius in 2019 as part of a pilot trial – the first time the US Navy had outsourced such work to local Japanese firms.

Last year, MHI became the first Japanese yard to secure a regular overhaul contract for the USS Miguel Keith, a Puller-class expeditionary mobile base.

Sumitomo Heavy Industries Marine & Engineering is another prominent MSRA holder. The company website says it has focused on repair work mainly for the US Navy in Yokosuka in recent years. They provide repair services to ships belonging to the Seventh Fleet, including nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, and “are engaged in repairing” US Army vessels including landing craft.

Sasebo Heavy Industries sits next to the Sasebo Naval Base and shares a dry dock with the US Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force. Having suspended new shipbuilding in 2022, the company now focuses exclusively on ship maintenance and repair.

Japan Marine United Corporation operates five ship-repair yards across the country, at Isogo and Tsurumi in Yokohama, as well as Kure, Maizuru and Innoshima. The Maizuru facility took part in the repair of the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Fitzgerald last December.

South Korea

Unlike in Japan, the US Navy does not have a direct ship-repair facility in South Korea. Instead, it collaborates with major local shipbuilders, primarily for logistical vessels. Notably, MSRA certifications for South Korean contractors have been mainly awarded in the past few years, reflecting the US Navy’s strategic shift towards MRO outsourcing.

In July 2024, Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) made history as the first South Korean shipyards to obtain MSRA from the US Navy, shortly after the former acquired the Philly Shipyard in Pennsylvania.

Hanwha Ocean conducts its repair works at the Geoje shipyard on an island off the southeastern coast near Busan.

It completed South Korea’s first MRO project – maintenance of the USNS Wally Schirra dry cargo and ammunition ship – in 2025 and also worked on the USNS Yukon, a replenishment oiler assigned to the US Navy’s 7th Fleet.

HHI secured the overhaul project for the Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo and ammunition vessel USNS Alan Shepard in August 2025 after efforts to tap into the US by forming an alliance with the US-based military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls. The work was carried out at a berth near HD Hyundai Mipo Dockyard in the southeastern city of Ulsan from last September.

HJ Heavy Industries, a mid-sized shipbuilder, became the third South Korean firm to pass US Navy evaluations to get an MSRA in January this year, after signing a contract in December to carry out a midlife maintenance contract for the 40,000-tonne Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo ship USNS Amelia Earhart at its Yeongdo shipyard in Busan.

SK Oceanplant, another major defence contractor that has built more than 30 South Korean naval and coastguard vessels including the latest Ulsan-class Batch-III frigates, officially signed the MSRA in February. The company operates a 430-metre (1,410 foot) ultra-large floating dock in its shipyard in Goseong on the southern coast and conducts maintenance for more than 30 commercial vessels annually.

Samsung Heavy Industries, one of South Korea’s “Big Three” shipbuilders alongside Hanwha Ocean and HHI, has reportedly begun the MSRA application process and aims to complete certification this year.

Singapore

Strategically located at the entrance of the Strait of Malacca, the crossroads connecting the West Pacific and Middle East, Singapore has long been a hub for US naval operations. Along with the SRF-JRMC’s Singapore detachment, the US Navy primarily works with two local MSRA-holding partners.

State-owned defence contractor ST Engineering Marine operates facilities such as its Benoi and Gul yards. Its recent MRO contracts came not only from the Pacific Fleet, but also the Military Sealift Command and Naval Supply Systems Command. It was awarded a contract in February for the regular overhaul of Safeguard-class rescue and salvage ship USNS Salvor.

Government-linked Sembcorp Marine held an MSRA before its merger with Keppel Offshore & Marine in 2023 to form Seatrium Limited. Its Tuas Yard has a repair dock that is 400 metres (1,310 feet) long and 14 metres deep, one of the deepest in Asia for mega vessels, while the Admiralty Yard is equipped with multiple dry docks and quays, including one that is 13 metres deep.

India

The US Navy has also expanded cooperation with India against the backdrop of deepening defence ties under the framework of its Indo-Pacific strategy. It has certified Indian shipbuilders Mazagon Dock and Larsen & Toubro with MSRAs in 2023. Mazagon’s facilities are in Mumbai and Larsen & Toubro runs the Kattupalli Shipyard in Chennai.

In 2024, the third Indian MSRA was awarded to state-run Cochin Shipyard. Under these agreements, the Indian contractors will primarily support ships under the US Navy’s Military Sealift Command.

The Philippines

Although the Philippines lacks an advanced domestic shipbuilding industry, its strategic location as a key hub in the South China Sea has led the US Navy to contract US-owned firms to operate maintenance and repair facilities in the country.

The Agila Subic Shipyard in Subic Bay, where the USS Benfold arrived four days after losing power and was repaired in July and August, was formerly operated by Hanjin Heavy Industries Philippines (HHIC-Phil) and is now owned by New York-based Cerberus Capital Management.

Colorado-based defence contractor Vectrus (now V2X after a merger) provides services at the site, which features a 500-metre long dock and forms part of the growing network of overseas facilities supporting US naval operations in the region.

item.title: [SCMP] Heading to America to bridge the gap in US-China relations
item.description:
Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case.

I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side.

As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here.
item.content:encoded:
Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case.

I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side.

As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here.

Beginning this month, I take up a one-year appointment as a senior visiting scholar at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia at the Harvard Kennedy School. My purpose is straightforward to state and harder to fulfil: to sit down with American thought leaders across the political spectrum and ask them where they think this relationship is headed, and whether conflict is as inevitable as it now appears.

To understand why this question matters so much, a brief look back is useful. The relationship began its current downward spiral in 2018, when the first Trump administration launched its opening salvo in the trade war. At the time, the confrontation felt sudden and jarring. It was not, in fact, sudden at all. Grievances had been quietly accumulating for decades across government, industry, trade, academia, science and technology. What changed in 2018 was that those grievances finally found their outlet.

Layered on top were structural anxieties. In Washington, there is the perceived erosion of American primacy in manufacturing and superpower status. In Beijing, there is a mirror-image worry: that a declining but still-dominant America, unwilling to accept the reality of a rising China, is bent on containing its development, through tariffs, technology export controls and alliances built for that purpose.

That mutual anxiety, in turn, fed less rational forces on both sides of the Pacific: incomplete narratives, hostile rhetoric, rumour dressed as fact, all doing damage to how each public sees the other. In Washington, there is a wry observation that American politicians agree on almost nothing except the need to get tough on China. In China, public sentiment towards the US has turned sour.

The goodwill accumulated over decades of engagement has largely evaporated, replaced by mutual suspicion and precaution – of which my scrubbed phone is a small but telling example.

None of this is to dismiss the seriousness of the moment. In the past fortnight alone, US Treasury officials have floated the possibility of sanctioning Chinese banks over their dealings with Iran, a suggestion that drew a sharp pushback from Beijing.

Long Guoqiang, deputy director general of the Development Research Centre of the State Council, a leading government think tank, captured the prevailing mood in Beijing when he warned recently that the US remains “the biggest external source of uncertainty affecting China’s path to modernisation”. He argues that American containment of China will persist and intensify over the long run, notwithstanding the trade war truce.

Long’s warning is not wrong. But a truce, however temporary, is also an opening. After their Beijing summit in May, President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are set to meet three more times this year: Xi is expected in Washington later this month, with further encounters likely on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 leaders’ meetings in November and December.

Much of the coverage of these meetings will, understandably, focus on tangible deliverables – deals on trade, investment, technology. But Beijing and Washington might also use the moment to look at the bigger picture, along three tracks that receive far less airtime than they should.

On global challenges, can both powers still cooperate on climate change and future pandemics, even if the current US administration shows little enthusiasm for the former?

On engagement, law enforcement cooperation – against transnational crime, the booming scam-centre operations along China’s periphery, and the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals into North America – is a shining example. Quiet cooperation on precursor chemicals continued even through the worst of the trade war, proof that narrow, mutually beneficial arrangements can survive broader hostility when both sides see a direct interest in results.

I am a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict

And on global regulation, can the two governments find common ground in governing artificial intelligence, space and other emerging technologies?

Right now, discourse in both capitals dwells overwhelmingly on the negative. Far less is said about where cooperation remains not just possible but necessary.

That is what I intend to spend the next year finding out. I am, by long habit of observation, a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict. From Cambridge, I plan to reach beyond the think tanks most familiar to a China watcher, including into quarters not typically friendly to Beijing’s view of the world, setting aside my instincts and assumptions as best I can.

What will I find by the time this fellowship ends? I do not know. But having spent three decades chronicling how perception so often diverges from reality in this relationship, I remain hopeful that reality, properly examined, still leaves room for two great powers to coexist – durably, and peacefully – for everyone’s sake.

item.title: [SCMP] 2025 was a tough year for Hong Kong’s bar industry, so how are new concepts carving a path forward?
item.description:
Despite this being the year Hong Kong hosted its first edition of World’s 50 Best Bars (with Asia’s 50 Best Bars held in nearby Macau), the scene as a whole suffers from headwinds stemming from declining interest in alcohol and dining out, combined with a significant price gap with the Greater Bay Area, to which tourists and weekend revellers are flocking, as the Post reported earlier this month.

Bars and restaurants close every year, but 2025 saw the closure of extremely recognisable venues that have been serving the city for anywhere between half of to beyond a decade. Foxglove, which celebrated a decade this year, closed its doors last week. The Daily Tot shuttered just a few weeks before that, preceded by Stockton (est. 2014) earlier in the year. Last year, Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour and Please Don’t Tell were closed to make way for major renovations at The Landmark, Mandarin Oriental. The Envoy, The Pottinger’s outdoor terrace bar, and its neighbouring speakeasy Room 309 also served their last drinks in 2024.

“I feel very sad that these bars closed down for good,” says Jo Lo, co-founder of Bar Mind, a minimalist cocktail bar in SoHo. “These are the bars [that] really opened my eyes to Asian and Hong Kong bar culture.” Before opening Bar Mind this year, Lo spent almost six years at Room 309 and The Envoy as part of Tastings Group. In 2022, she won Diageo World Class Hong Kong & Macau Bartender of the Year.
item.content:encoded:
Despite this being the year Hong Kong hosted its first edition of World’s 50 Best Bars (with Asia’s 50 Best Bars held in nearby Macau), the scene as a whole suffers from headwinds stemming from declining interest in alcohol and dining out, combined with a significant price gap with the Greater Bay Area, to which tourists and weekend revellers are flocking, as the Post reported earlier this month.

Bars and restaurants close every year, but 2025 saw the closure of extremely recognisable venues that have been serving the city for anywhere between half of to beyond a decade. Foxglove, which celebrated a decade this year, closed its doors last week. The Daily Tot shuttered just a few weeks before that, preceded by Stockton (est. 2014) earlier in the year. Last year, Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour and Please Don’t Tell were closed to make way for major renovations at The Landmark, Mandarin Oriental. The Envoy, The Pottinger’s outdoor terrace bar, and its neighbouring speakeasy Room 309 also served their last drinks in 2024.

“I feel very sad that these bars closed down for good,” says Jo Lo, co-founder of Bar Mind, a minimalist cocktail bar in SoHo. “These are the bars [that] really opened my eyes to Asian and Hong Kong bar culture.” Before opening Bar Mind this year, Lo spent almost six years at Room 309 and The Envoy as part of Tastings Group. In 2022, she won Diageo World Class Hong Kong & Macau Bartender of the Year.

“This year feels like a market correction,” says Ming Cheung, co-founder of 001. “Rents have readjusted in some areas, but not enough. Consumer spending is more cautious. It’s a perfect storm – pre-pandemic business models are colliding with post-pandemic economics and consumer behaviour. It’s a cleansing, but a painful one for the culture.” Originally founded near Gage Street Market in 2010, 001 closed in 2022 before finding a new home a year later in Tai Kwun.

Opening a successful concept in Hong Kong requires a delicate confluence of factors. Rent and operational costs have to be kept as lean as possible. Lo observes that breaking even can take anywhere from six months to two years even with significant initial investment, cost control and effective marketing. John Nugent, founder of The Diplomat and co-founder of Sugar King, emphasises the fundamentals of business planning – maintaining doomsday, middle-of-the-road and success scenarios; pivoting as needed; and knowing the product and clientele.

With costs, breaking even and engagement key to a concept’s survival, it’s easy to assume that bars must consistently predict what the drinking public will enjoy. While many recent closures were speakeasies opened in the 2010s, this year also saw an influx of neighbourhood bars. Bar Leone took home World’s Best Bar, as other “community first” concepts spread their wings: Mius, Oasis and Sugar King, to name a few, focus on simple drinks and convivial atmospheres to great success.

Nugent feels that predicting tastes is only part of the equation, however. “I think it’s a dangerous question to read into drinking preferences,” he says. “We want to make sure that every guest who walks into our venue is treated like they’re getting away from the doldrums of everyday life. Whether you’re serving a fast food item, a curated cocktail or a fine dining meal, you’re giving the best hospitality you can.

“We have to ask ourselves, ‘Is it the guest’s job to keep these places afloat or is the onus on us?’ How do we keep creating new and exciting ways for guests to come back? To take on these challenges, you really have to love the industry we’re in – otherwise, there’s no reason to get out of bed to take on these challenges.”

For Cheung, this focus on the guest makes training another key challenge. “In 2010, we needed people who could master technique,” she says. “Today, that’s the baseline. Now, we need storytellers, hosts, diplomats. They need to navigate social media, understand global trends, manage guest allergies and preferences with ease, and be ambassadors for a vast portfolio of spirits. The skill is in connection, making a guest feel uniquely seen in a 60-second interaction.”

“The challenge is sustaining interest past the two-year mark,” Cheung continues. “We need to consistently turn first-time visitors into regulars, and regulars into ambassadors. There’s no foot traffic to cushion the early months – just the steady, growing trust of people who make the effort to find you. It’s a marathon of consistent excellence, not a sprint.”

“Consistent quality in product and service leads to positive word of mouth and returning customers,” Lo notes. “The ‘hype’ window is like the honeymoon for a new establishment. It reflects the reality that initial excitement [can fade] unless sustained by quality and engagement.”

So is it due to these shifting sands, or a venue’s glaring inability to serve guests or offer something unique – to capture lightning in a half-to-two-year bottle – that causes it to close? Not necessarily. When 001’s original NoHo lease was ending, Cheung explains, the bar was not facing unmanageable financial pressures, but renewing would have locked the business into costs that Cheung and the team felt did not allow for growth or stability. The speakeasy, at its new location in Tai Kwun, celebrated its 15th anniversary last month.

Similarly, as the Post reported, Singular Concepts CEO David Sit attributed The Daily Tot’s closure to rent increases when it was attempting to renew its lease. “We hold onto the concept and the spirit of The Daily Tot, and hope to be back in the near future,” Sit stated in a press release. Reopening has come about for 001 and Dr Fern’s Gin Parlour – now The Doctor’s Residence at The Pottinger – though it is its own gamble.

“I’d say we were 80 per cent confident [we would reopen],” Cheung said. “We had the will, the brand, the team’s core and a strong reputation. But finding the right home – one that matched our ethos and made financial sense – was the 20 per cent gamble.” To reopen, a bar has to “protect its soul, not just the logo”, she advises. “Wait for the location that doesn’t just fit your budget, but fulfils your narrative. A rushed comeback can do more damage than a graceful exit.”

Some venues have indeed exited gracefully and given their mixologists room to develop something new. Nugent previously helmed the beverage programme at Lily & Bloom, a restaurant and bar in Lan Kwai Fong that closed in 2018. In 2020, he opened The Diplomat, a venue known as much for its bar bites and midnight cookies as its classics-based, martini-forward menu and one of the best Irish coffees in town. The opening of Sugar King over the summer has only added to the throngs of imbibers crowding Peel Street every weekend.

“The beauty, but also the curse of Hong Kong, is that it’s ever changing,” Nugent says. “These venues [that have closed] were incredible in their own right; they offered something that was part of the ethos of Hong Kong hospitality.

“We wish nothing but the best for anybody and everyone involved with these places. Who knows? One closure could [lead to] another opening of something even more incredible.”

Ultimately, whether it’s staving off closure, reopening or building something new, guest support and word of mouth go a long way towards keeping valued concepts alive. “One visit a month from a true regular is worth 10 one-time visits from trend chasers,” Cheung affirms. “Be a regular, come on a Tuesday, bring someone new. That’s the oxygen that lets a concept like ours live, breathe and evolve over 15 years.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump threatens Taiwan’s representative office, sparking debate over island’s US policy
item.description:
Taiwan’s representative office is among a list of entities US President Donald Trump has threatened to sue as part of his crusade against a progressive American think tank, triggering debate about the island’s US policy ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month.

Trump named the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office (Tecro) in a social media post on Monday attacking the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning Washington think tank, over a report disputing his claims about the effect of National Guard deployments on violent crime.

Trump called the think tank a “radical left scam” and threatened to seek US$5 billion in damages, adding that he was “strongly considering” including some of its donors in the lawsuit.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan’s representative office is among a list of entities US President Donald Trump has threatened to sue as part of his crusade against a progressive American think tank, triggering debate about the island’s US policy ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month.

Trump named the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office (Tecro) in a social media post on Monday attacking the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning Washington think tank, over a report disputing his claims about the effect of National Guard deployments on violent crime.

Trump called the think tank a “radical left scam” and threatened to seek US$5 billion in damages, adding that he was “strongly considering” including some of its donors in the lawsuit.

He named Tecro – Taiwan’s de facto embassy in the US – alongside the Japanese embassy, the Korea Foundation and the embassy of the United Arab Emirates as foreign supporters of the think tank.

The remarks have raised questions in Taiwan about whether Taipei’s funding of US think tanks has become a political liability under Trump, particularly ahead of his expected summit with Xi.

Chen I-hsin, head of the culture and communications committee of the Kuomintang, Taiwan’s main opposition party, described Trump’s remarks as an “unusual diplomatic warning”.

He questioned the value of using taxpayers’ money to support an institution strongly critical of the US leader, only for Taiwan to be singled out by Trump.

“[Taiwan’s] foreign ministry must immediately explain how much taxpayer money is still being provided to CAP since Trump returned to the White House,” Chen said.

He acknowledged that Taipei’s cooperation with US think tanks across the political spectrum predated the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) return to power in 2016, but said “diplomacy required adjusting to political changes”.

Chen said that if the DPP government continued providing substantial funding to institutions closely associated with US Democrats and strongly critical of Trump, it raised questions about whether Taipei’s diplomatic strategy had become unbalanced.

“Taiwan-US relations must not pay the price for the DPP’s misguided political bet,” he said, adding that the government should explain the situation to the public.

Taiwan’s foreign ministry defended the practice, saying it and its overseas missions had long worked with major US think tanks and academic institutions across the political spectrum.

It said the cooperation supported research into Indo-Pacific security, supply-chain resilience and critical technologies, while improving Americans’ understanding of Taiwan and the island’s ties with the US.

“Such cooperation does not involve Taiwan in US local politics and should not be turned into an issue for political manipulation in Taiwan,” it said.

The ministry added that Taipei would continue deepening cooperation with the Trump administration on the basis of mutual respect and mutual benefit.

Taiwan has funded prominent Washington think tanks for years as part of efforts to build support in the United States.

A 2020 investigation by The American Prospect magazine identified the Centre for American Progress, Brookings Institution, Centre for a New American Security, Centre for Strategic and International Studies and Hudson Institute as recipients of Taiwanese funding.

The report questioned whether researchers adequately disclosed their institutions’ Taiwanese funding when advocating stronger security and economic ties between Washington and Taipei.

Taipei later rejected suggestions that its funding influenced research, saying it respected academic freedom and that such programmes promoted scholarly exchanges and expert discussion.

Data from the Washington-based Think Tank Funding Tracker showed Taiwanese entities provided about US$6.77 million to 25 American think tanks between 2019 and 2024.

International relations and strategic studies scholar James Yifan Chen said Taipei still needed relationships with US think tanks given its reliance on Washington’s support, but should ensure its outreach was politically balanced.

“For over a decade, the DPP has relied heavily on US support … and often seeks partnerships with American think tanks that share similar values,” Chen said, adding that such an approach risked unsettling Trump and his Republican allies.

“Without formal ties, Taiwan must adopt a more balanced approach, building bipartisan relationships to avoid future embarrassments,” he said.

Chen added that Taiwan should cultivate ties across the US political spectrum and allocate its resources more strategically.

“Taiwan must avoid actions that could complicate the situation in the lead-up to the Trump-Xi summit,” he said.

Chen said he believed the planned September 24 meeting in Washington was “unlikely to provide much room for transactional bargaining” between Trump and Xi.

Instead, Xi was likely to seek to stabilise relations and offer incentives that aligned with Trump’s desire to strengthen the US economy ahead of the midterm elections, he said.

Dennis Lu-chung Weng, an associate professor of political science at Sam Houston State University in Texas, said Taipei should focus less on whether funding the Centre for American Progress was right or wrong and more on whether the broader political atmosphere in Washington was shifting ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting.

He said Trump’s decision to name Tecro was “not a positive development” because the US leader appeared to be ramping up the pressure from attacking the think tank’s work to drawing attention to those supporting the institution.

“For Trump, negotiations often begin well before anyone sits down at the negotiating table,” Weng said. “Public statements, legal threats and even naming the other side’s supporters can themselves form part of the negotiating process.”

There was no evidence Trump would take action against Tecro, Weng stressed, but if the list was not random, being named could be a political signal that Taiwan had entered his field of vision.

The real concern would be if the island were incorporated into Trump’s broader political calculations over US-China relations, Weng said.

“That would not be something that could simply be resolved with money.”

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The United States, like most nations, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but is opposed to any forcible change to the status quo and is committed to providing arms for its defence.

item.title: [SCMP] US Navy plans compact Silent Anvil torpedo as China’s submarine fleet surges
item.description:
As China expands its submarine fleet, the US Navy is looking to develop a compact air-launched torpedo that could enable more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines from farther away.

The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT).

While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller.
item.content:encoded:
As China expands its submarine fleet, the US Navy is looking to develop a compact air-launched torpedo that could enable more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines from farther away.

The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT).

While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller.

HAAWC adds a glide kit to a Mark 54 lightweight torpedo and can be launched by P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft from altitudes of up to 30,000 feet (9,140 metres).

According to the request for information, the navy wants the new weapon to weigh up to 268lbs (122kg) while measuring up to 70 inches (178cm) long and 7.5 inches (19cm) in diameter – dimensions intended to broaden the range of aircraft that could carry it.

The requirements also envisage that Silent Anvil would be compatible with aircraft carrier storage and handling systems, potentially allowing carrier-based platforms to field the weapon.

The US Navy said it was considering two approaches: a new integrated weapon designed to glide into the water before homing acoustically on its target, or a glide kit fitted to an existing torpedo.

The glide system could receive targeting updates during flight, helping it to release the torpedo closer to the submarine’s expected location. Once in the water, the torpedo would use its own acoustic sensor to find and attack the target.

The document does not mention China, nor does it name any potential adversary. But it comes as Beijing expands and modernises its submarine fleet amid intensifying US-China military competition in the western Pacific.

Peter Jones, a retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral and an adjunct professor with the Naval Studies Group at UNSW Canberra, said Silent Anvil could potentially enable many more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to serve as delivery platforms for weapons.

“The overall effect will be a more responsive anti-submarine capability,” Jones said. “For an adversary submariner, it means that any air platform could be a weapon carrier.”

But Jones said the Silent Anvil’s usefulness would also depend on whether the weapon could be produced cheaply enough to be widely deployed, while the aircraft carrying it would still rely on air, surface and underwater systems to find submarines.

Lyle Goldstein, director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities, said spreading the mission across more platforms could be particularly valuable because specialised US anti-submarine warfare aircraft such as the P-8 were few in number.

Large, slow anti-submarine warfare aircraft could struggle to operate in the vast and highly contested airspace of the Asia-Pacific, potentially increasing the value of drones operating from “very remote locations under austere conditions”, he added.

While separating detection platforms from those that attack submarines could make better use of resources, it could also complicate operations, Goldstein observed, citing the enormous distances involved, attempts to jam communications and attacks on logistics nodes.

James Holmes, a professor of maritime strategy at the US Naval War College who was speaking in a personal capacity, said that while the Silent Anvil concept “shows a lot of promise”, its effectiveness would have to be shown in practice.

“The difficulty here is ensuring connectivity among elements of the force,” Holmes said, especially as China’s “systems destruction warfare” concept involved disrupting the networks that allowed an adversary’s forces to operate together, including through electronic warfare.

The push to broaden US options for attacking submarines comes as Beijing rapidly builds up its undersea fleet.

Rear Admiral Mike Brookes, head of the US Office of Naval Intelligence, told a congressional commission in March that China could have up to 80 submarines by 2035, roughly half of them nuclear-powered – a major shift for a force that has historically relied heavily on conventionally powered boats.

The build-up is not only about numbers. China is also developing new submarine designs.

The South China Morning Post reported in July that satellite imagery and expert analysis indicated a previously unidentified attack submarine at Shanghai’s Jiangnan Shipyard. Its propulsion type remains uncertain.

Meanwhile, another next-generation nuclear-powered design has been spotted at Bohai Shipyard in Liaoning province, northeast China.

According to Goldstein, China’s newer nuclear-powered attack submarines could pose a growing challenge by operating farther into the central and eastern Pacific. “As this challenge grows, the US will be forced to devote more effort to the anti-submarine threat.”

Holmes observed that the undersea competition could increasingly resemble the Cold War rivalry between the navies of the US and the then Soviet Union, particularly in relation to a potential conflict involving Taiwan.

He compared the first island chain – an arc of islands from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines that underpins the US security strategy in the region – to the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, a key Cold War passage for Soviet submarines entering the Atlantic.

Holmes described both as geographic barriers to a wider ocean. “We are back to the future,” he said.

According to Holmes, the Luzon Strait and the Bashi Channel south of Taiwan are obvious routes for People’s Liberation Army Navy submarines seeking access to the western Pacific.

The depth and underwater conditions of these waterways would make them difficult places for submarine hunters, while frequent rough weather could further complicate operations above the surface, he said.

If successfully developed, Silent Anvil would be “highly relevant” in such a scenario, in his view. “Any system that would help seal up the PLA Navy’s access to the western Pacific would help the US and its allies stiffen a ‘denial defence’,” Holmes said.

Goldstein said he expected the US Navy to be closely coordinating potential anti-submarine operations with Australia and especially Japan, including through sharing technology and tactics.

Any conflict could require large stocks of anti-submarine weapons at forward bases in those countries, he said, but those bases and logistics nodes could be vulnerable to Chinese missile and drone strikes.

Companies have until September 29 to respond to the request, which calls for a complete system demonstration within 18 months of a development agreement, followed by production of about 180 prototype weapons over the following three years.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore MPs back ministerial pay rise, but agree money alone won’t lure talent
item.description:
While Singapore’s officials are among the highest-paid in the world, money alone cannot attract the brightest leaders to public service, lawmakers have said during a debate on the increase in ministerial salaries – a move supported by both opposition and ruling party MPs.

The parliamentary discussion on Thursday, which saw MPs share their personal reflections on stepping into public office, followed an announced rise in ministerial salary, which Prime Minister Lawrence Wong insisted was necessary for leadership renewal and to keep pace with the private sector.

Benchmark salaries of Wong’s cabinet will be increased by more than 60 per cent, ranging from S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) to S$3.6 million annually. Ministers will receive a one-off rise of up to 9 per cent next month, with subsequent increments subject to individual performance and responsibilities.
item.content:encoded:
While Singapore’s officials are among the highest-paid in the world, money alone cannot attract the brightest leaders to public service, lawmakers have said during a debate on the increase in ministerial salaries – a move supported by both opposition and ruling party MPs.

The parliamentary discussion on Thursday, which saw MPs share their personal reflections on stepping into public office, followed an announced rise in ministerial salary, which Prime Minister Lawrence Wong insisted was necessary for leadership renewal and to keep pace with the private sector.

Benchmark salaries of Wong’s cabinet will be increased by more than 60 per cent, ranging from S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) to S$3.6 million annually. Ministers will receive a one-off rise of up to 9 per cent next month, with subsequent increments subject to individual performance and responsibilities.

Singapore last adjusted the salaries of political holders in 2012, slashing wages by more than 35 per cent. A recommendation to increase the pay following a 2017 review was not adopted.

“If too many capable people conclude that political service asks for sacrifices which are just too great, then over time we will have fewer people prepared to step forward,” Wong said as he rounded up the debate that lasted over 3½ hours.

“Eventually, the quality of our leadership will suffer and Singapore will suffer the consequences.”

He called it a “mistaken framework” that the purpose of the salary structure was to entice people into politics with money since “motivation to serve” and “responding to the call” had to come first.

“We have to persuade good people that Singapore needs them, that the work matters, that they can make a difference. Then, if someone is prepared to step forward, remuneration becomes a practical consideration,” Wong said.

Earlier, opposition Workers’ Party chief Pritam Singh questioned if the city state’s high earners in the private sector were deterred from politics by lower pay or whether the issue was political responsibilities.

He argued that most of Singapore’s cabinet continued to be fielded from the public sector, while “only a small handful” chose to leave the private sector for politics.

“For some, it would not be out of order to suggest that no amount of money will persuade them to trade their suits and ties for grass-roots activities and to immerse themselves in municipal concerns and the rough and tumble of politics,” he said.

Singh in parliament reiterated his party’s view that ministers’ salaries should be a multiple of an MP’s allowance instead of pegged to the median wage of the top 1,000 earners in Singapore, with a discount. The approach of WP – the only opposition party in parliament – would have resulted in more modest increases over time, he said.

Wong argued that the WP’s formula would arrive at a similar figure and if the salary was benchmarked with inflation, a higher sum would be derived.

“For all intents and purposes, within this term of government, we agree on the implementation approach. Beyond that, we will have to consider the circumstances then,” Wong said, noting that another independent review would be done in five years.

Wong also countered the argument that Singapore’s office holders were among the highest earners in the world, saying political office holders in many countries were given pensions, allowances, housing and other benefits beyond their official salary package.

As prime minister, Wong’s salary would be increased from S$2.2 million to S$3.6 million. He pledged to donate the increment to good causes for five years and said on Thursday that he would not keep the tax benefits from his donation.

Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng, a former doctor and medical entrepreneur, shared his personal experience of giving up his career as group CEO and managing director of IHH Healthcare to enter politics in 2020, at the age of 55.

Tan said on Thursday that he made the move after a “growing inner realisation” that his experience in the private sector could be put to good use to give back to the country. He added that no realistic level of ministerial salary could have matched what he was earning in the private sector.

On attracting future talent, Tan said: “If we make entry into the public service come at too high a personal cost for too many capable Singaporeans, then over time we will indeed narrow the pool from which our country can draw its leaders and, members of the House, that would be a far greater cost than any salary debate.”

Singapore’s ministerial salary model ensured that its leaders were “not incentivised to look elsewhere” and act with citizens’ best interests in mind, said Christopher de Souza, a lawmaker from the ruling People’s Action Party.

Prolonged wage stagnation may lead political office holders to view their time in office as a stepping stone for their professional careers, he said, citing examples of state leaders from the United States and the United Kingdom who earned large sums from assets and corporate deals after leaving office.

“If politicians know that their future careers may depend on relationships built while in office, the public will inevitably wonder whether today’s decisions are made solely in the national interest, or whether tomorrow’s opportunities are also at the back of the minds of their leaders,” he said.

Several MPs raised concerns regarding negative public sentiment over ministerial pay increases and some asked for more information to be made public on how ministers’ performances were reviewed.

Wong said he understood the concerns, but there was never going to be a “politically convenient time” to adjust salaries.

“If every difficult circumstance becomes a reason not to act, then we will keep putting the issue off, and there will come a point where restraint ceases to be prudence and becomes neglect,” he said, adding that leadership renewal was urgent.

On how ministers’ performance bonuses were distributed, he cautioned against the assessment being made into a public popularity contest and said the cabinet was a team that Singaporeans should judge based on how the government as a whole performed.

“If we fall short, Singaporeans can choose another team to govern. That is the final accountability in our system,” Wong said.

The pay bump reignited a long-standing debate on the thorny issue, with opposition parties voicing swift criticism. Some pointed out ongoing economic uncertainty and rising unemployment rates, while others criticised the salary framework.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said the argument of recruiting and retaining talent was justifiable from a human resource perspective.

He said the amounts would, however, appear “eye-watering” to the public and raise questions about “other forms of inspiration” to serve the people.

“Even without the pay rises, political appointees still earn more than enough to afford a very, very comfortable standard of living.”

He suggested that indicators such as total fertility rate and progress on climate issues be included in the assessment for compensation for political office holders.

Currently, ministers’ salaries include a national bonus, which is linked to socio-economic indicators such as the growth rate of residents’ median income and Singapore’s real gross domestic product.

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s youth job crisis is driving graduates to German vocational apprenticeships
item.description:
Two years ago, Yuki Liu was a university student in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, studying traditional Chinese music and the pipa – a pear-shaped Chinese lute – weighing the usual paths considered by her peers: postgraduate degree or civil service exam.

Today, her day begins at 1am in Germany.

While many people sleep, she is already working as an apprentice at an industrial bakery in a small town outside Stuttgart in the country’s southwest, preparing the shop for the morning rush.
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago, Yuki Liu was a university student in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, studying traditional Chinese music and the pipa – a pear-shaped Chinese lute – weighing the usual paths considered by her peers: postgraduate degree or civil service exam.

Today, her day begins at 1am in Germany.

While many people sleep, she is already working as an apprentice at an industrial bakery in a small town outside Stuttgart in the country’s southwest, preparing the shop for the morning rush.

The turning point for Liu came as she approached graduation and grew increasingly unsure about the path her studies could offer her in China. “With a music degree, your only option is to teach,” she said. “Otherwise you starve.”

Liu came across Germany’s apprenticeship system almost by happenstance, discovering a path that the musician had never imagined: becoming a blue-collar worker in Europe’s largest economy.

Liu is among a growing number of young Chinese turning to Ausbildung, Germany’s dual vocational training system, as an alternative to an increasingly competitive graduate job market at home and as a potential route to staying in Europe. Many applicants, like her, already hold university degrees or have worked for well-known companies.

On Chinese social media, the pitch is straightforward: little upfront cost and the prospect of a job at the end. Apprentices are employed by a company in Germany and paid a training allowance while attending a state vocational school tuition-free. Most stay on as regular employees once they qualify.

Back in China, there is a popular cultural refrain that students and degree-holders often use to describe how hard it is to find a job: “graduation means unemployment”.

A record 12.7 million students graduated from Chinese universities this year, up 480,000 from 2025. Unemployment among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, rose to 17.9 per cent in July – an 11-month high.

For some, Ausbildung – literally translated as “education”, “training” or “apprenticeship” – offers more than a pay cheque. It is also one of the cheaper routes to relocating abroad, particularly for those looking to escape a working culture epitomised by a notorious “996” schedule – working from 9am to 9pm, six days a week.

Social media has helped fuel the appeal. Liu recalled a video on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – featuring a philosophy postgraduate student who had dropped out and moved to Germany to train as a gardener, listing what he found different about working there: no rat race, no overtime and no office politics. The video drew thousands of likes, with viewers asking in the comments how they could follow a similar path.

The financial incentives also blunt some reluctance towards blue-collar work. Workers in Germany with a recognised vocational qualification earned about €4,125 (US$4,800) a month before tax in April 2025, according to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office – roughly five times the average pay of production workers in China last year, data from the National Bureau of Statistics shows.

“You can really feel it: far more people are talking about it than before,” said Emilie Xie, a former media worker in China who is now applying to become a carer in Germany.

However, for some, reality often hits harder than the online pitch.

Lin Chenxi runs a youth hostel in Hamburg and helps place Chinese apprentices with German employers, supporting them after they arrive. “Only about a third of the students we placed made it through,” she said. “The other two-thirds either got weeded out or lost heart and left.”

The language, Lin said, can be the biggest hurdle. She explained how applicants need a B1 proficiency level in German – an intermediate stage in which they can handle everyday situations and communicate familiar topics – but many appear to have drilled their way through the German language exam in China, and they arrive unable to hold a conversation.

I feel like a screw on an assembly line

Yuki Liu

The promise of plentiful jobs can also be misleading. Germany lacked enough qualified workers to fill 369,500 skilled jobs in 2025, according to the German Economic Institute, with nursing among the hardest-hit professions. Some of the roles that are more accessible to Chinese applicants are said to include care work, baking and kitchen jobs.

“I feel like a screw on an assembly line,” Liu said, explaining how she spends about six hours every workday sorting deliveries and two hours making products. In nearly a year, she lamented, she had never taken a single item from raw ingredients to a finished loaf.

Apprentices spend about three years on a training allowance that averages €1,238 a month before tax, according to the Federal Statistical Office, with smaller firms typically paying less. Liu takes home €873, of which €680 goes towards rent. She said she is already considering her next restart, possibly by pursuing another apprenticeship.

Those realities may help explain the gap between the buzz on Chinese social media and the number actually taking the route. Germany counted 573 Chinese nationals in dual vocational training in 2024, up from 282 in 2020, according to the Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training.

The figures exclude nursing and other school-based programmes that attract many more Chinese applicants. Still, the overall number remains a fraction of China’s outbound workforce.

For Emilie Xie, though, none of this has changed her mind. “A degree isn’t hard currency any more,” she said. “It has become consumption, not an investment.”

Xie graduated from Hengshui High School – famed for its gruelling exam drilling – and went on to study at a university in Beijing. It was a path once seen as a ticket to a comfortable career. She worked in media before deciding to retrain herself.

Xie said she deliberately chose care work: the sector is short-staffed, relatively easy to enter and – she believed – harder for artificial intelligence to replace. She said she knew the job meant changing adult diapers and cleaning up after people, but she said she was ready for it.

For his part, Willie Wei had an advantage many other students lacked: he studied German as an undergraduate before dropping out of a journalism master’s degree programme in Beijing. He was hired by a large care provider for disabled people in Saxony on a regular employee contract, rather than an apprentice wage, with 32 days of paid leave and what he said was one of the better salaries in the sector.

“Things are falling into place, step by step,” he said, revealing his plan to apply for German citizenship once he qualifies.

Even so, looking back on his journey through the Ausbildung system, Wei said he would have preferred to have taken an academic path through a university – a route that he said he still may consider in the future.

item.title: [SCMP] Family firms power China’s economy – but what happens when the heirs refuse the throne?
item.description:
Many Chinese tend to label the offspring of the country’s nouveau riche private business founders with the pejorative “fuerdai”, literally “second-generation rich”.

They are seen as scions, waiting in the wings to inherit their family’s enterprises and the massive wealth their parents oversaw, a life in the lap of luxury guaranteed.

In reality, many of these transitions are plagued by a clash between generations, as the younger generation is unwilling – or unable – to keep the family business going, let alone allow it to thrive.
item.content:encoded:
Many Chinese tend to label the offspring of the country’s nouveau riche private business founders with the pejorative “fuerdai”, literally “second-generation rich”.

They are seen as scions, waiting in the wings to inherit their family’s enterprises and the massive wealth their parents oversaw, a life in the lap of luxury guaranteed.

In reality, many of these transitions are plagued by a clash between generations, as the younger generation is unwilling – or unable – to keep the family business going, let alone allow it to thrive.

The private sector, the backbone of China’s economy and employment, is now facing a growing succession crisis – one which may see businesses wind down or fold, observers warn, as family matters threaten to send broader tremors throughout the country.

In regions like China’s eastern Zhejiang province, a major economic centre, questions over inheritance are becoming more pressing.

“I cannot – and probably should not – take over from my father,” said Li Fante, whose family’s factory, like many other businesses in Zhejiang’s city of Wenling, has maintained steady profits.

However, he said the work was neither exciting nor lucrative enough to lure him in.

“We may not do as well as our parents have done, and the business is boring,” Li said.

There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother?

Li Fante, Wenling, Zhejiang province

When Li’s parents were approaching 70 years old, he said he made an agreement with them to wind down the family business, which produces rubber and plastic parts, after more than 30 years in the trade.

He said that disagreements in the family had contributed to the decision.

“For us, taking over from our fathers means the beginning of endless quarrels and clashes,” he said. “There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother?

“Business drive and acumen may not automatically pass from one generation to the next.”

Li, who is in his early 30s, used the proceeds from the sale of the factory’s land and its assets to invest in stocks and Shanghai property.

Although ostensibly a family matter, Li’s decision – and those taking place among wealthy households across the country – could impact the future of China’s private sector, which accounts for 60 per cent of gross domestic product and 80 per cent of urban employment.

More than 85 per cent of the country’s private enterprises are family-run, according to data from the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, and Zhejiang is a major site of succession debates.

The province is one of China’s richest, and its private sector contributes 70 per cent of local GDP and employs many of its residents.

The average age of founders from Zhejiang’s top 100 biggest private enterprises was 64 years old, according to a 2025 report from the local government.

“This means enterprises entering the succession phase are not isolated ones, but a huge swathe of the most vibrant and productive part of China’s private economy,” provincial authorities said.

Data from Wenling’s United Front Work Department showed that, in 2025, close to 60 per cent of local private firms with an annual industrial output of 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million) were in need of “urgent succession planning” to ensure continuity in operations as their founders reached 60 years old.

Of 114 private firms surveyed throughout Ningbo and neighbouring cities, including Wenling, 90 were still led by their founders, some aged 70 or older, and about 60 firms had neither a designated successor nor any second-generation family members in management.

Only 10 companies of the 114 covered in the survey, conducted between 2023 and 2025 by Ningbo University of Finance and Economics (NBUFE), had come under the control of the second generation.

A related NBUFE survey also found close to 20 per cent of the second-generation members of the 114 firms explicitly declined to take over, while 45 per cent remain undecided or prefer to pursue a career other than their family’s business.

Su Saier, a deputy professor at NBUFE who led the survey, said most private entrepreneurs in Ningbo – and across Zhejiang broadly – showed limited awareness of succession planning and lacked systematic, long-term arrangements.

“Founders have limited willingness to ‘relinquish’ control and there is also a lack of resilience and entrepreneurial drive among their children,” she said.

The risks of investment reduction, business closures and broader impact on the economy have researchers worried.

“The succession and continuity of private enterprises is no longer a family matter, but a question of regional economic vitality and industrial ecology,” Su warned.

“This is particularly true in regions known for their private sector that are China’s economic pillars, like Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Guangdong, where numerous private firms are embedded in industrial and supply-chain networks.

“If succession is not smooth at one enterprise, it could put employment, upstream and downstream production and even the broader industrial ecosystem on the line,” she said.

Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing, likened family-operated factories to capillaries in the massive Chinese economy.

“These factories may not be massive conglomerates themselves, but collectively they could be foundational to the Chinese manufacturing ecosystem,” Tang said.

“They usually specialise in a single component, or a minor link in the supply and production chain, that larger manufacturers usually outsource. If they shut down as their founders grey, the resilience and cost-effectiveness of Chinese manufacturing may be at stake going forward.”

Li, from the family factory in Wenling, agreed.

“The ageing of founders at many factories that do not have a successor may mean potential supply disruptions,” he said.

His family factory was one of many producers established in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It now sells moulded plastic auto parts to carmakers like Geely and BYD.

Handling succession is not just a test for business owners, but also a challenge for local cadres. If businesses in their jurisdictions wither, officials will have to tackle the subsequent impact on sentiment, jobs and fiscal income.

In one recent example, listed kitchenware maker Zhejiang Meida sold a controlling stake to an outside bidder for 1.29 billion yuan in July after its 85-year-old founder failed to convince his children to take over the business. Its stock price subsequently fell.

Meida is one of the largest listed firms in its home base of Haining, and employs thousands of workers. Local officials have stepped in following the sudden announcement to save local jobs and retain the local production base, according to people there familiar with the matter.

The succession issue has also caught the attention of top policymakers in recent years, with some viewing it as an issue that will make or break the future of the private sector of the world’s second-largest economy.

A 2023 Communist Party policy statement on promoting the private economy noted the need for “mentoring and guidance” for the younger generation of private entrepreneurs to ensure “orderly handover and succession”.

A dedicated law on the private economy, in effect since May 2025, requires qualified private entities to establish and improve their modern corporate governance system as an institutional foundation for sustainability and intergenerational succession.

Specific proposals, like recruiting professional managers to help run and modernise family businesses, have been raised.

But Li said this would not help much.

“By design, the founding family retains ownership, while professional managers brought in from the outside can leverage their knowledge and management skills to grow the company and get paid with salary, bonus and shares,” he said. “This idea sounds good on paper.

“The crux of the issue is that for a small family business, nothing is institutionalised,” he added.

“Many business decisions still rest on the founder’s experience, risk-taking, personal connections and even intuition and gut feeling. There is no business model. How can one modernise such a business?”

But NBUFE’s Su argued that to make more private businesses more sustainable, the test was how to transform them, regardless of who sat at the helm.

Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges

Zhejiang Daily

“The challenge goes beyond whether the second generation is willing to take over or not, but rather whether modern governance transformation can replace the founder’s personal abilities, experience and authority and adapt the company to the competitive environment of the new era.

“The key is who can drive the company’s sustainable development.”

Some high-profile examples can provide a model for such a transition.

On August 17, Li Shufu, founder of auto giant Geely Auto, put his long-time deputy An Conghui in the driving seat of the 345-billion-yuan business empire, passing over his children.

“The most feasible approach is to retain the advantages of the ‘family system’ so that shares can be held by the family, but management positions should be opened to the public, as much as possible to talent outside the family,” wrote Zhejiang Daily – a press organ of the provincial government – in a commentary piece following Li Shufu’s retirement.

“The goal is a modern enterprise system with clear property rights, well-defined boundaries between family and business executives for a sound corporate governance structure.”

Officials in the province are determined to tackle the issue, as time appears to be running out.

“The first generation of Zhejiang entrepreneurs who rose to prominence after the reform and opening-up since the 1980s are now seniors. For them – and local officials and governments as well – handing over the business has become a sword hanging overhead, and the window of time is steadily closing,” Zhejiang Daily said.

“Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges.”

item.title: [SCMP] 5 years after sweeping ban, China’s tutoring industry still bleeding parents dry
item.description:
Yin Yue, a mother with a 15-year-old daughter, feels like after-school academic tutoring is everywhere again in Guangzhou, the city where she lives in southern China.

Five years ago, China launched a sweeping crackdown that drove much of the industry out of sight. But prep centres had quietly begun popping up again in popular commercial areas across the city, said Yin, a pharmaceutical sales manager in her 40s.

In Guangzhou’s shopping malls, these centres are now among the busiest tenants, pulling in crowds of parents and schoolchildren on weekends and weekday evenings, according to Yin. During the summer and winter holidays, they sometimes get so busy that nearby shops and restaurants see an uptick in business.
item.content:encoded:
Yin Yue, a mother with a 15-year-old daughter, feels like after-school academic tutoring is everywhere again in Guangzhou, the city where she lives in southern China.

Five years ago, China launched a sweeping crackdown that drove much of the industry out of sight. But prep centres had quietly begun popping up again in popular commercial areas across the city, said Yin, a pharmaceutical sales manager in her 40s.

In Guangzhou’s shopping malls, these centres are now among the busiest tenants, pulling in crowds of parents and schoolchildren on weekends and weekday evenings, according to Yin. During the summer and winter holidays, they sometimes get so busy that nearby shops and restaurants see an uptick in business.

That would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago. In 2021, Beijing launched its “double reduction” campaign to outlaw for-profit tutoring in core school subjects such as maths and English, aiming to stamp out an academic rat race that was leading parents to spend eye-watering sums on extra classes for their children.

Thousands of providers closed or were forced to restructure during the intense national enforcement campaign that followed, as the authorities introduced tough punishments for tutors found operating without a licence.

Yet the crackdown did not dampen the intense competition in the country’s education system – or the demand for extra tutoring that it feeds. And that has allowed the industry to gradually make a comeback, aided by a pause in intensive, high-profile national clampdown campaigns.

Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before

Yin Yue, mother based in Guangdong province

Recent surveys and interviews with parents in major Chinese cities suggest that families across the country continue to spend heavily on after-school academic tutoring, even at a time when China’s uncertain job market and property downturn are dampening overall household consumption growth.

Yin’s daughter starts high school next month. To help her get a head-start on next semester’s curriculum, Yin spent more than 11,500 yuan (US$1,700) to send her on an intensive 12-day course covering maths, physics, chemistry and English.

In total, Yin said her family had spent close to 70,000 yuan on tutoring over the past year. She felt the extra classes were vital to help her daughter keep up with her peers – after all, they all had private tutors too.

“The stronger the students, the more their parents spend,” Yin said. “Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before.”

A survey of more than 2,100 parents in Zhongshan, another city in southern China, conducted by the Southern Metropolis Daily and released in late August, also found that after-school classes were still the norm.

Nearly 70 per cent of the parents surveyed said their children were currently attending subject-based after-school tutoring, while about another 20 per cent said they planned to arrange extra classes for them. Only 8.75 per cent said they had no plans for after-school tutoring.

More than 60 per cent of respondents said they spent at least 1,000 yuan per month on after-school tutoring, with 6.45 per cent spending over 5,000 yuan. This represents a big chunk of a typical household budget, given that Zhongshan’s per capita disposable income was about 35,000 yuan in the first half of 2026, according to official data.

The top three reasons parents gave for paying for tutoring were that their children were struggling to keep up with school coursework, the intense competition for admission to high schools and universities, and the fact that other students were also taking extra classes, according to the survey.

Among affluent Chinese families, the spending on tutoring can be far larger.

“In my son’s class, parents spend an average of 10,000 yuan a month on tutoring,” said Guan Jing, a parent based in Beijing.

Louis Tan, who runs a manufacturing business in Shenzhen, said he had budgeted 300,000 to 500,000 yuan for academic tutoring over the next three years, as his daughter prepared to take China’s national university entrance exams.

He had also set aside another 500,000 yuan for art classes, because his daughter hoped to attend China’s prestigious Central Academy of Fine Arts, Tan added.

“When I was young, a kid from a poor background could stand out on natural talent alone,” said Tan, who grew up in a poor rural community in southwestern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. “Today, they have to compete against peers getting tonnes of extra coaching.”

If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and your child doesn’t, she falls behind

Zhang Liang, father based in Hubei province

Families in smaller cities are also feeling the pressure. In Jingshan, a county-level city in central China’s Hubei province, truck driver Zhang Liang said he had spent more than 10,000 yuan a semester on tutoring for his 9-year-old daughter, plus 2,800 yuan for 14 days of summer classes.

The costs are a burden for the family, which earns about 15,000 yuan a month, but Zhang feels the classes are important for his daughter’s future.

“If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and yours doesn’t, she falls behind,” Zhang said. He worries that his kidney stones could one day stop him from driving long-haul trucks, leaving the family unable to afford the tutoring fees.

Education appears to be one of the few non-negotiable spending categories for Chinese households at a time of heightened economic uncertainty. China’s per capita consumption rose 3.7 per cent in the first half of the year, while spending on education, culture and recreation increased 4.9 per cent, according to official data.

Between 2020 and 2025, education, culture and recreation spending in China grew 71.7 per cent, National Bureau of Statistics data showed.

Xiong Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, said the core problem was the intense competition for places at China’s top schools, which extended from senior high school through to university. The fight for school places helps explain the resilience of demand for private tutoring, according to Xiong.

item.title: [SCMP] Economist Lan Xiaohuan on the balancing act needed to boost China’s consumption
item.description:
Lan Xiaohuan is a professor of economics at China Europe International Business School. His book, How China Works: An Introduction to China’s State-led Economic Development, has sold millions of copies in China and has been translated into multiple languages.

Here, he discusses the economic realities behind China’s record trade surplus, the case for a stronger social safety net, and how public data infrastructure shapes the artificial intelligence race with the United States.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Lan Xiaohuan is a professor of economics at China Europe International Business School. His book, How China Works: An Introduction to China’s State-led Economic Development, has sold millions of copies in China and has been translated into multiple languages.
